questions.stem: We ________ our food when the waiter suddenly dropped a tray of dishes.
questions.trap_type: Past continuous for ongoing background action — we were already eating when the waiter dropped the tray (interruption).
questions.learning_tip: We WERE EATING (ongoing past) when the waiter dropped the tray (sudden interruption). The eating was already happening → past continuous.

questions.stem: Mr Lim's fishball noodles are far ________ than anything Sam had ever tasted from a restaurant.
questions.trap_type: 'Most delicious' = superlative; 'deliciouser' is WRONG. MORE DELICIOUS = comparative.
questions.learning_tip: Long adjective → MORE + adjective = comparative. MORE DELICIOUS THAN restaurant noodles = comparing two things. 'Deliciouser' is ALWAYS WRONG. For long adjectives, use MORE.

questions.stem: "________ you tried the new roti prata stall yet?" asked Min.
questions.trap_type: 'Have you tried' = present perfect (experience up to now). Students use 'Did you try' (simple past, also possible but less natural with 'yet').
questions.learning_tip: 'Have you [done something] YET?' = asking about experience up to now → present perfect: HAVE you tried. 'Yet' is a signal for present perfect question.

questions.stem: The hawker centre is one of the most important parts of Singapore's food culture, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive present 'to be' ('is') → negative question tag.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present 'to be' → negative tag. The hawker centre IS important, ISN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. IS → ISN'T.

questions.stem: The auntie at the drinks stall gave Sam ________ glass of barley water free.
questions.trap_type: 'A glass' — 'glass' starts with a consonant sound → 'a'. Students may pick 'an' over-applying vowel rules.
questions.learning_tip: 'A' + consonant sound: a glass, a bowl, a plate. 'AN' + vowel sound: an orange, an egg. 'Glass' starts with G (consonant) → A glass.

questions.stem: ________ the food was spicy, the children ate it happily.
questions.trap_type: 'Although' = concession — the food was spicy BUT they still ate it happily. This is a contrast.
questions.learning_tip: ALTHOUGH = even though (surprising contrast). Spicy food + children happily eating = a contrast (usually spicy food makes children not want to eat). ALTHOUGH introduces the surprise.

C.label: Section C — Grammar Cloze
C.instructions: Read the passage below. Choose the most suitable word from the box and write its letter in each blank. Use each word ONCE only.
C.passage: My family loves going to the hawker centre near (1)___ house. Last Saturday, my father brought (2)___ there for lunch. We sat at a round table and looked at all the stalls. My sister pointed at the chicken rice stall and said, '(3)___ food always smells so good!' Father went to order the food and came back with five plates of chicken rice. He placed (4)___ carefully on the table. The chicken rice uncle saw (5)___ sitting together as a family and smiled. He walked over and gave us a small bowl of soup. '(6)___ is a gift from me,' he said kindly. My mother thanked (7)___ and said the chicken rice was (8)___ best she had ever tasted.

questions.trap_type: 'Near our house' — E = our (possessive, first person plural). Students may pick F (their).
questions.learning_tip: MY FAMILY = we/our. 'Near OUR house' = belonging to us. OUR = E (first person plural possessive).

questions.trap_type: 'Brought us there' — H = us (object pronoun). Students pick G (them).
questions.learning_tip: Father brought US (the family, including the speaker) there. US = object pronoun for WE. H = us.

questions.trap_type: 'Their food' — F = their (possessive for the stall/the people running it). Students pick D (its).
questions.learning_tip: The chicken rice stall's food = THEIR food (belonging to the stall people). THEIR = F (third person plural possessive).

questions.trap_type: 'Placed them on the table' — G = them (object pronoun for 'five plates'). Students pick C (it).
questions.learning_tip: Five plates = plural → object pronoun = THEM = G. 'IT' (C) is for singular objects.

questions.trap_type: H is already used in blank 2. Must redesign. 'He saw us sitting' → H(us). But H used. Redesign blank 2 or 5.
questions.answer_corrected: Blank 5: 'He saw (5)___ sitting together as a family' → needs US (H). But H is used in blank 2 too. Re-examine: If blank 2 uses a different word... OR redesign passage so only one blank needs 'us'. Resolution: blank 2 = 'brought (2)___ there' → could use G(them) if narrator speaks of family as 3rd person. But passage uses first person 'we'. Final fix: use 'the family' in blank 2 to free up H for blank 5.
questions.learning_tip: HE SAW US = he saw the family (object pronoun: us = H).

questions.trap_type: 'This/It is a gift from me' — C = it (referring to the soup bowl). Students pick D (its).
questions.learning_tip: 'IT is a gift from me' = referring to the soup bowl. IT = C (pronoun for a thing). ITS = possessive (its colour, its taste).

questions.trap_type: 'Thanked him' — the uncle is male. B = his? No: 'thanked him' = object pronoun = B(his)? No — 'him' is not in the box. Redesign: replace B(his) with B(him).
questions.answer_corrected: Word box redesigned: B = 'him'. 'My mother thanked HIM = B (the uncle, male, object).'
questions.learning_tip: After THANKED (verb), use object pronoun: thanked HIM (the male uncle). HIM = B.

questions.trap_type: 'It was her best' — A = her (possessive for 'my mother'). Students pick E (our) thinking of the whole family.
questions.learning_tip: MY MOTHER said the chicken rice was HER best = belonging to her (the mother's own experience). HER = A.

D.label: Section D — Vocabulary Cloze
D.instructions: Read the passage carefully. Choose the most suitable word from the box and write its letter in each blank. Use each word ONCE only.
D.passage: Last Saturday, my mother took me to the market to choose some fish for dinner. The (1)___ of the market was full of life. There were many people standing in a long (2)___ at the popular fish stall. We (3)___ patiently for our turn. When it was our time, Mother (4)___ two big sea bass because they looked very (5)___. The fishmonger was paid for the fish and wrapped them neatly. On the way home, Mother told me that sea bass was Father's favourite fish. She said he would be delighted when he saw what we were having for dinner.

questions.trap_type: 'The smell of the market' — G = smell. A market has a distinctive smell. Students pick 'sound' (not in box).
questions.learning_tip: A busy wet market has many food smells. The SMELL of the market = G. 'The smell was full of life' = the market was lively and fragrant.

questions.trap_type: 'Standing in a long queue' — F = queue (line of people waiting). Students pick 'crowd' (not in box).
questions.learning_tip: A QUEUE = a line of people waiting their turn. At a popular stall, people stand in a QUEUE = F.

questions.trap_type: 'Waited patiently for our turn' — H = waited. Students pick 'stood' (not in box).
questions.learning_tip: You WAIT for your turn in a queue. WAITED = H (past tense). 'Patiently' tells us HOW they waited.

questions.trap_type: 'Mother chose two sea bass' — A = chose (selected). Students pick 'bought' (E = paid) confusing choosing and paying.
questions.learning_tip: CHOSE = selected/picked. She CHOSE two sea bass = picked them. Paying comes AFTER choosing. 'Chose' (past of choose) = A.

questions.trap_type: 'They looked very fresh' — D = fresh (not old; recently caught). Students may pick 'big' (size, already described as 'big' in same sentence) or 'clean'.
questions.learning_tip: Fish from a market 'looked very FRESH' = newly caught, not old. FRESH fish = recently caught and in good condition. D = fresh.

E.label: Section E — Editing
E.instructions: The passage below has five mistakes. Each mistake is underlined. Write the correct word in the box next to each number.
E.passage: Last weekend, my family visited the famous Maxwell Food Centre in Chinatown. We arrived early so we could get there (33) favourite breakfast stall before the queue grew too long. The uncle at the stall visited (34) us there every week and recognised us right away. He learns (35) our order by heart and started preparing our food before we even spoke. He show (36) us how he makes the stock by simmering bones for over six hours. At the end, we read the stall owners's (37) story on the sign and felt even prouder to be regular customers.

errors.error_type: Homophone confusion — there (place) vs their (belonging to them)
errors.trap_type: 'there' (place) when 'their' (belonging to them/our family) is needed.
errors.learning_tip: THEIR = belonging to them. THERE = at that place. 'Get THEIR favourite breakfast stall' → belonging to us? YES → THEIR. THEIR = possession. THERE = location.

errors.error_type: Present tense required — habitual action (visit every week)
errors.trap_type: 'visited' = past tense. A habitual action needs present: we VISIT every week.
errors.learning_tip: 'Every week' = habitual action = PRESENT TENSE. We VISIT (not visited) every week. VISITED = past tense (one completed trip). Use VISIT for regular, repeated actions.

errors.error_type: Past tense required — regular verb (learn → learned)
errors.trap_type: 'learns' is present tense. The story is being told in past tense context.
errors.learning_tip: LEARN → LEARNED (regular past, add -ed). In a past tense narrative, use LEARNED. 'He learns our order' = WRONG in past context. Use LEARNED.

errors.error_type: Past tense required — regular verb (show → showed)
errors.trap_type: 'show' is base form. Past tense context requires 'showed'.
errors.learning_tip: SHOW → SHOWED (regular past, add -ed). In a past tense context, use SHOWED. 'He show us' = WRONG — wrong tense. Use SHOWED.

errors.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (owners', not owners's)
errors.trap_type: Students add 's after apostrophe for plural ending -s.
errors.learning_tip: Plural possessive: apostrophe AFTER -s! OWNERS' story = the story belonging to all the owners (the couple who run the stall). NEVER 'owners's'. Singular: owner's. Plural: owners'. Extra -s = WRONG.

questions.sentence1: Sam's mother asked the hawker a question.
questions.sentence2: Do you make the fishballs by hand every morning?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'Sam's mother asked...'
questions.model_answer: Sam's mother asked the hawker if he made the fishballs by hand every morning.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if does he make' (wrong order) or keep 'you'.
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'Do YOU make?' → asked IF HE MADE. Pronoun: you → he. Tense: do make → made. Word order is normal after 'if'.

questions.instruction: Rewrite using 'Both'.
questions.model_answer: Both Rani and her father like chicken rice.
questions.trap_type: Students keep 'likes' (singular) after 'Both A and B'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Both A and B' = plural → plural verb: Both Rani and her father LIKE (not likes) chicken rice.

G.label: Section G — Comprehension
G.passage:
Every morning, Mr Lim arrived at his stall at five o'clock, long before the rest of the hawker centre opened. He boiled the fishball soup for at least two hours to get the right taste. Mr Lim sold fishball noodles at Tampines Food Centre for over twenty years.

One rainy Tuesday, a young boy came to the stall alone. He looked at the menu and counted his coins carefully. 'Uncle,' he said quietly, 'I only have one dollar and fifty cents. Is that enough for a small bowl?'

Mr Lim looked at the boy. He knew the price was two dollars. But the boy's wet uniform and tired eyes told him the boy had come a long way in the rain. 'Of course,' said Mr Lim with a smile. 'One dollar fifty is enough today.'

He served the boy a full bowl — not a small one. He even added extra fishballs. The boy ate every bit of it and looked up at Mr Lim with bright eyes. 'Thank you, Uncle. This is the best I have ever eaten.'

Mr Lim waved his hand. 'Come back any time,' he said. And he meant it.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'cooked something slowly and gently in hot liquid'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Boiled' = high heat with large bubbles; 'fried' = cooked in oil; 'grilled' = cooked over flame. SIMMERED = cooked gently in liquid just below boiling.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: SIMMERED = cooked slowly and gently in hot liquid just below boiling point. Mr Lim SIMMERED the bones for six hours = kept them at a low, steady heat. SIMMER = gentle, slow cooking.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'Sam could not explain it'?

options.1: The way the stall was decorated
options.2: Why the fishball noodle soup tasted so different from anything he had eaten before
options.3: How Mr Lim made the broth
options.4: The amount of time he waited in the queue

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 3 thinking 'it' = the broth recipe. But 'could not explain IT' = a feeling about the taste, not a recipe.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'Sam could not explain IT.' IT = the mysterious quality of the taste — WHY the soup tasted so different and so much better. He could taste the difference but could not put it into words.

mcq_questions.stem: Why does the writer say Mr Lim's secret ingredient was 'time'?

options.1: Because Mr Lim was very old and experienced.
options.2: Because the long hours of slow cooking and years of practice were what made the soup taste so special.
options.3: Because Mr Lim's stall was open for a very long time.
options.4: Because Mr Lim took a very long time to serve each customer.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 3 thinking TIME = how long the stall has been open. But 'secret ingredient = time' refers to the COOKING PROCESS.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: The 'SECRET INGREDIENT = TIME' = a METAPHOR. Mr Lim SIMMERED the bones for SIX HOURS and spent YEARS perfecting his recipe. TIME = the patience and sustained effort that cannot be shortcut. Option 2 = the full meaning of 'time' here.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Sam had eaten Mr Lim's fishball noodles before? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says it was Sam's first visit to the stall — his mother told him about it but he had never tasted it before.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: it was Sam's FIRST VISIT. He had heard about it from his mother but never tasted it. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did Mr Lim know the boy had come a long way in the rain?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: He could see that the boy's uniform was wet and the boy looked tired.

open_ended_questions.stem: Apart from accepting the lower price, what else did Mr Lim do to help the boy? Give TWO things.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) He served the boy a FULL bowl instead of a small one. (ii) He added EXTRA fishballs to the bowl.

open_ended_questions.stem: At the end of the passage, the writer says 'And he meant it.' What did Mr Lim mean?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Mr Lim meant that the boy was truly welcome to come back any time — it was a sincere invitation, not just something polite to say.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on the passage, describe TWO character traits of Mr Lim with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) DEDICATED: Mr Lim arrived every morning at four o'clock to prepare his stock and did so for thirty years — showing total commitment to his craft without shortcuts. (ii) HUMBLE: when Sam's mother complimented the soup, Mr Lim simply smiled and said 'same recipe, every day' — showing he did not seek praise and just focused on his work.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'hardworking and kind' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: DEDICATED = arrived at FOUR O'CLOCK every morning for THIRTY YEARS. HUMBLE = just smiled and said 'same recipe, every day' — no boasting. Name trait + give evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: On the hottest day of the year, the playground was as ________ as a frying pan — even the metal slide was too hot to touch.
questions.trap_type: 'Cold','dark','wet' are opposite to the description. SCORCHING = extremely hot, like being near a flame.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The playground was AS SCORCHING AS a frying pan = comparing the intense heat to a hot pan on a stove. SCORCHING = extremely hot. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is always the correct simile form.

questions.stem: After the rain stopped, a beautiful ________ with seven colours appeared across the sky.
questions.trap_type: Thunder is a sound and lightning is a flash — neither has seven colours. Only a rainbow shows seven colours after rain.
questions.learning_tip: A RAINBOW appears when sunlight passes through water droplets after rain and splits into seven colours.

questions.stem: When the rain finally stopped, the children rushed outside to ________ the puddles and enjoy the cool air.
questions.trap_type: 'Run away from','give up on','break down' all describe negative actions. SPLASH AROUND IN = play happily in shallow water.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: SPLASH AROUND IN = play in water by hitting it and creating spray. Children SPLASHED AROUND IN the puddles = they jumped and played in the rain water. SPLASH + AROUND + IN work together as one meaning.

questions.stem: After the family survived the terrible flood with everyone safe and their home intact, they were ________ — it felt like a miracle.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = trouble; 'down in the dumps' = sad. OVER THE MOON = extremely happy and relieved.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OVER THE MOON = feeling extremely happy and relieved. The family was OVER THE MOON = overjoyed that everyone was safe. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!

questions.stem: Mother ________ us to bring our umbrellas before we left for school that rainy morning.
questions.trap_type: 'Suggested' implies a new idea; 'reminded' means telling someone about something they should already know but might forget.
questions.learning_tip: REMINDED = told someone again about something they might have forgotten. Mother REMINDED us = made sure we did not forget our umbrellas.

questions.stem: Nobody in the village ________ a storm as powerful as the one that struck last Thursday night.
questions.trap_type: NOBODY = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Nobody REMEMBERS = add -S. 'Nobody remember' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.

questions.stem: The Meteorological Service has ________ a weather warning for heavy rain and strong winds this weekend.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. ISSUE → ISSUED (regular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. The service HAS ISSUED a warning = done recently and now in effect. ISSUE → ISSUED (regular verb, add -d).

questions.stem: The children ________ in the park when the sky suddenly darkened and the first drops of rain began to fall.
questions.trap_type: 'The sky darkened' = sudden interrupting event. Children were already playing = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The sky DARKENED = sudden past event. Children were already in the middle of playing = WERE PLAYING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.

questions.stem: After the storm, the river was far ________ than before — it had swallowed the lower path completely.
questions.trap_type: 'Widest' = superlative; 'more wider' is WRONG. WIDER = comparative of 'wide'.
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective + -ER = comparative. Wide → WIDER. The river was WIDER THAN before = comparing two states. 'More wider' is ALWAYS WRONG — never add BOTH 'more' AND '-er'.

questions.stem: We could not go to the beach ________ the weather was too stormy that afternoon.
questions.trap_type: 'So' would reverse the order, placing the result before the reason. 'Because' correctly links the result to its reason.
questions.learning_tip: Could not go BECAUSE the weather was stormy. BECAUSE introduces the reason. The reason comes AFTER 'because'.

questions.stem: The rainy season in Singapore usually arrives in November and December, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive present simple ('arrives') → negative question tag. ARRIVES → doesn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present simple → negative tag. The rainy season ARRIVES in November, DOESN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. Present simple → DOES/DOESN'T. 'Doesn't it' (not 'isn't it' — that is for 'to be').

questions.stem: The typhoon ________ the island early yesterday morning, causing great damage.
questions.trap_type: 'Yesterday morning' = past. 'Hit' is invariant: hit → hit. Students often write 'hitted'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Hit' never changes its form: hit → hit → hit. 'Yesterday morning' = past → HIT. Never write 'hitted'.

questions.stem: "Look at ________ puddles outside! We must wear our boots today," said Mother.
questions.trap_type: 'Puddles' is plural so we need 'these' or 'those'. 'Look at' means the puddles are visible right outside = nearby = these.
questions.learning_tip: 'Puddles' = plural → these or those. 'Look at' = they are visible nearby. Near + plural = THESE.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Prepositions of time and place)

questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' or 'on' for a clock time. AT is the correct preposition for specific times.
questions.learning_tip: Use AT for specific clock times: AT six o'clock, AT noon, AT midnight.

questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' or 'at'. DURING means throughout a whole period of time such as a journey.
questions.learning_tip: DURING = throughout a period: DURING the journey, DURING the holiday, DURING the match.

questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' which means inside without motion from one end to the other. THROUGH means entering one side and exiting the other.
questions.learning_tip: THROUGH = enter one side and come out the other: drive THROUGH a tunnel, walk THROUGH a forest.

questions.trap_type: 'Arrived by noon' — 'by' shows the deadline or latest time. Students write 'at' (already used in blank 1) or 'in'.
questions.learning_tip: BY = no later than a specific time: arrived BY noon = got there no later than noon. It shows a deadline, not a precise moment.

questions.trap_type: Students write 'at' or 'on'. The rule is IN the morning / afternoon / evening for parts of the day.
questions.learning_tip: IN the morning, IN the afternoon, IN the evening — use IN for parts of the day. Exception: AT night.

questions.trap_type: 'During' is already used in blank 2. The jackets were worn ahead of entering the cold farm, so BEFORE is correct.
questions.learning_tip: BEFORE = earlier than an event. They wore jackets BEFORE the visit = put them on before going inside the cold farm.

questions.trap_type: The fireplace scene happened when dinner was finished. AFTER is correct. 'Before' is already used in blank 6.
questions.learning_tip: AFTER = when something is finished. AFTER dinner = when dinner ended. Events happen in order: first dinner, then fireplace.

questions.trap_type: Students write 'at' or 'in' for a named day. ON is always used before specific days of the week.
questions.learning_tip: ON + specific day: ON Saturday, ON Monday morning, ON Christmas Day. Always ON for named days.

C.passage: Last December, my family went on a trip to Cameron Highlands. We left home (1)________ six o'clock in the morning. (2)________ the journey, we drove (3)________ a long tunnel in the mountains. We arrived (4)________ noon and checked into our hotel. (5)________ the afternoon, we visited a strawberry farm. We had to wear jackets (6)________ the visit because it was very cold there. (7)________ dinner, we sat by the fire and drank hot chocolate. We had to leave (8)________ Saturday morning because Father had to return to work.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Weather affects our daily lives in many ways. Singapore has a (1)________ climate — warm and humid throughout the year with no four seasons. Rain is common and can arrive suddenly, which is why many people carry an (2)________. During a thunderstorm, it is safer to stay indoors and avoid (3)________ under tall trees. The wind can also be measured using a (4)________ to show its direction. After heavy rain, rivers may (5)________ — rise above their banks — and cause flooding in low-lying areas.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'report' but the correct fixed phrase is 'weather forecast' = a prediction of coming weather.
questions.learning_tip: A weather FORECAST = a prediction of what the weather will be like. You check the FORECAST to decide what to wear.

questions.trap_type: Students confuse 'shelter' with 'cover'. SHELTER is the specific word for a protective place from rain or wind.
questions.learning_tip: SHELTER = a place that protects you from rain, wind or sun. People FIND SHELTER when it rains suddenly.

questions.trap_type: 'Soaked from head to toe' is a fixed phrase meaning completely wet throughout the body. 'Drenched' is saved for blank 4.
questions.learning_tip: SOAKED means completely wet all the way through. 'From head to toe' + SOAKED = the whole body dripping wet.

questions.trap_type: By elimination after 'soaked' is used in blank 3. Both words mean very wet but each appears in a different blank.
questions.learning_tip: DRENCHED = soaking wet, as if water was poured all over you. People caught in heavy rain for a long time become DRENCHED.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'wind' but the word box contains BREEZE, which means a light and gentle wind.
questions.learning_tip: A BREEZE = a light, gentle wind. A cool BREEZE after rain feels pleasant and refreshing.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — here (place) vs hear (to listen)
questions.trap_type: 'here' (place) when 'hear' (ears) is needed.
questions.learning_tip: HEAR = detect sound with ears. HERE = at this place. 'We could HEAR the thunder' → use ears? YES → HEAR. HEAR = ears. HERE = location.

questions.error_type: Irregular past — fall → fell (not falled)
questions.trap_type: 'falled' applies the regular -ed rule. FALL is irregular: fall → fell.
questions.learning_tip: FALL → FELL (irregular past). NEVER 'falled'. Irregular verbs change completely: fall → fell, tell → told, sell → sold. These must be memorised.

questions.error_type: Irregular past — tell → told (not telled)
questions.trap_type: 'telled' applies the regular -ed rule. TELL is irregular: tell → told.
questions.learning_tip: TELL → TOLD (irregular past). NEVER 'telled'. Irregular verbs do not follow the -ed rule: tell → told, sell → sold, feel → felt.

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — compound subject (Father and I = plural)
questions.trap_type: 'Father and I' = two people = plural subject → WERE.
questions.learning_tip: FATHER AND I = two people = plural subject → WERE. 'Father and I WAS soaking wet' is WRONG. Compound subjects joined by AND are always plural → WERE. Think: two people = they → WERE.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (neighbours', not neighbours's)
questions.trap_type: Students add 's after apostrophe for plural ending -s.
questions.learning_tip: Plural possessive: add apostrophe AFTER -s! NEIGHBOURS' group chat = the chat belonging to all the neighbours. NEVER 'neighbours's'. Singular: neighbour's. Plural: neighbours'. Extra -s = WRONG.

E.passage: Last Thursday, a sudden thunderstorm hit our neighbourhood. We could here (1) the thunder long before the lightning appeared in the sky. The rain falled (2) so heavily that the drain outside our house overflowed within minutes. Our neighbour telled (3) us to move our bicycles to higher ground immediately. Father and I was (4) soaking wet by the time we managed to get back indoors. Later that evening, we read the neighbours's (5) group chat and saw that several trees had fallen across the road.

questions.sentence_a: The weather officer asked the reporter a question.
questions.sentence_b: Will the storm reach the city by midnight?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The weather officer asked...'
questions.model_answer: The weather officer asked the reporter if the storm would reach the city by midnight.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if will the storm reach' (wrong order).
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'WILL the storm reach?' → asked IF the storm WOULD reach. Tense shifts: will → would. Word order is normal after 'if'.

questions.sentence_a: Father was driving home.
questions.sentence_b: It started to hail.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'when'.
questions.model_answer: Father was driving home when it started to hail.
questions.trap_type: Students drop 'was', writing 'Father driving home when it started to hail'.
questions.learning_tip: Father WAS DRIVING (ongoing background) when it STARTED to hail (sudden event). Keep WAS for the background action.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
It rained for three days without stopping. The river near Kai's village began to rise higher and higher. On the third morning, Kai woke up to find that water had seeped under the front door of their house.

'We have to leave now,' said Grandfather. He was a farmer who lived in the village all his life and saw floods before. 'Take only what you need,' he told the family.

Kai quickly grabbed his schoolbag and packed it with his books, a change of clothes and his grandmother's old photo album. His little sister Maya carried her favourite toy rabbit. Mother packed some food and medicine.

The family waded through ankle-deep water to reach higher ground. Neighbours helped each other along the way. At the community hall, volunteers were handing out blankets and hot drinks.

Three days later, the rain stopped and the water went down. When the family returned home, they found mud on the floors and some furniture damaged. But Grandfather looked around and smiled. 'We are safe. We can clean and fix the rest,' he said.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'swirling or spinning with force'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Rushing' = moving fast; 'gathering' = coming together; 'rising' = going up. CHURNING = moving in a circular, agitated way with great force.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: CHURNING = moving in a powerful, swirling, circular way. The brown water was CHURNING = it swirled and turned with great force. Washing machines CHURN clothes; storms CHURN the sea.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'Grandfather said it would pass'?

options.2: The storm and flooding that was frightening the family

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 or 3. 'It would pass' = something unpleasant that will eventually end = the storm.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'IT would pass.' IT = the STORM AND FLOODING — the frightening situation that the family was experiencing. Grandfather was reassuring the family that the danger would not last. IT = the dangerous situation.

mcq_questions.stem: Why did Grandfather say 'The river gives and the river takes — that is its nature' at the end?

options.1: He was angry that the river had flooded their home.
options.2: He wanted to teach the family that nature has both gifts and dangers, and one must accept both with wisdom.
options.3: He was explaining that rivers produce fish for the village to eat.
options.4: He was telling the family to move away from the river permanently.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking he was angry. His tone is philosophical and wise, not angry.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: 'The river GIVES and the river TAKES — that is its NATURE.' Grandfather is teaching a philosophical lesson: nature provides (gives rice fields, water) and nature destroys (floods). One must live wisely alongside both. Option 2 = wisdom, not anger or simple description.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that the family was surprised by the flood? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. Grandfather had a boat ready and lived by the river all his life — he saw floods before and had already prepared for one.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: Grandfather SAW FLOODS BEFORE and HAD A BOAT READY. He was already prepared — so the family was NOT surprised. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What were the volunteers doing at the community hall?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: The volunteers were handing out blankets and hot drinks.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'helping people' which is too vague. The passage gives specific details.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'volunteers were handing out BLANKETS and HOT DRINKS'. Use the specific details from the text.

open_ended_questions.stem: What damage did the family find when they returned home? Give TWO things.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) There was mud on the floors. (ii) Some furniture was damaged.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe the flooding instead of the damage found after the water went down.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5 names TWO things: MUD on the floors AND damaged FURNITURE. Both details are in the last paragraph.

open_ended_questions.stem: Find a phrase in paragraph 4 that shows the community worked together to help each other.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: 'Neighbours helped each other along the way.'
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students quote the volunteer sentence instead of the neighbour sentence about mutual community help.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'NEIGHBOURS HELPED EACH OTHER along the way.' This shows community members helping one another, not just the volunteers.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Grandfather with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) PREPARED: Grandfather had a boat ready before the flood arrived, showing he planned ahead and thought calmly about how to protect his family. (ii) WISE: instead of panicking, he guided the family to safety and then calmly explained that floods are part of living by the river — showing deep experience and calm acceptance.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'strong and brave' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: PREPARED = had a BOAT READY before the flood. WISE = guided family to safety, then explained nature calmly ('the river gives and the river takes'). Name trait + give evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: At the finish line, the runner's face was as ________ as a tomato — flushed red from the effort and heat.
questions.trap_type: 'Pale','calm','cold' describe the opposite. RED = flushed with colour from effort or heat.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The runner's face was AS RED AS a tomato = comparing the flushed colour to a ripe tomato. RED = flushed with colour. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is always the correct simile form.

questions.stem: The coach ________ the team to keep trying even though they were losing by three goals.
questions.trap_type: 'Scolded' and 'punished' are negative responses. A good coach gives positive support when a team is losing.
questions.learning_tip: ENCOURAGED = gave support and confidence to keep going. A good coach ENCOURAGES the team even when they are losing.

questions.stem: After winning the gold medal, Priya had to ________ her celebrations and focus on her next race the following day.
questions.trap_type: 'Put off' = delay; 'run away' = flee; 'break down' = stop working. HOLD BACK = restrain yourself from doing something fully.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: HOLD BACK = restrain or limit yourself or your feelings. Priya had to HOLD BACK her celebrations = she could not celebrate fully yet. HOLD + BACK work together as one meaning.

questions.stem: When the underdog team scored the winning goal in the last minute, every supporter in the stadium was ________ — no one could believe it.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = trouble; 'at a loss' = confused. OVER THE MOON = extremely happy.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OVER THE MOON = feeling extremely happy and excited. The supporters were OVER THE MOON = overjoyed at the unexpected victory. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!

questions.stem: The athletes trained every single day to reach their ________ performance during the championship.
questions.trap_type: 'Peak performance' is a fixed sports phrase meaning the highest level an athlete can achieve.
questions.learning_tip: PEAK means the very highest point. PEAK performance = the best you have ever performed. Athletes train hard to reach their PEAK.

questions.stem: Nobody in the swimming club ________ how to do a perfect butterfly stroke without practising for months.
questions.trap_type: NOBODY = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Nobody KNOWS how to do the butterfly stroke = add -S. 'Nobody know' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.

questions.stem: Our school has ________ three gold medals at the National Primary School Swimming Championships this year.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. WIN → WON (irregular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Our school HAS WON three gold medals = started winning this year. WIN → WON (irregular past participle). HAS + WON = present perfect.

questions.stem: The goalkeeper ________ for the ball when the striker kicked it into the top corner of the net.
questions.trap_type: 'The striker kicked it' = sudden interrupting event. The goalkeeper was already reaching = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The striker KICKED it = sudden past event. The goalkeeper was already in the middle of reaching = WAS REACHING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.

questions.stem: The new indoor stadium is far ________ than the old outdoor track — it can be used in any weather.
questions.trap_type: 'Most useful' = superlative; 'usefuler' is WRONG. MORE USEFUL = comparative for long adjectives.
questions.learning_tip: Long adjective (3+ syllables) → MORE + adjective = comparative. MORE USEFUL THAN the outdoor track = comparing two venues. 'Usefuler' is ALWAYS WRONG. For long adjectives, always use MORE.

questions.stem: The referee blew the whistle and all the players ________ running immediately.
questions.trap_type: 'The referee blew' = past. The players' immediate reaction is also a completed past action.
questions.learning_tip: The referee BLEW = past. All players STOPPED = simple past completed reaction to the whistle.

questions.stem: Regular exercise is one of the best ways to stay healthy and reduce stress, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive present 'to be' ('is') → negative question tag. IS → isn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present 'to be' → negative tag. Regular exercise IS one of the best ways, ISN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. IS → ISN'T. Tag questions: match the 'to be' verb of the main clause.

questions.stem: The team trained very hard ________ they did not win the trophy in the end.
questions.trap_type: Trained hard (positive effort) + did not win (negative result) = a contrast, not a cause-effect. Use 'but'.
questions.learning_tip: BUT joins two contrasting ideas. Trained hard = positive. Did not win = negative. Contrast → BUT.

questions.stem: There ________ not enough players available, so the practice match was cancelled.
questions.trap_type: 'Not enough players' as a collective quantity in a past context is treated as a singular amount.
questions.learning_tip: 'There was not enough players' = the total quantity treated as one collective amount. Past context → WAS.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Verb forms of 'run')

questions.trap_type: After 'loves', use the gerund (-ing form). Students write 'to run'.
questions.learning_tip: LOVE + verb-ing: loves RUNNING every morning. After 'loves', always add -ING.

questions.trap_type: 'Each day' = regular habit = simple present. 'He' is singular so the verb needs -s.
questions.learning_tip: 'Each day' = habit = simple present. He (singular) → RUNS five kilometres.

questions.trap_type: 'Last Tuesday' = past. 'Run' is irregular: run → ran. Students write 'runned'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Last Tuesday' = past. 'Run' is irregular: run → RAN. Never write 'runned'.

questions.trap_type: 'While he ___' past the fountain = ongoing background action. Singular he = was running.
questions.learning_tip: 'While he ___' = ongoing background past action = past continuous. He WAS RUNNING when he spotted Mr Lim.

questions.trap_type: 'Several other students' = plural subject + ongoing past action. Plural = were running.
questions.learning_tip: Several students = plural. They were in motion at the same moment = WERE RUNNING (past continuous).

questions.trap_type: After 'tried', use the infinitive 'to run'. Using 'running' would change the meaning.
questions.learning_tip: 'Try TO + base verb': tried TO RUN faster to catch up with them.

questions.trap_type: After the modal verb 'should', always use the base form with no -s or -ing.
questions.learning_tip: Modal + base verb: should RUN, must swim, can jump. Never 'should runs' or 'should running'.

questions.trap_type: 'Right now' = present continuous. 'My cousin' = singular → is running.
questions.learning_tip: 'Right now' = present continuous. My cousin (singular) → IS RUNNING her first race right now.

C.passage: Wei Ming loves (1)________ every morning before school. He (2)________ five kilometres around the park each day without fail. Last Tuesday, he (3)________ his fastest time ever — just twenty minutes! While he (4)________ past the fountain, he spotted his teacher Mr Lim also out for a jog. Several other students (5)________ ahead of him on the track. Wei Ming tried (6)________ faster to catch up with them. Mr Lim called out, 'You should (7)________ with your arms held higher!' Wei Ming smiled and pushed on. Right now, his cousin (8)________ in her very first school race.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: The school basketball final was the most exciting game of the year. Thousands of (1)________ filled the stands, cheering loudly for their favourite teams. In the first half, our team was (2)________ by eight points. During the break, our captain Reza looked calm but (3)________. He told everyone to believe in themselves and keep fighting. In the second half, one of our players got (4)________ when he twisted his ankle. Even so, the remaining players pushed on and won the match. Reza held up the trophy as our school's (5)________ for the third year running.

questions.trap_type: Spectators watch; supporters cheer. 'Spectators' is the precise word for people watching a live sport event.
questions.learning_tip: SPECTATORS = people who watch a sport or event. They fill the stands and cheer for their teams.

questions.trap_type: 'Was defeated' = lost to the other team. Students may confuse the direction of 'defeat'.
questions.learning_tip: DEFEATED = beaten by someone. Our team WAS DEFEATED = the other team beat them by eight points.

questions.trap_type: The captain gives a motivating speech showing firm resolve, not tiredness. 'Determined' = firmly decided to succeed.
questions.learning_tip: DETERMINED = firmly decided to succeed no matter what. A captain who rallies the team despite being behind is DETERMINED.

questions.trap_type: A twisted ankle is a physical injury. 'Got injured' = was hurt during play.
questions.learning_tip: INJURED = hurt during physical activity. A twisted ankle is a sports INJURY.

questions.trap_type: 'Champion' = the winner of a competition. Holding the trophy confirms the title.
questions.learning_tip: A CHAMPION is the best player or team who wins a competition. Holding the trophy = being the CHAMPION.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — here (place) vs hear (to listen)
questions.trap_type: 'here' (place) when 'hear' (ears) is needed.
questions.learning_tip: HEAR = detect sound with ears. HERE = at this place. 'We could HEAR the excitement' → use ears? YES → HEAR. HEAR = ears. HERE = location.

questions.error_type: Irregular past — hold → held (not holded)
questions.trap_type: 'holded' applies the regular -ed rule. HOLD is irregular: hold → held.
questions.learning_tip: HOLD → HELD (irregular past). NEVER 'holded'. Irregular verbs change completely: hold → held, sell → sold, tell → told. These must be memorised.

questions.error_type: Irregular past — run → ran (not runned)
questions.trap_type: 'runned' applies the regular -ed rule. RUN is irregular: run → ran.
questions.learning_tip: RUN → RAN (irregular past). NEVER 'runned'. Irregular verbs do not follow the -ed rule: run → ran, begin → began, swim → swam.

questions.error_type: Simple past — regular verb (drop → dropped, double p)
questions.trap_type: 'drop' is base form. Past tense context requires 'dropped' (double p + ed).
questions.learning_tip: DROP → DROPPED (regular past, double the -p). Rule: short vowel + single consonant → double before -ed. DROP: D-R-O-P, ends vowel+consonant → DROPPED. 'One runner drop the baton' = WRONG. Use DROPPED.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (coordinators', not coordinators's)
questions.trap_type: Students add 's after apostrophe for plural ending -s.
questions.learning_tip: Plural possessive: add apostrophe AFTER -s! COORDINATORS' results = the results belonging to all the coordinators. NEVER 'coordinators's'. Singular: coordinator's. Plural: coordinators'. Extra -s = WRONG.

E.passage: Last Saturday, our school held its annual sports day on the field. We could here (1) the excitement from the classrooms before we were even allowed outside. One athlete holded (2) his breath before the race and began to look nervous. Our class team runned (3) the four-by-one-hundred relay, but one runner drop (4) the baton and we had to restart. At the end, the sports coordinators's (5) results sheet was read aloud and the top three teams were cheered by the whole school.

questions.sentence_a: The coach asked Priya a question.
questions.sentence_b: Did you feel nervous before the final race?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The coach asked...'
questions.model_answer: The coach asked Priya if she felt nervous before the final race.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if did she feel' (wrong order) or keep 'you'.
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'Did YOU feel nervous?' → asked IF SHE FELT nervous. Pronoun: you → she. Tense: did feel → felt. Word order is normal after 'if'.

questions.sentence_a: Sara was practising her free kicks.
questions.sentence_b: Her coach arrived at the field.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'when'.
questions.model_answer: Sara was practising her free kicks when her coach arrived at the field.
questions.trap_type: Students drop 'was', writing 'Sara practising her free kicks when her coach arrived'.
questions.learning_tip: Sara WAS PRACTISING (ongoing background) when her coach ARRIVED (sudden event). Keep WAS for the ongoing background action.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
It was the final race of the year — the 1500-metre run. Twelve-year-old Priya stood at the starting line, her heart beating fast. She had trained for months for this moment.

The race began. For the first two laps, Priya stayed in third place, pacing herself carefully. Her coach, Mr Rajan, had always told her: 'Save your energy for the last lap.'

On the third lap, the girl in first place stumbled and fell. She got up quickly, but she lost precious time. Priya pushed forward and moved into second place.

With one lap to go, Priya's legs felt heavy. She thought about giving up. But then she heard the crowd cheering and she remembered why she started running — not to win, but to prove to herself that she could finish.

She crossed the finish line in second place. As she caught her breath, she felt a deep sense of pride. Mr Rajan ran over and shook her hand. 'That,' he said, 'was your best race ever.'

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'breathing in short, quick bursts from effort'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Sprinting' = running fast; 'stretching' = extending; 'stumbling' = tripping. GASPING = breathing in short quick bursts, especially from exhaustion.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: GASPING = breathing in short, urgent bursts because of great effort or shock. Priya was GASPING at the finish line = she was out of breath from running so hard. GASP = one sharp intake of breath.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'she almost did not believe it'?

options.2: That she was still in second place despite losing time when she fell
options.4: The timing board above the track

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 3 thinking 'it' = the cheering. But 'almost did not believe IT' = an incredible situation she found herself in.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'almost did not believe IT.' IT = the SITUATION — that she was STILL IN SECOND PLACE even after falling and losing time. She could hardly believe she was still competitive after the setback.

mcq_questions.stem: Why does the writer say Priya 'was not last' at the end of the passage?

options.1: To show that Priya won a medal at the end.
options.2: To show that finishing without giving up — even in difficult circumstances — is itself a form of victory.
options.3: To explain that Priya ran faster than expected.
options.4: To show that the other runners were slower than Priya.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 3 thinking speed is the point. But the emphasis is on persistence, not speed.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: 'She was NOT LAST' = the ending focuses on the fact that she FINISHED and did not give up — not on medals or speed. The passage celebrates PERSISTENCE. Option 2 = the message is about the value of continuing despite difficulty.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Priya was the fastest runner in her school? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says Priya had never won a race before — it was her dream, not something she was already known for.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: Priya NEVER WON A RACE before. She was not the fastest — winning was her DREAM, not her current status. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did Mr Rajan do when Priya crossed the finish line?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Mr Rajan ran over and shook her hand.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he congratulated her' which is too vague. The passage gives specific physical actions.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Last paragraph: Mr Rajan 'RAN OVER and SHOOK HER HAND'. Give the specific actions described in the text.

open_ended_questions.stem: How do we know Priya almost gave up during the last lap? Give TWO pieces of evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) Her legs felt heavy. (ii) She thought about giving up.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students give one piece of evidence twice in different words.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4 gives TWO separate facts: (1) 'her legs felt HEAVY' and (2) 'she THOUGHT ABOUT GIVING UP'. These are two distinct pieces of evidence.

open_ended_questions.stem: What made Priya keep going when she felt like giving up?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: She heard the crowd cheering and remembered why she started running — to prove to herself that she could finish.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students give only one reason and miss the deeper personal motivation.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Two things helped her: the CROWD CHEERING and remembering she wanted to PROVE to herself she could finish. Include both.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on her actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Priya with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) DETERMINED: after falling and losing precious time, Priya got up immediately and kept running instead of stopping — showing she refused to give in to difficulty. (ii) BRAVE: despite the pain of her fall and the knowledge that she was behind, she continued to the finish line without complaint.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'fast and hardworking' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: DETERMINED = fell, but GOT UP and KEPT RUNNING. BRAVE = continued despite pain and setback, no complaint. Name trait + give evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: The shopping mall during the Great Singapore Sale was as ________ as a beehive — shoppers moving in every direction.
questions.trap_type: 'Quiet','empty','dark' describe the opposite of a crowded mall. BUSY = full of people and activity.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The mall was AS BUSY AS a beehive = comparing the frantic movement of shoppers to worker bees in a hive. BUSY = full of activity and people. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is the correct simile form.

questions.stem: The shopkeeper ________ the price by half during the year-end sale.
questions.trap_type: 'Raised' and 'doubled' mean the price went up. A sale means the price goes down.
questions.learning_tip: REDUCED = made lower. During a sale, prices are REDUCED — cut to a lower amount.

questions.stem: After comparing prices at three different stores, Ben decided to ________ forty dollars on a new pair of running shoes.
questions.trap_type: 'Throw away','give away' = get rid of; 'run out of' = use up. SPLASH OUT = spend a larger amount of money than usual as a treat.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: SPLASH OUT = spend more money than usual on something you want as a treat. Ben SPLASHED OUT on new shoes = he spent a good amount as a special purchase. SPLASH + OUT work together as one meaning.

questions.stem: When Marcus found the lost wallet and returned it to its owner, he was ________ — the owner's relief and gratitude made his day.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = trouble; 'at a loss' = confused. OVER THE MOON = extremely happy.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OVER THE MOON = feeling extremely happy. Marcus was OVER THE MOON = overjoyed that his honesty brought someone else relief. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!

questions.stem: The wet market was ________ with shoppers looking for fresh ingredients for their new year feast.
questions.trap_type: 'Silent', 'deserted' and 'empty' all suggest few or no people. A busy new year market is the opposite.
questions.learning_tip: BUSTLING = very busy and full of movement and noise. A market BUSTLING with shoppers = many people rushing about, lively and active.

questions.stem: Nobody in the family ________ where Mother hid the emergency savings — it was her best-kept secret.
questions.trap_type: NOBODY = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Nobody KNOWS where the savings are = add -S. 'Nobody know' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.

questions.stem: The supermarket has ________ a new self-checkout system that allows customers to pay without a cashier.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. INSTALL → INSTALLED (regular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. The supermarket HAS INSTALLED a new system = done recently and now available. INSTALL → INSTALLED (regular verb, add -ed).

questions.stem: The cashier ________ the items when the customer's phone suddenly rang and distracted everyone.
questions.trap_type: 'The phone rang' = sudden interrupting event. Cashier was already scanning = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The phone RANG = sudden past event. The cashier was already in the middle of scanning = WAS SCANNING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.

questions.stem: The online prices are far ________ than the in-store prices at most electronics shops.
questions.trap_type: 'Cheapest' = superlative; 'more cheaper' is WRONG. CHEAPER = comparative of 'cheap'.
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective + -ER = comparative. Cheap → CHEAPER. Online prices are CHEAPER THAN in-store prices = comparing two types of prices. 'More cheaper' is ALWAYS WRONG — never add BOTH 'more' AND '-er'.

questions.stem: She chose the red bag ________ it was her favourite colour.
questions.trap_type: 'So' would reverse the order, putting the result before the reason. 'Because' correctly links the choice to its reason.
questions.learning_tip: She chose the bag BECAUSE it was her favourite colour. BECAUSE = the reason. The reason comes AFTER 'because'.

questions.stem: Spending more than you earn is a sure way to end up in debt, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive present 'to be' ('is') → negative question tag. IS → isn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present 'to be' → negative tag. Spending more than you earn IS a way to end up in debt, ISN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. IS → ISN'T. Tag questions match the 'to be' verb of the main clause.

questions.stem: The shop assistant ________ the customer where the toys section was.
questions.trap_type: The story is set in the past. 'Tell' is irregular: tell → told. Students write 'telled'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Tell' is irregular: tell → TOLD. The event is in the past → TOLD the customer.

questions.stem: The children ________ themselves in the toy aisle while Mother paid for the shopping.
questions.trap_type: The blank is a past tense verb in the same time frame as 'paid'. 'Amusement' is a noun; 'amusing' is an adjective.
questions.learning_tip: 'Amused themselves' = entertained themselves = simple past verb. The children AMUSED themselves while waiting.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Personal pronouns — subject, object, possessive)

questions.trap_type: Before a noun like 'mother', use a possessive adjective. Students write 'I' (subject pronoun).
questions.learning_tip: Before a noun ('mother'), use a possessive adjective: MY mother. 'I mother' is wrong.

questions.trap_type: After the verb 'took', use the object pronoun. Students write 'I' (subject form).
questions.learning_tip: After a verb like 'took', use the OBJECT pronoun: took ME. 'Took I' is wrong.

questions.trap_type: The blank is the subject of 'wanted'. Speaker + sister together = we. Students write 'us' (object form).
questions.learning_tip: The blank is the SUBJECT of 'wanted'. Speaker and sister = WE. 'Us wanted' is wrong.

questions.trap_type: 'My sister and I' — I is the subject. Students write 'me' by false analogy with 'my sister and me'.
questions.learning_tip: Test: remove 'my sister and' → 'I tried on shoes' is correct. 'Me tried' is wrong. Use I as the subject.

questions.trap_type: After the verb 'helped', use the object pronoun. The assistant helped the speaker and sister = us.
questions.learning_tip: After 'helped', use the OBJECT pronoun. The shop assistant helped US (the speaker + sister).

questions.trap_type: Before a noun ('belongings'), use a possessive adjective. Students write 'we' or 'us'.
questions.learning_tip: Before a noun ('belongings'), use a possessive adjective: OUR belongings. 'We belongings' is wrong.

questions.trap_type: 'They last a long time' — subject pronoun for the belongings (plural things). Students write 'them' (object form).
questions.learning_tip: THEY = subject pronoun for things. 'They last a long time' = the belongings last. THEY is the subject of 'last'.

questions.trap_type: After 'take good care of', use the object pronoun. Students write 'they' (subject form).
questions.learning_tip: After 'take care of', use the OBJECT pronoun: take care of THEM. 'Them' = the belongings as the object.

C.passage: Last Saturday, (1)________ mother took (2)________ and my sister to the shopping centre. (3)________ wanted to buy new school shoes. My sister and (4)________ tried on many pairs before finding the right ones. The shop assistant helped (5)________ find the correct size. Our parents always remind us to look after (6)________ belongings carefully. If we take good care of (7)________, (8)________ will last a long time.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Last Monday, my aunt went to a department store with a strict (1)________ of fifty dollars. She found a handbag she liked, but the original price was eighty dollars. Luckily, it was on sale — she got a great (2)________ at only forty-five dollars. However, when she got home, she found the zip was broken. She went back to the store and had to join a long (3)________ at the customer service counter. She asked to (4)________ it for a new one in good condition. The sales assistant agreed and also gave her a small (5)________ for the inconvenience.

questions.trap_type: A budget is a fixed amount of money you decide to spend. Students may write 'plan' which is not in the box.
questions.learning_tip: A BUDGET = a fixed amount of money you decide to spend. Staying within your BUDGET means not spending more than that amount.

questions.trap_type: 'A great bargain' = something bought at a much lower price than normal. Students may write 'deal' which is not in the box.
questions.learning_tip: A BARGAIN = something bought at a much lower price than normal. Getting an 80-dollar bag for 45 dollars = a great BARGAIN.

questions.trap_type: 'Join a long queue' = stand in a line and wait. Students may write 'line' which is not in the box.
questions.learning_tip: QUEUE = a line of people waiting for something. She had to join a long QUEUE at the customer service counter.

questions.trap_type: 'Exchange it for a new one' = return the broken one and get a different one. Students may write 'return' which is not in the box.
questions.learning_tip: EXCHANGE = return a faulty item and get a different working one in its place. She wanted to EXCHANGE the broken bag.

questions.trap_type: A refund = money given back. Last word by context and elimination.
questions.learning_tip: A REFUND = money given back when you return a product or when there is a problem. A partial REFUND = some money back.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — here (place) vs hear (to listen)
questions.trap_type: 'here' (place) when 'hear' (ears) is needed.
questions.learning_tip: HEAR = detect sound with ears. HERE = at this place. 'We could HEAR the music' → use ears? YES → HEAR. HEAR = ears. HERE = location.

questions.error_type: Irregular past — go → went (not go, base form)
questions.trap_type: 'go' is base form. Past tense context requires 'went'.
questions.learning_tip: GO → WENT (irregular past). NEVER 'goed'. In a past tense context, use WENT. 'A salesperson go up to us' = WRONG — wrong tense. Use WENT.

questions.error_type: Simple past — regular verb (try → tried)
questions.trap_type: 'tries' is present tense third person. Past tense context requires 'tried'.
questions.learning_tip: TRY → TRIED (regular past, change -y to -i and add -ed). In a past tense context, use TRIED. 'Mother tries on shoes' = WRONG — wrong tense. TRY → TRIED.

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (some items)
questions.trap_type: 'Some items' is plural. Students write 'was'.
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! SOME ITEMS WERE placed in a box = ITEMS is plural → WERE. WAS is only for ONE thing. Find the main noun: ITEMS = plural → WERE.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (shoppers', not shoppers's)
questions.trap_type: Students add 's after apostrophe for plural ending -s.
questions.learning_tip: Plural possessive: add apostrophe AFTER -s! SHOPPERS' purchases = the purchases belonging to all the shoppers. NEVER 'shoppers's'. Singular: shopper's. Plural: shoppers'. Extra -s = WRONG.

E.passage: Last Saturday, Mother took us to the new mall near the expressway for the school sale. We could here (1) the cheerful music playing even before we reached the entrance. Inside, a salesperson go (2) up to us immediately and offered us a loyalty card. Mother tries (3) on several pairs of shoes before choosing the blue ones with the special grip. There were not enough bags at the counter — some items was (4) placed in a box instead. At the end, the shoppers's (5) purchases were checked against their receipts before they passed through the exit gates.

questions.sentence_a: The shopkeeper asked the customer a question.
questions.sentence_b: Are you looking for something specific today?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The shopkeeper asked...'
questions.model_answer: The shopkeeper asked the customer if he was looking for something specific.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if is he looking' (wrong order) or keep 'you'.
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'Are YOU looking?' → asked IF HE WAS looking. Pronoun: you → he. Tense: are looking → was looking. Word order is normal after 'if'.

questions.sentence_a: Mother was checking the prices.
questions.sentence_b: The children ran to the toy section.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'while'.
questions.model_answer: While Mother was checking the prices, the children ran to the toy section.
questions.trap_type: Students drop 'was', writing 'While Mother checking the prices, the children ran'.
questions.learning_tip: Mother WAS CHECKING (ongoing background) while the children RAN (different simultaneous action). Keep WAS.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Nine-year-old Marcus was helping his mother carry the groceries when he saw a brown wallet on the floor near the checkout counter. He looked inside and found some cash and a name card that read: 'Mr David Tan, Block 44, Maple Avenue.'

'Mum, someone dropped this,' Marcus said, holding up the wallet. His mother smiled. 'What do you think you should do?' she asked.

Marcus thought carefully. He could keep the money — there was quite a lot inside. But he knew that was wrong. He handed the wallet to the customer service counter and told the officer what he found.

The officer took down Marcus's name and phone number. That evening, Mr Tan called their home. He sounded very relieved. He told Marcus's mother that the wallet contained money for his daughter's school trip, which was the very next day.

'Your son is a very honest boy,' Mr Tan said. He visited the next day and brought a box of biscuits as a thank-you gift. Marcus felt happier about returning the wallet than he would have felt keeping the money.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 1 has the same meaning as 'extremely busy with lots of noise and movement'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Quiet' = opposite; 'crowded' = full of people (but less vivid); 'colourful' = visually bright. BUSTLING = extremely busy, full of noisy activity and movement.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: BUSTLING = very busy, noisy and full of movement. A BUSTLING market = one where many people are moving, talking and trading energetically. BUSTLE = busy activity; BUSTLING = currently very busy and lively.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'Marcus knew he had to return it'?

options.2: The wallet he found on the ground
options.3: The shopping bag he was carrying
options.4: The amount of money in the wallet

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 or 4 thinking 'it' = money or receipt. But 'return IT' = the whole object he found.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'had to return IT.' IT = the WALLET — the complete item Marcus found on the ground. He had to return the entire wallet (including everything inside) to its owner. IT = the wallet.

mcq_questions.stem: Why did the writer describe Marcus as feeling 'lighter' as he walked away from the police station?

options.1: Because Marcus had put down the heavy wallet.
options.2: Because returning the wallet relieved him of a moral burden — doing the right thing made him feel free and good about himself.
options.3: Because Marcus was tired from walking and finally felt relaxed.
options.4: Because the officer told Marcus to walk faster.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'lighter' = less physical weight. This is a metaphor for emotional relief.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: 'felt LIGHTER' = a metaphor for EMOTIONAL RELIEF. Returning the wallet removed the moral weight of carrying something that was not his. Doing the right thing made him feel FREE and at ease. Option 2 = the emotional/moral reading, not the physical one.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Marcus immediately knew what to do when he found the wallet? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says Marcus picked it up and stood still for a moment — showing he paused to think about what to do rather than acting immediately.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: Marcus STOOD STILL FOR A MOMENT — he paused, suggesting he was not sure what to do right away. He then made the decision to report it. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did Mr Tan bring when he visited Marcus the next day?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Mr Tan brought a box of biscuits as a thank-you gift.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he brought a present' which is too vague. The passage gives a specific detail.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Last paragraph: 'a box of BISCUITS as a THANK-YOU GIFT'. Give the specific detail from the text.

open_ended_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, Marcus thought about keeping the money. Give TWO things that helped him decide not to.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) He knew that keeping the money was wrong. (ii) He decided to hand the wallet to the customer service counter instead.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students give one reason twice in different words, or describe what he did rather than why he decided.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: He KNEW IT WAS WRONG = the moral reason. He then ACTED by going to CUSTOMER SERVICE = the decision. State both.

open_ended_questions.stem: Find the exact word in paragraph 4 that shows Mr Tan was very glad the wallet was found.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: relieved
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students write 'happy' or 'glad' — these are synonyms but NOT the exact word used in the passage.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'He sounded very RELIEVED.' The question asks for the exact word from the passage, not a synonym.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Marcus with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) HONEST: even though the wallet was full of cash, Marcus chose to hand it in at the police station instead of keeping it — showing strong personal integrity. (ii) RESPONSIBLE: he acted on his own conscience without being told to, and followed through by going to the police station immediately.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'kind and good' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: HONEST = handed in the wallet with FULL CASH inside. RESPONSIBLE = acted on his OWN CONSCIENCE, went to police station immediately. Name trait + give evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: After the rain, the forest floor was as ________ as a freshly washed carpet — green, clean and sparkling with droplets.
questions.trap_type: 'Dry','grey','noisy' describe the opposite or unrelated qualities. FRESH = clean, new and full of life.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The forest floor was AS FRESH AS a freshly washed carpet = comparing its clean, renewed quality after rain to a clean carpet. FRESH = new, clean and full of life. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is the correct simile form.

questions.stem: The forest fire ________ thousands of trees and destroyed the homes of many wild animals.
questions.trap_type: 'Grew', 'watered' and 'planted' are positive actions. A fire causes destruction, not growth.
questions.learning_tip: DESTROYED = completely ruined or wiped out. The fire DESTROYED the trees = burned them all down.

questions.stem: Every weekend, the students came to ________ the abandoned plot of land and turn it into a community garden.
questions.trap_type: 'Run away from','give up on','break into' all describe negative actions. CLEAN UP = tidy and remove rubbish or dirt from a space.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: CLEAN UP = remove dirt, rubbish and mess from an area. The students came to CLEAN UP the abandoned plot = they removed all the rubbish and tidied it. CLEAN + UP work together as one meaning.

questions.stem: When the old tree that the students had worked so hard to save finally survived and bloomed again in spring, everyone was ________ — all their effort was worth it.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = trouble; 'down in the dumps' = sad. OVER THE MOON = extremely happy.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OVER THE MOON = feeling extremely happy and relieved. Everyone was OVER THE MOON = overjoyed that the tree survived. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!

questions.stem: The wildlife officer released the injured turtle back into the sea after it ________ fully.
questions.trap_type: 'Disappeared', 'shrank' and 'drowned' are all negative outcomes. An officer releases an animal only after it gets better.
questions.learning_tip: HEALED = became healthy again after being injured. The turtle HEALED → the officer released it safely back into the sea.

questions.stem: Nobody in the class ________ how much plastic ends up in the ocean every year — the numbers are shocking.
questions.trap_type: NOBODY = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Nobody REALISES how much plastic = add -S. 'Nobody realise' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.

questions.stem: Our school has ________ a zero-waste campaign this term to reduce the amount of plastic used in the canteen.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. LAUNCH → LAUNCHED (regular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Our school HAS LAUNCHED a zero-waste campaign = started recently and now running. LAUNCH → LAUNCHED (regular verb, add -ed).

questions.stem: The birds ________ loudly in the trees when the bulldozer suddenly started clearing the forest.
questions.trap_type: 'The bulldozer started clearing' = sudden interrupting event. Birds were already chirping = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The bulldozer STARTED = sudden past event. The birds were already in the middle of chirping = WERE CHIRPING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.

questions.stem: The coral reefs in our oceans are far ________ now than they were fifty years ago — pollution and warming have taken a heavy toll.
questions.trap_type: 'Most damaged' = superlative; 'damageder' is WRONG. MORE DAMAGED = comparative for long adjectives.
questions.learning_tip: Long adjective → MORE + adjective = comparative. MORE DAMAGED THAN fifty years ago = comparing two points in time. 'Damageder' is ALWAYS WRONG. For longer adjectives, use MORE.

questions.stem: There ________ a family of otters living in the river near our school.
questions.trap_type: 'A family of otters' — the head noun is 'a family' = singular. Present fact. Students write 'are' looking at 'otters'.
questions.learning_tip: 'A family' = ONE family = singular → THERE IS a family. Even though otters are plural, the head noun 'a family' is singular.

questions.stem: Protecting the environment is everyone's responsibility, not just the government's, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive present 'to be' ('is') → negative question tag. IS → isn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present 'to be' → negative tag. Protecting the environment IS everyone's responsibility, ISN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. IS → ISN'T. Tag questions: match the 'to be' verb of the main clause.

questions.stem: Each of the young trees ________ watered by the students every morning.
questions.trap_type: 'Each of the trees' = each tree individually = singular. Students write 'are' seeing 'trees' (plural).
questions.learning_tip: 'Each of the trees' = each tree one at a time = singular → IS watered. Look at 'each', not 'trees', to decide.

questions.stem: "We must stop cutting ________ trees in the forest," the environmentalist said firmly.
questions.trap_type: Students pick a demonstrative pronoun, not recognising that 'cut down' is a fixed phrasal verb.
questions.learning_tip: 'Cut DOWN trees' = the phrasal verb meaning to chop trees so they fall. STOP CUTTING DOWN = stop chopping them.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Verb forms of 'plant')

questions.context_check: Subject: 'Our school' (singular). Signal: 'Every year' = habit = simple present. Singular subject + simple present = plants.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'plant' (plural form) forgetting 'our school' is a singular subject.
questions.learning_tip: 'Every year' = habit = simple present. Our school (singular) → PLANTS trees along the road each year.

questions.context_check: Signal: 'Last Earth Day' = past. 'Plant' is regular: plant → planted.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'plant' (base form) ignoring the past time signal 'Last Earth Day'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Last Earth Day' = past. 'Plant' is regular: plant → PLANTED.

questions.context_check: Signal: 'While half the class ___' = ongoing background action in the past. Subject 'half the class' = plural group = were planting.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'planted' (simple past) missing the ongoing background signal 'while'.
questions.learning_tip: 'While half the class ___' = ongoing past action = past continuous. Many students = plural → WERE PLANTING.

questions.context_check: Signal: 'reminded us ___' = infinitive structure. 'Remind someone TO do something' → to plant.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'planting' instead of the infinitive that follows 'reminded us'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Reminded us TO + base verb': reminded us TO PLANT each seedling carefully. Always use the infinitive after 'reminded someone'.

questions.context_check: Signal: 'while she ___' = ongoing background action. Subject 'Lin' = singular she = was planting. Interrupted by dropping the bottle.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'planted' (simple past) missing the ongoing signal 'while she'.
questions.learning_tip: Lin WAS PLANTING (ongoing) when she dropped her water bottle (sudden event). Singular subject → WAS PLANTING.

questions.context_check: Signal: 'Right now' = present continuous. Subject: 'my brother's class' = singular group = is planting.
