questions.trap_type: Students write 'plants' (simple present habit) missing the 'right now' signal for present continuous.
questions.learning_tip: 'Right now' = present continuous. My brother's class (one class, singular) → IS PLANTING trees behind the canteen.

questions.context_check: Signal: 'loves ___' = gerund after 'loves'. Pattern: love + verb-ing.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'to plant' instead of the gerund after 'loves'.
questions.learning_tip: LOVE + verb-ing: Our principal loves PLANTING trees. After 'loves', always add -ING.

questions.context_check: Signal: 'should ___' = modal verb + base form. Never add -s or -ing after a modal.
questions.trap_type: Students add -s or use 'planting' after the modal verb 'should'.
questions.learning_tip: After modal verbs (should, must, can, will), always use the BASE form: should PLANT. Never 'should plants' or 'should planting'.

C.passage: Every year, our school (1)________ trees along the roadside as part of its green programme. Last Earth Day, students from all classes (2)________ over two hundred seedlings in the school compound. Class 3A was especially enthusiastic — while half the class (3)________ trees near the science block, the other half watered the existing plants. Our teacher reminded us (4)________ each seedling carefully so the roots would take hold. My friend Lin (5)________ a small mango tree when she accidentally dropped her water bottle. Right now, my brother's class (6)________ trees behind the canteen. Our principal loves (7)________ trees and has said we should (8)________ at least one new tree every month.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Nature provides everything we need to survive. Trees produce the (1)________ we breathe and absorb harmful carbon dioxide. Rivers and streams supply clean (2)________ for drinking and farming. When forests are cut down, animals lose their (3)________ — the natural environment where they live and raise their young. Humans must reduce (4)________ — damage caused to air, water and land by harmful substances. Every small effort to (5)________ — reuse, reduce and recycle — helps protect the planet for future generations.

questions.trap_type: 'Rubbish dropped in parks and rivers' = throwing rubbish in public = littering.
questions.learning_tip: LITTERING = dropping or throwing rubbish in public places. It harms the environment and makes surroundings ugly.

questions.trap_type: 'Catching too many fish' = overfishing. Students may not know this compound word.
questions.learning_tip: OVERFISHING = catching too many fish from the sea, leaving too few to reproduce and survive. 'Over-' = too much.

questions.trap_type: 'From leftover food and vegetable peels' = organic material that becomes compost. Students may write 'fertiliser' which is not in the box.
questions.learning_tip: COMPOST = decayed food and plant material mixed into soil to make it richer. Made from leftover food and vegetable peels.

questions.trap_type: 'Without using any chemicals' = done the way nature itself does it = natural.
questions.learning_tip: NATURAL = occurring in nature, without man-made chemicals. Compost enriches soil in a NATURAL way.

questions.trap_type: 'To protect our environment' = to keep it safe from harm. Last word by context and elimination.
questions.learning_tip: PROTECT = keep something safe from harm. We must PROTECT the environment so all living things can thrive.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — here (place) vs hear (to listen)
questions.trap_type: 'here' (place) when 'hear' (ears) is needed.
questions.learning_tip: HEAR = detect sound with ears. HERE = at this place. 'We could HEAR the birdsong' → use ears? YES → HEAR. HEAR = ears. HERE = location.

questions.error_type: Spelling — joined (join + ed, not jointed)
questions.trap_type: 'jointed' adds -ed to 'joint' not 'join'. The correct base is JOIN → JOINED.
questions.learning_tip: JOIN → JOINED (just add -ed). 'Jointed' = a different word (connected by a joint). NEVER 'jointed' for JOIN. Spell clearly: J-O-I-N + ED = JOINED.

questions.error_type: Irregular past — tell → told (not telled)
questions.trap_type: 'telled' applies the regular -ed rule. TELL is irregular: tell → told.
questions.learning_tip: TELL → TOLD (irregular past). NEVER 'telled'. Irregular verbs: tell → told, sell → sold, fall → fell. These must be memorised.

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the students)
questions.trap_type: 'The students' is plural. Students write 'was'.
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! THE STUDENTS WERE amazed = STUDENTS is plural → WERE. WAS is only for ONE thing. STUDENTS = plural → WERE.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (participants', not participants's)
questions.trap_type: Students add 's after apostrophe for plural ending -s.
questions.learning_tip: Plural possessive: add apostrophe AFTER -s! PARTICIPANTS' observation sheets = the sheets belonging to all the participants. NEVER 'participants's'. Singular: participant's. Plural: participants'. Extra -s = WRONG.

E.passage: Last Sunday, our class joined a nature walk at the reservoir nature trail. We could here (1) birdsong from the moment we stepped off the bus. Our guide jointed (2) us at the entrance and explained the rules: no litter, no loud noise. She telled (3) us that even a small piece of rubbish can harm the wildlife living near the water. As we walked, the students was (4) amazed by the variety of birds and insects they spotted along the way. At the end, the participants's (5) observation sheets were collected for a class display back at school.

questions.sentence_a: The nature guide asked the children a question.
questions.sentence_b: Have you ever seen a wild otter before?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The nature guide asked...'
questions.model_answer: The nature guide asked the children if they had ever seen a wild otter before.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if have they ever seen' (wrong order) or keep 'you'.
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'Have YOU ever seen?' → asked IF THEY HAD EVER seen. Pronoun: you → they. Tense: have → had. Word order is normal after 'if'.

questions.sentence_a: The students were collecting fallen leaves.
questions.sentence_b: A butterfly landed on one of the bags.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'when'.
questions.model_answer: The students were collecting fallen leaves when a butterfly landed on one of the bags.
questions.trap_type: Students drop 'were', writing 'The students collecting fallen leaves when a butterfly landed'.
questions.learning_tip: The students WERE COLLECTING (ongoing background) when a butterfly LANDED (sudden event). Keep WERE for the ongoing action.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
At the centre of Birchwood Primary School stood a magnificent old raintree. Its wide branches spread across the entire field, giving shade to students during recess. According to the school's history book, the tree was planted by the school's founder over eighty years ago.

One morning, the principal announced that the raintree had to be cut down because its roots were cracking the floor of the school hall. Many students were upset. A group of Primary 5 students decided to do something about it.

They started a petition and collected over three hundred signatures from students, teachers and parents. They also researched ways to save old trees without cutting them down. One student found that roots could be guided away from buildings using special underground barriers.

The principal read the petition carefully. Impressed by the students' effort and research, she agreed to bring in a tree expert before making the final decision.

The expert visited and suggested installing root barriers underground to guide the roots away from the hall. It would cost more, but the tree could be saved.

A month later, the work was done. The old raintree still stood, and students still gathered under its shade during recess, just as they always did.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'not moving at all, completely still'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Whispering','leaning','reaching' all involve some movement. MOTIONLESS = completely still, not moving at all.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: MOTIONLESS = completely without movement. The children stood MOTIONLESS = they did not move a single muscle while watching the birds. MOTION = movement; MOTIONLESS = no movement at all (-LESS = without).

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'Kai realised he had never noticed it before'?

options.1: The bird that landed on the branch
options.2: How much beauty and life existed in nature close to his home, which he had walked past without seeing
options.3: The notebook he used to record his observations

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'it' = the bird. But 'never noticed IT before' = something that was always there but unseen.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'never noticed IT before.' IT = THE NATURAL WORLD around his home — the birds, the trees, the sounds. Kai realised he had walked past all this BEAUTY without ever paying attention to it. IT = the richness of nature near his home.

mcq_questions.stem: Why does the writer end the passage with 'the old tree was still there — and so were they'?

options.1: To show that the students were tired and did not want to leave.
options.2: To show that protecting the tree and caring for nature helped both the tree and the students grow and endure.
options.3: To explain that the tree was so old it would outlast the students.
options.4: To suggest the students should come back to visit more often.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 or 3. The ending is poetic and symbolic — 'they' = the students and the relationship between humans and nature.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: 'the old tree was still THERE — and so WERE THEY.' Both the tree AND the students endured and grew. The writer is drawing a parallel: just as the tree survived through care, the students' CONNECTION TO NATURE also survived and deepened. Option 2 = the symbolic parallel meaning.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that the old tree was in danger of being cut down? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: True. The passage says the town council planned to remove the old tree to make way for a road — showing it was under threat.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: the TOWN COUNCIL PLANNED TO REMOVE the old tree to make way for a road. This means the tree was in danger of being cut down. Answer is TRUE.

open_ended_questions.stem: How many signatures did the students collect for their petition?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: They collected over three hundred signatures.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'many signatures' which is too vague.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: 'over THREE HUNDRED signatures'. Use the exact number from the text.

open_ended_questions.stem: What TWO things did the group of Primary 5 students do to try to save the tree?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) They started a petition and collected signatures. (ii) They researched ways to save old trees without cutting them down.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students give one action twice or mention the expert, who was brought in by the principal — not by the students.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: (1) they started a PETITION and (2) they RESEARCHED ways to save trees. The expert was the principal's decision later.

open_ended_questions.stem: What was the raintree used for by students at recess?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Students gathered under its shade during recess.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'to play' or 'to rest' which are too general.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: 'giving SHADE to students during RECESS'. The tree gave shade and students gathered beneath it at recess.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on their actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of the students with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) DETERMINED: the students wrote letters, made signs and appealed to the council to save the tree — showing they did not give up even when facing official opposition. (ii) CARING: they gave up their weekends to water and tend to the tree, showing genuine concern for nature beyond their own personal gain.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'hardworking and kind' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: DETERMINED = wrote letters, made signs, appealed to council — did not give up. CARING = gave up weekends to water and tend the tree. Name trait + give evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: Grandma's kitchen smelled as ________ as a bakery — warm bread, cinnamon and butter filled every corner.
questions.trap_type: 'Cold','noisy','empty' don't match the warm comforting smell description. SWEET = pleasant, warm, sugary smell.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The kitchen smelled AS SWEET AS a bakery = comparing the home's smell to a freshly baked bakery. SWEET = pleasantly fragrant. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is always the correct simile form.

questions.stem: The chef added a ________ of salt to the dish to improve its flavour.
questions.trap_type: A bowl, bucket and bottle are all large amounts. Salt is added in tiny amounts — a pinch.
questions.learning_tip: A PINCH = a very small amount you can pick up between two fingers. Recipes say 'a pinch of salt' for a tiny amount.

questions.stem: After the big meal, Mother asked the children to ________ the dishes and put them away in the cupboard.
questions.trap_type: 'Put off' = delay; 'run away' = flee; 'give in' = surrender. WASH UP = clean the dishes after a meal.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: WASH UP = clean the dishes and utensils after eating. Mother asked them to WASH UP the dishes = clean them with soap and water. WASH + UP work together as one meaning.

questions.stem: When the judges tasted Grandma's secret recipe soup and gave her first prize, she was ________ — it was her dream come true.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = trouble; 'at a loss' = confused. OVER THE MOON = extremely happy.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OVER THE MOON = feeling extremely happy and delighted. Grandma was OVER THE MOON = her happiness was at its very highest. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!

questions.stem: The recipe said to ________ the mixture until it became smooth and there were no more lumps.
questions.trap_type: 'Fry' uses oil; 'fold' = gently combine; 'peel' removes skin. Only 'whisk' = beat rapidly to make smooth.
questions.learning_tip: WHISK = beat a mixture quickly to make it smooth and airy. You whisk eggs or cake batter. The clue 'no more lumps' tells you the action makes things smooth.

questions.stem: Nobody in the cooking class ________ how to make roti prata from scratch — it is one of the hardest dishes to master.
questions.trap_type: NOBODY = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Nobody KNOWS = add -S. 'Nobody know' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.

questions.stem: Our school canteen has ________ a new healthy menu with less sugar and more vegetables this term.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. INTRODUCE → INTRODUCED (regular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. The canteen HAS INTRODUCED a new menu = done recently and now in use. INTRODUCE → INTRODUCED (regular verb, add -d).

questions.stem: Father ________ the fish in the pan when the smoke alarm suddenly went off.
questions.trap_type: 'The smoke alarm went off' = sudden interrupting event. Father was already frying = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The alarm WENT OFF = sudden past event. Father was already in the middle of frying = WAS FRYING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.

questions.stem: Grandma's laksa is far ________ than any laksa Kai has ever tasted at a restaurant.
questions.trap_type: 'Tastiest' = superlative; 'more tastier' is WRONG. TASTIER = comparative of 'tasty' (ending -y: change y to i, add -er).
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective ending in -Y → change Y to I, add -ER. Tasty → TASTIER. Grandma's laksa is TASTIER THAN the restaurant's. 'More tastier' is ALWAYS WRONG — never add BOTH 'more' AND '-er'.

questions.stem: The noodles tasted very bland ________ no one had added any seasoning at all.
questions.trap_type: 'So' would reverse the order, placing the result before the reason.
questions.learning_tip: Tasted bland BECAUSE no one added seasoning. BECAUSE = the reason. The reason comes AFTER 'because'.

questions.stem: Grandma's secret recipe has been in the family for over fifty years, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive present perfect ('has been') → negative question tag. HAS → hasn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present perfect → negative tag. The recipe HAS BEEN in the family for fifty years, HASN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. HAS → HASN'T. Present perfect tag: has/have → hasn't/haven't.

questions.stem: The youngest chef in the kitchen ________ the curry by adding too many chillies by mistake.
questions.trap_type: The story is in past context. 'Spoil' is regular: spoil → spoiled. Students write 'spoilt' (both accepted but 'spoiled' preferred here).
questions.learning_tip: 'Spoil' = ruined. Past tense = SPOILED (regular). The story is in past tense → SPOILED the curry.

questions.stem: "You must not touch ________ hot pan on the stove," Mother warned the children firmly.
questions.trap_type: 'Hot pan' is singular (→ this or that). The pan is right there on the stove = nearby = this.
questions.learning_tip: The hot pan is RIGHT THERE on the stove = nearby. Pan = singular. Near + singular = THIS hot pan.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Prepositions in a kitchen context)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We started (1)________ ten o'clock'. Signal: specific clock time → AT. 'At ten o'clock' is the only correct preposition for a named clock time.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' or 'on' for a clock time. AT is the correct preposition for specific times.
questions.learning_tip: Use AT for specific clock times: AT ten o'clock, AT noon, AT midnight.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Grandma mixed flour (2)________ butter'. Signal: combining two ingredients → 'mixed A WITH B'. WITH shows what is combined.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'and' (a conjunction, not a preposition) or 'in'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Mix A WITH B' = combine A and B together. Grandma mixed flour WITH butter to make the dough.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'she rolled it (3)________ a flat sheet'. Signal: transformation — the dough changed shape by rolling → rolled INTO a flat sheet. INTO shows the result of a change.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' (location, no movement) instead of 'into' (movement/transformation).
questions.learning_tip: 'Rolled it INTO a flat sheet' = transformed it by rolling. INTO = changing form or entering something.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'she cut small circles (4)________ the sheet'. Signal: removing shapes out of the source material → cut FROM the sheet. FROM shows the source or origin.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' or 'on' instead of 'from', which shows the source of the cut shapes.
questions.learning_tip: 'Cut circles FROM the sheet' = removed the circles from the source material. FROM shows where something comes from.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'placed each tart (5)________ the baking tray'. Signal: resting on the surface of the tray → ON. ON = touching the top of a surface.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' (inside, not on top) or 'into' (entering, not resting on a surface).
questions.learning_tip: ON = resting on a surface: placed the tarts ON the tray. Use ON for things touching the top of a surface.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'put the tray (6)________ the oven'. Signal: inside the oven to bake → IN. Food goes IN the oven (enclosed space).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'into' (movement entering) instead of 'in' (location inside the oven where it stays).
questions.learning_tip: Food goes IN the oven = inside the enclosed oven space. 'Place IN the oven' = put inside the oven to bake.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'baked them (7)________ twenty minutes'. Signal: duration of time → FOR. 'Baked for twenty minutes' = how long the baking lasted.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'at' or 'in' instead of 'for', which shows duration.
questions.learning_tip: FOR + duration: baked FOR twenty minutes, waited FOR an hour. FOR shows how long something lasts.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'we waited (8)________ they turned golden brown'. Signal: continuing up to a specific endpoint → UNTIL. UNTIL = up to the point when something happens.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'for' (already used in blank 7) or 'when' (not a preposition here).
questions.learning_tip: UNTIL = up to the point when something happens: waited UNTIL they turned golden brown = kept waiting up to that moment.

C.passage: Last Sunday, I helped my grandmother make pineapple tarts. We started (1)________ ten o'clock in the morning. Grandma mixed flour (2)________ butter to make the pastry dough. Then she rolled it (3)________ a flat sheet on the kitchen table. Next, she cut small circles (4)________ the sheet using a round cutter. I helped place each tart (5)________ the baking tray carefully. We then put the tray (6)________ the oven and baked them (7)________ twenty minutes. The kitchen smelled wonderful as we waited (8)________ they turned golden brown.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Food is an important part of every culture. Before cooking, a chef must (1)________ all the ingredients to make sure nothing is missing. Most dishes need the right (2)________ of heat — too high and food burns; too low and it stays raw. A good cook also knows the correct (3)________ for each ingredient — a pinch of salt is very different from a handful. Every recipe requires fresh (4)________ to bring out the best flavour. A meal cooked with love and patience always (5)________ better than one that is rushed.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'method' which is not in the box. A recipe is a set of cooking instructions.
questions.learning_tip: A RECIPE = a set of instructions telling you what ingredients to use and how to cook a dish.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'item' or 'food' which are not in the box.
questions.learning_tip: An INGREDIENT = one of the items used to make a food dish. The main ingredient is the most important one.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'piece' or 'serving' which are not in the box. A portion = the amount served to one person.
questions.learning_tip: A PORTION = the amount of food served to one person. A generous PORTION = a large, plentiful serving.

questions.trap_type: Students may not know this word. The clue 'everyone wanted to start eating straight away' = the food looked very attractive.
questions.learning_tip: APPETISING = looking or smelling so good that it makes you want to eat. Golden food that looks APPETISING is very attractive.

questions.trap_type: The clue is 'because Father had forgotten to add salt and pepper' = no flavour = bland.
questions.learning_tip: BLAND = having very little flavour. Food without salt, pepper or seasoning tastes BLAND.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — here (place) vs hear (to listen)
questions.trap_type: 'here' (place) when 'hear' (ears) is needed.
questions.learning_tip: HEAR = detect sound with ears. HERE = at this place. 'We could HEAR the sizzling' → use ears? YES → HEAR. HEAR = ears. HERE = location.

questions.error_type: Spelling — decide + d (not decied)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'decied' misspelling 'decided'. DECIDE ends in silent -e: add only -d.
questions.learning_tip: DECIDE → DECIDED. Rule: silent -e at the end → just add -D. DECIDE + D = DECIDED. 'Decied' is WRONG — do not rearrange the letters.

questions.error_type: Spelling — clean + ed (no double n, clean ends in two consonants)
questions.trap_type: Students double the -n. CLEAN ends in two consonants (n already) → just add -ed, no doubling.
questions.learning_tip: CLEAN → CLEANED (just add -ed, no double n). Rule: only double the final consonant when the word ends in ONE vowel + ONE consonant: run → running. CLEAN ends in -AN (two consonants) → just add -ED.

questions.error_type: Irregular past — eat → ate (not eated)
questions.trap_type: 'eated' applies the regular -ed rule. EAT is irregular: eat → ate.
questions.learning_tip: EAT → ATE (irregular past). NEVER 'eated'. Irregular verbs change completely: eat → ate, swim → swam, run → ran. These must be memorised.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (cooks', not cooks's)
questions.trap_type: Students add 's after apostrophe for plural ending in -s.
questions.learning_tip: Plural possessive: add apostrophe AFTER -s! COOKS' notebook = the notebook belonging to all the cooks. NEVER 'cooks's'. Singular: cook's. Plural: cooks'. Extra -s after apostrophe = WRONG.

E.passage: Last Sunday, our family cooked a big meal together to celebrate Grandma's birthday. We could here (1) the sizzling sounds of food being fried from the other room. First, we decied (2) to make her favourite dish — prawn noodle soup. Father began cutting the vegetables but accidentally cleanned (3) the knife with the wrong cloth. The soup was left to simmer, but it eated (4) away some of the flavour because we forgot to cover the pot. After the meal, we signed the cooks's (5) notebook with a message of thanks for Grandma.

questions.sentence_a: The cooking teacher asked the class a question.
questions.sentence_b: Have you ever cooked a meal by yourself?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The cooking teacher asked...'
questions.model_answer: The cooking teacher asked the class if they had ever cooked a meal by themselves.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if have they ever cooked' (wrong order) or keep 'you/yourself'.
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'Have YOU ever cooked?' → asked IF THEY had ever cooked. Pronoun: you → they. Tense: have → had. Word order is normal after 'if'.

questions.sentence_a: Grandma was stirring the porridge.
questions.sentence_b: A neighbour knocked on the door.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'when'.
questions.model_answer: Grandma was stirring the porridge when a neighbour knocked on the door.
questions.trap_type: Students drop 'was', writing 'Grandma stirring the porridge when a neighbour knocked'.
questions.learning_tip: Grandma WAS STIRRING (ongoing background) when a neighbour KNOCKED (sudden event). Keep WAS for the ongoing background action.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Every Chinese New Year, Great-Aunt Lian made her famous pineapple tarts. People said they were the best in the whole neighbourhood. Families would come from nearby streets just to get a small tin of them.

This year, Great-Aunt Lian was eighty years old. Her hands shook a little as she rolled the pastry, but her eyes were sharp and her instructions were clear. Twelve-year-old Nadia sat beside her, watching every movement carefully.

'The secret,' said Great-Aunt Lian, 'is not the recipe. It is the patience.' She showed Nadia how to press each small circle of pastry gently, how to place just the right amount of filling in the centre, and how to seal the edges without cracking them.

By the afternoon, they made three hundred tarts. Nadia's back ached and her fingers were sticky with sugar, but she did not complain. She was too busy learning.

'You have good hands,' said Great-Aunt Lian at the end of the day. 'Next year, you can make them yourself.'

Nadia felt a warmth spread through her chest. She realised that Great-Aunt Lian was not just teaching her to bake. She was passing down something that words alone could not explain.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'cooked slowly and gently in hot liquid'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Boiled' = cooked at high heat with bubbles; 'grilled' = cooked over flame; 'stirred' = mixed. SIMMERED = cooked gently in hot liquid just below boiling point.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: SIMMERED = cooked slowly in hot liquid just below boiling point — gentle bubbles, not a rolling boil. Grandma SIMMERED the soup = she kept it at a low, steady heat for a long time.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'she had never shared it with anyone outside the family'?

options.2: The secret recipe that passed down through generations

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 or 3. 'Never shared IT with anyone' = the secret recipe — something precious and private.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'never shared IT with anyone outside the family.' IT = the SECRET RECIPE. Something so precious Grandma kept it only within the family. Context before IT: discussion of the family recipe tradition.

mcq_questions.stem: Why did Kai feel 'something he could not name' when he watched Grandma cook?

options.1: He was confused about which ingredient to add next.
options.2: He felt a deep sense of love and belonging that words could not fully describe.
options.3: He felt hungry and wanted to eat immediately.
options.4: He was worried that Grandma was cooking too slowly.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 or 3. 'Something he could not name' = an emotion too deep for words.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: 'something he COULD NOT NAME' = an emotion beyond words. In context — watching Grandma cook her secret recipe with love — this is a feeling of BELONGING and LOVE. Option 2 = the emotion the passage describes indirectly.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Grandma's recipe was well-known throughout the neighbourhood? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says the recipe was a family secret — Grandma never shared it with anyone outside the family, so the neighbourhood did not know it.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: the recipe was a FAMILY SECRET. Grandma NEVER SHARED it outside the family. Therefore the neighbourhood did not know it. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: How many tarts did Nadia and Great-Aunt Lian make by the afternoon?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: They made three hundred tarts.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'many tarts' which is too vague.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'they made THREE HUNDRED tarts.' Use the exact number from the text.

open_ended_questions.stem: Even though Nadia's back ached and her fingers were sticky, she did not complain. Give TWO reasons from the passage why she kept going.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) She was too busy learning from Great-Aunt Lian to think about the discomfort. (ii) She valued the opportunity to learn this special skill from her great-aunt.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe the physical discomfort rather than the reasons she kept going.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'She was TOO BUSY LEARNING.' The passage tells you directly — she was focused on LEARNING. Infer she also valued the opportunity.

open_ended_questions.stem: Find ONE phrase in paragraph 2 that shows Great-Aunt Lian was still alert and careful despite her age.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: 'Her eyes were sharp and her instructions were clear.'
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students quote 'her hands shook a little' which shows physical weakness, not alertness.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2 contrasts weakness and strength: hands shook (weakness) BUT 'her EYES WERE SHARP and her instructions were CLEAR' (alertness). The question asks for alertness.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on the passage, describe TWO character traits of Grandma with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) GENEROUS: Grandma chose to share her secret recipe with Kai, trusting him to carry it forward — showing she put family love above secrecy. (ii) PATIENT: she cooked the soup slowly for hours, never rushing, showing she believed that good food — like good relationships — could not be hurried.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'kind and skilful' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: GENEROUS = chose to SHARE her secret recipe with Kai. PATIENT = cooked SLOWLY FOR HOURS, never rushed. Name trait + give evidence from passage = full marks.

questions.stem: The express train shot through the tunnel as ________ as an arrow — it was there and gone in seconds.
questions.trap_type: 'Slow' is the opposite. 'Quiet' and 'heavy' don't describe speed. FAST = moving with great speed.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The train was AS FAST AS an arrow = comparing its speed to an arrow shot from a bow. FAST = moving with great speed. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is the correct simile form.

questions.stem: Father reminded us to ________ our seatbelts as soon as we got into the car.
questions.trap_type: 'Remove' is the opposite — it means take off. 'Break' would damage the seatbelt.
questions.learning_tip: FASTEN your seatbelt = click it securely into place. This is the standard safety instruction in any vehicle.

questions.stem: After a long journey, the family was tired and happy to ________ the taxi and finally reach their hotel.
questions.trap_type: 'Run away from' = flee; 'break into' = enter by force; 'stay in' = remain. GET OUT OF = leave a vehicle or enclosed space.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: GET OUT OF = leave a vehicle or place. The family wanted to GET OUT OF the taxi = step out of it. GET + OUT + OF work together. Contrast: get in(to) a taxi (enter) vs get out of a taxi (leave).

questions.stem: When Anya's plane finally landed after the long flight, she was ________ — she counted down the hours.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = trouble; 'at a loss' = confused. OVER THE MOON = extremely happy and relieved.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OVER THE MOON = feeling extremely happy and relieved. Anya was OVER THE MOON = overjoyed to finally land. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!

questions.stem: The cyclist ________ around the fallen branch on the road and continued riding safely.
questions.trap_type: 'Swerved' = turned sharply to avoid something. 'Stopped' = came to a halt, not went around.
questions.learning_tip: SWERVED = turned suddenly to the left or right to avoid something. The cyclist SWERVED = turned quickly to miss the branch.

questions.stem: Nobody on the crowded platform ________ which train to take — the announcement board had stopped working.
questions.trap_type: NOBODY = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Nobody KNOWS = add -S. 'Nobody know' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.

questions.stem: The Land Transport Authority has ________ two new MRT lines in the eastern part of Singapore this year.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. OPEN → OPENED (regular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. The LTA HAS OPENED two new MRT lines = done recently and now in use. OPEN → OPENED (regular verb).

questions.stem: The passengers ________ in the queue when the bus finally pulled up to the stop.
questions.trap_type: 'The bus finally pulled up' = sudden past event. Passengers were already waiting = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The bus PULLED UP = sudden past event. Passengers were already in the middle of waiting = WERE WAITING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.

questions.stem: The new expressway is much ________ than the old road — cars can now travel the same distance in half the time.
questions.trap_type: 'Fastest' = superlative; 'more faster' is WRONG. FASTER = comparative of 'fast'.
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective + -ER = comparative. Fast → FASTER. The expressway is FASTER THAN the old road = comparing two routes. 'More faster' is ALWAYS WRONG — never add BOTH 'more' AND '-er'.

questions.stem: Every passenger on the bus ________ required to tap their card on the reader before boarding.
questions.trap_type: 'Every passenger' = each one individually = singular. Present fact. Students write 'are' thinking of many passengers.
questions.learning_tip: 'Every passenger' = each one individually = singular → IS required. EVERY always takes a singular verb.

questions.stem: Taking the MRT during peak hour can be extremely crowded and stressful, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive modal ('can be') → negative question tag. CAN → can't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive modal → negative tag. Taking the MRT CAN be crowded, CAN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. Modal 'can' → 'can't'. Match the auxiliary of the main clause.

questions.stem: "Please keep ________ bags under the seat in front of you," the flight attendant announced.
questions.trap_type: Before a noun ('bags'), use a possessive adjective. 'You' is a subject pronoun and cannot describe a noun.
questions.learning_tip: Before 'bags' (a noun), use a POSSESSIVE ADJECTIVE: YOUR bags. 'You bags' is wrong — 'you' cannot describe a noun.

questions.stem: The lorry driver ________ at the junction and waved the children safely across the road.
questions.trap_type: The story is in past tense. 'Stop' is regular: stop → stopped. Students write 'stop' (base form).
questions.learning_tip: The story is in past tense. 'Stop' is regular: stop → STOPPED. Both actions (stopped and waved) are simple past.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Verb forms of 'drive')

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Uncle Ravi loves (1)________ his family on road trips'. Signal: 'loves + ___' = gerund (verb-ing). Pattern: love + verb-ing → driving.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'to drive' instead of the gerund after 'loves'.
questions.learning_tip: LOVE + verb-ing: loves DRIVING his family on trips. After 'loves', always add -ING.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'He (2)________ carefully and always follows traffic rules'. Signal: 'always' = habitual truth about Uncle Ravi. Subject 'He' = singular → simple present → drives.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'drive' (plural form) forgetting that 'He' is a singular subject.
questions.learning_tip: 'Always' = a regular habit = simple present. He (singular) → DRIVES carefully and follows traffic rules.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Last year, he (3)________ us all the way to Penang'. Signal: 'Last year' = past. 'Drive' is irregular: drive → drove.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'drived', not knowing 'drive' is irregular.
questions.learning_tip: 'Last year' = past. 'Drive' is irregular: drive → DROVE. Never write 'drived'.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'While he (4)________ through the mountains, we saw a waterfall'. Signal: 'While he ___' = ongoing background action. Subject 'he' = singular → was driving. Interrupted by 'we saw'.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'drove' (simple past) missing the ongoing background signal 'while'.
questions.learning_tip: 'While he ___' = ongoing background past action = past continuous. He WAS DRIVING through the mountains when we spotted the waterfall.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The other cars (5)________ slowly because the road was narrow'. Signal: same past time frame, plural subject 'the other cars' + ongoing action → were driving.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'drove' (simple past) instead of the past continuous for an ongoing parallel action.
questions.learning_tip: The other cars = plural. They were also moving at that same past moment = WERE DRIVING (past continuous).

questions.context_check: Passage: 'My cousin wants (6)________ when she grows up'. Signal: 'wants + ___' = infinitive. Pattern: want + to + base verb → to drive.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'driving' instead of the infinitive after 'wants'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Want TO + base verb': wants TO DRIVE when she grows up. Always use the infinitive after 'wants'.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Uncle Ravi says she should (7)________ carefully'. Signal: 'should + ___' = modal verb + base form. Never add -s or -ing after a modal.
questions.trap_type: Students add -s or -ing after the modal verb 'should'.
questions.learning_tip: After modal verbs (should, must, can, will), always use the BASE form: should DRIVE. Never 'should drives' or 'should driving'.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Right now, she (8)________ in the car park on her first lesson'. Signal: 'Right now' = present continuous. Subject 'she' = singular → is driving.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'drives' (simple present habit) missing the 'right now' signal for present continuous.
questions.learning_tip: 'Right now' = present continuous. She (singular) → IS DRIVING in the car park on her first lesson.

C.passage: Uncle Ravi loves (1)________ his family on road trips during the school holidays. He (2)________ carefully and always follows all traffic rules. Last year, he (3)________ us all the way from Singapore to Penang. While he (4)________ through the mountains, we spotted a beautiful waterfall beside the road. The other cars (5)________ slowly because the road was narrow and winding. My cousin wants (6)________ when she grows up, just like her father. Uncle Ravi says she should (7)________ carefully and never rush. Right now, she (8)________ in the car park on her very first lesson.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Travelling by different modes of transport offers different experiences. A (1)________ is someone who travels between home and work every day, often using public transport. Long journeys by bus or train can feel (2)________ if the seats are comfortable and the scenery is beautiful. Some routes pass through a (3)________ — a long passage built under a hill or the seabed. At major cities, an (4)________ is an official entry point where passports and luggage are checked. Responsible travellers always follow (5)________ — the rules about how to behave and travel safely.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'arrival'. DEPARTURE = the time the flight leaves, not arrives.
questions.learning_tip: DEPARTURE = the act of leaving / the scheduled time a flight leaves. We arrived two hours before DEPARTURE = before the flight was due to leave.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'cancelled'. DELAYED = made later than planned, not cancelled entirely.
questions.learning_tip: DELAYED = made to happen later than planned. A delayed flight = one that leaves later than its scheduled time.

questions.trap_type: Students may pick 'departure' (already used). BOARDING = getting onto the plane; a boarding announcement tells you it is time to go on.
questions.learning_tip: BOARDING = getting onto a plane or ship. A BOARDING announcement tells you it is time to go to the gate and get on.

questions.trap_type: Students may not know this aviation word. The clue 'made the plane shake' defines turbulence directly.
questions.learning_tip: TURBULENCE = rough air movements that cause a plane to shake and bump. Pilots ask passengers to fasten seatbelts during TURBULENCE.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'airport'. DESTINATION = the place you are travelling to, which here is Tokyo.
questions.learning_tip: A DESTINATION = the place you are travelling to. When we finally arrived at our DESTINATION = we reached Tokyo.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — here (place) vs hear (to listen)
questions.trap_type: 'here' (place) when 'hear' (ears) is needed.
questions.learning_tip: HEAR = detect sound with ears. HERE = at this place. 'We could HEAR the rain' → use ears? YES → HEAR. HEAR = ears. HERE = location.

questions.error_type: Irregular past — take → took (not taked)
questions.trap_type: 'taked' applies regular -ed rule. TAKE is irregular: take → took.
questions.learning_tip: TAKE → TOOK (irregular past). NEVER 'taked'. Irregular verbs do not follow the -ed rule: take → took, make → made, shake → shook.

questions.error_type: Adverb required after action verb (rode/travelled)
questions.trap_type: 'smooth' (adjective) after an action. The ride moving = adverb needed.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (the ride was/moved), use an ADVERB. The ride was SMOOTHLY? No — 'the ride' is a noun, so actually 'smooth' describes the ride (adjective after linking verb). BUT 'rode smooth' needs 'smoothly'. Check: verb or noun? Here 'rode' = verb → SMOOTHLY.

questions.error_type: Simple past — regular verb (spot → spotted)
questions.trap_type: 'spot' is base form. In past tense context, add -ted: spotted.
questions.learning_tip: SPOT → SPOTTED (regular past, double the 't'). Rule: short vowel + single consonant → double before -ed. SPOT: S-P-O-T, ends vowel+consonant → SPOTTED. 'The bus spot a landslide' = WRONG. Use SPOTTED.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (drivers', not drivers's)
questions.trap_type: Students add 's after apostrophe for plural ending -s.
questions.learning_tip: Plural possessive: add apostrophe AFTER -s! DRIVERS' report = the report belonging to all the drivers. NEVER 'drivers's'. Singular: driver's. Plural: drivers'. Extra -s = WRONG.

E.passage: Last month, our family took a long-distance bus trip to visit our relatives in the north. We could here (1) the sound of rain pattering against the windows as we left the city. The driver taked (2) a rest at a service station halfway through the journey. The ride was smooth (3) and most passengers fell asleep quickly in their seats. Suddenly, the bus spot (4) a landslide on the road ahead and had to take a detour. Later, when we finally arrived, the drivers's (5) report was checked by the transport supervisor before we disembarked.

questions.sentence_a: The conductor asked the passengers a question.
questions.sentence_b: Do you have your tickets ready?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The conductor asked...'
questions.model_answer: The conductor asked the passengers if they had their tickets ready.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if do they have' (wrong order) or keep 'you/your'.
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'Do YOU have YOUR tickets?' → asked IF THEY HAD THEIR tickets. Pronoun: you → they, your → their. Tense: do have → had. Word order is normal after 'if'.

questions.sentence_a: The bus driver was checking the tickets.
questions.sentence_b: A passenger dropped her bag.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'when'.
questions.model_answer: The bus driver was checking the tickets when a passenger dropped her bag.
questions.trap_type: Students drop 'was', writing 'The bus driver checking the tickets when a passenger dropped her bag'.
questions.learning_tip: The driver WAS CHECKING (ongoing background) when a passenger DROPPED her bag (sudden event). Keep WAS for the ongoing action.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
The school holidays were over and twelve-year-old Zara was on her way home to Singapore after spending three weeks with her grandparents in Kuala Lumpur. She was travelling alone for the first time.

At the KL Sentral station, Zara's grandmother hugged her tightly. 'Call us when you arrive,' she said. Zara nodded, trying to look confident, although her heart was beating a little fast.

On the train, Zara found her seat and placed her backpack on the overhead rack. A kind elderly man in the next seat asked her where she was going. When she told him, he smiled. 'Singapore! I used to live there thirty years ago,' he said.

They talked all the way to Johor Bahru. The man told Zara about the Singapore he remembered — the food, the people and the kampung house he grew up in. Zara listened with great interest.

When the train pulled into Woodlands Checkpoint, Zara shook the old man's hand and thanked him for the conversation. As she joined the immigration queue, she felt calmer and more confident than she did at the start of the journey.

Her father was waiting at the station exit, waving and smiling. Zara ran towards him, no longer thinking about the nervousness she felt hours before.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 1 has the same meaning as 'moving very slowly in heavy traffic'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Speeding' = moving fast; 'rushing' = moving hurriedly; 'gliding' = moving smoothly. CRAWLING = moving very slowly, like a creature that crawls.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: CRAWLING = moving very slowly. Traffic that CRAWLS = moves at almost no speed. The buses were CRAWLING in the jam = they barely moved. CRAWL normally means to move on hands and knees, but it also describes very slow movement.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'Anya could not take her eyes off it'?

options.2: The view from the train window as they crossed the causeway

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'it' = the ticket. But 'could not take her eyes OFF IT' = something visually captivating outside = the view.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'could not take her eyes off IT.' You 'take your eyes off' something you are looking at intently. IT = the VIEW from the window — described just before as the causeway stretching over the water. She was captivated by what she saw outside.

mcq_questions.stem: Why did Anya say 'I think I could get used to this' at the end of the passage?

options.1: Because she found train travel more comfortable than she expected.
options.2: Because she enjoyed the excitement, the views and the sense of adventure that travel brought.
options.3: Because she wanted to become a train driver when she grew up.
options.4: Because she was happy to finally get off the train.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking she liked the seat. The sentence reflects a broader appreciation of the travel experience.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: 'could get USED TO THIS' = she could happily make this a regular part of her life. THIS = not just the train seat, but everything — the EXCITEMENT, the VIEWS, the sense of ADVENTURE. Option 2 = the full experience she is embracing.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Anya enjoyed travelling by train? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: True. The passage says Anya pressed her face against the window and could not look away — showing she found the journey exciting and enjoyable.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: Anya PRESSED HER FACE AGAINST THE WINDOW and COULD NOT LOOK AWAY. These actions show excitement and enjoyment — not boredom. Answer is TRUE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did the old man tell Zara about his past connection with Singapore?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: He told her that he used to live in Singapore thirty years ago.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he liked Singapore' which is too vague.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: 'I USED TO LIVE there THIRTY YEARS ago.' Give the specific detail from the text.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did the old man talk to Zara about during the train journey? Give TWO things.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: He talked about (i) the food in Singapore he remembered, and (ii) the people and the kampung house he grew up in. (Accept any two of: food / people / kampung house.)
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students give only one topic or describe Zara's reaction instead of the topics discussed.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: he talked about the FOOD, the PEOPLE and the KAMPUNG HOUSE. Give any two specific topics.

open_ended_questions.stem: Find a phrase in the last paragraph that shows Zara was no longer nervous at the end of the journey.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: 'No longer thinking about the nervousness she felt hours before.'
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students quote 'ran towards him' which shows eagerness but does not directly state that the nervousness was gone.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Last paragraph: 'NO LONGER THINKING ABOUT THE NERVOUSNESS she felt hours before.' This directly states that her earlier nervousness was gone.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on her actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Anya with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) CURIOUS: Anya pressed her face against the window and could not take her eyes off the changing scenery — showing a genuine hunger to explore and observe new things. (ii) ADVENTUROUS: when the train crossed the causeway, instead of feeling nervous, she leaned forward with excitement — showing she embraced new experiences rather than fearing them.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'excited and happy' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: CURIOUS = pressed face to window, could not look away. ADVENTUROUS = leaned forward with excitement when crossing the causeway — embraced the unknown. Name trait + give evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: On the first day of Chinese New Year, Grandma's living room was as ________ as a garden in spring — red flowers, golden lanterns and laughter everywhere.
questions.trap_type: 'Quiet','empty','dark' describe the opposite of a festive room. COLOURFUL = having many bright, vivid colours.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The room was AS COLOURFUL AS a garden in spring = comparing the festive decorations to a blooming spring garden. COLOURFUL = vivid and full of bright colours. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is the correct simile form.

questions.stem: Children ________ with joy when the fireworks lit up the night sky on National Day.
questions.trap_type: 'Cried' could mean sadness or excitement, but 'cheered' specifically means shouting with joy.
questions.learning_tip: CHEERED = shouted with joy and excitement. Children CHEER when they see something thrilling like fireworks.

questions.stem: After the new year meal, the children helped to ________ the dishes and prepare the table for the exchange of ang pao.
questions.trap_type: 'Put off' = delay; 'run away' = flee; 'give in' = surrender. CLEAR UP = tidy and clean a space after use.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: CLEAR UP = tidy and remove mess from a place. The children helped to CLEAR UP the dishes = they tidied the table after eating. CLEAR + UP work together as one meaning.

questions.stem: When the lion dance performers arrived at their door and brought good luck, the whole family was ________ — everyone cheered and clapped.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = trouble; 'down in the dumps' = sad. OVER THE MOON = extremely happy.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OVER THE MOON = feeling extremely happy and delighted. The family was OVER THE MOON = their joy was at its very highest when the lion dance arrived. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!

questions.stem: During the fasting month, Muslims ________ from eating and drinking from dawn until sunset each day.
questions.trap_type: 'Resist' = fight against temptation. 'Refrain from' = the fixed formal phrase meaning deliberately choose not to do something.
questions.learning_tip: REFRAIN FROM = choose not to do something as a matter of discipline. Muslims REFRAIN FROM eating during the fasting hours.

questions.stem: Everyone in our extended family ________ to Grandpa's house for reunion dinner without fail every year.
questions.trap_type: EVERYONE = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: EVERYONE / NOBODY / SOMEONE = Singular! Everyone COMES to Grandpa's house = add -S. 'Everyone come' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.

questions.stem: Our school has ________ a special multicultural festival to celebrate Deepavali, Hari Raya and Chinese New Year together this term.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. ORGANISE → ORGANISED (regular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Our school HAS ORGANISED a festival = planned and carried it out recently. ORGANISE → ORGANISED (add -d for regular verbs ending in -e).

questions.stem: Mother ________ the rendang in the kitchen when the first guests knocked on the door.
questions.trap_type: 'The guests knocked on the door' = sudden interrupting event. Mother was already cooking = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The guests KNOCKED = sudden past event. Mother was already in the middle of cooking = WAS COOKING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.

questions.stem: The Deepavali light display at Little India was far ________ this year than last year — there were twice as many lanterns.
questions.trap_type: 'Brightest' = superlative; 'more brighter' is WRONG. BRIGHTER = comparative of 'bright'.
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective + -ER = comparative. Bright → BRIGHTER. The display was BRIGHTER THAN last year = comparing two years. 'More brighter' is ALWAYS WRONG — never add BOTH 'more' AND '-er'.

questions.stem: We stayed up past midnight ________ we wanted to watch the countdown on New Year's Eve.
questions.trap_type: 'So' reverses the order. 'Because' correctly links the action to its reason.
questions.learning_tip: Stayed up late BECAUSE we wanted to watch. BECAUSE = the reason. The reason comes AFTER 'because'.

questions.stem: The Chingay parade is one of the most spectacular events in Singapore every year, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive present 'to be' ('is') → negative question tag. IS → isn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present 'to be' → negative tag. The parade IS one of the most spectacular events, ISN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. IS → ISN'T. Tag questions match the verb of the main clause.

questions.stem: "May I visit ________ grandparents with you this weekend?" Zara asked her friend.
questions.trap_type: Before a noun ('grandparents'), use a possessive adjective. 'You' is a subject pronoun and cannot describe a noun.
questions.learning_tip: Before 'grandparents' (a noun), use a POSSESSIVE ADJECTIVE: YOUR grandparents. 'You grandparents' is wrong.

questions.stem: The lion dance performers ________ energetically for over an hour before taking a short rest.
questions.trap_type: The festival described is a past event. 'Dance' is regular: dance → danced. Students write 'dance' (base form).
questions.learning_tip: The festival is described in past context. 'Dance' is regular: dance → DANCED (add -d).

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Personal pronouns — subject, object and possessive)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Last Deepavali, (1)________ celebrated with both sides of my family.' Signal: blank is the SUBJECT of 'celebrated'. Speaker + family = we (first person plural subject).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'us' (object form) instead of 'we' (subject form).
questions.learning_tip: The blank is the SUBJECT of 'celebrated'. The speaker and family = WE. 'Us celebrated' is wrong.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(2)________ brought a huge tray of murukku.' Signal: blank is the SUBJECT of 'brought'. Refers to the uncle's wife (female) = she (third person singular female subject).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'her' (object form) instead of 'she' (subject form).
questions.learning_tip: The uncle's wife is the SUBJECT of 'brought'. She = female = SHE. 'Her brought' is wrong.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(3)________ husband spent the morning drawing kolam.' Signal: blank is BEFORE the noun 'husband' = possessive adjective. Refers to the uncle's wife (female) = her (third person singular female possessive adjective).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'she' (subject pronoun) instead of 'her' (possessive adjective before a noun).
questions.learning_tip: Before 'husband' (a noun), use a POSSESSIVE ADJECTIVE: HER husband. 'She husband' is wrong.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'the children gathered while (4)________ parents prepared the feast.' Signal: blank is BEFORE the noun 'parents' = possessive adjective. Speaker is one of the children; the children's parents = our (first person plural possessive adjective).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'their' which is not in the word box, or 'we' (subject pronoun, not possessive adjective).
questions.learning_tip: Before 'parents' (a noun), use possessive adjective: OUR parents (the speaker is also one of the children). 'We parents' is wrong.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(5)________ placed the final dish at the centre of the table.' Signal: blank is the SUBJECT of 'placed'. Refers to Uncle (male) = he (third person singular male subject).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'his' (possessive) instead of 'he' (subject pronoun).
questions.learning_tip: Uncle is the SUBJECT of 'placed'. Uncle = male = HE placed the dish. 'His placed' is wrong.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(6)________ thanked Mother warmly.' Signal: blank is the SUBJECT of 'thanked'. Refers to the children (plural) = they (third person plural subject).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'them' (object form) instead of 'they' (subject form).
questions.learning_tip: The children = plural = THEY thanked Mother. THEY is the subject pronoun for a group. 'Them thanked' is wrong.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'My little cousin started crying, but (7)________ mother quickly comforted him.' Signal: blank is BEFORE the noun 'mother' = possessive adjective. The cousin is a boy = his (third person singular male possessive adjective).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'her' (already used for blank 3) or 'he' (subject pronoun, not possessive adjective).
questions.learning_tip: Before 'mother' (a noun), use a possessive adjective. The cousin is a boy → HIS mother. 'He mother' is wrong.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'comforted him with a sweet and distracted (8)________ with a song.' Signal: blank is the OBJECT of 'distracted'. Refers to the children (plural) = them (third person plural object pronoun).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'they' (subject form) instead of 'them' (object form after a verb).
questions.learning_tip: After the verb 'distracted', use the OBJECT pronoun: distracted THEM. 'Them' = the children as the object. 'Distracted they' is wrong.

C.passage: Last Deepavali, (1)________ celebrated with both sides of my family. My uncle's wife came early to help decorate. (2)________ brought a huge tray of murukku for everyone. (3)________ husband spent the morning drawing kolam at the front door. All the children gathered in the living room while (4)________ parents prepared the feast in the kitchen. Uncle carried out the final dish and (5)________ placed it at the centre of the table. The children were delighted — (6)________ thanked Mother warmly. My little cousin started crying, but (7)________ mother quickly comforted him with a sweet and distracted (8)________ with a song.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Every year during Chinese New Year, our extended family comes together and we are (1)________ after months of being apart. The house becomes (2)________ with music, laughter and the chatter of young and old. Grandparents share stories about the old (3)________ they followed as children, such as sweeping the house before the new year to chase away bad luck. Relatives are always (4)________ — they bring food, gifts and red packets for everyone. These are more than just habits; they are (5)________ that have been passed down for generations and give our family a deep sense of belonging.

questions.trap_type: 'Reunited after months of being apart' = coming back together after separation. Students may write 'together' which is not in the box.
questions.learning_tip: REUNITED = brought back together after being apart. Families are REUNITED at festivals after not seeing each other for months.

questions.trap_type: 'Lively with music, laughter and chatter' = full of energy and activity. Students may write 'noisy' which is not in the box.
questions.learning_tip: LIVELY = full of life, energy and activity. A house filled with music and laughter is LIVELY.

questions.trap_type: Students confuse 'customs' with 'traditions' (blank 5). CUSTOMS = specific practices; TRADITIONS = broader long-established heritage passed down.
questions.learning_tip: CUSTOMS = specific practices or behaviours traditional in a culture, like sweeping the house before new year.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'they bring food, gifts and red packets' = giving a lot freely = generous.
questions.learning_tip: GENEROUS = willing to give a lot freely. Relatives who bring lots of food, gifts and red packets are being GENEROUS.

questions.trap_type: 'Passed down for generations' = long-established heritage = traditions. 'Customs' was used in blank 3.
questions.learning_tip: TRADITIONS = long-established practices passed from generation to generation. They give a sense of identity and belonging.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — here (place) vs hear (to listen)
questions.trap_type: 'here' (place) when 'hear' (ears) is needed.
questions.learning_tip: HEAR = detect sound with ears. HERE = at this place. 'We could HEAR music' → use ears? YES → HEAR. HEAR = ears. HERE = location.

questions.error_type: Spelling — invited (not inivted)
questions.trap_type: Students scramble 'invited' as 'inivted'. INVITED: i-n-v-i-t-e-d.
questions.learning_tip: INVITED: I-N-V-I-T-E-D. Spell it slowly: IN-VITE-D. The common error is to write 'inivted' — the -v- comes before -i-. INVITE → INVITED (add -d for silent -e words).

questions.error_type: Spelling — arrived (double r before -ed)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'arived' with one -r. ARRIVE has double -r: a-r-r-i-v-e-d.
questions.learning_tip: ARRIVED: A-R-R-I-V-E-D. Note the DOUBLE R: arrive → arrived. The double -r is part of the base word ARRIVE, not added during conjugation. Always remember: arRIVE → arRIVED.

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the children)
questions.trap_type: 'The children' is plural. Students write 'was'.
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! The CHILDREN WERE given sweets = CHILDREN is plural → WERE. WAS is only for ONE thing. CHILDREN = plural → WERE.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (guests', not guests's)
questions.trap_type: Students add 's after apostrophe for plural ending -s.
questions.learning_tip: Plural possessive: add apostrophe AFTER -s! GUESTS' shoes = the shoes belonging to all the guests. NEVER 'guests's'. Singular: guest's. Plural: guests'. Extra -s after apostrophe = WRONG.

E.passage: Last year, our family celebrated Deepavali with our neighbours for the first time. We could here (1) the sound of music and laughter coming from Mrs Kumar's flat before we even reached her door. When we arrived, we found that she inivted (2) twenty guests from our block. The house was so beautifully decorated that we arived (3) speechless at the entrance. The children was (4) given sweets and sparklers before the fireworks began on the rooftop. At the end of the evening, all of the guests's (5) shoes were neatly lined up outside the front door.

questions.sentence_a: The teacher asked the class a question.
questions.sentence_b: Do you celebrate any special festivals at home?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The teacher asked...'
questions.model_answer: The teacher asked the class if they celebrated any special festivals at home.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if do they celebrate' (wrong order) or keep 'you'.
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'Do YOU celebrate?' → asked IF THEY CELEBRATED. Pronoun: you → they. Tense: do celebrate → celebrated. Word order is normal after 'if'.

questions.sentence_a: Grandmother was kneading the dough.
questions.sentence_b: The guests rang the doorbell.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'when'.
questions.model_answer: Grandmother was kneading the dough when the guests rang the doorbell.
questions.trap_type: Students drop 'was', writing 'Grandmother kneading the dough when the guests rang the doorbell'.
questions.learning_tip: Grandmother WAS KNEADING (ongoing background) when the guests RANG (sudden event). Keep WAS for the ongoing background action.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Eight-year-old Aiman looked forward to Hari Raya every year. This year, Grandma promised to teach him how to make ketupat — the diamond-shaped rice cakes wrapped in coconut leaves.

On the morning of Hari Raya, the whole family was busy. Father hung up the green lights along the corridor. Mother arranged the kuih on trays in the living room. Grandma sat in the kitchen, her nimble fingers weaving the coconut leaves into shape.

'Come, Aiman,' she called. Aiman sat beside her and watched every movement carefully. 'It looks easy, but you need patience,' Grandma said with a smile.

Aiman tried. His first attempt was too loose and the coconut leaves came apart. His second attempt was too tight. But on his third try, Grandma nodded. 'Better,' she said quietly.

By noon, they made over fifty pieces of ketupat. When the guests arrived, Aiman could not wait to tell them he helped make the ketupat himself. One uncle tasted a piece and said, 'This is the best ketupat I have ever eaten!'

Aiman beamed with pride. He knew the uncle was probably exaggerating, but it did not matter. It was the best Hari Raya he ever had.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'a strong, pleasant smell'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Colour', 'texture', 'noise' relate to sight and touch/sound. FRAGRANCE = a pleasant, sweet smell.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: FRAGRANCE = a sweet, pleasant smell. The fragrance of Grandma's cooking FILLED the house = the lovely smell spread everywhere. FRAGRANT = adjective (fragrant flowers); FRAGRANCE = noun (the smell itself).

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'Omar said he would never forget it'?

options.1: The food that was served at the celebration
options.2: The moment the whole family sat down and prayed together before the meal
options.3: The decorations hung around the house
options.4: The fireworks display later that night

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'it' = the food. But 'would never forget IT' = a meaningful moment, not just food.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'would never forget IT.' IT = the MEANINGFUL MOMENT — the whole family sitting and praying together before the meal. This is the moment described just before the pronoun, and it is the emotional peak of the paragraph.

mcq_questions.stem: Why does the writer describe the house as 'alive' at the end of the passage?

options.1: Because there were real plants growing inside the house.
options.2: Because the sounds, colours and movement of the celebration filled every corner with energy and joy.
options.3: Because the family was very loud and noisy during dinner.
options.4: Because the lights were left on all night.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 3 thinking 'alive' = noisy. ALIVE WITH = full of vibrant energy — a more complete picture.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: 'ALIVE WITH' = full of active energy, colour and sound. The house was ALIVE = it felt like a living, breathing space filled with joy. This is an EXTENDED METAPHOR — the house is compared to something living. Option 2 = the full picture the writer creates.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Omar had celebrated Hari Raya at his grandparents' house before? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: True. The passage says the family went to the grandparents' house every Hari Raya — so Omar celebrated there every year.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: 'They went to the grandparents' house EVERY HARI RAYA.' EVERY = without exception, year after year. So YES, he celebrated there before. Answer is TRUE.

open_ended_questions.stem: How many pieces of ketupat did Aiman and Grandma make by noon?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: They made over fifty pieces of ketupat.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'many pieces' which is too vague.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: 'they made over FIFTY pieces of ketupat.' Use the exact number from the text.

open_ended_questions.stem: Grandma said 'It looks easy, but you need patience.' Give TWO pieces of evidence from the passage that show making ketupat really does require patience.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) Aiman's first attempt was too loose and came apart. (ii) It took him three tries before Grandma said 'Better'.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students give the same piece of evidence twice in different words, or mention how many tarts they made.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Evidence: (1) FIRST attempt FAILED (too loose, came apart); (2) it took THREE TRIES before even getting a 'Better' from Grandma.

open_ended_questions.stem: Find the word in paragraph 2 that describes Grandma's fingers and tells us why she was skilled at making ketupat.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: nimble
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students write 'fast' or 'quick' which are synonyms but not the exact word from the passage.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'her NIMBLE fingers weaving the coconut leaves.' NIMBLE = quick, light and skilful with your hands.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on the passage, describe TWO character traits of Grandma with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) WELCOMING: Grandma prepared food and decorations for the whole family before anyone arrived — showing she put effort into making everyone feel celebrated and included. (ii) TRADITIONAL: she insisted on performing the family prayers before the meal, showing she valued keeping cultural and family traditions alive for the next generation.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'caring and hardworking' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: WELCOMING = prepared food and decorations BEFORE anyone arrived. TRADITIONAL = insisted on performing FAMILY PRAYERS before the meal. Name trait + give evidence from passage = full marks.

questions.stem: The volunteer's smile was as ________ as a ray of sunshine — it made even the most worried patient feel a little better.
questions.trap_type: 'Cold','dull','distant' describe unfriendly or dim things. WARM = giving a feeling of comfort and friendliness.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The smile was AS WARM AS a ray of sunshine = comparing its comforting effect to the warmth of sunlight. WARM = giving comfort and friendliness. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is the correct simile form.

questions.stem: The volunteers ________ food and blankets to the flood victims at the relief centre.
questions.trap_type: 'Took away', 'threw away' and 'hid away' all suggest removing or hiding, not distributing to people in need.
questions.learning_tip: HANDED OUT = gave things to many people one by one. Volunteers HAND OUT supplies to those who need them.

questions.stem: The charity volunteers decided to ________ free meals to the elderly residents of the neighbourhood.
questions.trap_type: 'Take away' = remove; 'run away' = flee; 'break down' = stop working. GIVE AWAY = give something to people for free.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: GIVE AWAY = give something to others for free without expecting anything in return. The volunteers GAVE AWAY free meals = they distributed meals at no cost. GIVE + AWAY work together as one meaning.

questions.stem: When Mrs Tan heard that the neighbourhood community raised enough money to fix the elderly man's roof, she was ________ — she helped to organise the effort for weeks.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = trouble; 'at a loss' = confused. OVER THE MOON = extremely happy.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OVER THE MOON = feeling extremely happy. Mrs Tan was OVER THE MOON = overjoyed that the community succeeded. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!

questions.stem: Despite her busy schedule, the doctor ________ time every weekend to visit patients at the elderly home.
questions.trap_type: 'Wasted' and 'lost' suggest time was not used well. 'Made time' = deliberately created time despite being busy.
questions.learning_tip: 'MAKE TIME' = deliberately set aside time for something even when you are busy. The doctor MADE TIME = created space in her schedule to help.

questions.stem: Nobody in our block ________ the elderly Mr Wong better than Mei — she visits him every single week.
questions.trap_type: NOBODY = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Nobody KNOWS Mr Wong better = add -S. 'Nobody know' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.

questions.stem: The community centre has ________ a new befriending programme for lonely elderly residents this month.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. LAUNCH → LAUNCHED (regular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. The centre HAS LAUNCHED a new programme = started recently and now running. LAUNCH → LAUNCHED (regular verb, add -ed).

questions.stem: The volunteers ________ bags of rice when the delivery lorry broke down unexpectedly.
questions.trap_type: 'The lorry broke down' = sudden interrupting event. Volunteers were already loading = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The lorry BROKE DOWN = sudden past event. The volunteers were already in the middle of loading = WERE LOADING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.

questions.stem: A kind word is far ________ than silence when someone is feeling sad and alone.
questions.trap_type: 'Most powerful' = superlative; 'powerfuler' is WRONG. MORE POWERFUL = comparative for long adjectives.
questions.learning_tip: Long adjective (3+ syllables) → MORE + adjective = comparative. MORE POWERFUL THAN silence = comparing a kind word to silence. 'Powerfuler' is ALWAYS WRONG. For long adjectives, always use MORE.

questions.stem: Mei donated her old toys to the children's home ________ she wanted to make them happy.
questions.trap_type: 'So' reverses the order. 'Because' correctly links the action to its reason.
questions.learning_tip: Donated toys BECAUSE she wanted to make them happy. BECAUSE = the reason. The reason comes AFTER 'because'.

questions.stem: Helping others is one of the most rewarding things you can do in life, ________ it?
