questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The roar was AS LOUD AS thunder = comparing the lion's roar to the power of thunder. LOUD = producing great sound. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is the correct simile form — never use an adverb.

questions.stem: The zookeeper ________ fresh fruit and vegetables to the elephants at feeding time every morning.
questions.trap_type: 'Threw away' means discarded. 'Hid' means concealed. Only 'distributed' = handed out to multiple animals.
questions.learning_tip: DISTRIBUTED = gave things out to several people or animals one by one. The zookeeper DISTRIBUTED food to the elephants.

questions.stem: After a long day at the zoo, the children were too tired to ________ and had to be carried to the car.
questions.trap_type: 'Stay on' = remain; 'sit down' = take a seat; 'give up' = stop trying. WALK ON = continue walking forward.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: WALK ON = continue moving forward without stopping. The children were too tired to WALK ON = they could not continue walking. WALK + ON work together as one meaning.

questions.stem: When the baby elephant walked up and touched the little girl's hand with its trunk, she was ________ — it was the best moment of her life.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = in trouble; 'at a loss' = confused. OVER THE MOON = extremely happy.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OVER THE MOON = feeling extremely happy and excited. She was OVER THE MOON = the best feeling of happiness. The moon is so far — being 'over' it means the very highest happiness!

questions.stem: The zoo's ________ programme helped bring the number of endangered rhinos back from very low numbers.
questions.trap_type: 'Destruction' and 'hunting' harm animals. 'Decorating' is irrelevant. Only 'breeding' = a programme to reproduce and increase animal numbers.
questions.learning_tip: BREEDING = producing offspring, especially as part of a conservation programme. A BREEDING programme helps endangered animals reproduce safely.

questions.stem: Nobody in our group ________ a polar bear at a zoo before — this was our very first time.
questions.trap_type: NOBODY = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Nobody SEES = add -S. 'Nobody see' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.

questions.stem: The zoo has ________ a new underwater viewing tunnel for visitors to watch the sea lions swim.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. OPEN → OPENED (regular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. The zoo HAS OPENED a new tunnel = it was completed recently and is now available to visitors. OPEN → OPENED (regular verb).

questions.stem: The monkey ________ from branch to branch when the keeper called it back for feeding time.
questions.trap_type: 'The keeper called it back' = sudden interrupting event. The monkey was already swinging = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The keeper CALLED IT BACK = sudden past event. The monkey was already in the middle of swinging = WAS SWINGING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.

questions.stem: The giraffe enclosure is far ________ than the lion area — you can walk all the way around it in ten minutes.
questions.trap_type: 'Largest' = superlative; 'more larger' is WRONG. LARGER = comparative of 'large'.
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective + -ER = comparative. Large → LARGER. The giraffe enclosure is LARGER THAN the lion area = comparing two areas. 'More larger' is ALWAYS WRONG — never add BOTH 'more' AND '-er'.

questions.stem: We queued for twenty minutes ________ we could watch the sea lion feeding show.
questions.trap_type: 'Because' introduces a past reason. 'So that' introduces a forward-looking purpose — they queued FOR THE PURPOSE of watching the show.
questions.learning_tip: SO THAT = in order to achieve a goal. We queued SO THAT we could watch the show. This shows the purpose of the action.

questions.stem: The penguin feeding show is one of the most popular attractions at the zoo, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive present 'to be' ('is') → negative question tag. IS → isn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present 'to be' → negative tag. The show IS popular, ISN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. IS → ISN'T. Tag questions: match the 'to be' verb of the main clause.

questions.stem: "Look at ________ baby orangutan over there — it is holding on to its mother!" said Jas.
questions.trap_type: 'Baby orangutan' is singular (→ this or that). 'Over there' = far away from the speaker = that.
questions.learning_tip: 'Baby orangutan' = singular → this or that. 'Over there' = the animal is far away = THAT baby orangutan.

questions.stem: The children enjoyed ________ so much that they asked to visit the zoo again the very next weekend.
questions.trap_type: 'The children enjoyed themselves' = reflexive pronoun for third person plural. Students pick 'them' (object) or 'they' (subject).
questions.learning_tip: 'The children enjoyed THEMSELVES' = they had a great time. THEMSELVES is the reflexive pronoun for 'they' (third person plural).

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Prepositions of place and movement)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We arrived (1)________ the zoo entrance at half past nine.' Signal: specific location point = AT. 'Arrived AT the entrance' = AT is used for arrival at a specific place.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' (inside the zoo) or 'on' (surface). AT is correct for a named arrival point.
questions.learning_tip: Use AT for a specific location point: arrived AT the zoo entrance, waited AT the gate. AT shows you are at that exact spot.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The flamingos were standing (2)________ a shallow pool near the entrance.' Signal: inside the pool (enclosed water area) = IN. Animals stand IN water, not ON it.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'on' (surface) instead of 'in' (inside an enclosed space or liquid).
questions.learning_tip: IN = inside an enclosed space or immersed in something. The flamingos stood IN a shallow pool = their legs were inside the water.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We walked (3)________ the winding path that led to the big cat section.' Signal: following the length of a path = ALONG. 'Walked ALONG the path' = followed its direction.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'on' (surface of the path) instead of 'along' (following the path's direction and length).
questions.learning_tip: ALONG = following the line or length of something: walk ALONG a path, walk ALONG the river. It shows movement in the direction of something extended.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We walked (4)________ a glass tunnel where sharks swam above our heads.' Signal: entering one side and exiting the other side of an enclosed space = THROUGH. 'Walked THROUGH a tunnel' = passed inside from one end to the other.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' (inside but not passing through) instead of 'through' (entering and exiting).
questions.learning_tip: THROUGH = enter one side and come out the other: walk THROUGH a tunnel, drive THROUGH a forest. It shows complete passage inside something.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We then walked (5)________ the reptile house without going inside.' Signal: moved beside and beyond a place without entering = PAST. 'Walked PAST the reptile house' = went by it without stopping.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'by' which has a similar meaning but 'past' is more specific for walking by something without entering.
questions.learning_tip: PAST = moved alongside and beyond a place without stopping or entering. We walked PAST the reptile house = we went by it without going in.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'My little brother sat (6)________ me on the bench while we rested.' Signal: next to, at the side of a person = BESIDE. 'Sat BESIDE me' = sat right next to me.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'next' (incomplete — 'next to' needs two words) or 'near' (not in the box). BESIDE = at the side of.
questions.learning_tip: BESIDE = right next to something or someone. My brother sat BESIDE me = he sat right next to me on the same bench.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The zookeeper placed a large watermelon (7)________ the ground for the elephant.' Signal: resting on the surface of the ground = ON. 'Placed ON the ground' = put it on the surface.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' (inside the ground) or 'at' (a specific location point). ON = resting on a surface.
questions.learning_tip: ON = resting on a surface: placed ON the ground, put ON the table. Use ON for things touching the top of a surface.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The elephant picked it up with its trunk and dropped it (8)________ its mouth.' Signal: movement entering an enclosed space = INTO. 'Dropped INTO its mouth' = the watermelon moved and entered the mouth.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' (location inside) instead of 'into' (movement entering). INTO shows the direction of entry.
questions.learning_tip: INTO = movement entering a space: dropped INTO its mouth, jumped INTO the water. INTO shows something moving and entering an enclosed space.

C.passage: Every morning, a zookeeper (1)________ the animals at six o'clock before the zoo opens. Yesterday, she (2)________ the gorillas first, then the flamingos. Right now, she (3)________ the elephant enclosure with fresh water. Last week, a new keeper (4)________ the penguins while the regular keeper was on leave. Later today, the team plans (5)________ the pandas their afternoon bamboo. Sometimes, two keepers (6)________ the large animals like rhinos together for safety. Years ago, the zoo (7)________ only twenty species; now it has over three hundred. This morning, a baby orangutan (8)________ carefully with its mother in the viewing area.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: At the zoo's safari section, we saw animals that live in the wild in Africa. The zebras and giraffes (1)________ freely across a wide open area that looked like their natural (2)________. The zookeeper explained that some of these animals are (3)________ because their numbers in the wild are very low. One of the tigers was in a large (4)________ surrounded by thick glass so visitors could watch it safely. During the visit, we also (5)________ a rare white lion resting in the shade. It was the first time I had ever seen one.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'walked' which is not in the box. ROAMED = wandered freely over a large area.
questions.learning_tip: ROAMED = wandered or moved freely over a wide area. The zebras ROAMED across the open space = moved around freely.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'home' which is not in the box. HABITAT = the natural environment where an animal lives.
questions.learning_tip: HABITAT = the natural environment where a plant or animal normally lives. The savannah is the natural HABITAT of zebras and giraffes.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'their numbers in the wild are very low' = at risk of dying out = endangered.
questions.learning_tip: ENDANGERED = at serious risk of becoming extinct because the population is very low. ENDANGERED animals need protection.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'cage' which is not in the box. ENCLOSURE = a fenced or walled area where animals are kept in a zoo.
questions.learning_tip: An ENCLOSURE = a fenced or walled area in a zoo where animals are kept. The tiger was in a large glass ENCLOSURE.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'saw' which is not in the box. SPOTTED = noticed or caught sight of something, often something rare.
questions.learning_tip: SPOTTED = noticed something, especially something that is rare or hard to find. We SPOTTED a rare white lion = we caught sight of it.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — here (place) vs hear (to listen)
questions.trap_type: 'here' (place) when 'hear' (ears) is needed.
questions.learning_tip: HEAR = detect sound with ears. HERE = at this place. 'We could HEAR the animals' → use ears? YES → HEAR. HEAR = ears. HERE = location.

questions.error_type: Irregular past — go → went (not goed)
questions.trap_type: 'goed' applies the regular -ed rule. GO is irregular: go → went.
questions.learning_tip: GO → WENT (irregular past). NEVER 'goed'. GO changes completely in past tense: go → went. Irregular verbs do not follow the -ed rule.

questions.error_type: Irregular past — find → found (not finded)
questions.trap_type: 'finded' applies the regular -ed rule. FIND is irregular: find → found.
questions.learning_tip: FIND → FOUND (irregular past). NEVER 'finded'. Irregular verbs change completely: find → found, bind → bound, wind → wound. Memorise these.

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the children)
questions.trap_type: 'The children' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! The CHILDREN WERE amazed = CHILDREN is plural → WERE. WAS is only for ONE thing. CHILDREN = plural → WERE.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (zookeepers', not zookeepers's)
questions.trap_type: Students add 's after apostrophe for plural ending in -s.
questions.learning_tip: Plural possessive: add apostrophe AFTER -s! ZOOKEEPERS' guestbook = the book belonging to all the zookeepers. NEVER 'zookeepers's'. Singular: zookeeper's. Plural: zookeepers'. Extra -s after apostrophe = WRONG.

E.passage: Last Saturday, our class visited the city zoo as part of a school excursion. When we arrived, we could here (1) the animals before we could see them. The guide showed us the map and we goed (2) straight to the reptile section first. There, a keeper finded (3) a small gecko hiding behind a rock and showed it to us carefully. The children was (4) amazed by the number of different species in just one enclosure. At the end, we signed the zookeepers's (5) guestbook and left our feedback about the visit.

questions.sentence_a: The zookeeper asked the children a question.
questions.sentence_b: Can you guess what the cheetah eats?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The zookeeper asked...'
questions.model_answer: The zookeeper asked the children if they could guess what the cheetah ate.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if can they guess' (wrong word order) or keep 'you'.
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'Can YOU guess?' → asked IF THEY COULD guess. Pronoun: you → they. Tense: can → could. Word order is normal after 'if'.

questions.sentence_a: The queue for the elephant ride was very long.
questions.sentence_b: We decided to skip it and watch the bird show instead.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'so'.
questions.model_answer: The queue for the elephant ride was very long, so we decided to skip it and watch the bird show instead.
questions.trap_type: Students reverse the clauses, writing 'We decided to skip it so the queue for the elephant ride was very long'.
questions.learning_tip: Long queue = CAUSE. Decided to skip = RESULT. Cause + SO + result. The cause always comes BEFORE 'so'.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Class 3B was on a school trip to the wildlife park. The students were excited, clutching their clipboards and worksheets. Their task was to observe one animal closely and write down three interesting facts about it.

Most students rushed to the lion enclosure or the elephant zone. But ten-year-old Faiz walked quietly to a smaller enclosure at the side. There, lying in the shade of a tall rock, was a cheetah.

The cheetah was asleep. Its spotted coat rose and fell with each slow breath. Faiz sat down on a bench and watched. He did not write anything yet. He just looked.

After ten minutes, the cheetah opened one eye. It looked directly at Faiz. Then it stretched, yawned and curled up again.

Faiz smiled and began to write. He wrote about the cheetah's spotted coat, its long tail that helped it balance when running, and the black lines on its face that looked like tear marks.

'You spent the whole time at one enclosure?' his friend asked after the trip.

'Yes,' said Faiz. 'And I learned more than anyone else today.'

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'not moving at all and very still'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Crouched' = bent down; 'stretched' = extended; 'alert' = watchful and ready. MOTIONLESS = completely still, not moving at all.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: MOTIONLESS = completely without movement. The cheetah was MOTIONLESS = it did not move even a single muscle. MOTION = movement; MOTIONLESS = no movement at all (the suffix -LESS = without).

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'Kira pressed her nose against it and stared'?

options.2: The glass viewing panel of the cheetah enclosure

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 3 thinking 'it' = the camera. But 'pressed her nose against IT and stared' = she was pressing against the glass to look at the cheetah.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'pressed her nose against IT.' What do you press your nose against to look into an enclosure? The GLASS PANEL. IT = the glass viewing panel. Context clue: she stared at the sleeping cheetah through it.

mcq_questions.stem: Why did Kira say 'I think it's dreaming about running' at the end of the passage?

options.1: Because she could see the cheetah's legs moving in its sleep.
options.2: Because she imagined that even a sleeping cheetah's spirit belonged to the wild, where it would run free.
options.3: Because the zookeeper told her cheetahs dream about running.
options.4: Because Kira wanted to make her classmates laugh.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking she saw movement. The sentence is poetic/imaginative — Kira is projecting her idea of the cheetah's inner nature.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: Kira said 'I THINK it's dreaming about running.' This is her IMAGINATION — she sees a wild animal constrained in a zoo and imagines its spirit longing to run free. It is a poetic, empathetic statement, not a factual observation.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Kira visited the zoo many times before? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says it was Kira's first visit to the zoo — she had never seen most of the animals in real life before.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: 'FIRST visit to the zoo.' FIRST = it had never happened before. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did the cheetah do after it opened one eye and looked at Faiz?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: It stretched, yawned and curled up again.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'it went back to sleep' which misses the specific actions described.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: the cheetah 'STRETCHED, YAWNED and CURLED UP again.' Give the specific sequence of actions.

open_ended_questions.stem: What THREE facts did Faiz write about the cheetah? Name any TWO.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) Its spotted coat. (ii) Its long tail that helped it balance when running. (Accept also: the black lines on its face that looked like tear marks.)
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe what the cheetah did (stretched, yawned) instead of the facts Faiz wrote down.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: Faiz wrote about (1) the SPOTTED COAT, (2) the long TAIL that helped it balance, and (3) the black lines like tear marks. Give any two.

open_ended_questions.stem: Find a phrase in paragraph 3 that shows Faiz was observing the cheetah very patiently.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: 'He just looked.'
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students quote 'He sat down on a bench' which describes his position, not his patient observation.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: 'He did not write anything yet. He JUST LOOKED.' This phrase shows he was simply watching patiently without rushing to write.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on her actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Kira with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) OBSERVANT: Kira noticed the sleeping cheetah before anyone else in the group and was the first to press her nose against the glass to look — showing she paid close attention to her surroundings. (ii) IMAGINATIVE: rather than simply noting the cheetah was asleep, she imagined it was dreaming about running — showing a creative and empathetic way of seeing the world.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'curious and kind' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: OBSERVANT = noticed the sleeping cheetah FIRST, pressed nose against glass. IMAGINATIVE = said it was 'dreaming about running' — a creative, empathetic statement. Name trait + evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: The puppy's eyes were as ________ as two shining buttons — black, round and full of life.
questions.trap_type: 'Dull' = lacking light; 'large' = big (but doesn't capture the shining quality); 'rough' = not smooth. BRIGHT = giving off a strong, clear light.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The puppy's eyes were AS BRIGHT AS shining buttons = comparing the sparkle of the eyes to polished buttons. BRIGHT = giving off a clear, strong light. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is the correct simile form.

questions.stem: The vet ________ the injured cat carefully to check for any broken bones.
questions.trap_type: 'Dropped' and 'released' would harm or free the cat. Only 'examined' = looked at and checked carefully.
questions.learning_tip: EXAMINED = looked at something or someone very carefully to find out information. A vet EXAMINES an animal to check its health.

questions.stem: Before going on holiday, Priya asked her neighbour to ________ her goldfish while she was away.
questions.trap_type: 'Give up' = stop trying; 'run away' = flee; 'break into' = enter by force. LOOK AFTER = take care of someone or something.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: LOOK AFTER = take care of someone or something, especially while the owner is away. Priya asked her neighbour to LOOK AFTER her goldfish = keep it fed, alive and safe. LOOK + AFTER work together.

questions.stem: When the vet confirmed that the dog's leg was not broken, the whole family was ________ — they were so worried.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = in trouble; 'at a loss' = confused. OVER THE MOON = extremely happy and relieved.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OVER THE MOON = feeling extremely happy, delighted or relieved. The family was OVER THE MOON = they were overjoyed to hear good news about their pet. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!

questions.stem: The fish tank needed to be kept ________ to keep the tropical fish healthy and active.
questions.trap_type: 'Frozen' = too cold; 'dim' = dark; 'arid' = very dry. Only 'immaculate' = perfectly clean, which is what a fish tank needs.
questions.learning_tip: IMMACULATE = perfectly clean, without any dirt or mess. A fish tank must be kept IMMACULATE so the fish stay healthy.

questions.stem: Nobody in our neighbourhood ________ a pet as well-trained as Scout the golden retriever.
questions.trap_type: NOBODY = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Nobody OWNS = add -S. 'Nobody own' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.

questions.stem: The animal shelter has ________ over two hundred dogs to loving families since it opened last year.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. REHOME → REHOMED (regular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. The shelter HAS REHOMED two hundred dogs = started last year and still going. REHOME → REHOMED (regular verb, add -d).

questions.stem: The dog ________ on its blanket when the doorbell rang and startled it awake.
questions.trap_type: 'The doorbell rang' = sudden interrupting event. The dog was already sleeping = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The doorbell RANG = sudden past event. The dog was already in the middle of sleeping = WAS SLEEPING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.

questions.stem: Priya's cat is much ________ than the vet expected — it ran to the door as soon as they arrived home.
questions.trap_type: 'Most lively' = superlative; 'more livelier' is WRONG. LIVELIER = comparative of 'lively' (ending in -y: change y to i, add -er).
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective ending in -Y → change Y to I, add -ER. Lively → LIVELIER. The cat is LIVELIER THAN expected = comparing current state to expectations. 'More livelier' is ALWAYS WRONG.

questions.stem: The parrot ________ the words it hears so often that it can now say full sentences.
questions.trap_type: 'So often' = a regular habit = simple present. 'The parrot' is singular → repeats.
questions.learning_tip: 'So often' = a regular, habitual action = simple present. The parrot (singular) → REPEATS the words it hears.

questions.stem: Looking after a pet is a big responsibility that requires daily care, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive present simple ('requires') → negative question tag. REQUIRES → doesn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present simple → negative tag. Looking after a pet REQUIRES daily care, DOESN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. Present simple → DOES/DOESN'T. 'Doesn't it' (not 'isn't it' — that is for 'to be').

questions.stem: The vet told Priya ________ her cat twice a day and bring it back in a week.
questions.trap_type: 'Told someone to do something' = reported speech structure: told + object + to + base verb → to medicate.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told someone TO + base verb': told Priya TO MEDICATE her cat. After 'told + object', use the infinitive with 'to'.

questions.stem: The injured bird ________ by a kind student who found it on the playing field.
questions.trap_type: The bird was the receiver of the action (it did not rescue itself). Past passive = was rescued.
questions.learning_tip: The bird did not rescue itself — someone rescued it. Use the PASSIVE: was RESCUED. Passive = was/were + past participle.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Verb forms of 'feed')

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Lily enjoys (1)________ her two goldfish every morning before school.' Signal: 'enjoys + ___' = gerund (verb-ing). Pattern: enjoy + verb-ing → feeding.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'to feed' instead of the gerund after 'enjoys'.
questions.learning_tip: ENJOY + verb-ing: enjoys FEEDING her goldfish. After 'enjoys', always add -ING.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'She (2)________ them exactly the right amount each time so they stay healthy.' Signal: 'each time' = regular habit = simple present. Subject 'She' = singular → feeds.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'feed' (plural form) forgetting that 'She' is singular.
questions.learning_tip: 'Each time' = a regular habit = simple present. She (singular) → FEEDS them the right amount.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Last week, she (3)________ them a little too much and the water turned cloudy.' Signal: 'Last week' = past. 'Feed' is irregular: feed → fed.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'feeded', not knowing 'feed' is irregular.
questions.learning_tip: 'Last week' = past. 'Feed' is irregular: feed → FED. Never write 'feeded'.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'While she (4)________ them one morning, she noticed one fish was not moving.' Signal: 'While she ___' = ongoing background action in the past. Subject 'she' = singular → was feeding. Interrupted by 'she noticed'.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'fed' (simple past) missing the ongoing signal 'while she'.
questions.learning_tip: 'While she ___' = ongoing background past action = past continuous. She WAS FEEDING the fish when she noticed the problem.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Her younger brothers (5)________ the family rabbit in the garden at the same time.' Signal: same past time frame, plural subject 'her younger brothers' + ongoing parallel action → were feeding.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'fed' (simple past) instead of past continuous for an ongoing parallel action.
questions.learning_tip: Her younger brothers = plural. They were doing it at the same past moment = WERE FEEDING (past continuous).

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The vet reminded Lily (6)________ her fish only once a day from then on.' Signal: 'reminded + object + ___' = infinitive. Pattern: remind someone + to + base verb → to feed.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'feeding' instead of the infinitive after 'reminded Lily'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Reminded someone TO + base verb': reminded Lily TO FEED her fish only once a day.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'She says we should never (7)________ pet fish more than they need.' Signal: 'should + ___' = modal verb + base form. Never add -s or -ing after a modal.
questions.trap_type: Students add -s or -ing after the modal verb 'should'.
questions.learning_tip: After modal verbs (should, must, can, will), always use the BASE form: should FEED. Never 'should feeds' or 'should feeding'.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Right now, Lily (8)________ her fish carefully, making sure she gives them just the right amount.' Signal: 'Right now' = present continuous. Subject 'Lily' = singular → is feeding.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'feeds' (simple present habit) missing the 'right now' signal for present continuous.
questions.learning_tip: 'Right now' = present continuous. Lily (singular) → IS FEEDING her fish carefully right now.

C.passage: Lily enjoys (1)________ her two goldfish every morning before school. She (2)________ them exactly the right amount each time so they stay healthy. Last week, she (3)________ them a little too much and the water turned cloudy. While she (4)________ them one morning, she noticed one fish was not moving. Her younger brothers (5)________ the family rabbit in the garden at the same time, so she called out to her mother for help. The vet reminded Lily (6)________ her fish only once a day from then on. She says we should never (7)________ pet fish more than they need, as overfeeding can harm them. Right now, Lily (8)________ her fish carefully, making sure she gives them just the right amount.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Pets bring joy and responsibility into our homes. Every pet needs a balanced (1)________ — the right mix of food for its breed and size. Dogs must be taken for regular (2)________ to keep them fit and give them fresh air each day. Every responsible owner gets their pet (3)________ by a vet at least once a year to check for illness. A pet also needs a warm, safe (4)________ — whether a basket, a cage or a tank — to rest and feel secure. Learning what your pet needs every day is the true meaning of being a (5)________ owner.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'against common dog diseases so he would not fall ill' = given vaccines = vaccinated.
questions.learning_tip: VACCINATED = given a vaccine (an injection) to protect against disease. A dog must be VACCINATED to stay healthy and visit public places.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'if the dog got lost, the vet could scan him' = a tiny chip placed under the skin = microchipped.
questions.learning_tip: MICROCHIPPED = had a tiny electronic chip inserted under the skin. If a pet is lost, a vet can SCAN the microchip to find the owner's details.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'brush' which is not in the box. GROOM = clean and maintain an animal's fur and appearance.
questions.learning_tip: GROOM = clean and tidy an animal's coat, nails and overall appearance. Owners brush their pets to GROOM them.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'follows every command without any fuss' = does what is asked = obedient.
questions.learning_tip: OBEDIENT = does what it is told without argument. A well-trained dog is OBEDIENT and follows its owner's commands.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'loves to cuddle and lick your hand' = shows love and warmth = affectionate.
questions.learning_tip: AFFECTIONATE = showing love and warmth through actions like cuddling and touching. A dog that loves to cuddle is very AFFECTIONATE.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — here (place) vs hear (to listen)
questions.trap_type: 'here' (place) when 'hear' (ears) is needed.
questions.learning_tip: HEAR = detect sound with ears. HERE = at this place. 'We could HEAR the mewing' → use ears? YES → HEAR. HEAR = ears. HERE = location.

questions.error_type: Irregular past — bring → brought (not bringed)
questions.trap_type: 'bringed' applies the regular -ed rule. BRING is irregular: bring → brought.
questions.learning_tip: BRING → BROUGHT (irregular past). NEVER 'bringed'. Irregular verbs change completely: bring → brought, buy → bought, catch → caught. Memorise these.

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — singular subject (the mother cat)
questions.trap_type: 'The mother cat' is singular. Students write 'were' thinking of the kittens.
questions.learning_tip: Singular subject → singular verb! The MOTHER CAT WAS gentle = THE MOTHER CAT is one animal → WAS. Find the main noun: THE MOTHER CAT = singular → WAS, not WERE.

questions.error_type: Adverb required after action verb (held)
questions.trap_type: 'careful' (adjective) after action verb 'held'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (HELD), use an ADVERB. Ben held the kitten CAREFULLY = how did he hold it? CAREFULLY (adverb, -ly). 'Careful' describes nouns; 'carefully' describes HOW the action is done.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (pets', not pets's)
questions.trap_type: Students add 's after apostrophe for plural ending in -s.
questions.learning_tip: Plural possessive: add apostrophe AFTER -s! PETS' journal = the journal for all the pets. NEVER 'pets's'. Singular: pet's. Plural: pets'. Extra -s after apostrophe = WRONG for plural nouns ending in -s.

E.passage: Last week, our neighbour's cat had kittens and we were allowed to visit them. We could here (1) the tiny mewing sounds before we even opened the door. Ben bringed (2) a small blanket to keep the kittens warm during the visit. The mother cat were (3) very gentle but kept a watchful eye on each kitten the whole time. Ben held the smallest kitten careful (4) in both hands so as not to disturb it. Later, he wrote down his thoughts in the pets's (5) observation journal that the vet kept at the clinic.

questions.sentence_a: The vet said to Priya, 'Your rabbit needs more fresh vegetables in its diet.'
questions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using reported speech: The vet told Priya that ________.
questions.model_answer: The vet told Priya that her rabbit needed more fresh vegetables in its diet.
questions.trap_type: Students keep 'your' instead of changing to 'her', or keep 'needs' instead of changing to 'needed' in reported speech.
questions.learning_tip: In reported speech: (1) change 'your' → 'her', (2) change 'needs' → 'needed'. The vet told Priya that HER rabbit NEEDED more fresh vegetables.

questions.sentence_a: The vet asked Priya a question.
questions.sentence_b: Does your rabbit eat fresh vegetables every day?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The vet asked...'
questions.model_answer: The vet asked Priya if her rabbit ate fresh vegetables every day.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if does her rabbit eat' (wrong word order) or keep 'your'.
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'Does YOUR rabbit eat?' → asked IF HER rabbit ATE. Pronoun: your → her. Tense: does eat → ate. Word order is normal after 'if'.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
When Aiden was six years old, his parents brought home a small brown puppy. Aiden named him Scout. From the first day, the two were inseparable. Scout slept at the foot of Aiden's bed and waited by the door every afternoon for him to come home from school.

As Scout grew older, Aiden took on more responsibility. He learned to measure Scout's food carefully, brush his coat every evening and take him for walks even when it was raining. His mother watched quietly and smiled. Her shy, quiet boy was growing more confident every day.

One morning in Aiden's third year of primary school, Scout fell ill. He refused to eat and lay still in his basket with dull, half-closed eyes. Aiden was frightened. He sat beside Scout and stroked his fur gently, whispering, 'You'll be okay.'

At the vet's clinic, the doctor examined Scout and said he had a stomach infection. 'He will need medicine twice a day for five days,' she said.

Aiden gave Scout his medicine every morning and evening without missing a single dose. By the fifth day, Scout was wagging his tail again.

That evening, Aiden hugged Scout tightly. He realised that caring for a pet was not just about the fun parts. It was about being there — even on the hard days.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'moved back and forth with great energy'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Cowered' = crouched in fear; 'leaped' = jumped; 'barked' = made dog sound. WAGGED = moved tail back and forth repeatedly with excitement.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: WAGGED = moved a tail back and forth rapidly, usually showing excitement or happiness. Scout's tail WAGGED = it moved from side to side energetically when Scout was happy.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'Ben could not believe it'?

options.2: That Scout recognised Ben after three whole years apart
options.3: That the vet said Scout was healthy
options.4: The size of Scout's new kennel

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 3 thinking 'it' = health news. But 'Ben could not believe IT' = the incredible moment of Scout recognising him after years.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'Ben could not believe IT.' What was unbelievable? That SCOUT RECOGNISED BEN after THREE YEARS apart. IT = that remarkable reunion moment of being remembered.

mcq_questions.stem: What does 'he grew up, but Scout had not aged' most likely suggest about how Ben felt?

options.1: Ben was happy that Scout was younger than him.
options.2: Ben felt a mix of tenderness and sadness, realising that his childhood bond with Scout still existed even though time had passed.
options.3: Ben was disappointed that Scout was still a puppy.
options.4: Ben felt that Scout did not recognise him because dogs age differently.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 4 thinking the dog didn't recognise him. The sentence is reflective and emotional — Ben is moved by the bond that time cannot break.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: 'he grew up but Scout had not aged' = Ben is moved by the contrast — he is older and changed, but the DOG'S LOVE and RECOGNITION remain unchanged. Option 2 = emotional insight into the lasting bond between boy and dog.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Ben still lived with Scout? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says Ben had not seen Scout for three years because his family moved away — so Scout was left with his grandparents.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: Ben had not seen Scout for THREE YEARS because his family MOVED AWAY. Scout stayed with his grandparents. Ben no longer lived with Scout. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did the vet say was wrong with Scout?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: The vet said Scout had a stomach infection.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he was sick' which is too vague.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'he had a STOMACH INFECTION.' Give the specific diagnosis from the passage.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did Aiden's mother know that caring for Scout was changing Aiden? Give TWO pieces of evidence from paragraph 2.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) Aiden learned to measure Scout's food carefully and brush his coat every evening. (ii) He took Scout for walks even when it was raining, which showed growing responsibility. His mother noticed her shy, quiet boy growing more confident.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe what Aiden did without linking it to the change his mother observed.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: His mother saw Aiden becoming more RESPONSIBLE (measuring food, brushing, walking in rain) and growing more CONFIDENT. Link the actions to the change.

open_ended_questions.stem: How do we know Aiden was a caring and dedicated owner when Scout was ill? Find ONE piece of evidence from paragraphs 4 and 5.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Aiden gave Scout his medicine every morning and evening without missing a single dose.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he took Scout to the vet' which was his parents' action. The question asks about Aiden's own dedication.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: Aiden gave medicine EVERY MORNING AND EVENING WITHOUT MISSING A SINGLE DOSE. This shows dedication — he did not skip once.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on the passage, describe TWO character traits of Ben with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) CARING: when Ben saw Scout after three years, he immediately knelt down and embraced the dog — showing he had not forgotten their bond and still deeply loved his pet. (ii) REFLECTIVE: Ben noticed that 'he grew up, but Scout had not aged' — showing he could think about the passage of time and what their relationship meant.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'loving and sad' without precise traits or textual evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: CARING = immediately embraced Scout, showing lasting love. REFLECTIVE = said 'he grew up but Scout had not aged' = thinking about time, change and their bond. Name trait + evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: On a dark rainy evening, the wet road was as ________ as a mirror — every headlight reflected perfectly on the surface.
questions.trap_type: 'Rough' and 'dull' don't describe a wet reflective surface. 'Dark' = lacking light. SLIPPERY = difficult to walk or drive on without sliding.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The wet road was AS SLIPPERY AS a mirror = comparing how smooth and dangerous the road surface was to a mirror. SLIPPERY = hard to grip; you might slide. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is the correct simile form.

questions.stem: The safety officer reminded the students to ________ their bicycle helmets before riding on the road.
questions.trap_type: 'Remove' is the opposite — it means take off. 'Fasten' = click and secure in place.
questions.learning_tip: FASTEN = click or secure something in place. Always FASTEN your helmet before riding so it stays on and protects your head.

questions.stem: In a fire emergency, it is important to ________ the building immediately and gather at the designated meeting point.
questions.trap_type: 'Stay in' and 'run into' are the opposite of safe behaviour. 'Break into' = enter by force. GET OUT OF = leave a place or situation.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: GET OUT OF = leave a place, especially in an emergency. In a fire, GET OUT OF the building immediately = leave it at once. GET + OUT + OF work together as one meaning.

questions.stem: After the fire drill ended and everyone was found safe and accounted for, the principal was ________ — no one was hurt.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = in trouble; 'down in the dumps' = sad. OVER THE MOON = extremely happy and relieved.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OVER THE MOON = feeling extremely happy and relieved. The principal was OVER THE MOON = overjoyed that everyone was safe. Idioms cannot be understood word by word — the moon has nothing to do with it!

questions.stem: The paramedic acted ________ and reached the scene of the accident within three minutes of the call.
questions.trap_type: 'Leisurely' = slowly and without hurry; 'reluctantly' = unwillingly; 'carelessly' = without attention. Only 'promptly' = quickly and without delay, which is essential in emergencies.
questions.learning_tip: PROMPTLY = quickly and without any delay. In an emergency, paramedics must arrive PROMPTLY so they can help as soon as possible.

questions.stem: Everyone in the fire safety class ________ how important it is to check smoke detectors every month.
questions.trap_type: EVERYONE = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: EVERYONE / NOBODY / SOMEONE = Singular! Everyone KNOWS = add -S. 'Everyone know' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.

questions.stem: The town council has ________ new traffic lights at the busy junction near the school this month.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. INSTALL → INSTALLED (regular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. The council HAS INSTALLED new traffic lights = done recently and now in use. INSTALL → INSTALLED (regular verb, add -ed).

questions.stem: The children ________ on the pavement when a car suddenly swerved onto the kerb.
questions.trap_type: 'The car suddenly swerved' = sudden interrupting event. Children were already walking = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The car SUDDENLY SWERVED = sudden past event. The children were already in the middle of walking = WERE WALKING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.

questions.stem: The new pedestrian crossing is much ________ than the old one — it has flashing lights and a countdown timer.
questions.trap_type: 'Most safe' = superlative; 'more safer' is WRONG. SAFER = comparative of 'safe'.
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective + -ER = comparative. Safe → SAFER. The new crossing is SAFER THAN the old one = comparing two crossings. 'More safer' is ALWAYS WRONG — never add BOTH 'more' AND '-er'.

questions.stem: Always look both ways before crossing ________ you do not get hit by oncoming traffic.
questions.trap_type: 'Because' introduces a past reason. 'So that' introduces a forward-looking purpose — you look both ways FOR THE PURPOSE of not getting hit.
questions.learning_tip: SO THAT = in order to achieve a goal. Look both ways SO THAT you do not get hit — this is the purpose of the action.

questions.stem: Wearing a helmet when cycling can save your life, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive present 'can' → negative question tag. CAN → can't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive modal verb → negative tag. Wearing a helmet CAN save your life, CAN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. Modal 'can' → 'can't'. Match the auxiliary verb of the main clause.

questions.stem: The safety officer told the pupils ________ their phones while crossing the road.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: 'told someone not to do something' = told + object + not to + base verb → not to use.
questions.learning_tip: Negative reported speech: told them NOT TO + base verb. The officer told pupils NOT TO USE their phones while crossing. Always put 'not' before 'to'.

questions.stem: The broken step on the staircase ________ repaired by the building manager last Monday.
questions.trap_type: The step did not repair itself — it was repaired by the manager. Past passive = was repaired.
questions.learning_tip: The step was the receiver of the action. Use the PASSIVE: was REPAIRED. Passive = was/were + past participle. 'Last Monday' = past → was repaired.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Verb forms of 'cross')

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Our teacher reminds us that (1)________ the road safely requires full attention.' Signal: subject of the sentence = gerund as noun. 'Crossing the road' = the subject of the sentence, functioning as a noun (gerund).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'to cross' instead of the gerund used as the subject of the sentence.
questions.learning_tip: A gerund (verb-ing) can act as the SUBJECT of a sentence. CROSSING the road requires full attention — 'crossing' is the subject here.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Every day, our school warden (2)________ the road with the younger students after school.' Signal: 'Every day' = regular habit = simple present. Subject 'our school warden' = singular → crosses.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'cross' (plural form) forgetting that 'our school warden' is singular.
questions.learning_tip: 'Every day' = habit = simple present. Our school warden (singular) → CROSSES the road with the students.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Last Tuesday, my sister and I carefully (3)________ at the pedestrian crossing near our school.' Signal: 'Last Tuesday' = past. 'Cross' is regular: cross → crossed.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'cross' (base form) ignoring the past time signal 'Last Tuesday'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Last Tuesday' = past. 'Cross' is regular: cross → CROSSED.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'While she (4)________ the road, a motorcycle ran through a red light.' Signal: 'While she ___' = ongoing background action in the past. Subject 'she' = singular → was crossing. Interrupted by 'a motorcycle ran through a red light'.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'crossed' (simple past) missing the ongoing background signal 'while she'.
questions.learning_tip: 'While she ___' = ongoing past action = past continuous. She WAS CROSSING the road when the motorcycle ran the red light.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Some other pedestrians (5)________ at the same junction at that moment.' Signal: same past time frame, plural subject 'some other pedestrians' + ongoing parallel action → were crossing.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'crossed' (simple past) instead of past continuous for an ongoing parallel action.
questions.learning_tip: Some other pedestrians = plural. They were doing it at the same past moment = WERE CROSSING (past continuous).

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The warden reminded everyone (6)________ only at the green man signal.' Signal: 'reminded everyone + ___' = infinitive. Pattern: remind someone + to + base verb → to cross.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'crossing' instead of the infinitive after 'reminded everyone'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Reminded everyone TO + base verb': reminded everyone TO CROSS only at the green man signal.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The traffic police say we should always (7)________ at a designated pedestrian crossing.' Signal: 'should + ___' = modal verb + base form. Never add -s or -ing after a modal.
questions.trap_type: Students add -es or -ing after the modal verb 'should'.
questions.learning_tip: After modal verbs (should, must, can, will), always use the BASE form: should CROSS. Never 'should crosses' or 'should crossing'.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Right now, the warden (8)________ the road with a group of Primary One students.' Signal: 'Right now' = present continuous. Subject 'the warden' = singular → is crossing.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'crosses' (simple present habit) missing the 'right now' signal for present continuous.
questions.learning_tip: 'Right now' = present continuous. The warden (singular) → IS CROSSING the road with the students right now.

C.passage: Road safety is everyone's responsibility. Every morning, students (1)________ the road carefully before stepping off the pavement. Yesterday, a young boy nearly (2)________ while chasing a ball into the street. Right now, the lollipop lady (3)________ children across the busy junction near the school. Last term, our class (4)________ a special traffic safety workshop run by the police. Next Friday, the school plans (5)________ the new reflective armbands to all students. Every day, cyclists on our estate (6)________ the cycle path beside the main road. Years ago, drivers (7)________ this road at high speed; now there are speed cameras. At present, council workers (8)________ new road markings near the bus stop.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: At home, safety is just as important as on the road. Every family should know what to do in an (1)________ such as a fire or a gas leak. One important (2)________ is to keep a working fire extinguisher in the kitchen. Cooking oil and some cleaning products are (3)________ — they can catch fire very easily, so they must be stored safely away from heat. The yellow warning signs on these products are there to signal a (4)________ to users. Whenever you handle such products, do so with great (5)________ and always follow the instructions on the label.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'such as a fire or a gas leak' = a sudden serious situation = emergency.
questions.learning_tip: An EMERGENCY = a sudden and serious situation that requires immediate action. A fire or gas leak at home is an EMERGENCY.

questions.trap_type: Students may confuse 'precaution' with 'caution' (blank 5). A PRECAUTION = an action taken in advance to prevent a problem.
questions.learning_tip: A PRECAUTION = an action taken ahead of time to prevent something bad from happening. Keeping a fire extinguisher is a PRECAUTION against fires.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'they can catch fire very easily' = able to catch fire easily = flammable.
questions.learning_tip: FLAMMABLE = easily set on fire. Cooking oil and some chemicals are FLAMMABLE and must be kept away from heat and open flames.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'danger' which is not in the box. HAZARD = a specific risk or source of danger.
questions.learning_tip: A HAZARD = something that can cause danger or harm. Warning signs on products tell users there is a HAZARD — a specific risk to be aware of.

questions.trap_type: Students may confuse 'caution' with 'precaution' (blank 2). CAUTION = care and attention when doing something.
questions.learning_tip: CAUTION = great care and attention, especially when doing something risky. Handle flammable products with CAUTION = be very careful.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — here (place) vs hear (to listen)
questions.trap_type: 'here' (place) when 'hear' (ears) is needed.
questions.learning_tip: HEAR = detect sound with ears. HERE = at this place. 'We could HEAR cars passing' → use ears? YES → HEAR. HEAR = ears. HERE = location.

questions.error_type: Irregular past — run → ran (not runned)
questions.trap_type: 'runned' applies the regular -ed rule. RUN is irregular: run → ran.
questions.learning_tip: RUN → RAN (irregular past). NEVER 'runned'. Irregular verbs do not follow the -ed rule: run → ran, begin → began, swim → swam.

questions.error_type: Adverb required after action verb (cross)
questions.trap_type: 'safe' (adjective) after action verb 'cross'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (CROSS), use an ADVERB. We must always cross SAFELY = how do we cross? SAFELY (adverb, -ly). 'Safe' describes nouns; 'safely' describes HOW the action is done.

questions.error_type: Irregular past — take → took (not taked)
questions.trap_type: 'taked' applies the regular -ed rule. TAKE is irregular: take → took.
questions.learning_tip: TAKE → TOOK (irregular past). NEVER 'taked'. Irregular verbs change completely: take → took, make → made, shake → shook.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (speakers', not speakers's)
questions.trap_type: Students add 's after apostrophe for plural ending in -s.
questions.learning_tip: Plural possessive: add apostrophe AFTER -s! SPEAKERS' slides = the slides belonging to all the speakers. NEVER 'speakers's'. Singular: speaker's. Plural: speakers'. Extra -s after apostrophe = WRONG.

E.passage: Last Wednesday, our school held a road safety workshop for all Primary Three students. The workshop leader asked us to stay quiet — we could here (1) cars passing outside and needed to concentrate. The speaker told us that a child once runned (2) into the road after a ball and was nearly hit. 'Always stop, look and listen,' she said. She explained that road accidents happen because people do not stop to think before crossing — and that we must always be safe (3) whenever we cross. A student then taked (4) a wrong turn during the practice drill and had to be guided back by a teacher. At the end, the speakers's (5) presentation slides were printed and given to each student to take home.

questions.sentence_a: The teacher said to the class, 'Never play near the swimming pool without an adult present.'
questions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using reported speech: The teacher told the class ________.
questions.model_answer: The teacher told the class never to play near the swimming pool without an adult present.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'told the class to never play' (incorrect word order) or keep 'never play' without changing to infinitive form.
questions.learning_tip: Negative reported speech with 'never': told the class NEVER TO PLAY. Change the imperative 'Never play' to 'never to play' in reported speech.

questions.sentence_a: The safety officer asked the students a question.
questions.sentence_b: Do you always look both ways before crossing?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The safety officer asked...'
questions.model_answer: The safety officer asked the students if they always looked both ways before crossing.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if do they always look' (wrong word order) or keep 'you'.
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'Do YOU always look?' → asked IF THEY ALWAYS LOOKED. Pronoun: you → they. Tense: do look → looked. Word order is normal after 'if'.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
It was a bright Tuesday afternoon when eight-year-old Nora noticed something that made her stop in her tracks. An elderly man was trying to cross a busy road, but he looked confused and kept stepping forward and pulling back each time a car went by.

Nora hesitated. She was already late for her piano lesson, and her mother was waiting for her at the community centre just two blocks away. But the sight of the old man struggling made her feel uneasy.

She walked up to him. 'Excuse me, sir. Would you like me to help you cross?' she asked politely.

The old man looked at her with grateful eyes. 'Thank you, child. My eyesight is not very good these days.'

Nora held his arm gently and looked both ways carefully before guiding him across at the pedestrian crossing. On the other side, the old man thanked her warmly and went on his way.

When Nora arrived at the community centre, she explained to her mother what happened. Her mother did not say a single word about the lateness. Instead, she pulled Nora close and said quietly, 'I am very proud of you.'

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 1 has the same meaning as 'came to a complete stop'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Rushed' = moved fast; 'watched' = looked carefully; 'signalled' = gave a sign. HALTED = stopped completely, especially suddenly.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: HALTED = came to a complete, sudden stop. The car HALTED at the red light = it stopped completely. HALT = stop; HALTED = past tense of 'halt'.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 2, what does 'it' refer to in 'Kai knew it was his fault'?

options.2: The fact that he had not looked both ways before cycling out of the driveway
options.3: The red light that was not working

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'it' = the bicycle. But 'IT was his fault' = IT = the accident/situation that happened because he did not check.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'Kai KNEW IT was his fault.' IT = the SITUATION — the near-accident that happened because HE DID NOT LOOK BOTH WAYS before cycling out. It refers to the careless action, not the bicycle.

mcq_questions.stem: Why does the writer describe Kai's heart as 'pounding for a different reason' at the end of the passage?

options.1: Because Kai was still afraid of the driver who nearly hit him.
options.2: Because his heart pounded from relief and the determination never to be careless again.
options.3: Because he was running very fast to get home.
options.4: Because the road safety officer made him nervous.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 3 thinking he was running. 'A different reason' = not fear anymore — but a new emotion: relief and resolve.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: earlier, his heart pounded from FEAR. Now it pounds for 'A DIFFERENT REASON' = RELIEF at being safe, combined with a new DETERMINATION to be more careful. Option 2 = the contrast the writer is drawing between fear and resolve.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Kai was concentrating fully on the road when the car nearly hit him? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says Kai was looking at his phone and not paying attention to the road when the car swerved past him.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: Kai was LOOKING AT HIS PHONE and NOT PAYING ATTENTION to the road. This is why the near-accident happened. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: Why did the elderly man have difficulty crossing the road?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: His eyesight was not very good, so he could not see the traffic clearly.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he was old' which is too general. The passage gives a specific reason.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'My EYESIGHT is not very good these days.' The specific reason is his poor eyesight — not just his age.

open_ended_questions.stem: How do we know Nora crossed the road safely with the elderly man? Give TWO things she did.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) She held his arm gently to guide him. (ii) She looked both ways carefully before crossing at the pedestrian crossing.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe only one action or say 'she helped him' which is too vague.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: (1) she HELD HIS ARM gently and (2) she LOOKED BOTH WAYS carefully before crossing AT THE PEDESTRIAN CROSSING. Two specific safe actions.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did Nora's mother react when Nora arrived late at the community centre?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Her mother did not say a word about the lateness. Instead, she pulled Nora close and said she was very proud of her.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'her mother was angry' which is the opposite of what happened.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Last paragraph: her mother 'did not say a single word about the LATENESS' and instead told Nora she was 'very PROUD' of her. The mother approved, not complained.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Kai with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) RESPONSIBLE: after the near-accident, Kai did not make excuses — he admitted it was his own fault for not looking both ways and for using his phone while cycling. (ii) REFLECTIVE: standing at the kerb, he made a firm decision to always check before crossing in future — showing he could learn from a frightening experience.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'careful and scared' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: RESPONSIBLE = admitted IT WAS HIS FAULT without excuses. REFLECTIVE = made a firm DECISION to change his behaviour. Name trait + give evidence from passage = full marks.

questions.stem: The astronaut floated through the space station as ________ as a feather drifting in still air — weightless and completely silent.
questions.trap_type: 'Heavy','noisy' and 'rigid' describe the opposite of weightless movement. LIGHT = without heaviness.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The astronaut was AS LIGHT AS a feather = comparing weightless movement to a feather floating. LIGHT = without weight. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is the correct simile form — never use an adverb.

questions.stem: Scientists use powerful ________ to study distant stars and galaxies from Earth.
questions.trap_type: 'Microscopes' zoom in on tiny things; 'stethoscopes' are for heartbeats; 'periscopes' are used in submarines. Only 'telescopes' are for viewing distant objects in space.
questions.learning_tip: A TELESCOPE = an instrument that uses lenses to make distant objects appear closer. Scientists use TELESCOPES to study stars and planets far away.

questions.stem: After years of research, scientists finally managed to ________ the mystery of how black holes are formed.
questions.trap_type: 'Ignore' = pay no attention; 'create' = make something new. FIGURE OUT = understand or solve after thinking carefully.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: FIGURE OUT = understand or solve a problem by thinking carefully. Scientists FIGURED OUT the mystery = they worked out the answer after long research. FIGURE + OUT work together.

questions.stem: When Priya finally saw the Milky Way through the telescope, she was ________ — it was more beautiful than she ever imagined.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = in trouble. OVER THE MOON = extremely happy and thrilled.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OVER THE MOON = feeling extremely happy and excited. Priya was OVER THE MOON = she was thrilled beyond words. Idioms cannot be understood word by word — being 'over the moon' means reaching the highest happiness!

questions.stem: Scientists discovered the asteroid was ________ towards Earth at tremendous speed and raised an alert.
questions.trap_type: 'Retreating' means moving away; 'drifting' means moving slowly without direction; 'hovering' means staying in one spot. Only 'hurtling' = moving at great speed in a specific direction.
questions.learning_tip: HURTLING = moving at very great speed in a particular direction, often dangerously. The asteroid was HURTLING towards Earth = racing towards it at tremendous speed.

questions.stem: Nobody in our science class ________ a real meteorite before — the one in the museum was our first.
questions.trap_type: NOBODY = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Nobody TOUCHES = add -S. 'Nobody touch' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.

questions.stem: Scientists have ________ more than five thousand planets outside our solar system since the 1990s.
questions.trap_type: HAVE + past participle = present perfect. DISCOVER → DISCOVERED (regular).
questions.learning_tip: HAVE + past participle = present perfect. Scientists HAVE DISCOVERED five thousand planets = started in the 1990s and still finding more. DISCOVER → DISCOVERED (regular verb, add -ed).

questions.stem: The students ________ through the telescope when the shooting star flashed across the sky.
questions.trap_type: 'The shooting star flashed' = sudden interrupting event. Students were already looking = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The shooting star FLASHED = sudden past event. Students were already looking = WERE LOOKING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when something interrupts.

questions.stem: Jupiter is far ________ than any other planet in our solar system — it is twice the size of all the others combined.
questions.trap_type: 'Largest' = superlative; 'more larger' is WRONG. LARGER = comparative of 'large'.
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective + -ER = comparative. Large → LARGER. Jupiter is LARGER THAN = comparing it to other planets. 'More larger' is ALWAYS WRONG — never add BOTH 'more' AND '-er'. FAR + comparative = much more.

questions.stem: The rocket launched ________ midnight so that scientists could observe it against the dark sky.
questions.trap_type: 'Midnight' is a specific time point. 'In' is for months/years/parts of day; 'on' is for days; 'at' is for specific times including midnight.
questions.learning_tip: Use AT for specific time points: AT midnight, AT noon, AT six o'clock. 'Midnight' is a precise moment → AT midnight.

questions.stem: The moon landing in 1969 was one of the greatest achievements in human history, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive past 'to be' ('was') → negative question tag. WAS → wasn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive past 'to be' → negative tag. The moon landing WAS a great achievement, WASN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE tag. WAS → WASN'T. Past 'to be': was/were → wasn't/weren't.

questions.stem: The space probe ________ by engineers at the control centre when it sent back its first images.
questions.trap_type: The probe did not guide itself — engineers guided it. Past passive = was guided.
questions.learning_tip: The probe was the receiver of the action. Use the PASSIVE: WAS GUIDED. Passive = was/were + past participle. Engineers guided it → it WAS GUIDED by engineers.

questions.stem: The science teacher told her students ________ the positions of the planets before the test next Friday.
questions.trap_type: 'Told someone to do something' = reported speech structure: told + object + to + base verb → to memorise.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told someone TO + base verb': told her students TO MEMORISE the positions. After 'told + object', use the infinitive with 'to'.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Verb forms of 'explore')

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Since she was young, Dr Tan has loved (1)________ the mysteries of outer space.' Signal: 'loved + ___' = gerund (verb-ing). Pattern: love + verb-ing → exploring.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'to explore' instead of the gerund after 'loved'.
questions.learning_tip: LOVE + verb-ing: loved EXPLORING the mysteries of space. After 'loved', always add -ING.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Her team (2)________ new data from the Mars rover every week.' Signal: 'every week' = regular habit = simple present. Subject 'Her team' = singular collective → explores.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'explore' (plural form) forgetting that 'her team' is treated as a singular collective subject.
questions.learning_tip: 'Every week' = habit = simple present. Her team (singular collective) → EXPLORES new data every week.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Last year, the rover (3)________ a deep canyon on the surface of Mars for the first time.' Signal: 'Last year' = past. 'Explore' is regular: explore → explored.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'explore' (base form) ignoring the past signal 'Last year'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Last year' = past. 'Explore' is regular: explore → EXPLORED.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'While the rover (4)________ the canyon floor, it detected an unusual rock formation.' Signal: 'While the rover ___' = ongoing background action in the past. Subject 'the rover' = singular → was exploring. Interrupted by 'it detected'.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'explored' (simple past) missing the ongoing signal 'while the rover'.
questions.learning_tip: 'While the rover ___' = ongoing background past action = past continuous. The rover WAS EXPLORING when it detected the unusual rock.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Two separate probes (5)________ different regions of the planet at the same time.' Signal: same past time frame, plural subject 'two separate probes' + ongoing parallel action → were exploring.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'explored' (simple past) instead of past continuous for an ongoing parallel action.
questions.learning_tip: Two separate probes = plural. They were doing it at the same past moment = WERE EXPLORING (past continuous).

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Scientists hope (6)________ the moons of Jupiter in a future mission.' Signal: 'hope + ___' = infinitive. Pattern: hope + to + base verb → to explore.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'exploring' instead of the infinitive after 'hope'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Hope TO + base verb': hope TO EXPLORE the moons of Jupiter. Use the infinitive after 'hope'.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Dr Tan says humans should (7)________ space with care and respect for its vastness.' Signal: 'should + ___' = modal verb + base form. Never add -s or -ing after a modal.
questions.trap_type: Students add -s or -ing after the modal verb 'should'.
questions.learning_tip: After modal verbs (should, must, can, will), always use the BASE form: should EXPLORE. Never 'should explores' or 'should exploring'.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Right now, the newest rover (8)________ a region near the Martian south pole for signs of frozen water.' Signal: 'Right now' = present continuous. Subject 'the newest rover' = singular → is exploring.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'explores' (simple present habit) missing the 'right now' signal for present continuous.
questions.learning_tip: 'Right now' = present continuous. The newest rover (singular) → IS EXPLORING a region near the Martian south pole.

C.passage: Every child (1)________ about space travel at some point. Priya (2)________ about visiting the Space Station last night. Last year, our class (3)________ the science of stars in an exciting project. Right now, a new rocket (4)________ its way to the outer planets. Last Tuesday, the students (5)________ the rings of Saturn through the school telescope. Next year, the government plans (6)________ a new observatory. Many children were once (7)________ to become astronauts when they grew up. Currently, a team of engineers (8)________ new ways to make space travel more affordable.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Space is vast and full of wonders. Each planet sits in its own (1)________ — a fixed path around the Sun that it follows year after year. Earth's (2)________ is a thin layer of gases that traps heat and makes life possible. The Moon is Earth's only natural (3)________, circling our planet every twenty-eight days. When a space rock crashes into a planet, it leaves a circular hollow called a (4)________. Beyond our solar system lie billions of stars grouped into a (5)________ — a vast spinning structure held together by gravity.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'universe' which is not in the box. A GALAXY = a huge system of billions of stars.
questions.learning_tip: A GALAXY = a system of billions of stars held together by gravity. The Milky Way is the GALAXY that contains our solar system.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'path' which is not in the box. ORBIT = the curved path a planet or moon takes around a star or planet.
questions.learning_tip: An ORBIT = the curved path that a planet, moon or satellite travels around a larger body in space. Earth's ORBIT around the Sun takes 365 days.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'circles our planet' = a natural satellite. Students may write 'moon' but SATELLITE is the precise scientific term used here.
questions.learning_tip: A SATELLITE = an object that orbits a planet. The Moon is a natural SATELLITE of Earth. Man-made satellites are also sent into orbit.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'layer of gases surrounding the planet' = atmosphere. Students may write 'sky' which is not in the box.
questions.learning_tip: ATMOSPHERE = the layer of gases surrounding a planet. Earth's ATMOSPHERE protects us from harmful radiation and provides the air we breathe.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'large bowl-shaped holes made when rocks crashed' = craters. Students may write 'holes' which is not in the box.
questions.learning_tip: A CRATER = a large, bowl-shaped hollow on the surface of a planet or moon, formed when a rock from space crashes into it.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — here (place) vs hear (to listen)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'here' (at this place) when the sentence needs 'hear' (to detect sound with ears).
questions.learning_tip: HEAR = detect sound with ears. HERE = at this place. Test: 'We could HEAR the excitement' → use ears? YES → HEAR. HEAR = ears. HERE = place.

questions.error_type: Spelling — -ing rule: silent -e is dropped, consonant is NOT doubled
questions.trap_type: Students double the 'n' in 'shining', producing 'shinning'. 'Shine' ends in a vowel-consonant-e pattern: drop the -e and add -ing. Do NOT double the final consonant.
questions.learning_tip: 'Shine' ends in vowel-consonant-e (-i-n-e): drop the -e and add -ing → SHINING. Only double the consonant when a SHORT vowel precedes a single consonant (e.g., run → running).

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the stars)
questions.trap_type: 'The stars' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: 'The stars' = plural → WERE visible. WAS is only for singular subjects.

questions.error_type: Irregular plural — consonant + y → drop y, add -ies
questions.trap_type: Students add -s directly to 'discovery', producing 'discoverys'. When a word ends in consonant + y, change y to i and add -es.
questions.learning_tip: 'Discovery' ends in consonant + y → change y to i and add -es: discovery → DISCOVERIES. Same rule: story → stories, city → cities.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (scientists', not scientists's)
questions.trap_type: Students add 's after apostrophe for a plural noun ending in -s.
questions.learning_tip: Plural possessive: add apostrophe AFTER -s! SCIENTISTS' report = belonging to all scientists. NEVER 'scientists's'. Singular: scientist's. Plural: scientists'. Extra -s = WRONG for plural nouns ending in -s.

E.passage: Last Saturday, my family went to a star-gazing event at the science park. We could here (1) the excitement in the crowd as the first telescope was pointed at the moon. The night sky was clear and the stars were shinning (2) brightly in every direction. The stars was (3) so numerous that it was impossible to count them all. A scientist told us about the recent discoverys (4) made by the Mars rovers. At the end, the scientists's (5) report was read aloud before we drove home.

questions.sentence_a: The astronaut asked mission control a question.
questions.sentence_b: Is the shuttle ready for launch?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The astronaut asked...'
questions.model_answer: The astronaut asked if the shuttle was ready for launch.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked if the shuttle is ready' (no tense shift).
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'IS the shuttle ready?' → asked IF the shuttle WAS ready. Tense shifts: is → was. Word order is normal after 'if'.

questions.sentence_a: A team of engineers built the new space telescope.
questions.instruction: Rewrite in the passive voice: The new space telescope ________.
questions.model_answer: The new space telescope was built by a team of engineers.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'The new space telescope built by a team of engineers' — missing the auxiliary verb 'was'.
questions.learning_tip: Passive = subject + WAS/WERE + past participle + by + agent. The new space telescope WAS BUILT BY a team of engineers.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
