Eleven-year-old Priya wanted to be an astronaut from the age of four. Her bedroom ceiling was covered with glow-in-the-dark stars, and her bookshelf held more books about space than about anything else.

One evening, her school organised a visit to the Science Centre for a special planetarium show. Priya arrived thirty minutes early, claiming a seat in the very front row. While the other students chatted and played on their phones, Priya sat perfectly still, staring up at the dark dome above her.

When the show began, the dome lit up with thousands of simulated stars. The narrator explained how stars are born inside giant clouds of gas and dust called nebulae. Priya leaned forward in her seat, her notebook open on her lap. She wrote down every fact, every name and every number.

Afterward, a scientist named Dr Ariff stayed to answer questions. One by one, the other students gave short answers and walked away. But Priya stayed. She asked about the temperature at the core of a star, how long it takes light to travel from the nearest star to Earth and whether any current missions were searching for planets like ours.

Dr Ariff looked at her with a wide smile. 'You know,' he said, 'I have been visiting schools for fifteen years. I have never met a student quite like you.'

Priya did not know what to say. She just looked back up at the dome, which was now dark and still. She smiled quietly to herself.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'completely unable to look away due to fascination'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: TRANSFIXED = unable to look away due to fascination.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: TRANSFIXED = completely held by something so fascinating you cannot look away. TRANSFIXED by the stars = staring, unable to move.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'Priya leaned forward, her notebook open on it'?

options.3: Her lap where the notebook rested

mcq_questions.trap_type: 'It' = the surface the notebook rests on = her lap.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'notebook open on IT.' The notebook is placed on something. IT = her LAP. A detail showing how focused and prepared Priya was.

mcq_questions.stem: Why does the writer say Priya's hand 'shot up immediately' when Dr Ariff asked for questions?

options.2: Priya was so genuinely curious she could not wait to ask.
options.3: Priya was the only student awake.

mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Shot up IMMEDIATELY' = instinctive genuine curiosity, not showing off.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: 'Shot up IMMEDIATELY' + notebook open + transfixed throughout = GENUINE BURNING CURIOSITY. Evidence in the text = the real reason.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Priya visited a planetarium before? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says this was Priya's first visit to the planetarium — she had never seen a show like this before.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: 'FIRST visit to the planetarium.' FIRST = never happened before. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: Name THREE questions that Priya asked Dr Ariff after the show.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: She asked about (i) the temperature at the core of a star, (ii) how long it takes light to travel from the nearest star to Earth, and (iii) whether any current missions were searching for planets like ours.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students name only one or two questions instead of all three.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: Priya asked THREE things — (1) TEMPERATURE at a star's core, (2) how long LIGHT takes to travel from the nearest star, (3) whether missions seek PLANETS like Earth.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did Priya's behaviour during the show differ from that of the other students? Give TWO differences.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) While the other students chatted and played on their phones, Priya sat perfectly still and stared at the dome. (ii) Priya wrote down every fact in her notebook, while the other students did not appear to take any notes.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students give the same difference twice in different words.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: students chatted and used phones; Priya sat STILL and stared. Paragraph 3: Priya wrote in her NOTEBOOK; no mention of others doing the same. Two clear differences.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did Dr Ariff mean when he said 'I have never met a student quite like you'?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: He meant that Priya was exceptional — her deep curiosity, focused attention and intelligent questions were unlike anything in his fifteen years of visiting schools.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he thought she was good' which is too vague.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Dr Ariff visited schools for FIFTEEN YEARS and never met anyone like Priya. He means she was truly EXCEPTIONAL in her curiosity and the depth of her questions — not just 'good'.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on her actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Priya with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) CURIOUS: Priya kept a notebook open during the show and immediately raised her hand for questions — showing a deep, genuine desire to learn more. (ii) FOCUSED: while others chatted and used phones, Priya sat still and stared at the dome, not distracted by anything around her.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'smart and excited' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: CURIOUS = notebook open, hand shot up immediately. FOCUSED = sat still, stared at dome, ignored distractions. Name trait + evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: The freshly painted mural was as ________ as a sunset — brilliant reds, golds and blues stretching from one end of the wall to the other.
questions.trap_type: 'Dull' = lacking colour (opposite); 'small' = limited size; 'rough' = not smooth. COLOURFUL = having many bright, vivid colours.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The mural was AS COLOURFUL AS a sunset = comparing its vivid colours to a spectacular sunset. COLOURFUL = having many bright, vivid colours. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is the correct simile form.

questions.stem: The sculptor used a small knife to ________ a horse from a block of wood.
questions.trap_type: 'Pour' is for liquids; 'scatter' means to spread things; 'assemble' means to put parts together. Only 'carve' = cut a shape from a solid material.
questions.learning_tip: CARVE = cut into a solid material like wood or stone to create a shape. A sculptor CARVES figures out of wood or marble.

questions.stem: In the middle of painting, Mei realised she had ________ blue paint and had to mix more from scratch.
questions.trap_type: 'Given away' = given for free; 'looked after' = cared for; 'put away' = stored. RUN OUT OF = used up all of something so none remained.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: RUN OUT OF = use up all of something so there is none left. Mei RAN OUT OF blue paint = she used every last drop. RUN + OUT + OF work together as one meaning — never separate them.

questions.stem: When Omar's painting won first place, he was ________ — it was the proudest moment of his school life.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = feeling ill; 'in hot water' = in trouble. ON CLOUD NINE = feeling extremely happy and delighted.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: ON CLOUD NINE = feeling extremely happy and elated. Omar was ON CLOUD NINE = he felt wonderful when he won. There is no actual cloud — it means the highest possible level of happiness!

questions.stem: The painting was so ________ in colour and detail that it looked almost like a real photograph.
questions.trap_type: 'Dull', 'faded' and 'blurred' all suggest poor colour or lack of clarity. Only 'vivid' = bright, strong and very clear.
questions.learning_tip: VIVID = very bright, strong and clear in colour or detail. A VIVID painting has rich, striking colours that make it look almost real.

questions.stem: Everyone in the art class ________ a different style of brush stroke for the shading exercise.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'try'. EVERYONE = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: EVERYONE / NOBODY / SOMEONE = Singular! Always use verb+S. Everyone TRIES = add -S. 'Everyone try' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.

questions.stem: Our school has ________ a new art studio this term, with proper easels and professional brushes.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. OPEN → OPENED (regular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. The school HAS OPENED a new studio = it was done recently and the studio is now available. OPEN → OPENED (add -ed for regular verbs).

questions.stem: The potter ________ the clay on the wheel when the electricity suddenly went out.
questions.trap_type: 'The electricity went out' = sudden interrupting event. The potter was already shaping = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The electricity WENT OUT = sudden past event. The potter was already in the middle of shaping = WAS SHAPING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.

questions.stem: Mei's watercolour painting was far ________ than any work she had produced before — the colours blended perfectly.
questions.trap_type: 'Most beautiful' = superlative; 'beautifuler' is WRONG. MORE BEAUTIFUL = comparative of long adjective.
questions.learning_tip: Long adjective (3+ syllables) → MORE + adjective = comparative. MORE BEAUTIFUL THAN = comparing this painting to her earlier work. 'Beautifuler' is ALWAYS WRONG. FAR + MORE = much more beautiful.

questions.stem: The winning artwork was displayed ________ the main entrance so that all visitors could see it.
questions.trap_type: 'In the entrance' suggests inside an enclosed space; 'on' is for surfaces; 'at' is correct for a specific location point.
questions.learning_tip: AT = at a specific location point: displayed AT the main entrance, waited AT the gate. AT shows you are at that named spot.

questions.stem: The school art competition is held every year in November, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive present 'to be' ('is held') → negative question tag. 'Is' → isn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present 'to be' → negative tag. The competition IS held every year, ISN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. IS → ISN'T. Remember: use 'to be' tags for passive sentences too (is held → isn't it).

questions.stem: The mural ________ by a group of student volunteers over the course of three weekends.
questions.trap_type: The mural did not paint itself — volunteers painted it. Past passive = was painted.
questions.learning_tip: The mural was the receiver of the action. Use the PASSIVE: WAS PAINTED. Passive = was/were + past participle.

questions.stem: The art teacher told the class ________ their brushes in the wrong container.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: 'told someone not to do something' = told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: Negative reported speech: told them NOT TO + base verb. The teacher told the class NOT TO LEAVE their brushes in the wrong container.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Verb forms of 'paint')

questions.context_check: Passage: 'My grandfather enjoys (1)________ landscapes in his spare time.' Signal: 'enjoys + ___' = gerund (verb-ing). Pattern: enjoy + verb-ing → painting.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'to paint' instead of the gerund after 'enjoys'.
questions.learning_tip: ENJOY + verb-ing: enjoys PAINTING landscapes. After 'enjoys', always add -ING.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'He (2)________ at least one new picture every month without fail.' Signal: 'every month' = regular habit = simple present. Subject 'He' = singular → paints.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'paint' (plural form) forgetting that 'He' is singular.
questions.learning_tip: 'Every month' = habit = simple present. He (singular) → PAINTS at least one new picture.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Last summer, he (3)________ a large mural on the wall of our community centre.' Signal: 'Last summer' = past. 'Paint' is regular: paint → painted.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'paint' (base form) ignoring the past signal 'Last summer'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Last summer' = past. 'Paint' is regular: paint → PAINTED.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'While he (4)________ the upper section of the mural, a sudden rain shower forced him to stop.' Signal: 'While he ___' = ongoing background action in the past. Subject 'he' = singular → was painting. Interrupted by 'a sudden rain shower forced him to stop'.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'painted' (simple past) missing the ongoing signal 'while he'.
questions.learning_tip: 'While he ___' = ongoing background past action = past continuous. He WAS PAINTING the upper section when the rain shower came.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Two of his friends (5)________ the lower section at the same time to help him finish faster.' Signal: same past time frame, plural subject 'two of his friends' + ongoing parallel action → were painting.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'painted' (simple past) instead of past continuous for an ongoing parallel action.
questions.learning_tip: Two of his friends = plural. They were doing it at the same past moment = WERE PAINTING (past continuous).

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Grandfather always wanted (6)________ a mural that the whole neighbourhood could enjoy.' Signal: 'wanted + ___' = infinitive. Pattern: want + to + base verb → to paint.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'painting' instead of the infinitive after 'wanted'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Want TO + base verb': wanted TO PAINT a mural the neighbourhood could enjoy. Always use the infinitive after 'wanted'.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'He says anyone can (7)________ if they are willing to practise and be patient.' Signal: 'can + ___' = modal verb + base form. Never add -s or -ing after a modal.
questions.trap_type: Students add -s or -ing after the modal verb 'can'.
questions.learning_tip: After modal verbs (can, should, must, will), always use the BASE form: can PAINT. Never 'can paints' or 'can painting'.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Right now, Grandfather (8)________ a sunset scene on a fresh canvas in the garden.' Signal: 'Right now' = present continuous. Subject 'Grandfather' = singular → is painting.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'paints' (simple present habit) missing the 'right now' signal for present continuous.
questions.learning_tip: 'Right now' = present continuous. Grandfather (singular) → IS PAINTING a sunset scene right now.

C.passage: My grandfather enjoys (1)________ landscapes in his spare time. He (2)________ at least one new picture every month without fail. Last summer, he (3)________ a large mural on the wall of our community centre. While he (4)________ the upper section of the mural, a sudden rain shower forced him to stop for the day. Two of his friends (5)________ the lower section at the same time to help him finish faster. Grandfather always wanted (6)________ a mural that the whole neighbourhood could enjoy and be proud of. He says anyone can (7)________ if they are willing to practise and be patient. Right now, Grandfather (8)________ a sunset scene on a fresh canvas in the garden.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Art can take many forms. A (1)________ is a piece of cloth that artists stretch over a frame and paint on. Before painting, an artist usually makes a (2)________ — a quick pencil drawing to plan the image. Finding (3)________ — a spark of creativity — can be the hardest part of the creative process. The (4)________ of a surface describes how rough, smooth, bumpy or soft it feels to the touch. When an artist has enough work, they may organise an (5)________ — a public display where people can view and buy their pieces.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'drawing' which is not in the box. A SKETCH = a rough, quick drawing used to plan a final artwork.
questions.learning_tip: A SKETCH = a rough, quick drawing used to plan the layout of a final artwork. Artists SKETCH their ideas in pencil before painting.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'paper' which is not in the box. A CANVAS = a woven fabric stretched over a frame, used for painting.
questions.learning_tip: A CANVAS = a piece of woven fabric stretched tightly over a wooden frame. Most oil and acrylic paintings are done on a CANVAS.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'how the surface feels — smooth, rough or bumpy' = texture. Students may write 'surface' which is not in the box.
questions.learning_tip: TEXTURE = the feel or appearance of a surface — whether it is smooth, rough, bumpy or soft. The TEXTURE of a painting affects how it looks under different lighting.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'find their ___' from unexpected places = the idea or motivation to create = inspiration.
questions.learning_tip: INSPIRATION = a feeling of enthusiasm and the desire to create something. Artists find INSPIRATION in nature, people and everyday surroundings.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'show' which is not in the box. An EXHIBITION = a public display of artworks for people to view.
questions.learning_tip: An EXHIBITION = a public display of artworks, photographs or other items. Artists hold EXHIBITIONS so the public can view their work.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — no (negative) vs know (to have knowledge)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'no' (negative/zero) when the sentence needs 'know' (to have knowledge).
questions.learning_tip: KNOW = to have knowledge or understanding. NO = not any / negative answer. 'Difficult to NO where to begin' → can you say 'to have knowledge where to begin'? YES → KNOW. KNOW = knowledge. NO = negative.

questions.error_type: Spelling — -ing rule: silent -e is dropped before -ing
questions.trap_type: Students keep the final -e when adding -ing to 'glue', producing 'glueing'. The rule is: drop the silent -e before adding -ing.
questions.learning_tip: 'Glue' ends in silent -e: drop the -e before adding -ing → GLUING. Same rule: make → making, hope → hoping, come → coming.

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the colours)
questions.trap_type: 'The colours' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: 'The colours' = plural → WERE so bright. WAS is only for singular subjects.

questions.error_type: Irregular plural — leaf → leaves (f/fe → ves)
questions.trap_type: Students add -s directly to 'leaf', producing 'leafs'. Words ending in -f or -fe often change to -ves in the plural.
questions.learning_tip: 'Leaf' follows the -f → -ves rule: leaf → LEAVES. Same pattern: knife → knives, half → halves, scarf → scarves.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (students', not students's)
questions.trap_type: Students add 's after the apostrophe for a plural noun ending in -s.
questions.learning_tip: Plural possessive: just add apostrophe AFTER the -s! The STUDENTS' paintings = the paintings belonging to all students. NEVER 'students's'. Singular: student's. Plural: students'. Extra -s after apostrophe = WRONG for plurals ending in -s.

E.passage: Last Thursday, our class worked on a collaborative mural in the school hall. It is always difficult to no (1) where to begin when you face a blank wall. One student accidentally split the glue while glueing (2) tiny pieces of tissue paper onto the canvas. The art supplies was (3) arranged neatly on the tables before the lesson began. Some students stuck real leafs (4) onto their work to add a natural texture. The students's (5) paintings were displayed along the corridor for the whole school to enjoy.

questions.sentence_a: You mix yellow and blue paint.
questions.sentence_b: You get green.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'If'.
questions.model_answer: If you mix yellow and blue paint, you get green.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'If you will mix yellow and blue paint, you will get green' — adding 'will' in the 'if' clause, which is incorrect in first conditional.
questions.learning_tip: In an 'If' sentence stating a general truth: IF + simple present, simple present. If you MIX yellow and blue, you GET green. Never use 'will' in the 'if' clause for general facts.

questions.sentence_a: The art teacher asked the class a question.
questions.sentence_b: Have you ever mixed your own colours?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The art teacher asked...'
questions.model_answer: The art teacher asked the class if they had ever mixed their own colours.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked the class if have they ever mixed' (wrong word order) or keep 'you' instead of changing to 'they'.
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'Have YOU ever mixed?' → asked IF THEY had ever mixed. Pronoun: you → they. Tense: have → had. Word order is NORMAL after 'if' — no inversion.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Every Thursday after school, twelve-year-old Omar went to the community art room. He went every Thursday for six months, but he never finished a single painting. He would start boldly — choosing the brightest colours, sweeping the brush across the canvas in long strokes — and then, halfway through, he would stop. Something always felt wrong.

'It doesn't look right,' he would mutter, and leave the half-finished canvas on the shelf.

The art teacher, Mrs Yip, noticed. One day, she placed a fresh canvas in front of Omar and sat down beside him.

'Why do you always stop?' she asked.

'Because it never looks the way I imagine it,' he said quietly.

Mrs Yip nodded slowly. 'That feeling,' she said, 'means you have a real eye for art. The gap between what you imagine and what you can do is exactly where improvement lives.'

Omar looked at the blank canvas. 'So I should keep going even when it looks wrong?'

'Especially then,' said Mrs Yip.

That afternoon, Omar started a painting of the view from the art room window. He painted past the point where he usually stopped. The result was not perfect. But for the first time, he had a finished painting — and it was his.

He looked at it for a long time. Then he picked up his brush and started another one.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'not satisfied with something because it is not as good as you hoped'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Distracted' = unable to focus; 'determined' = resolved; 'discouraged' = lost confidence. DISSATISFIED = not pleased because something did not meet your expectations.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: DISSATISFIED = not satisfied; not happy with the result because it does not match what you hoped for. Omar was DISSATISFIED = his painting never looked as good as the picture in his mind. DIS- = a prefix meaning 'not'.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 4, what does 'it' refer to in 'he finally let it dry and stepped back to look'?

options.2: The window he was looking at
options.3: The painting he had just completed of the view from the art room

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'it' = the paintbrush. But 'let IT dry' = wait for the WET PAINTING to dry.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'let IT dry' — what needs to dry? A wet PAINTING. IT = the painting Omar just completed of the view from the art room window. You let paint dry — not a paintbrush.

mcq_questions.stem: Why did Omar immediately start another painting at the end of the passage?

options.1: Because Mrs Yip told him to paint more.
options.2: Because he wanted to finish his homework quickly.
options.3: Because finishing one painting made him want to keep improving and create more.
options.4: Because he was not happy with his first painting.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 4 thinking he was unhappy. The ending is positive — he looked at the painting for a long time, then picked up his brush again.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: He 'looked at it for a LONG TIME, then picked up his brush.' This is a positive moment — completing one work inspired him to create another. Option 3 = the passage implies growth, not dissatisfaction.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Omar gave up on his paintings before finishing them? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: True. The passage says Omar always stopped halfway through — he never finished a single painting before Mrs Yip spoke to him.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'False, he kept going.' The passage clearly says he always stopped halfway.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: 'He always STOPPED HALFWAY through.' This means he never completed a painting. Answer is TRUE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did Omar do at the very end of the passage?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: He looked at his finished painting for a long time, then picked up his brush and started another one.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he was happy with his painting' which misses the specific action at the very end.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Last paragraph: 'he picked up his BRUSH and started ANOTHER one.' The specific action is that he immediately started a new painting.

open_ended_questions.stem: How do we know Omar cared deeply about his art even before Mrs Yip spoke to him? Give TWO pieces of evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) He came to the art room every Thursday for six months without stopping. (ii) He always started boldly with bright colours and long strokes, showing enthusiasm, but stopped when it did not meet his high standards.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he tried hard' which is too general. Must use specific evidence from the passage.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Evidence: (1) he came EVERY THURSDAY for SIX MONTHS = commitment; (2) he started BOLDLY with bright colours each time but STOPPED when it looked wrong = high personal standards, not lack of care.

open_ended_questions.stem: In paragraph 6, Mrs Yip said 'That feeling means you have a real eye for art.' What does 'that feeling' refer to?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: 'That feeling' refers to Omar's dissatisfaction when his painting did not match the picture in his imagination.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'that feeling means he is good at art' which misses what the feeling actually is.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Mrs Yip is referring to the feeling Omar described in paragraph 5: the frustration when 'it never looks the way I IMAGINE IT.' 'That feeling' = DISSATISFACTION with the gap between imagination and result.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Omar with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) PASSIONATE: Omar came to the art room every Thursday for six months — even before Mrs Yip spoke to him, showing he truly loved art and kept returning despite his frustration. (ii) RESILIENT: after Mrs Yip's advice, he pushed through his feelings of dissatisfaction and completed his first painting, then immediately started another.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'hardworking and brave' without precise trait names or textual evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: PASSIONATE = came to art room for SIX MONTHS — shows love for art. RESILIENT = pushed through frustration, completed the painting, then STARTED ANOTHER. Name trait + evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: When the orchestra played the opening note together, the sound was as ________ as a clap of thunder — powerful and unexpected.
questions.trap_type: 'Soft' and 'quiet' are opposites of thunder's sound. 'Distant' = far away. LOUD = producing a lot of sound.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The sound was AS LOUD AS thunder = comparing the orchestra's opening to the power of thunder. LOUD = producing strong, powerful sound. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is always the correct simile form.

questions.stem: The young violinist practised her piece until she could play it without looking at the ________.
questions.trap_type: 'Instrument' is what she plays; 'curtain' and 'spotlight' are stage elements. Only 'score' = the written sheet of music a musician reads.
questions.learning_tip: A SCORE = the written or printed music that a musician reads while playing. Playing without the SCORE means playing entirely from memory.

questions.stem: After months of practice, Jamal finally felt ready to ________ at the school concert without any nerves.
questions.trap_type: 'Give away' = give for free; 'run away' = flee; 'break down' = stop working. SHOW OFF = perform or display a skill to impress others.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: SHOW OFF = display a skill or talent to impress people. Jamal wanted to SHOW OFF his piano skills = perform and let everyone see what he could do. SHOW + OFF work together as one meaning.

questions.stem: When the audience gave a standing ovation after his performance, Jamal was ________ — all the months of hard practice were worth it.
questions.trap_type: 'Under the weather' = ill; 'in hot water' = in trouble; 'at a loss' = confused. ON CLOUD NINE = extremely happy and thrilled.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: ON CLOUD NINE = feeling extremely happy, as if floating on the highest cloud. Jamal was ON CLOUD NINE = he was overjoyed by the standing ovation. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!

questions.stem: The guitarist ________ a new melody during the break, which later became the band's most popular song.
questions.trap_type: 'Demolished' means destroyed; 'repeated' means played again; 'downloaded' is a digital action. Only 'composed' = created original music.
questions.learning_tip: COMPOSED = created an original piece of music. The guitarist COMPOSED a new melody = he created it from scratch.

questions.stem: Nobody in the school orchestra ________ as many hours of practice as Jamal — he rehearses every single day.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'put'. NOBODY = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Nobody PUTS in as many hours = add -S. 'Nobody put' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.

questions.stem: The school band has ________ the same song for this year's concert as they performed last year.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. CHOOSE → CHOSEN (irregular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. The band HAS CHOSEN the same song = they decided recently and the choice stands now. CHOOSE → CHOSEN (irregular past participle).

questions.stem: Jamal ________ the final movement when he suddenly hit the wrong key in front of the audience.
questions.trap_type: 'Suddenly hit the wrong key' = sudden interrupting event. Jamal was already playing = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: He SUDDENLY HIT the wrong key = sudden past event. Jamal was already in the middle of playing = WAS PLAYING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when something interrupts.

questions.stem: The new concert hall is much ________ than the old assembly room — it holds three times as many audience members.
questions.trap_type: 'Largest' = superlative; 'more larger' is WRONG. LARGER = comparative of 'large'.
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective + -ER = comparative. Large → LARGER. The new hall is LARGER THAN the old room = comparing two places. 'More larger' is ALWAYS WRONG — never add BOTH 'more' AND '-er'.

questions.stem: The musicians rehearsed ________ the stage before the evening show started.
questions.trap_type: 'In' suggests enclosed space; 'at' is for a location point; 'over' = above. Only 'on' = on the surface of the stage where performers stand.
questions.learning_tip: ON = on the surface of something: rehearsed ON the stage, stood ON the platform. Performers work ON a stage, not 'in' it.

questions.stem: The audience thoroughly enjoyed the performance last Friday evening, ________ they?
questions.trap_type: Positive past simple ('enjoyed') → negative question tag. 'Enjoyed' → didn't they.
questions.learning_tip: Positive past simple → negative tag. The audience ENJOYED the performance, DIDN'T they? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE. Past simple regular verb → DID/DIDN'T. ENJOYED → DIDN'T they (not 'weren't' — that is for 'to be').

questions.stem: The solo performance ________ by the youngest member of the orchestra last Saturday night.
questions.trap_type: The performance did not give itself — the youngest member gave it. Past passive = was given.
questions.learning_tip: The performance was the receiver of the action. Use the PASSIVE: WAS GIVEN. Passive = was/were + past participle. 'Last Saturday night' = past.

questions.stem: The music teacher told the students ________ their instruments before leaving the music room.
questions.trap_type: 'Told someone to do something' = reported speech: told + object + to + base verb → to put away.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told someone TO + base verb': told the students TO PUT AWAY their instruments. After 'told + object', use the infinitive with 'to'.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Personal pronouns — subject, object and possessive)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Maya has played the piano since (1)________ was five years old.' Signal: blank = SUBJECT of 'was'. Maya = female = she (third person singular female subject pronoun).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'her' (object form) instead of 'she' (subject form).
questions.learning_tip: The blank is the SUBJECT of 'was'. Maya = female = SHE. 'Her was five' is wrong.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Last year, (2)________ teacher entered her in the school talent show.' Signal: blank = BEFORE the noun 'teacher' = possessive adjective. Maya = female = her (third person singular female possessive adjective).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'she' (subject pronoun) instead of 'her' (possessive adjective before a noun).
questions.learning_tip: Before 'teacher' (a noun), use a POSSESSIVE ADJECTIVE: HER teacher. 'She teacher' is wrong.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The audience watched (3)________ perform an original piece alongside Maya without any mistakes.' Signal: blank = OBJECT of 'watched'. Refers to Raju = male = him (third person singular male object pronoun).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'he' (subject form) instead of 'him' (object form after a verb).
questions.learning_tip: After the verb 'watched', use the OBJECT pronoun: watched HIM perform. 'Watched he' is wrong.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'On stage beside her was Raju, the guitarist. (4)________ tuned his guitar just before the performance began.' Signal: blank = SUBJECT of 'tuned'. Raju = male = he (third person singular male subject pronoun).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'his' (possessive) instead of 'he' (subject pronoun).
questions.learning_tip: Raju is the SUBJECT of 'tuned'. Raju = male = HE tuned his guitar. 'His tuned' is wrong.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(5)________ guitar playing added warmth to the performance.' Signal: blank = BEFORE the noun 'guitar playing' = possessive adjective. Raju = male = his (third person singular male possessive adjective).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'he' (subject pronoun) instead of 'his' (possessive adjective before a noun).
questions.learning_tip: Before 'guitar playing' (a noun phrase), use a POSSESSIVE ADJECTIVE: HIS guitar playing. 'He guitar playing' is wrong.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'When the two performers took their final bow, (6)________ received a standing ovation.' Signal: blank = SUBJECT of 'received'. Maya and Raju = two people = plural = they (third person plural subject pronoun).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'them' (object form) instead of 'they' (subject form).
questions.learning_tip: Maya and Raju = two people = THEY received a standing ovation. THEY is the subject pronoun for a group. 'Them received' is wrong.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The principal congratulated (7)________ on stage in front of the whole school.' Signal: blank = OBJECT of 'congratulated'. Maya and Raju = them (third person plural object pronoun).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'they' (subject form) instead of 'them' (object form after a verb).
questions.learning_tip: After the verb 'congratulated', use the OBJECT pronoun: congratulated THEM. 'Congratulated they' is wrong.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Maya and Raju said (8)________ performance was the proudest moment of their lives.' Signal: blank = BEFORE the noun 'performance' = possessive adjective. Maya and Raju = plural = their (third person plural possessive adjective).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'they' (subject) or 'them' (object) instead of 'their' (possessive adjective before a noun).
questions.learning_tip: Before 'performance' (a noun), use a POSSESSIVE ADJECTIVE: THEIR performance. 'They performance' and 'them performance' are both wrong.

C.passage: Maya has played the piano since (1)________ was five years old. Last year, (2)________ teacher entered her in the school talent show. The audience watched (3)________ perform an original piece alongside Maya without any mistakes. On stage beside her was Raju, the guitarist. (4)________ tuned his guitar just before the performance began. (5)________ guitar playing added warmth and depth to Maya's piano melodies. When the two performers took their final bow, (6)________ received a standing ovation from the whole school. The principal congratulated (7)________ on stage in front of everyone. Maya and Raju said (8)________ performance was the proudest moment of their lives so far.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Our school held its annual concert last Friday evening. Every class had (1)________ at least one song or dance piece on the stage in front of parents and guests. The weeks before the concert were full of hard work — the choir went through (2)________ after (3)________ in the school hall, making sure every note and movement was in place. When the choir finally sang together, their voices blended in perfect (4)________ that filled the hall with a warm and rich sound. During the final (5)________, all sixty singers joined their voices as one, and many parents felt deeply moved.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'shown' or 'done' which are not in the box. PERFORMED = took part in a public performance on stage.
questions.learning_tip: PERFORMED = took part in a performance in front of an audience. Every class PERFORMED at least one piece on stage.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'the weeks before the concert' and 'making sure every note was in place' = a rehearsal = a practice session before a performance.
questions.learning_tip: A REHEARSAL = a practice session before a public performance. The choir attended many REHEARSALS to prepare for the concert.

questions.trap_type: 'Rehearsal after rehearsal' = the word is used twice in the same phrase to show repetition. Both blanks 2 and 3 use the same word.
questions.learning_tip: 'Rehearsal after REHEARSAL' = one practice session after another, repeatedly. This shows how many times they practised before the concert.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'tune' which is not in the box. HARMONY = the pleasing combination of different musical notes sung or played together.
questions.learning_tip: HARMONY = different notes sung or played at the same time that sound pleasing together. A choir sings in perfect HARMONY when all voices blend well.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'verse' which is not in the box. A CHORUS = the repeated section of a song that all performers sing together.
questions.learning_tip: A CHORUS = the part of a song where all performers join in and sing together, usually the most memorable and repeated section.

sections.D_note: Note: word_box has 5 words but 'rehearsal' is used twice in blanks 2 and 3 — both are intentional (rehearsal after rehearsal). The word_box below lists it once but the passage and model require it in both blanks. This is an intentional design where the repeated word tests whether students recognise the phrase structure.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — here (place) vs hear (to listen)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'here' (at this place) when the sentence needs 'hear' (to detect sound with ears).
questions.learning_tip: HEAR = detect sound with ears. HERE = at this place. Test: 'you could HEAR the audience' → can you use your ears to detect this? YES → HEAR. HERE means 'at this location' — that does not fit. HEAR = ears. HERE = location.

questions.error_type: Irregular plural — piano → pianos (not pianoes)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'pianoes' following the rule for words ending in -o (e.g. tomatoes). But PIANO is a foreign/musical word that just adds -s.
questions.learning_tip: Most words ending in -O from foreign languages just add -S: piano → PIANOS, photo → PHOTOS, solo → SOLOS, radio → RADIOS. NEVER 'pianoes'. The -OES rule applies to native words like tomato, potato, hero.

questions.error_type: Spelling — beautifully (double l before -y suffix: beautiful + -ly = beautifully)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'beautifuly' with one -l. BEAUTIFUL ends in -l, so adding -ly = -lly.
questions.learning_tip: BEAUTIFUL + -LY = BEAUTIFULLY (double L). Rule: when an adjective ends in -L, add -LY → the L doubles! Careful → carefully, beautiful → beautifully, wonderful → wonderfully. 'Beautifuly' is ALWAYS WRONG.

questions.error_type: Irregular plural — mouse → mice (not mouses)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'mouses' applying regular -s plural rule. MOUSE is irregular: mouse → mice.
questions.learning_tip: MOUSE → MICE (irregular plural). These are irregular — the word completely changes. Never 'mouses'. Other irregular pairs: man → men, tooth → teeth, goose → geese. Learn these by heart!

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (musicians', not musicians's)
questions.trap_type: Students add 's after the apostrophe for a plural noun ending in -s.
questions.learning_tip: Plural possessive: add apostrophe AFTER the -s! The MUSICIANS' bows = the bows belonging to all the musicians. NEVER 'musicians's'. Singular: musician's. Plural: musicians'. Extra -s after apostrophe = WRONG for plural nouns ending in -s.

E.passage: Last Friday, our school held its annual music concert in the main hall. We waited nervously near the stage — you could here (1) the audience chatting loudly through the curtain. One of the pianoes (2) was slightly out of tune, but the students performed magnificently. The performance was so beautifuly (3) done that many parents wiped tears from their eyes. At one point, a family of mouses (4) were spotted under the front row of seats. At the end, the musicians's (5) bows were met with thunderous applause from the audience.

questions.sentence_a: Mr Chua asked Jamal a question.
questions.sentence_b: Did you hear the mistake you made?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'Mr Chua asked...'
questions.model_answer: Mr Chua asked Jamal if he heard the mistake he made.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked Jamal if did he hear' (wrong word order) or keep 'you' instead of 'he'.
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'Did YOU hear?' → asked IF HE heard. Pronoun: you → he. Tense: did hear → heard. Word order is NORMAL after 'if' — no inversion.

questions.sentence_a: The conductor raised his baton.
questions.sentence_b: The orchestra played the opening note.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'As soon as'.
questions.model_answer: As soon as the conductor raised his baton, the orchestra played the opening note.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'The orchestra played the opening note as soon as the conductor raised his baton' — both orders are acceptable but leading with 'as soon as' is the target structure.
questions.learning_tip: AS SOON AS = immediately when. AS SOON AS the conductor RAISED his baton, the orchestra PLAYED — showing that one action happened the moment the other did.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Twelve-year-old Jamal practised the same piano piece for four months. It was a difficult piece, full of fast runs and sudden changes in volume, and he knew every note by heart. Tonight was the school concert, and he was the closing act.

When Jamal walked onto the stage, the lights were bright and the hall was packed. He sat at the grand piano, placed his hands on the keys and began.

The first half went perfectly. Then, in the third movement, his fingers slipped. He hit a wrong note — loud and clear in the quiet hall. He felt his face go red.

But Jamal did not stop. He steadied himself, took a breath and kept playing. The mistake faded behind him as the music carried on.

When the last note rang out, there was a moment of silence. Then the audience erupted. They rose to their feet and clapped. His music teacher, Mr Chua, was standing at the side of the stage with a wide smile.

'That was the bravest thing I have seen on this stage in twenty years,' Mr Chua said afterwards. 'Anyone can play a perfect piece. But only a true musician carries on after making a mistake.'

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 1 has the same meaning as 'completely memorised without needing to look'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Rehearsed' = practised; 'performed' = presented; 'perfectly' = without error. BY HEART = memorised completely so you can recall it without looking.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: BY HEART = memorised completely and perfectly, without needing any notes or reminders. Jamal knew the piece BY HEART = every note was stored in his memory. 'Learn BY HEART' is a fixed expression.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'He steadied himself, took a breath and kept playing it'?

options.2: The piano he was sitting at
options.3: The piece of music he was performing

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'it' = the wrong note. But 'kept playing IT' = continued the performance.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'kept playing IT.' What was Jamal playing throughout the concert? The PIECE OF MUSIC. He kept playing IT = he did not stop the performance. The mistake happened during the piece, so IT = the piece.

mcq_questions.stem: What does Mr Chua mean when he says 'Only a true musician carries on after making a mistake'?

options.2: The ability to recover and continue despite a mistake shows true musicianship.
options.3: Mr Chua was angry that Jamal made a mistake.
options.4: Jamal's mistake was so small that nobody noticed it.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'true musician = no mistakes'. Mr Chua is praising Jamal for continuing — not suggesting perfection.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: 'CARRIES ON after making a mistake' = continues despite the error. A 'true musician' = someone with real skill and character, not someone who never makes mistakes. The praise is about RECOVERY, not perfection.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Jamal felt confident just before his performance? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says Jamal's hands were trembling and his heart was pounding before he walked onto the stage — showing he was nervous, not confident.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, he practised for months.' Practice does not automatically equal confidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: Jamal's HANDS WERE TREMBLING and his HEART WAS POUNDING = signs of nervousness, not confidence. Despite four months of practice, he was still nervous before performing. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did the audience do when Jamal played the last note?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: There was a moment of silence and then the audience erupted, rose to their feet and clapped.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'they applauded' without mentioning that they rose to their feet.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: 'There was a moment of SILENCE. Then the audience ERUPTED. They ROSE TO THEIR FEET and CLAPPED.' Give the specific sequence of reactions.

open_ended_questions.stem: How do we know Jamal was very well prepared for the concert? Give TWO pieces of evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) He practised the same piece for four months. (ii) He knew every note of the piece by heart.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students give one piece of evidence twice in different words.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: (1) he PRACTISED for FOUR MONTHS and (2) he 'knew every note BY HEART'. Both are distinct pieces of evidence for his preparation.

open_ended_questions.stem: Find a phrase in paragraph 4 that shows Jamal deliberately chose to keep performing despite the mistake.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: 'He steadied himself, took a breath and kept playing.'
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students quote 'the mistake faded behind him' which describes the result, not the deliberate choice Jamal made.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'He STEADIED HIMSELF, took a breath and KEPT PLAYING.' These actions show deliberate choice and self-control — not an accident.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Jamal with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) DETERMINED: Jamal practised the same piece for four months and knew every note by heart — showing he was willing to put in sustained effort to reach his goal. (ii) COURAGEOUS: after making a mistake on stage, he steadied himself and kept playing instead of stopping — showing he could face failure and push through it.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'talented and hardworking' without precise trait names or specific textual evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: DETERMINED = practised for FOUR MONTHS, knew every note BY HEART. COURAGEOUS = made a mistake, steadied himself and KEPT PLAYING. Name trait + evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: On a sunny Saturday, the park was as ________ as a beehive — children running in every direction and laughter filling the air.
questions.trap_type: 'Quiet' and 'empty' are opposites of a beehive's activity. 'Dark' = lacking light. BUSY = full of activity and movement.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The park was AS BUSY AS a beehive = comparing the park's activity to the constant buzzing movement of bees in a hive. BUSY = full of activity. AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is always the correct simile form.

questions.stem: The park warden asked visitors to ________ their rubbish in the bins provided and not leave it on the grass.
questions.trap_type: 'Scatter' and 'drop' mean to leave things carelessly. 'Display' = show publicly. Only 'dispose of' = throw away properly in the correct place.
questions.learning_tip: DISPOSE OF = get rid of something properly, especially by putting it in the right bin or container. Always DISPOSE OF rubbish correctly to keep the park clean.

questions.stem: After the renovation, the children were excited to ________ the new adventure playground for the very first time.
questions.trap_type: 'Run away from' = flee; 'break into' = enter by force; 'give up on' = stop trying. TRY OUT = test or use something for the first time to see what it is like.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: TRY OUT = test or experience something for the first time. The children wanted to TRY OUT the new playground = use it and discover what it was like. TRY + OUT work together as one meaning.

questions.stem: When Hana heard that the old playground would be demolished, she felt ________ — it was the place where so many of her best memories were made.
questions.trap_type: 'Over the moon' = very happy (opposite); 'under the weather' = ill; 'on top of the world' = very happy. DOWN IN THE DUMPS = feeling sad and low.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: DOWN IN THE DUMPS = feeling sad, low and miserable. Hana felt DOWN IN THE DUMPS = she was unhappy and dejected about losing the playground. Idioms cannot be understood word by word — she was not literally in a dump!

questions.stem: The playground equipment was ________ and repainted over the school holiday to make it safe and attractive again.
questions.trap_type: 'Abandoned' = left and not maintained; 'demolished' = knocked down entirely; 'cluttered' = messy and overcrowded. Only 'renovated' = repaired and restored to good condition.
questions.learning_tip: RENOVATED = repaired, restored and improved something old or worn. The playground was RENOVATED = repaired and repainted to make it safe and new-looking again.

questions.stem: Everyone in the neighbourhood ________ how much the children love the old playground near the canal.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'know'. EVERYONE = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: EVERYONE / NOBODY / SOMEONE = Singular! Everyone KNOWS = add -S. 'Everyone know' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs in the present tense.

questions.stem: The town council has ________ over two million dollars on park improvements across the city this year.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. SPEND → SPENT (irregular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. The council HAS SPENT two million dollars = started spending this year and the total is complete. SPEND → SPENT (irregular past participle).

questions.stem: The dog ________ in the fountain when its owner realised and ran over to pull it out.
questions.trap_type: 'The owner realised and ran over' = sudden interrupting event. The dog was already splashing = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The owner REALISED and RAN OVER = sudden past event. The dog was already in the middle of splashing = WAS SPLASHING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.

questions.stem: The new adventure playground is much ________ than the old one — it has a climbing wall, a zip line and a water play area.
questions.trap_type: 'Most exciting' = superlative; 'excitinger' is WRONG. MORE EXCITING = comparative of long adjective.
questions.learning_tip: Long adjective (3+ syllables) → MORE + adjective = comparative. MORE EXCITING THAN = comparing two playgrounds. 'Excitinger' is ALWAYS WRONG. For long adjectives, always use MORE.

questions.stem: The children met ________ the park entrance and then walked to the playground together.
questions.trap_type: 'In' suggests inside an enclosed space; 'on' is for surfaces; 'along' = following a path. Only 'at' is correct for a specific meeting point.
questions.learning_tip: AT = at a specific location point: met AT the park entrance, waited AT the gate. AT shows you are at that exact named spot.

questions.stem: The new park benches are made from recycled materials, ________ they?
questions.trap_type: Positive present 'to be' passive ('are made') → negative question tag. 'Are' → aren't they.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present 'to be' passive → negative tag. The benches ARE made from recycled materials, AREN'T they? ARE → AREN'T. Remember: passive sentences use 'to be' tags, not 'do/did' tags.

questions.stem: The broken climbing frame ________ by the town council within two days of receiving the report.
questions.trap_type: The frame did not fix itself — the town council fixed it. Past passive = was fixed.
questions.learning_tip: The climbing frame was the receiver of the action. Use the PASSIVE: WAS FIXED. Passive = was/were + past participle.

questions.stem: The park warden reminded visitors ________ their dogs on a leash inside the park at all times.
questions.trap_type: 'Reminded someone to do something' = reported speech structure: reminded + object + to + base verb → to keep.
questions.learning_tip: 'Reminded visitors TO + base verb': reminded visitors TO KEEP their dogs on a leash. After 'reminded + object', use the infinitive with 'to'.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Prepositions of time and place)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We usually go to the park (1)________ Sunday mornings.' Signal: specific named day = ON. 'ON Sunday mornings' — ON is used before specific days of the week.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' or 'at' for a named day. ON is the correct preposition before specific days.
questions.learning_tip: ON + specific day: ON Sunday mornings, ON Monday, ON Christmas Day. Always use ON before named days.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We arrive (2)________ the park entrance just after eight o'clock.' Signal: specific location point (arrival) = AT. 'Arrived AT the entrance' — AT is used for specific named arrival points.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' (inside the park) or 'on' (surface). AT is correct for a named arrival point.
questions.learning_tip: AT = a specific location or arrival point: arrive AT the entrance, wait AT the gate. AT shows you are at that exact named spot.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'My favourite bench is (3)________ the koi pond at the eastern side of the park.' Signal: in the vicinity of, but not inside = NEAR. 'NEAR the koi pond' = close to it, beside it.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'at' (exact point) or 'in' (inside). NEAR = close to but not at the exact same spot.
questions.learning_tip: NEAR = close to something, but not at the exact same spot. My bench is NEAR the koi pond = it is close to the pond but not inside it.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We always rest (4)________ the large rain tree that gives shade to the whole picnic area.' Signal: below something overhead = UNDER. 'Rested UNDER the rain tree' = in the shade directly below the tree.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'below' (not in the box) or 'near' (already used). UNDER = directly below something that is above you.
questions.learning_tip: UNDER = directly below something that is overhead. We rested UNDER the tree = directly beneath it, sheltered by its branches above.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The playground is (5)________ the fitness corner and the community garden.' Signal: in the middle of two specific named places = BETWEEN. 'BETWEEN A and B' — exactly two things.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'among' (for three or more things) or 'near' (already used). BETWEEN is correct for exactly two specific named places.
questions.learning_tip: BETWEEN = in the middle of exactly two specific things. The playground is BETWEEN the fitness corner and the community garden — two specific places.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The ducks swim (6)________ the pond near the centre of the park.' Signal: inside a body of water (enclosed space) = IN. Animals swim IN a pond, not ON it.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'on' (surface) instead of 'in' (inside a body of water). Ducks swim inside the water, not on top of it.
questions.learning_tip: IN = inside an enclosed space or body of water. The ducks swim IN the pond = they are inside the water. 'On the pond' would mean on the surface (like a boat).

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Father always stretches (7)________ his morning jog around the park.' Signal: earlier than / prior to the jog = BEFORE. He stretches BEFORE the jog = the stretching happens first, then the jog.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'after' (after the jog, not before) or 'during' (not in the box). BEFORE = prior to, earlier than.
questions.learning_tip: BEFORE = earlier in time than something else. Father stretches BEFORE his jog = the stretching happens first. AFTER would mean he stretches when the jog is finished.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We stop for cold drinks at the café (8)________ our walk.' Signal: when the walk is finished = AFTER. They stop for drinks AFTER the walk = the walk ends, then they stop at the café.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'before' (already used in blank 7) or 'during' (not in the box). AFTER = when something is finished.
questions.learning_tip: AFTER = when something is finished. We stop for drinks AFTER our walk = we finish the walk first, then go for drinks.

C.passage: Every Saturday morning, our family meets (1)________ the park gate before sunrise. We always sit (2)________ the big tree near the fountain. The children run (3)________ the grass and chase the ducks. Families gather (4)________ the water feature to take photos. Dogs are allowed only (5)________ the gravel paths and must be kept on leads. The bench (6)________ the two oak trees is always the most popular spot. Older residents often arrive (7)________ the other visitors to claim the shady seats. We usually leave (8)________ lunch, tired but happy from our morning out.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Bishan-Ang Mo Kio Park is one of the most beautiful parks in Singapore. A winding river (1)________ through the park, creating a natural path for visitors to follow. The park is filled with (2)________ green grass and tall trees that provide shade on hot afternoons. Families (3)________ along the riverbank on weekends, stopping to watch dragonflies and ducks. The cool breeze from the river felt (4)________ after a long week of school and work. For young children, there is also an (5)________ course with climbing nets, balance beams and stepping stones that challenge them to move in different ways.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'flowed' which is not in the box. MEANDERED = moved in a slow, winding path with many curves.
questions.learning_tip: MEANDERED = moved slowly and in a winding, curving path. A river MEANDERS through a park = it flows in gentle curves rather than a straight line.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'green' or 'thick' which are not in the box. LUSH = growing strongly and richly, full of healthy plants.
questions.learning_tip: LUSH = growing strongly and richly, very green and full of life. LUSH grass or plants are healthy, vibrant and thick.

questions.trap_type: Students may write 'walked' which is not in the box. STROLLED = walked slowly and in a relaxed way, without any hurry.
questions.learning_tip: STROLLED = walked slowly and in a relaxed, leisurely way. Families STROLLED along the riverbank = they walked slowly and enjoyed the surroundings.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'cool breeze after a long week' = something that makes you feel better and more energetic = refreshing.
questions.learning_tip: REFRESHING = making you feel pleasantly cool, rested or energised. A cool breeze is REFRESHING after a long, tiring week.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'climbing nets, balance beams and stepping stones that challenge them' = a course with things to get past = obstacle course.
questions.learning_tip: An OBSTACLE = something that you have to get past or overcome. An OBSTACLE course has physical challenges like nets, beams and stepping stones to move through.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Adverb required after action verb (ran)
questions.trap_type: 'quick' (adjective) after action verb 'ran'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (RAN), use an ADVERB. Hana ran QUICKLY = how did she run? QUICKLY (adverb, -ly). 'Quick' describes nouns; 'quickly' describes HOW the action is done.

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — there (place) vs their (belonging to them)
questions.trap_type: 'there' (a place) when the sentence needs 'their' (belonging to the ducks).
questions.learning_tip: THEIR = belonging to them. THERE = at that place. Test: 'splashing in THEIR corner' → belonging to the ducks? YES → THEIR. THEIR = possession. THERE = location. Never confuse them!

questions.error_type: Irregular plural — goose → geese (not gooses)
questions.trap_type: 'gooses' applying the regular -s rule. GOOSE is irregular: goose → geese.
questions.learning_tip: GOOSE → GEESE (irregular plural). The word completely changes. NEVER 'gooses'. Other irregular pairs: mouse → mice, tooth → teeth, foot → feet. These must be memorised — they do not follow the -s rule.

questions.error_type: Spelling — -ing rule: silent -e is dropped before adding -ing
questions.trap_type: 'slideing' keeping the -e. Rule: drop silent -e before -ing.
questions.learning_tip: Rule: Silent -E → DROP before adding -ING. SLIDE → SLID + ING = SLIDING. 'Slideing' is WRONG. Same rule: make → making, ride → riding, write → writing. Drop the -e, then add -ing.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (teachers', not teachers's)
questions.trap_type: Students add 's after apostrophe for a plural noun ending in -s.
questions.learning_tip: Plural possessive: add apostrophe AFTER -s! TEACHERS' feedback = belonging to all teachers. NEVER 'teachers's'. Singular: teacher's. Plural: teachers'. Extra -s after apostrophe = WRONG.

E.passage: Last Sunday, our class visited the community park for a nature observation project. Hana ran quick (1) ahead to claim a spot near the pond. At the pond, she noticed the ducks splashing in there (2) favourite corner near the reeds. A pair of gooses (3) waddled along the bank, drawing everyone's attention. As the group moved towards the climbing frame, someone got stuck on the slideing (4) section. The teachers's (5) feedback forms were collected and shared with the class the next morning.

questions.sentence_a: The park warden asked the children a question.
questions.sentence_b: Are you here to see the new playground?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The park warden asked...'
questions.model_answer: The park warden asked the children if they were there to see the new playground.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'asked the children if are they there' (wrong word order) or keep 'you/here' instead of 'they/there'.
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF + subject + verb (normal order). 'Are YOU here?' → asked IF THEY WERE THERE. Pronoun: you → they. Place: here → there. Tense: are → were. Word order is normal after 'if'.

questions.sentence_a: Father was reading his newspaper on the bench.
questions.sentence_b: The children were playing on the swings nearby.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'while'.
questions.model_answer: While Father was reading his newspaper on the bench, the children were playing on the swings nearby.
questions.trap_type: Students drop 'was' or 'were', writing 'While Father reading his newspaper, the children playing on the swings'.
questions.learning_tip: WHILE shows two ongoing actions happening at the same time. Keep WAS and WERE: While Father WAS READING, the children WERE PLAYING. Both past continuous verbs stay.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
For nine-year-old Hana, the old playground at the end of her block was the best place in the world. It had a rusty slide that squeaked, a single roundabout and two swings. Nothing about it was new or exciting. But it was where Hana learned to pump the swings on her own, where she made her best friend Siti on a rainy Wednesday afternoon, and where she always went when she felt sad or happy or simply restless.

One afternoon, Hana came home from school to find a notice pasted on the gate. The playground would be demolished the following week to make way for a new multi-purpose fitness area.

Hana felt a sudden tightness in her chest. She ran to the playground, sat on her favourite swing and pushed off slowly. The chain creaked. The sky was turning orange.

'Are you upset?' asked a voice. It was Siti, sitting on the other swing.

'It's just a playground,' Hana said. But her voice was quiet.

'I know,' said Siti. 'But it was our playground.'

The two of them swung in silence as the sun went down. When the streetlights came on, they finally walked home. Hana did not say anything, but she felt a little lighter.

The new fitness area opened three months later. It had bright equipment and a smooth path for jogging. Hana used it sometimes. But she never forgot the rusty swing that squeaked.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 4 has the same meaning as 'gradually fell apart or broke down over time'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Rebuilt' and 'replaced' = making new; 'repainted' = painted again. CRUMBLED = fell apart gradually into small pieces over time.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: CRUMBLED = gradually fell apart or broke into small pieces over time. The old equipment CRUMBLED = it slowly deteriorated from years of use and weather. CRUMBLE = fall apart piece by piece.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'Hana felt a sudden tightness in it'?

options.3: Her chest — she felt the emotional weight of the news

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'it' = the playground. But 'Hana felt a tightness in IT' = tightness is felt in the body — specifically her chest.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'Hana felt a sudden tightness in IT.' Where do people feel emotional tightness? In the CHEST. IT = her chest. This is a physical sensation expressing an emotional response — the news made her feel tight in her chest.

mcq_questions.stem: What was Siti trying to communicate when she said 'I know. But it was OUR playground'?

options.1: She was angry that no one asked for the children's permission before demolishing it.
options.2: She agreed the playground was old but was emphasising the personal and emotional meaning it held for them.
options.3: She was suggesting that the new playground would never be as good.
options.4: She wanted the playground to be repaired rather than replaced.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking she was angry. 'I KNOW' = she acknowledges the facts. The emphasis is on 'OUR' — personal meaning, not ownership or anger.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: 'I KNOW. But it was OUR playground.' 'I know' = she agrees it was old/broken. 'OUR' = emphasis on the personal and shared memories tied to that specific place. Not anger — but emotional attachment to shared history.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that the old playground was in good condition? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says the old playground had a rusty slide that squeaked and equipment that was worn and crumbling — it was clearly in poor condition.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, the children loved it.' Loving a place does not mean it is in good condition.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: 'RUSTY slide that SQUEAKED', 'CRUMBLING equipment.' These details show the playground was in poor condition — old, damaged and deteriorating. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: Where did Hana meet her best friend Siti for the first time?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Hana met Siti at the old playground on a rainy Wednesday afternoon.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'at school' which is not supported by the passage.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: 'She MADE her best friend Siti on A RAINY WEDNESDAY AFTERNOON' — at the playground. Both details are needed.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did Hana feel at the end of the passage? How was this different from how she felt in paragraph 3?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: In paragraph 3, Hana felt shocked and sad — she felt a sudden tightness in her chest. By the end of the passage, after spending time with Siti, she 'felt a little lighter', meaning she felt slightly better and less burdened, even though she was still sad about losing the playground.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe only one emotional state without showing the contrast.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Contrast: Paragraph 3 = 'TIGHTNESS in her chest' (sudden distress). End of passage = 'felt a LITTLE LIGHTER' (slightly better after being with Siti). Show both to answer completely.

open_ended_questions.stem: In paragraph 1, Hana said the old playground was 'the best place in the world'. Find TWO specific reasons from the passage that explain why she felt this way.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) It was where she learned to pump the swings on her own. (ii) It was where she made her best friend Siti.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'because she liked playing there' which is too general.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1 gives THREE specific reasons: (1) where she LEARNED TO PUMP THE SWINGS, (2) where she MADE HER BEST FRIEND SITI, (3) where she always went when she felt any strong emotion. Give any two.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on her actions and words throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Hana with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) SENTIMENTAL: Hana felt a tightness in her chest when she heard about the demolition, and she recalled learning to pump the swings and meeting Siti there — showing she deeply valued memories tied to places. (ii) OPEN-MINDED: by the end, she smiled at the new playground, realising new memories could be made there too — showing she could accept change.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'sad and happy' without precise trait names or specific textual evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: SENTIMENTAL = felt tightness in chest, recalled specific memories at the old playground. OPEN-MINDED = smiled at the new playground, accepted that new memories are possible. Name trait + give evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: The octopus ________ a cloud of dark ink to confuse the shark and escaped into a crevice.
questions.trap_type: 'Swallowed' and 'absorbed' suggest taking something in. 'Released' = let something out, which is what an octopus does with ink.
questions.learning_tip: RELEASED = let something out or set something free. An octopus RELEASES a cloud of ink to escape from predators.

questions.stem: The giant manta ray drifted through the water as ________ as a cloud floating across a summer sky — effortless and silent.
questions.trap_type: 'Noisy' and 'rapid' describe opposite qualities. 'Clumsy' = awkward, which contrasts with the image. GRACEFUL = moving in a smooth, elegant and effortless way.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The manta ray was AS GRACEFUL AS a cloud = comparing its smooth, effortless movement to a drifting cloud. GRACEFUL = elegant and smooth (adjective). AS + ADJECTIVE + AS is the correct simile form — never use an adverb.

questions.stem: Scientists discovered a new species of deep-sea fish that was completely ________ to science.
questions.trap_type: 'Familiar' and 'common' are the opposite of a new discovery. 'Unknown' = not yet known or recorded by science.
questions.learning_tip: UNKNOWN = not yet discovered, named or recorded. A species UNKNOWN to science is one that no scientist has ever studied or documented before.

questions.stem: The children spent all afternoon exploring the rock pools — they were in ________, pointing at every crab and starfish they found.
questions.trap_type: 'Hot water' = in trouble; 'thin ice' = in a risky situation; 'deep trouble' = serious problems. IN SEVENTH HEAVEN = feeling extremely happy and delighted.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: IN SEVENTH HEAVEN = feeling extremely happy, as if you are in a perfect, joyful place. The children were IN SEVENTH HEAVEN = they were absolutely thrilled exploring the rock pools. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!

questions.stem: The documentary warned viewers to ________ single-use plastics that end up in the ocean and harm sea creatures.
questions.trap_type: 'Hold on' = wait; 'run into' = encounter; 'give in' = surrender. CUT OUT = stop using or consuming something entirely.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: CUT OUT = stop doing or using something entirely. CUT OUT single-use plastics = stop using them completely. CUT + OUT work together. 'I need to cut out junk food' = stop eating it.

questions.stem: Nobody in the diving team ________ a creature as rare as the blue-ringed octopus this close to shore before.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'see'. NOBODY = singular → verb+S in simple present.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Always use verb+S. Nobody SEES = add -S. 'Nobody see' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.

questions.stem: Our school has ________ an online marine life project that students can contribute to from home.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. LAUNCH → LAUNCHED (regular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Our school HAS LAUNCHED the project = it started recently and is now running. LAUNCH → LAUNCHED (regular verb, add -ed).

questions.stem: The dolphins ________ playfully around the boat when the captain spotted a school of tuna in the distance.
questions.trap_type: 'The captain spotted tuna' = sudden interrupting event. Dolphins were already swimming = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The captain SPOTTED tuna = sudden past event. The dolphins were already in the middle of swimming = WERE SWIMMING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.

questions.stem: The blue whale is far ________ than any other animal on Earth — it can grow up to thirty metres long.
questions.trap_type: 'Largest' = superlative (for 3+); 'more larger' = WRONG double comparative. LARGER = comparative (comparing two groups).
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective + -ER = comparative. Large → LARGER. The blue whale is LARGER THAN any other animal = comparing it to all others. 'More larger' is ALWAYS WRONG — never add both 'more' AND '-er'.

questions.stem: There is so ________ we still do not know about the deep ocean — scientists estimate we have explored less than twenty percent of it.
questions.trap_type: 'Much' needs 'so much' but cannot be used with uncountable noun alone here; 'few' and 'many' are for countable nouns. LITTLE = not much (for uncountable nouns like 'what we know').
questions.learning_tip: LITTLE + uncountable noun / concept = not much of it. There is SO LITTLE we know = the amount of knowledge is small. LITTLE = not much (uncountable). MUCH = a large amount (uncountable). FEW / MANY = for countable things.

questions.stem: Each of the clownfish in the tank ________ bright orange and white stripes on its body.
questions.trap_type: 'Each of the clownfish' = each one individually = singular. Present fact. Students write 'have' thinking of many fish.
questions.learning_tip: 'Each of the clownfish' = each one at a time = singular → HAS bright orange and white stripes. EACH always uses a singular verb.

questions.stem: The rare blue whale ________ by a team of marine biologists off the coast of Sri Lanka last month.
questions.trap_type: The whale did not spot itself — the marine biologists spotted it. Past passive = was spotted.
questions.learning_tip: The whale was the receiver of the action. Use the PASSIVE: WAS SPOTTED. Passive = was/were + past participle.

questions.stem: The marine conservationist told visitors ________ into the water to touch or disturb the coral.
