questions.learning_tip: AFTER + [the first event], [the second event]. AFTER the class ARRIVED, they WENT to the exhibition. The event after 'after' happened FIRST.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Class 3E arrived at the Heritage Museum on a Tuesday morning. Their teacher, Mr Loh, had one rule: look with your eyes, not your hands.

The first gallery was full of ancient pottery from South-East Asia. While the guide was explaining the history of a particular clay pot, a boy named Ivan leaned too close. He lost his balance, and his elbow caught the edge of a rope barrier. The barrier toppled, and the museum's smallest pot — a replica, thankfully — fell and shattered on the marble floor.

Everyone went very still. Ivan's face turned red. He looked at Mr Loh.

Mr Loh did not shout. He walked over to the museum attendant, spoke quietly and then came back. 'It was a replica,' he said calmly. 'No harm done. Now, what can everyone learn from this?'

A girl named Rina put her hand up. 'To respect the rules,' she said.

'Good,' said Mr Loh. 'And also — it is easier to break something than to make it.' He picked up one of the large shards and held it up. 'Look at this. A craftsman spent weeks shaping this pot. And it took one second to break.'

Ivan nodded slowly. He did not say anything for the rest of the museum visit. But when they reached the ancient weaving gallery at the end, he was the most careful one there.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 1 has the same meaning as 'broke suddenly into many small pieces'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Toppled' = fell over; 'leaned' = bent. SHATTERED = broke suddenly into many pieces.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: SHATTERED = broke suddenly and completely into many pieces. The pot SHATTERED on the marble floor = it smashed. SHATTER = break violently into small pieces.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'Mr Loh already knew what it was'?

options.1: The broken pieces on the floor
options.3: The fact that the pot was a replica, not the real ancient one
options.4: The lesson Mr Loh planned to teach

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1. 'It' = the pot's nature — that it was a copy.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'IT' refers to what the pot WAS — a REPLICA. Mr Loh already knew IT = he knew the pot was a copy. Context: 'He walked over slowly, crouched down, and smiled.'

mcq_questions.stem: Why was Ivan described as 'the most careful one' in the weaving gallery?

options.1: Because he was always the most careful student.
options.2: Because the broken pot taught him to understand how fragile and precious things are.
options.3: Because Mr Loh gave him a warning before the weaving gallery.
options.4: Because the weaving exhibits were more delicate.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Ivan was NOT always careful — he broke the pot. This change was caused by the lesson.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: Ivan was NOT always careful (he broke the pot by leaning too close). In the weaving gallery, 'he was the most careful.' This CHANGE happened BECAUSE the broken pot taught him a lesson about care.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 2, is it True or False that Ivan broke the pot on purpose? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says Ivan leaned too close, lost his balance and his elbow hit the barrier — it was an accident, not deliberate.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, he touched the barrier.' He hit it accidentally when he lost his balance.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'Ivan leaned too close, LOST HIS BALANCE, and his elbow HIT the rope barrier.' These words show an ACCIDENT. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did the pot break?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Ivan leaned too close, lost his balance, and his elbow hit the rope barrier. The barrier toppled and knocked the pot off its stand.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'Ivan touched the pot' which is inaccurate — he hit the barrier with his elbow, not the pot directly.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: Ivan's ELBOW hit the rope BARRIER, which toppled and caused the pot to fall. He did not directly touch the pot.

open_ended_questions.stem: What TWO lessons did Mr Loh teach the class after the pot broke?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) To respect the rules. (ii) It is easier to break something than to make it.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students give only one lesson or repeat the same lesson in different words.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraphs 5–6: (1) 'To RESPECT THE RULES' (Rina's answer that Mr Loh approved). (2) 'It is EASIER to break something than to make it.' Both are explicit lessons in the text.

open_ended_questions.stem: Find ONE phrase from the passage that shows Ivan truly understood the lesson by the end of the visit.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: 'He was the most careful one there.'
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students quote 'He did not say anything' which shows silence, not necessarily understanding.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Last paragraph: 'he was THE MOST CAREFUL ONE there.' This action shows he genuinely understood and changed his behaviour — the clearest evidence of learning.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his actions in the passage, describe TWO character traits of Mr Loh with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) CALM: when the pot shattered, instead of scolding Ivan, Mr Loh walked over slowly and smiled — showing he did not panic or react in anger. (ii) THOUGHTFUL: he used the broken pot as a teaching moment, turning the accident into a lesson about care and respect for things made with effort.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'kind and patient' without precise trait names or specific evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: CALM = walked SLOWLY, SMILED (not angry). THOUGHTFUL = turned the broken pot into a TEACHING MOMENT. Name trait → give evidence from passage = full marks.

questions.stem: The explorer ________ through the dense jungle, pushing branches aside as he searched for the hidden ruins.
questions.trap_type: 'Floated' and 'soared' are for water/air movement; 'tiptoed' is too careful and slow. Only 'trekked' = travelled on foot over difficult terrain.
questions.learning_tip: TREKKED = walked a long, difficult journey on foot, especially through wild terrain. Explorers TREK through jungles and mountains.

questions.stem: The old map was as ________ as tissue paper — one wrong touch and it might crumble to dust.
questions.trap_type: 'Thick', 'bright' and 'heavy' don't describe something easily damaged. FRAGILE = easily broken.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The map was AS FRAGILE AS tissue paper = comparing how easily it could be damaged to thin, delicate tissue paper. FRAGILE = easily broken — handle with care!

questions.stem: The children ________ their way through the abandoned warehouse, unsure of what they might find.
questions.trap_type: 'Raced', 'stormed' and 'leaped' all imply speed or force. Only 'crept' = moved slowly and quietly, trying not to be heard or noticed.
questions.learning_tip: CREPT = moved slowly, quietly and carefully, trying not to make noise. The children CREPT through the warehouse = moved with caution and silence.

questions.stem: Finding a single clue in the enormous abandoned warehouse was like looking for a ________ — almost impossible.
questions.trap_type: 'A piece of cake' = easy (opposite!). NEEDLE IN A HAYSTACK = something extremely difficult to find.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: A NEEDLE IN A HAYSTACK = something almost impossible to find among many things. The warehouse was so big that finding one small clue was A NEEDLE IN A HAYSTACK. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!

questions.stem: The detective carefully ________ the secret passage and found a trail of muddy footprints leading deeper inside.
questions.trap_type: 'Ran away from' = fled; 'gave up on' = stopped. LOOKED INTO = investigated carefully.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: LOOK INTO = investigate something carefully. The detective LOOKED INTO the passage = she examined it to find clues. LOOK + INTO work together as one meaning.

questions.stem: Nobody in the adventure club ________ a clue this difficult before — it has everyone completely baffled.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'solve'. NOBODY = singular → verb+S.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Nobody SOLVES = add -S. 'Nobody solve' is WRONG. In present tense, singular indefinite pronouns always take verb+S.

questions.stem: The young detectives have ________ three hidden clues since they started their investigation this morning.
questions.trap_type: HAVE + past participle = present perfect. FIND → FOUND (irregular).
questions.learning_tip: HAVE + past participle = present perfect. The detectives HAVE FOUND three clues = started finding this morning and have three so far. FIND → FOUND (irregular past participle).

questions.stem: The explorers ________ across the rope bridge when it began to sway violently in the wind.
questions.trap_type: 'The bridge began to sway' = sudden interrupting event. Explorers were already crossing = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The bridge BEGAN TO SWAY = sudden past event. Explorers were already in the middle of crossing = WERE CROSSING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when something interrupts.

questions.stem: The tunnel on the left was much ________ than the one on the right — and far more dangerous to enter alone.
questions.trap_type: 'Darkest' = superlative; 'more darker' = WRONG. DARKER = comparative of 'dark'.
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective + -ER = comparative. Dark → DARKER. The left tunnel was DARKER THAN the right = comparing only two. 'More darker' is ALWAYS WRONG — never add BOTH 'more' AND '-er'.

questions.stem: The children searched ________ the attic from morning until evening but still could not find the old diary.
questions.trap_type: 'At' is a location point; 'on' is a surface; 'in' is inside a space. Only 'through' = moving around and examining every part of a space.
questions.learning_tip: SEARCHED THROUGH = examined every part of something. They searched THROUGH the attic = looked in every corner and box. 'Through' shows comprehensive coverage.

questions.stem: Each of the coded messages in the detective game ________ a different secret phrase to unlock.
questions.trap_type: 'Each of the coded messages' = each one individually = singular. Present fact. Students write 'contain' thinking of many messages.
questions.learning_tip: 'Each of the coded messages' = each one at a time = singular → CONTAINS a different secret phrase. EACH always uses a singular verb.

questions.stem: The ancient scroll ________ in a clay pot buried under the ruins of the old temple.
questions.trap_type: The scroll did not find itself. Past passive = was found.
questions.learning_tip: The scroll was the receiver of the action. Past passive = WAS FOUND. Passive = was/were + past participle.

questions.stem: The expedition leader told her team ________ the cave alone under any circumstances.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told someone not to do something = told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told her team NOT TO + base verb': told her team NOT TO ENTER the cave alone. After 'told + object', always use 'not to' + base verb.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Verb forms of 'discover')

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Young adventurers love (1)________ hidden places and solving puzzles.' Signal: 'love + ___' = gerund (verb-ing). Pattern: love + verb-ing → discovering.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'to discover' instead of the gerund after 'love'.
questions.learning_tip: LOVE + verb-ing: love DISCOVERING hidden places. After 'love', always add -ING.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Every year, someone (2)________ a new piece of ancient history in an unexpected place.' Signal: 'Every year' = regular habit = simple present. Subject 'someone' = singular → discovers.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'discover' (plural form) forgetting 'someone' is singular.
questions.learning_tip: 'Every year' = habit = simple present. Someone (singular) → DISCOVERS a new piece of ancient history.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Last summer, a team of divers (3)________ a sunken ship off the coast of Batam.' Signal: 'Last summer' = past. 'Discover' is regular: discover → discovered.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'discover' (base form) ignoring the past signal 'Last summer'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Last summer' = past. 'Discover' is regular: discover → DISCOVERED.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'While the lead diver (4)________ the lower deck, a shark appeared nearby.' Signal: 'While the lead diver ___' = ongoing background action in the past. Subject 'the lead diver' = singular → was discovering. Interrupted by 'a shark appeared'.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'discovered' (simple past) missing the ongoing signal 'while the lead diver'.
questions.learning_tip: 'While the lead diver ___' = ongoing background past action = past continuous. The lead diver WAS DISCOVERING the lower deck when the shark appeared.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The other divers (5)________ ancient coins in the upper hull at the same time.' Signal: same past time frame, plural subject 'the other divers' + ongoing parallel action → were discovering.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'discovered' (simple past) instead of past continuous for an ongoing parallel action.
questions.learning_tip: The other divers = plural. They were doing it at the same past moment = WERE DISCOVERING (past continuous).

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Every explorer dreams (6)________ something truly remarkable.' Signal: 'dreams + ___' = infinitive. Pattern: dream + to + base verb → to discover.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'discovering' instead of the infinitive after 'dreams'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Dream TO + base verb': dreams TO DISCOVER something remarkable. Use the infinitive after 'dream'.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'One day, scientists may (7)________ what lies beneath the Antarctic ice sheet.' Signal: 'may + ___' = modal verb + base form. Never add -s or -ing after a modal.
questions.trap_type: Students add -s or -ing after the modal verb 'may'.
questions.learning_tip: After modal verbs (may, should, must, can), always use the BASE form: may DISCOVER. Never 'may discovers' or 'may discovering'.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Right now, a research team (8)________ ancient remains in a cave in Borneo.' Signal: 'Right now' = present continuous. Subject 'a research team' = singular → is discovering.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'discovers' (simple present habit) missing the 'right now' signal for present continuous.
questions.learning_tip: 'Right now' = present continuous. A research team (singular) → IS DISCOVERING ancient remains right now.

C.passage: Young adventurers love (1)________ hidden places and solving puzzles about the past. Every year, someone (2)________ a new piece of ancient history in an unexpected place. Last summer, a team of divers (3)________ a sunken ship off the coast of Batam. While the lead diver (4)________ the lower deck, a shark appeared and circled the wreck. The other divers (5)________ ancient coins in the upper hull at the same time. Every explorer dreams (6)________ something truly remarkable that changes what we know about history. One day, scientists may (7)________ what lies beneath the Antarctic ice sheet. Right now, a research team (8)________ ancient remains deep inside a cave in Borneo.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Mystery stories often begin with something strange or hidden. A key setting is the (1)________ house or location — empty and forgotten, full of secrets. Important clues may be (2)________ — hidden from view by clever tricks or physical barriers. A good mystery always leads to an (3)________ — a careful search for the truth. Many mysteries end when the last thread is (4)________ — the final connection between all the clues. These adventures remind us that even the most (5)________ journey can lead to something remarkable if we are brave enough to begin.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'after finding an old iron key' and 'followed the clues' = a systematic inquiry = investigation.
questions.learning_tip: An INVESTIGATION = a careful search for facts to solve a mystery or problem. The friends began their INVESTIGATION after finding the key.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'the whole mystery ___ before their eyes like a story being read aloud' = became clear and solved = unravelled.
questions.learning_tip: UNRAVELLED = became clear and solved, as if a tangled thread was being straightened out. The mystery UNRAVELLED = the solution revealed itself step by step.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'a place nobody had entered for years' = no longer used or occupied = abandoned.
questions.learning_tip: ABANDONED = left empty and unused, often for a long time. An ABANDONED building has no occupants and falls into disrepair.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'thorns and broken steps, had to move carefully to avoid falling' = full of danger = perilous.
questions.learning_tip: PERILOUS = full of serious danger. A PERILOUS path = one that is dangerous to cross, with many risks of getting hurt.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'beneath a loose floorboard' = hidden from sight = concealed.
questions.learning_tip: CONCEALED = hidden from sight, kept out of view. The tin box was CONCEALED beneath the floorboard = it was hidden there.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Adverb required after action verb (crept)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'slow' (adjective) after the action verb 'crept'. A verb needs an adverb to describe how.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (crept), use an ADVERB: crept SLOWLY. 'Slow' is an adjective — it describes nouns, not actions.

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — its (possessive) vs it's (it is)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'its' (possessive) when the meaning is 'it is'.
questions.learning_tip: IT'S = it is (contraction). ITS = belonging to it (possessive). Test: 'ITS strange' → can you say 'IT IS strange'? YES → use IT'S. IT'S = IT IS. ITS has no apostrophe because possessives (his, her, its) never need one.

questions.error_type: Spelling — -ing rule: silent -e is dropped before -ing
questions.trap_type: Students keep the final -e when adding -ing to 'hide', producing 'hideing'. Drop the silent -e before adding -ing.
questions.learning_tip: 'Hide' ends in silent -e: drop the -e before adding -ing → HIDING. Same rule: make → making, slide → sliding, give → giving.

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the footprints)
questions.trap_type: 'The footprints' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: 'The footprints' = plural → WERE all facing the same direction. WAS is only for singular subjects.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (detectives', not detectives's)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'detectives's' adding an extra 's' after the apostrophe. For a plural noun ending in -s, add only an apostrophe: detectives'.
questions.learning_tip: Plural possessive for nouns ending in -s: just add an apostrophe after the -s: detectives' notebook = the notebook belonging to the detectives (plural). Never 'detectives's'.

E.passage: Last Thursday after school, three friends decided to investigate the strange scratching sounds coming from the old storeroom. They crept slow (1) down the corridor, hearts pounding. They turned a corner and spotted a gap in the wall — its (2) strange that nobody noticed it before. They found a small cat hideing (3) behind a stack of boxes. The muddy paw prints was (4) all over the dusty floor. Later, when they wrote up their findings, the detectives's (5) notebook was filled with detailed sketches and notes about the little cat's hiding spot.

questions.sentence_a: The explorer was mapping the cave.
questions.sentence_b: She suddenly noticed strange symbols on the wall.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'while'.
questions.model_answer: While the explorer was mapping the cave, she suddenly noticed strange symbols on the wall.
questions.trap_type: Students drop 'was', writing 'While the explorer mapping the cave, she suddenly noticed strange symbols'.
questions.learning_tip: WHILE + ongoing action (past continuous), sudden event (simple past). While the explorer WAS MAPPING, she suddenly NOTICED. Keep WAS for the ongoing action.

questions.sentence_a: The detective found the hidden door.
questions.sentence_b: The hidden door led to a secret underground room.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using the relative pronoun 'which'.
questions.model_answer: The detective found the hidden door, which led to a secret underground room.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'The detective found the hidden door which it led to a secret underground room' — adding an extra 'it' after 'which'.
questions.learning_tip: Use 'which' to add information about a THING. The detective found the hidden door, WHICH led to a secret underground room. Never add 'it' after 'which'.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
It was Priya who noticed it first. While she was leaning against the crumbling wall of the old shophouse, her hand felt something beneath the peeling paint — a raised edge, like the border of a frame. She looked closer. There, barely visible under decades of old white paint, was a map.

She called the others: her neighbour Reuben and her cousin Amara. Together, they spent the next forty minutes carefully brushing away loose paint with their fingers. Slowly, a hand-drawn map of the neighbourhood came into view — but the neighbourhood looked very different from how it did today.

There were pathways that no longer existed. Buildings that were now carparks. And at the centre of the map, circled in red ink, was a location that none of them recognised: 'The Keeper's Room'.

'This must be from decades ago,' Reuben said.

'We have to find out where this room is,' said Amara.

Preya photographed the map with her phone. She knew the local history group met every Saturday morning. She also knew her grandmother once lived in this neighbourhood since she was a child.

That Saturday, she brought the photograph as well as her grandmother.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 1 has the same meaning as 'almost impossible to see'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Crumbling' = falling apart; 'peeling' = coming off in strips. BARELY VISIBLE = almost impossible to see.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: BARELY VISIBLE = almost impossible to see. The map was BARELY VISIBLE under the old paint = so faint that Priya almost missed it. BARELY = almost not at all. VISIBLE = able to be seen.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'it was labelled The Keeper's Room'?

options.1: The old map hidden under the paint
options.2: The red circle drawn at the centre of the map
options.3: The wall of the abandoned shophouse

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1. 'It' = the specific red CIRCLE that was labelled.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'IT was labelled The Keeper's Room.' IT = the RED CIRCLE at the centre of the map. 'A circle marked in red ink — IT was labelled...' IT refers to the circle, not the whole map.

mcq_questions.stem: Why did Priya decide to bring her grandmother to the history group meeting?

options.1: Because her grandmother was a member of the history group.
options.2: Because her grandmother might recognise places from when she once lived in the area.
options.3: Because she wanted her grandmother to draw a new map.
options.4: Because the history group required an adult.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1. The grandmother's value was her personal knowledge of the area, not membership.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: Priya knew her grandmother ONCE LIVED in this neighbourhood. So the grandmother might RECOGNISE places on the old map. Priya brought her because of personal knowledge of the area.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Priya was looking for a map when she found it? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says Priya was leaning against the wall and her hand felt something by accident — she was not searching for anything.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, she found the map.' She found it by accident while leaning, not because she was searching.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: 'While she was LEANING AGAINST the wall, her hand FELT something beneath the peeling paint.' She was not looking — it was an ACCIDENTAL discovery. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What was marked at the centre of the map?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: A location circled in red ink called 'The Keeper's Room'.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'a circle' without naming what the circle marked.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: 'at the centre of the map, circled in RED INK, was a location: THE KEEPER'S ROOM.' Name both the marking and the location.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did the map show that the neighbourhood had changed? Give TWO specific examples from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) The map showed pathways that no longer existed. (ii) It showed buildings that were now carparks.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'the neighbourhood looks different now' without naming the specific changes.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: (1) 'PATHWAYS that no longer existed' and (2) 'buildings that were now CARPARKS.' Give both specific changes from the text.

open_ended_questions.stem: Why did Priya think of TWO sources of help to find 'The Keeper's Room'?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: She thought of the local history group and her grandmother, because the history group meets regularly and knows local history, and her grandmother has lived in the neighbourhood since she was a child.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students mention only one source of help.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 6: Priya thought of (1) the LOCAL HISTORY GROUP that meets on Saturdays and (2) her GRANDMOTHER who lived in the neighbourhood since childhood. Two different sources.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on her actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Priya with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) OBSERVANT: she was the first to notice the raised edge beneath the paint — most people would lean against a wall without noticing anything unusual. (ii) RESOURCEFUL: when she could not solve the mystery alone, she thought of TWO sources of help — the local history group and her grandmother — using all available resources.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'curious and clever' without precise traits or specific evidence from the text.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: OBSERVANT = FIRST to notice the raised edge beneath the paint. RESOURCEFUL = thought of TWO different sources of help. Name the trait → give specific evidence from the passage = full marks.

questions.stem: The gardener used a small rake to ________ the dry leaves into a pile before composting them.
questions.trap_type: 'Scatter' means spread out; 'bury' means put underground; 'flatten' = press down. Only 'gather' = bring together into a group.
questions.learning_tip: GATHER = bring things together into one place. The gardener GATHERS fallen leaves into a pile before composting them.

questions.stem: The tomato seedlings were as ________ as little green jewels — tiny, bright and perfect in every way.
questions.trap_type: 'Heavy' and 'dull' are opposites of bright; 'delicate' describes fragility not colour. BRIGHT = giving off a strong, clear light or colour.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The seedlings were AS BRIGHT AS little green jewels = comparing their vivid green colour to sparkling jewels. Similes always use 'as ... as' to compare two different things.

questions.stem: The seeds needed rich, ________ soil to germinate quickly and grow into strong seedlings.
questions.trap_type: 'Stony', 'arid' and 'frozen' all describe soil that prevents plant growth. Only 'fertile' = rich in nutrients and ideal for growing plants.
questions.learning_tip: FERTILE = rich in nutrients and ideal for growing plants. FERTILE soil produces healthy crops and strong seedlings.

questions.stem: Mr Tan has ________ for growing vegetables — everything he plants comes up healthy and full.
questions.trap_type: 'A black eye' = an injury; 'cold feet' = fear; 'a big mouth' = talks too much. A GREEN THUMB = a natural talent for growing plants.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: A GREEN THUMB = a natural talent for gardening. 'Mr Tan has A GREEN THUMB' = he is naturally good at growing plants. Idioms cannot be understood word by word — green thumb is NOT about finger colour!

questions.stem: After the harvest festival, the students decided to ________ the old vegetable beds and plant fresh seeds.
questions.trap_type: 'Give in' = surrender; 'break down' = stop working; 'run out' = exhaust supply. DIG UP = remove something by digging it out of the ground.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: DIG UP = remove something from the ground by digging. The students DIG UP the old beds = they use a spade to lift and clear the soil. DIG + UP work together as one meaning.

questions.stem: Everyone in the gardening club ________ a different plant to care for each term.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'choose' thinking 'everyone in the club' = many people. EVERYONE = singular → verb+S in present tense.
questions.learning_tip: EVERYONE / NOBODY / SOMEONE / EACH = Singular! Always use verb+S. Everyone CHOOSES = add -S. 'Everyone choose' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.

questions.stem: The sunflower ________ almost two metres tall by the end of the summer holidays.
questions.trap_type: 'By the end of the summer holidays' = completed past event. 'Grow' is irregular: grow → grew.
questions.learning_tip: 'Grow' is irregular: grow → GREW. By the end of summer = completed past event → GREW almost two metres tall.

questions.stem: Grandmother ________ the tomato seedlings when a sudden downpour flooded the pots.
questions.trap_type: 'A sudden downpour flooded the pots' is the sudden interrupting event. Grandmother was already repotting = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The downpour FLOODED the pots = sudden past event. Grandmother was already repotting at that moment = WAS REPOTTING.

questions.stem: There ________ several caterpillars eating the lettuce leaves in the garden this morning.
questions.trap_type: 'Several caterpillars' = plural. 'This morning' = present context. Plural + present = are.
questions.learning_tip: 'Several caterpillars' = plural. Present context → THERE ARE several caterpillars in the garden this morning.

questions.stem: You planted those seeds last Monday, ________ you?
questions.trap_type: The main clause is positive past ('planted') → the question tag must be negative. 'Planted' = past simple → auxiliary 'did'. Negative tag = didn't.
questions.learning_tip: Question tag for positive simple past: [positive statement] + DIDN'T + subject? 'You PLANTED those seeds, DIDN'T you?' Positive → negative tag; past → 'did'.

questions.stem: These herbs are very easy to grow indoors, ________ they?
questions.trap_type: The main clause is positive present ('are') → the question tag must be negative. 'These herbs are' = plural present → negative tag = aren't.
questions.learning_tip: Question tag for 'These herbs ARE': positive present plural → negative tag = AREN'T. 'These herbs ARE easy to grow, AREN'T they?'

questions.stem: The herbs ________ by children in the community garden with guidance from volunteer gardeners.
questions.trap_type: 'Herbs' = plural. Present regular process. Passive = are planted. Students write 'is planted' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: 'Herbs' = plural + present passive → ARE PLANTED. Passive = am/is/are + past participle. Plural subject = ARE.

questions.stem: The horticulture teacher told the students ________ the seedlings too often or the roots would rot.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told someone not to do something = told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told students NOT TO + base verb': told the students NOT TO WATER the seedlings too often.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Prepositions: by, with, without, from, to, of, for, about)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'My uncle taught me everything I know (1)________ gardening.' Signal: 'taught me everything about' = the topic or subject matter = ABOUT. 'Know ABOUT gardening' = concerning the topic of gardening.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'of' instead of 'about'. 'Know ABOUT' = concerning a topic; 'know OF' = know that something exists, which is different.
questions.learning_tip: ABOUT = concerning a topic. 'Know ABOUT gardening' = have knowledge concerning gardening. 'About' shows the subject of the knowledge.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'He digs the soil (2)________ a long-handled spade each morning.' Signal: using a tool = WITH. 'Digs WITH a spade' = the spade is the tool used.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'by' instead of 'with'. 'By' shows method in passive sentences; 'with' shows the physical tool being used.
questions.learning_tip: WITH = using a physical tool or instrument. He digs WITH a spade = he uses the spade to dig. 'With' shows what tool is being used.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'He propagates new plants (3)________ taking cuttings from healthy stems.' Signal: method or means in an active sentence = BY. 'BY taking cuttings' = the method he uses.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'with' instead of 'by'. 'With' is for tools; 'by' shows the method or process used to achieve something.
questions.learning_tip: BY = the method or process used. He propagates plants BY taking cuttings = the method he uses is taking cuttings. 'By' + verb-ing shows how something is done.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'A cactus can survive (4)________ water for weeks because it stores moisture in its thick stems.' Signal: in the absence of something = WITHOUT. 'Survive WITHOUT water' = in the absence of water.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'from' (source) or 'for' (duration). 'Without' = in the absence of something.
questions.learning_tip: WITHOUT = in the absence of something. A cactus can survive WITHOUT water = it does not need water the way other plants do.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The seeds he plants come (5)________ all over the world.' Signal: origin or source = FROM. 'Come FROM all over the world' = their origin is different countries.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'of' instead of 'from'. 'Come FROM' = originating from a place; 'of' shows membership or composition.
questions.learning_tip: FROM = showing origin or source. The seeds come FROM all over the world = they originate from many different countries.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The smell (6)________ jasmine fills the garden every evening at dusk.' Signal: belonging or association = OF. 'The smell OF jasmine' = the smell that belongs to / comes from jasmine.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'from' instead of 'of'. 'The smell OF something' is the fixed noun phrase; 'of' shows association/belonging.
questions.learning_tip: OF = showing belonging or association. 'The smell OF jasmine' = the smell belonging to / characteristic of jasmine. 'Smell of' is a fixed phrase.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'My uncle has been gardening (7)________ over thirty years.' Signal: duration of time in present perfect context = FOR. 'Gardening FOR over thirty years' = the length of time he has been doing it.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'since' (not in the box) or 'of' instead of 'for'. FOR is used with a duration of time in present perfect sentences.
questions.learning_tip: FOR + duration of time: gardening FOR over thirty years = the length of time he has been doing it. FOR shows how long something has lasted.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'He donates fresh vegetables (8)________ the elderly residents in our neighbourhood every week.' Signal: recipient of an action = TO. 'Donates TO someone' = giving direction toward a recipient.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'for' instead of 'to'. 'Donate TO someone' = the person who receives; 'for' would show purpose, not recipient.
questions.learning_tip: TO = showing the recipient of an action. He donates vegetables TO the elderly residents = they are the ones who receive the vegetables.

C.passage: My uncle taught me everything I know (1)________ gardening. He digs the soil (2)________ a long-handled spade each morning before the sun gets too strong. He propagates new plants (3)________ taking cuttings from healthy stems and placing them in water until roots appear. He told me that a cactus can survive (4)________ water for weeks because it stores moisture in its thick stems. The seeds he plants come (5)________ all over the world — from Japan, India and South America. The smell (6)________ jasmine fills the garden every evening at dusk and makes the whole compound feel peaceful. My uncle has been gardening (7)________ over thirty years. Every week, he donates fresh vegetables (8)________ the elderly residents in our neighbourhood.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: A garden needs careful attention all year round. The best soil is (1)________ — rich in nutrients that feed plant roots. Gardeners often add organic material to help seeds (2)________ and push through the earth. Once a young (3)________ appears above the soil, it needs regular water and light to grow. Many plants depend on insects like bees to (4)________ them, carrying pollen between flowers. After months of care, gardeners enjoy the (5)________, picking ripe fruit and vegetables to eat or share.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'seeds need warmth and moisture' and 'tiny shoot pushes through the soil' = the process of a seed beginning to grow = germinate.
questions.learning_tip: GERMINATE = begin to grow from a seed. A seed GERMINATES when warmth, moisture and light trigger the first shoots to appear.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'young plant' and 'moved into a bigger pot as it grows stronger' = a young plant just sprouted from a seed = seedling.
questions.learning_tip: A SEEDLING = a very young plant that has just sprouted from a seed. SEEDLINGS are moved to larger pots as they grow.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'carrying pollen from one flower to another, which helps fruits to form' = the process of transferring pollen = pollinate.
questions.learning_tip: POLLINATE = transfer pollen from one flower to another to enable fertilisation and fruit formation. Bees POLLINATE flowers as they collect nectar.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'picking the ripe ones' after three months of growth = collecting crops at the right time = harvest.
questions.learning_tip: HARVEST = collect crops when they are ripe and ready to eat. HARVESTING vegetables means picking them at the right time.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'from kitchen waste such as vegetable peels... mixed into the soil to give extra nutrients' = decayed organic material used as fertiliser = compost.
questions.learning_tip: COMPOST = decayed organic material made from food waste and plant matter, used to enrich soil. COMPOST improves soil quality and feeds plants naturally.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Adverb required after action verb (pruned)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'careful' (adjective) after the action verb 'pruned'. A verb needs an adverb to describe how the action was done.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (pruned), use an ADVERB: pruned CAREFULLY. 'Careful' is an adjective — it describes nouns, not actions.

questions.error_type: Irregular plural — leaf → leaves (f → ves)
questions.trap_type: Students add -s to 'leaf', producing 'leafs'. Words ending in -f often change to -ves in the plural.
questions.learning_tip: 'Leaf' follows the -f → -ves rule: leaf → LEAVES. Same pattern: knife → knives, half → halves, loaf → loaves.

questions.error_type: Spelling — sprinkling (not sprinckling)
questions.trap_type: Students insert an extra 'c' in 'sprinkling', writing 'sprinckling'. The word comes from 'sprinkle' + -ing (drop silent e).
questions.learning_tip: 'Sprinkle' ends in silent -e: drop -e and add -ing → SPRINKLING. No extra 'c'. Spell it: s-p-r-i-n-k-l-i-n-g.

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the sunflowers)
questions.trap_type: 'The sunflowers' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: 'The sunflowers' = plural → WERE all facing east. WAS is only for singular subjects.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (gardeners', not gardeners's)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'gardeners's' adding an extra 's' after the apostrophe. For a plural noun ending in -s, add only an apostrophe.
questions.learning_tip: Plural possessive for nouns ending in -s: add only an apostrophe after the -s: the GARDENERS' tools = the tools belonging to the gardeners (plural).

E.passage: Last Saturday, we visited a community garden near the market. A volunteer pruned the rose bushes careful (1), removing all the dead branches near the base. We also noticed that some of the leafs (2) were eaten by insects. Another volunteer was sprinckling (3) water gently over the young seedlings in the shade house. By midday, the sunflowers was (4) all facing east, tracking the movement of the sun. We were shown the gardeners's (5) toolshed, which was filled with rakes, hoses and bags of fertiliser.

questions.sentence_a: She waters her plants every day.
questions.sentence_b: She will have a beautiful garden in spring.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'If'.
questions.model_answer: If she waters her plants every day, she will have a beautiful garden in spring.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'If she will water her plants every day, she will have a beautiful garden' — incorrectly adding 'will' in the 'if' clause.
questions.learning_tip: Conditional: IF + simple present, simple future. If she WATERS her plants, she WILL HAVE a beautiful garden. Never 'will' in the 'if' clause.

questions.sentence_a: The gardener planted a row of sunflowers.
questions.sentence_b: The sunflowers brighten up the whole neighbourhood.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using the relative pronoun 'which'.
questions.model_answer: The gardener planted a row of sunflowers, which brighten up the whole neighbourhood.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'The gardener planted a row of sunflowers which they brighten up the neighbourhood' — adding 'they' after 'which'.
questions.learning_tip: Use 'which' to add information about a THING. The gardener planted sunflowers, WHICH brighten up the neighbourhood. Do NOT add 'they' after 'which'.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
When the principal of Greenfield Primary announced that an unused rooftop would be turned into a garden, the students were curious but unconvinced. 'What is the point of growing vegetables at school?' one student asked.

By the end of the year, those same students could not imagine school without it.

The project began in January with the students digging compost into large planters and sowing seeds of spinach, chilli and cherry tomatoes. At first, progress was slow and some seeds did not sprout at all. But by March, the rooftop had green shoots pushing upward from every planter.

The garden changed the way many students thought about food. Before the project, several admitted they had never thought about where vegetables came from. After growing them, they paid more attention to what they ate and wasted far less food at lunch.

The garden also brought students together. Children from different classes worked side by side during gardening sessions, learning each other's names. A boy named Darren, who had previously kept to himself, became one of the most active gardeners. By the end of the year, he made three close friends through the garden.

In December, the students organised a small harvest festival. They cooked a simple vegetable soup using everything they grew, and invited parents and teachers to join them.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 1 has the same meaning as 'full of enthusiasm and interest'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Curious' = wanting to know; 'confused' = not understanding; 'satisfied' = content. EAGER = full of enthusiasm and keen to do something.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: EAGER = showing keenness and enthusiasm. The students were EAGER = they were enthusiastic and ready to begin. Look for word clues: 'full of enthusiasm' = EAGER.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'this' refer to in 'None of them expected this'?

options.1: The arrival of the gardening tools
options.2: That their plants would grow so quickly and produce real vegetables to eat
options.3: The instruction to water the plants every day
options.4: That Darren would become interested in the garden

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'this' = the tools. But the paragraph shows surprise at the actual results — real food growing from their work.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'THIS' refers to the nearest previous idea. In paragraph 3, 'this' = the fact that their plants actually GREW and produced real vegetables — an unexpected outcome.

mcq_questions.stem: What does Darren's story in paragraph 5 suggest about the garden's effect on students?

options.1: The garden was only useful for students who were already interested in nature.
options.2: The garden helped students who struggled academically improve their grades.
options.3: The garden could bring out new strengths in students who seemed quiet or withdrawn.
options.4: The garden was most useful for teaching students how to cook.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 2 thinking the garden helped grades. The passage focuses on Darren's social transformation, not academics.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: INFERENCE: Darren 'kept to himself' (shy/withdrawn) but became 'one of the most active gardeners' (social, engaged). The garden BROUGHT OUT NEW STRENGTHS in a quiet student.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that the students immediately knew how to grow vegetables when the project started? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says the students were eager but curious — they had not grown vegetables before and needed to learn from scratch.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, they were eager.' Being eager is not the same as already knowing how.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: EAGER = wanting to try. 'Curious' = wanting to find out. Both words show the students did NOT already know — they were learning for the first time. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did the students learn about food from growing their own vegetables?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: They learned where food comes from and began to pay more attention to what they ate.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe only the effect without identifying the cause, or give only general statements.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: CAUSE = they GREW the vegetables themselves and understood where food comes from. EFFECT = they paid more attention to what they ate and WASTED FAR LESS FOOD. Link cause to effect clearly.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did the garden change Darren? Give TWO specific details from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) Darren had previously kept to himself, but the garden made him one of the most active gardeners. (ii) By the end of the year, he made three close friends through the garden.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he became happier' without referencing specific details from the passage.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: (1) he went from 'keeping to himself' to being one of the MOST ACTIVE gardeners; (2) he made THREE CLOSE FRIENDS through gardening. Both details are explicit.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did the students use the vegetables from the garden in December?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: They cooked a simple vegetable soup using everything from the garden and invited parents and teachers to join them.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'they had a celebration' without describing what they did with the vegetables.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 6: they cooked VEGETABLE SOUP using everything from the garden and invited PARENTS and teachers to join them at the harvest festival.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on the passage, describe TWO character traits of the students who joined the gardening club. Give evidence for each.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) PERSISTENT: the students kept tending their plants through all seasons — from planting in January to harvesting in December — showing they did not give up even when progress was slow. (ii) CARING: they used their harvest to cook soup for parents and teachers, showing they wanted to share the results of their work with others.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'hardworking and kind' without precise traits or evidence. Name the trait and then give specific textual evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: Name the trait + give evidence from the passage. PERSISTENT = kept going for a full year. CARING = cooked for others. Trait + Evidence = full marks.

questions.stem: The princess ________ a deep sleep for one hundred years until the prince arrived.
questions.trap_type: 'Entered' is too general; 'avoided' and 'refused' are the opposite of sleeping. Only 'slumbered' = slept deeply and peacefully.
questions.learning_tip: SLUMBERED = slept deeply and peacefully, often for a long time. In fairy tales, enchanted characters SLUMBER for many years.

questions.stem: The dragon's roar echoed through the valley, as ________ as rolling thunder across a stormy sky.
questions.trap_type: 'Quiet' and 'soft' are opposites of thunder's sound. 'Swift' = fast, not relating to sound. LOUD = making a great amount of sound.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The dragon's roar was AS LOUD AS rolling thunder = comparing its sound to a thunderstorm. Similes always use 'as ... as' to compare two different things directly.

questions.stem: The brave knight ________ the fierce dragon with a sharp sword to rescue the village.
questions.trap_type: 'Fled from' means ran away from; 'admired' is a positive feeling; 'invited' is friendly. Only 'defeated' = overcame in battle.
questions.learning_tip: DEFEATED = overcame an opponent in a fight or contest. The knight DEFEATED the dragon = won the battle against it.

questions.stem: The young knight lived ________ after defeating the dragon and rescuing the village.

options.4: at the drop of a hat

questions.trap_type: 'Out of the blue' = unexpectedly; 'under the weather' = feeling ill; 'at the drop of a hat' = immediately. HAPPILY EVER AFTER = a fairy tale ending of permanent happiness.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: HAPPILY EVER AFTER = a life of permanent happiness, especially at the end of a fairy tale. 'He lived HAPPILY EVER AFTER' = he was happy for the rest of his life. This idiom comes from classic fairy tales!

questions.stem: The young hero had to ________ the dragon's lair and rescue the princess before sunrise.
questions.trap_type: 'Run away from' = flee; 'give up on' = stop trying; 'look up to' = admire. BREAK INTO = enter a place by force.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: BREAK INTO = enter a place by force or without permission. The hero had to BREAK INTO the lair = he forced his way in. BREAK + INTO work together — never separate them!

questions.stem: Nobody in the fairy tale ________ that the old woman at the door is actually a powerful enchantress.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'know' thinking 'nobody in the fairy tale' = many people. NOBODY = singular → verb+S in present tense.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / SOMEONE = Singular! Always use verb+S in present tense. Nobody KNOWS = add -S. 'Nobody know' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns take singular verbs.

questions.stem: The miller's daughter ________ the strange little man's riddle and broke the curse.
questions.trap_type: The story is set in the past. 'Solve' is regular: solve → solved.
questions.learning_tip: The fairy tale is told in the past. 'Solve' is regular: solve → SOLVED. She SOLVED the riddle = completed the action in the past.

questions.stem: The three bears ________ their porridge when Goldilocks crept into their cottage.
questions.trap_type: 'Goldilocks crept into the cottage' is the sudden interrupting event. The bears were already eating = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: Goldilocks CREPT IN = sudden past event. The bears were already eating at that moment = WERE EATING (ongoing background).

questions.stem: The fairy tale ________ enjoyed by generations of children all over the world for many centuries.
questions.trap_type: 'For many centuries' + implied continuation to the present = present perfect. 'The fairy tale' = singular → has been.
questions.learning_tip: 'For many centuries' (up to now) = present perfect. 'The fairy tale' = singular → HAS BEEN enjoyed. The enjoyment began long ago and continues.

questions.stem: The dragon lives in that cave over there, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Main clause is positive present simple ('lives') → negative tag. 'The dragon lives' = singular present simple → auxiliary 'does'. Negative tag = doesn't.
questions.learning_tip: Question tag for positive simple present singular: [positive] + DOESN'T + subject? The dragon LIVES there, DOESN'T it? Positive → negative tag; present simple → does.

questions.stem: The children were not frightened by the giant's roar, ________ they?
questions.trap_type: Main clause is NEGATIVE past ('were not') → question tag must be POSITIVE. 'They were not' → positive tag = were they.
questions.learning_tip: Question tag for negative past: [negative statement] + WERE + subject? The children WERE NOT frightened, WERE they? Negative statement → positive tag; past 'were' → 'were'.

questions.stem: The enchanted castle ________ discovered deep in the forest by the wandering prince.
questions.trap_type: The castle did not discover itself. Past passive = was discovered.
questions.learning_tip: The castle was the receiver of the action. Past passive = WAS DISCOVERED. Passive = was/were + past participle.

questions.stem: The fairy godmother told Cinderella ________ home before the clock struck midnight.
questions.trap_type: 'Told someone to do something' = reported speech: told + object + to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told Cinderella TO + base verb': told Cinderella TO RETURN home before midnight.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Reflexive pronouns)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The queen looked at (1)________ in the magic mirror and asked who was the fairest in the land.' Signal: subject = 'the queen' (female singular) + reflexive object of 'looked at' = HERSELF. The queen looked at her own reflection.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'himself' (male) or 'itself'. The queen = female singular → HERSELF.
questions.learning_tip: HERSELF = the reflexive pronoun for she/her. The queen looked at HERSELF in the mirror = looked at her own reflection.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The prince proved (2)________ worthy of the kingdom by completing the three tasks.' Signal: subject = 'the prince' (male singular) + reflexive object of 'proved' = HIMSELF. The prince proved his own worth.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'herself' (female) or 'itself'. The prince = male singular → HIMSELF.
questions.learning_tip: HIMSELF = the reflexive pronoun for he/him. The prince proved HIMSELF worthy = demonstrated his own worthiness.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The enchanted broom moved (3)________, sweeping the floor without anyone holding it.' Signal: subject = 'the broom' (thing/neuter singular) + reflexive = ITSELF. The broom moved by its own power.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'himself' or 'herself'. The broom = a thing (neuter) = ITSELF.
questions.learning_tip: ITSELF = the reflexive pronoun for it (things/animals). The broom moved ITSELF = moved by its own power without anyone touching it.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The three little pigs built their houses (4)________ without any help from their mother.' Signal: subject = 'the three little pigs' (plural, third person) + reflexive of 'built' = THEMSELVES. They did the building on their own.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'ourselves' (first person) or 'yourselves' (second person). The three pigs = third person plural → THEMSELVES.
questions.learning_tip: THEMSELVES = the reflexive pronoun for they/them (third person plural). The pigs built THEMSELVES = they did it without any outside help.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'I thought to (5)________, this wolf does not seem as frightening as the stories say.' Signal: subject = 'I' (first person singular) + reflexive of 'thought to' = MYSELF. 'I thought to myself' = an internal private thought.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'himself' or 'herself'. The speaker = 'I' = first person singular → MYSELF.
questions.learning_tip: MYSELF = the reflexive pronoun for I. 'I thought to MYSELF' = I had a private thought inside my own head. MYSELF is always used when the subject is 'I'.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The old wizard said to the young apprentice, "You must believe in (6)________ if you wish to master magic."' Signal: subject of the embedded clause = 'you' (second person singular) + reflexive = YOURSELF.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'himself' or 'itself'. The wizard speaks to 'you' = second person singular → YOURSELF.
questions.learning_tip: YOURSELF = the reflexive pronoun for you (singular). 'Believe in YOURSELF' = have confidence in your own abilities.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We found (7)________ lost deep inside the enchanted forest with no path home.' Signal: subject = 'we' (first person plural) + reflexive of 'found' = OURSELVES. We discovered our own situation.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'themselves' (third person) or 'yourself' (second person). 'We' = first person plural → OURSELVES.
questions.learning_tip: OURSELVES = the reflexive pronoun for we/us (first person plural). We found OURSELVES lost = we discovered (realised) our own situation.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The fairy said, "Now go and enjoy (8)________ at the ball before midnight strikes."' Signal: subject of the command = 'you' (second person plural — addressed to Cinderella and her helpers together) + reflexive = YOURSELVES.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'yourself' (singular) instead of 'yourselves' (plural group). The fairy addresses the whole group going to the ball → plural → YOURSELVES.
questions.learning_tip: YOURSELVES = the reflexive pronoun for you (plural group). 'Enjoy YOURSELVES' = have a good time (said to a group). YOURSELF is for one person; YOURSELVES is for more than one.

C.passage: In the fairy tale, the hero told (1)________ that he was brave enough to face the dragon alone. The princess locked (2)________ in the tower and refused to cry. The dragon stretched (3)________ out on the treasure and fell asleep. The villagers promised (4)________ they would be safe if someone defeated the beast. The king said to his knights, 'Prepare (5)________ for battle!' The youngest knight thought (6)________ 'I can do this.' The dragon could not help (7)________ admiring the knight's courage. At last, everyone allowed (8)________ to celebrate the victory with a great feast.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Fairy tales often begin with a world that is (1)________ — filled with magic, talking creatures and impossible things. Many feature a humble hero who is (2)________, meaning ordinary and not gifted with special powers. When the hero makes a brave choice, a wish may be (3)________ by a fairy or spirit. Evil characters who (4)________ into thin air are often defeated by love or honesty. These old stories have become (5)________ — tales so widely known and retold that everyone recognises them by name.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'a wish to be ___ by a magical creature' = given or fulfilled = granted.
questions.learning_tip: ENCHANTED = under a magic spell, filled with magic. An ENCHANTED world = a magical place where ordinary rules do not apply. In fairy tales, places and people are often enchanted.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'without a trace, leaving the hero alone' = disappeared suddenly and completely = vanished.
questions.learning_tip: MORTAL = an ordinary human being (not magical or immortal). A MORTAL hero = a normal person without special powers. Mortals can be hurt and can die — unlike gods or magical beings.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'ordinary rules do not apply, animals can speak and objects come to life' = under a magical spell = enchanted.
questions.learning_tip: GRANTED = officially given or approved. A wish is GRANTED = it is made to come true. In fairy tales, genies and fairies GRANT wishes. GRANT = give someone what they asked for.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'gods walk among ___ humans' = humans who can die, as opposed to immortal gods = mortal.
questions.learning_tip: VANISHED = disappeared suddenly and completely. The villain VANISHED = she was gone without a trace. VANISH = disappear; VANISHED = past tense.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'a tale so famous and retold so many times that it feels part of a culture's identity' = a legend.
questions.learning_tip: A LEGEND = a very old story that many people know and that has been told for generations. These stories become LEGENDS = they are so famous that everyone knows them.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Adverb required after action verb (roared)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'fierce' (adjective) after the action verb 'roared'. A verb needs an adverb to describe how the action was done.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (roared), use an ADVERB: roared FIERCELY. 'Fierce' is an adjective — it describes nouns, not actions.

questions.error_type: Irregular plural — ox → oxen
questions.trap_type: Students add -es to 'ox', producing 'oxes'. 'Ox' has a completely irregular plural form.
questions.learning_tip: 'Ox' has an irregular plural: ox → OXEN. Never write 'oxes'. Other irregular plurals: child → children, goose → geese.

questions.error_type: Spelling — -ing rule: silent -e is dropped before -ing
questions.trap_type: Students keep the final -e when adding -ing to 'make', producing 'makeing'. Drop the silent -e before adding -ing.
questions.learning_tip: 'Make' ends in silent -e: drop the -e before adding -ing → MAKING. Same rule: write → writing, ride → riding, give → giving.

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the villagers)
questions.trap_type: 'The villagers' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: 'The villagers' = plural → WERE frightened. WAS is only for singular subjects.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — irregular plural possessive (heroes', not hero's's)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'hero's's' confusing singular and plural possessives. The plural of 'hero' is 'heroes'. Plural possessive of heroes = heroes' (apostrophe after s).
questions.learning_tip: 'Hero' → plural = 'heroes'. Plural possessive = HEROES' (add apostrophe after the -s). 'Hero's' is the singular possessive. 'Heroes's' and 'hero's's' are both wrong.

E.passage: Once upon a time, a dragon lived on a hill above a small village. Every night, it roared fierce (1) and blew flames into the sky. The farmer who lived nearest to the hill used his two oxes (2) to plough the fields far away from the dragon. A travelling blacksmith began makeing (3) a special suit of armour to protect the village hero. The villagers was (4) so frightened that nobody dared leave their homes after dark. At last, the two hero's's (5) journey to the dragon's lair ended in a great victory, and peace returned to the valley.

questions.sentence_a: The princess touched the spindle.
questions.sentence_b: She immediately fell into a deep sleep.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'As soon as'.
questions.model_answer: As soon as the princess touched the spindle, she immediately fell into a deep sleep.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'The princess touched the spindle as soon as she immediately fell' — reversing the order.
questions.learning_tip: AS SOON AS + [the trigger], [the immediate result]. AS SOON AS the princess TOUCHED the spindle, she FELL into a deep sleep. The trigger comes after 'as soon as'.

questions.sentence_a: Jack climbed the beanstalk.
questions.sentence_b: The beanstalk reached all the way up to the giant's castle.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using the relative pronoun 'which'.
questions.model_answer: Jack climbed the beanstalk, which reached all the way up to the giant's castle.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'Jack climbed the beanstalk which it reached all the way up to the giant's castle' — adding 'it' after 'which'.
questions.learning_tip: Use 'which' to add information about a THING. Jack climbed the beanstalk, WHICH reached up to the giant's castle. Do NOT add 'it' after 'which'.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Long ago, a poor fisherman caught a golden fish in his net. The fish spoke in a clear, calm voice. 'Release me,' it said, 'and I will grant you one wish.'

The fisherman thought carefully. His family needed many things — a better boat, a larger house, enough food for winter. But instead, he made a simple request. 'I wish for my daughter to be healed,' he said, 'for she has been unwell for three years.'

The golden fish was quiet for a moment. Then it said, 'Your wish is granted.' The fish slipped back into the sea and disappeared.

When the fisherman returned home, his daughter was sitting up in bed, her cheeks pink and her eyes bright. She smiled when she saw him and said she felt better since noon.

The fisherman's neighbours were astonished. They asked him how he had managed it. He told them about the golden fish.

'You wasted the wish!' one neighbour said. 'You could have asked for gold, or a palace!'

The fisherman simply shook his head. He had no regrets.

Years later, when his daughter grew up to be a kind and generous woman, everyone in the village agreed that the fisherman made the wisest choice of all.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'shining with a golden light'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Enormous' = very large; 'trembling' = shaking; 'ancient' = very old. GLEAMING = shining with a steady golden or silver light.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: GLEAMING = shining brightly with a soft, golden light. The fish was GLEAMING = it gave off a beautiful golden glow. GLEAM = shine; GLEAMING = currently shining.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'he knew it was the right choice'?

options.2: His decision to wish for his daughter's health rather than wealth
options.3: The fishing rod he used to catch the fish

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'it' = the fish. But 'it' refers to the fisherman's decision — the choice he made.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PRONOUN REFERENCE: 'IT' refers to the fisherman's DECISION — the choice he made to wish for his daughter's health. The paragraph says 'he thought for a long time, then he knew IT was the right choice.' IT = his decision.

mcq_questions.stem: Why did the neighbours say the fisherman had wasted his wish?

options.1: Because they thought he should have wished for more fish.
options.2: Because they believed gold and palaces were more valuable than a person's health.
options.3: Because they did not know his daughter was ill.
options.4: Because they thought the golden fish would grant more wishes later.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking they wanted more fish. The passage says they suggested gold or a palace — material things.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph text: neighbours said 'he could have asked for GOLD or a PALACE.' They valued material wealth over health — showing they measured the wish's worth by money, not love.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that the fisherman caught the golden fish on purpose? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says the fisherman cast his net as usual and was surprised when something golden appeared — he did not go looking for a magical fish.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, he caught it.' He caught it by accident, not on purpose.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: The fisherman cast his net 'as usual' = his normal routine. He was SURPRISED when the golden fish appeared. If he planned it, the passage would say so. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did the fisherman's neighbours say when they heard about the wish he made?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: They said he had wasted the wish and that he could have asked for gold or a palace.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'they were surprised' without quoting what they actually said.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 6: 'You WASTED the wish! You could have asked for GOLD, or a palace!' Quote the specific reaction, not just describe it.

open_ended_questions.stem: What was the CAUSE of the daughter's recovery, and what was the EFFECT it had on the fisherman when he returned home?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: CAUSE: The golden fish granted the fisherman's wish for his daughter to be healed. EFFECT: When the fisherman returned home, his daughter was sitting up in bed with pink cheeks and bright eyes, smiling — she had recovered fully.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe only the daughter's recovery without explaining what caused it.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: CAUSE = the golden fish GRANTED the wish. EFFECT = the daughter was SITTING UP in bed, cheeks pink, eyes bright, smiling. Link the cause (the wish) clearly to the effect (her recovery).

open_ended_questions.stem: Find ONE phrase from the last paragraph that shows the fisherman was satisfied with his decision.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: 'He had no regrets.'
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students quote from an earlier paragraph about the wish itself instead of the end of the passage.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 7: 'He had NO REGRETS.' This phrase directly tells us he was completely satisfied with the choice he made.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his actions in the passage, describe TWO character traits of the fisherman with evidence from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) SELFLESS: when given a rare wish, the fisherman chose his daughter's health over wealth for himself — showing he put others' needs before his own. (ii) WISE: he ignored his neighbours' mocking and stayed firm in his decision, knowing that health and love matter more than gold.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'kind and brave' without precise traits or evidence from the passage.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: Name the trait + give evidence. SELFLESS = chose daughter's health over gold. WISE = ignored mockers and held firm. Trait + Evidence from passage = full marks.

questions.stem: The boy ________ the notice board for any message about his missing bicycle but found nothing.
questions.trap_type: 'Ignored' means paid no attention; 'decorated' means added ornaments; 'removed' means took away. Only 'scanned' = looked quickly across a surface to find something specific.
questions.learning_tip: SCANNED = looked quickly across something to find specific information. He SCANNED the notice board = looked rapidly for any relevant message.

questions.stem: The lost kitten ________ under the staircase for two days before a neighbour found it.
questions.trap_type: 'Paraded' means walked proudly; 'galloped' = ran fast; 'scattered' = spread in different directions. Only 'huddled' = crouched close together for warmth or safety.
questions.learning_tip: HUDDLED = crouched or pressed close together in a small space, often for warmth or safety. The lost kitten HUDDLED under the stairs = curled up tightly in a small space.

questions.stem: Finding the owner of a lost wallet in a crowded city is like looking for a ________ — almost impossible without a clue.
questions.trap_type: 'A piece of cake' = something easy (opposite meaning); 'fish in water' = comfortable; 'drop in the ocean' = a tiny amount. NEEDLE IN A HAYSTACK = something almost impossible to find.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: A NEEDLE IN A HAYSTACK = something extremely difficult to find because it is hidden among many other things. Finding a lost owner is 'like A NEEDLE IN A HAYSTACK' = almost impossible. Idioms cannot be understood word by word!

questions.stem: The lost puppy's face was as ________ as a wilted flower — tired, drooping and in need of care.
questions.trap_type: 'Fierce' = aggressive; 'cheerful' = happy (opposite); 'alert' = watchful. FORLORN = appearing sad and abandoned.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The puppy's face was AS FORLORN AS a wilted flower = comparing its sad, drooping look to a flower that has not been watered. FORLORN = pitifully sad and lonely.

questions.stem: After finding the wallet on the bus, the honest girl decided to ________ it at the nearest police station.
questions.trap_type: 'Throw away' = discard; 'run off with' = steal; 'leave behind' = abandon. HAND IN = give something to someone in authority.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: HAND IN = give something to a person in authority (teacher, police, lost property office). She HANDED IN the wallet = she gave it to the police. HAND + IN work together — this means to submit or surrender something officially.

questions.stem: Someone in this class ________ a water bottle in the canteen every single week.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'leave' thinking 'someone in class' = many people. SOMEONE = singular → verb+S in present tense.
questions.learning_tip: SOMEONE / EVERYONE / NOBODY / ANYONE = Singular! Always use verb+S. Someone LEAVES = add -S. 'Someone leave' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns always take singular present-tense verbs.

questions.stem: Ravi ________ his school pass somewhere between the canteen and the library last Thursday.
questions.trap_type: 'Last Thursday' = past. 'Lose' is irregular: lose → lost.
questions.learning_tip: 'Lose' is irregular: lose → LOST. 'Last Thursday' = past → LOST his school pass.

questions.stem: The teacher ________ the classroom for the missing scissors when a student found them in her own bag.
questions.trap_type: 'A student found them in her bag' is the sudden interrupting event. The teacher was already searching = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The student FOUND them = sudden past event. The teacher was already searching at that moment = WAS SEARCHING (ongoing background).

questions.stem: The lost wallet ________ to the owner by a kind student who found it in the school field.
questions.trap_type: The wallet did not return itself — the student returned it. Past passive = was returned.
questions.learning_tip: The wallet was the receiver of the action. Past passive = WAS RETURNED. Passive = was/were + past participle.

questions.stem: The library book was not where you left it, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Main clause is NEGATIVE past ('was not') → question tag must be POSITIVE. 'Was not' → positive tag = was.
questions.learning_tip: Question tag for negative past: [negative statement] + WAS + subject? The book WAS NOT there, WAS it? Negative → positive tag; past 'was' → 'was'.

questions.stem: You have handed in all the found items to the general office, ________ you?
questions.trap_type: Main clause is positive present perfect ('have handed') → negative tag. 'You have' → negative tag = haven't you.
questions.learning_tip: Question tag for positive present perfect: [positive] + HAVEN'T + subject? 'You HAVE handed in the items, HAVEN'T you?' Positive → negative tag; 'have' → 'haven't'.

questions.stem: There ________ no trace of the missing child's backpack anywhere near the playground.
questions.trap_type: 'No trace' = singular uncountable concept. Past event. Students write 'were' thinking of multiple items.
questions.learning_tip: 'No trace' = singular uncountable concept. Past event → THERE WAS no trace of the backpack.

questions.stem: The general office assistant told students ________ their names and class when handing in lost items.
questions.trap_type: 'Told someone to do something' = reported speech: told + object + to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told students TO + base verb': told students TO WRITE their names and class on a slip before handing in items.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Verb forms of 'find')

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Siti enjoys (1)________ lost objects and returning them to their owners.' Signal: 'enjoys + ___' = gerund (verb-ing). Pattern: enjoy + verb-ing → finding.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'to find' instead of the gerund after 'enjoys'.
questions.learning_tip: ENJOY + verb-ing: enjoys FINDING lost objects. After 'enjoys', always add -ING.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'She always (2)________ something interesting in the school's lost and found box every week.' Signal: 'always' = regular habit = simple present. Subject 'She' = singular → finds.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'find' (plural form) forgetting that 'She' is singular.
questions.learning_tip: 'Always' = a regular habit = simple present. She (singular) → FINDS something interesting every week.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Last Monday, she (3)________ a wallet with over fifty dollars and a student ID card inside.' Signal: 'Last Monday' = past. 'Find' is irregular: find → found.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'finded', not knowing 'find' is irregular.
questions.learning_tip: 'Last Monday' = past. 'Find' is irregular: find → FOUND. Never write 'finded'.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'While she (4)________ the owner's contact number, the student arrived at the office himself.' Signal: 'While she ___' = ongoing background action in the past. Subject 'she' = singular → was finding. Interrupted by 'the student arrived'.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'found' (simple past) missing the ongoing signal 'while she'.
questions.learning_tip: 'While she ___' = ongoing background past action = past continuous. She WAS FINDING the contact number when the student arrived.
