open_ended_questions.model_answer: She said it was strong and dark, with a sweetness that crept in at the end.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'it tasted very good' which is too vague.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 7: 'It was STRONG AND DARK, with a SWEETNESS that crept in at the end.' Use the specific words from the passage.

open_ended_questions.stem: What was the CAUSE of the journalist's visit to Uncle Beng's stall? What EFFECT did drinking the coffee have on her?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: CAUSE: The journalist was writing an article about the last of Singapore's traditional kopi stallholders, so she came to interview Uncle Beng. EFFECT: She drank the coffee slowly and found it unlike anything she had tasted in a modern café — it was strong and dark with a sweetness at the end, suggesting it deeply impressed her.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe only one of the two required elements.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: CAUSE: she was writing an ARTICLE about traditional kopi stallholders. EFFECT: she found the coffee UNLIKE anything in a modern café — it impressed her deeply.

open_ended_questions.stem: What does Uncle Beng's answer about his daughter tell us about the future of his coffee stall?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: It shows that Uncle Beng is passing down his skills to his daughter, so the stall and its traditions are likely to continue after him.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he has a daughter' without explaining what this means for the stall's future.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Last paragraph: 'My DAUGHTER IS LEARNING — she starts at five every morning.' This shows the tradition is being passed on = the stall will likely CONTINUE.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his words and actions in the passage, describe TWO character traits of Uncle Beng with evidence from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Uncle Beng is a calm and proud craftsman. Firstly, his calmness is shown when the journalist asked if he worried about old traditions disappearing — he simply poured the coffee with a 'steady hand' and gave a thoughtful, unhurried answer, showing he was not anxious. Secondly, his pride in his craft is shown when he said 'real kopi will always find its people' — he was confident in the value of what he made and did not feel threatened by modern trends.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say he is 'kind and old' without naming precise character traits or giving specific evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Name precise TRAITS then give EVIDENCE: (1) CALM — poured coffee with a STEADY HAND and gave an unhurried answer; (2) PROUD — confidently said 'real kopi will always find its people'.

questions.stem: The young chess player showed remarkable ________ by defeating a player three times her age.
questions.trap_type: 'Weakness', 'boredom' and 'carelessness' are all negative. Only 'aptitude' = a natural ability or talent for something.
questions.learning_tip: APTITUDE = a natural ability or talent for something. She showed great APTITUDE for chess = she had a natural skill that was apparent very early.

questions.stem: The musician ________ on her debut album for two years before releasing it to the public.
questions.trap_type: 'Gave up' = stopped; 'ignored' = paid no attention; 'scattered' = spread. Only 'laboured' = worked hard and persistently over a long period.
questions.learning_tip: LABOURED = worked very hard and for a long time on something. She LABOURED on her album for two years = put in great sustained effort.

questions.stem: The ballet dancer's performance left the audience ________, unable to look away for even a moment.
questions.trap_type: 'Bored', 'confused' and 'distracted' all suggest negative or disengaged reactions. Only 'spellbound' = completely captivated and transfixed.
questions.learning_tip: SPELLBOUND = so fascinated or captivated that you cannot look away. A great performance leaves the audience SPELLBOUND.

questions.stem: Lena ________ her natural talent for design by studying architecture at university.
questions.trap_type: 'Wasted', 'hid' and 'ignored' are all opposite to developing a talent. Only 'pursued' = followed and worked towards something with determination.
questions.learning_tip: PURSUED = followed or worked towards something with determination and effort. She PURSUED her talent = studied and developed it further rather than ignoring it.

questions.stem: The young scientist's discovery was so ________ that it appeared in a leading international journal.
questions.trap_type: 'Trivial', 'forgettable' and 'ordinary' all suggest unimportance. Only 'groundbreaking' = completely new and revolutionary.
questions.learning_tip: GROUNDBREAKING = completely new and innovative, changing the way people think about something. A GROUNDBREAKING discovery changes existing knowledge.

questions.stem: Every year, the school ________ a talent showcase to give students a platform to share their gifts.
questions.trap_type: 'Every year' = regular habit = simple present. 'The school' is singular → verb needs -s.
questions.learning_tip: 'Every year' = regular habit = simple present. The school (singular) → HOLDS a talent showcase.

questions.stem: The young writer ________ her first short story and submitted it to a national competition.
questions.trap_type: Completed past action. 'Complete' is regular: complete → completed.
questions.learning_tip: Completed past action. 'Complete' is regular: complete → COMPLETED. She completed and submitted.

questions.stem: The young chef ________ a new dish when the restaurant critic walked in unexpectedly.
questions.trap_type: 'The critic walked in unexpectedly' = sudden interrupting event. The chef was already preparing = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The critic WALKED IN = sudden past event. The chef was already preparing at that moment = WAS PREPARING.

questions.stem: The school has never produced a student of this calibre before, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Main clause is NEGATIVE present perfect ('has never') → POSITIVE tag. 'Has never' → positive tag = has it.
questions.learning_tip: Question tag for negative present perfect: [negative] + HAS + subject? 'The school HAS NEVER produced such a student, HAS it?' Negative → positive tag.

questions.stem: The portrait of the young artist was stunning, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Main clause is positive past ('was stunning') → negative tag. 'Was' → wasn't.
questions.learning_tip: Question tag for positive past: [positive] + WASN'T + subject? The portrait WAS stunning, WASN'T it? Positive → negative tag.

questions.stem: There ________ a great deal of applause when the young violinist finished her performance.
questions.trap_type: 'A great deal of applause' = singular uncountable. Past event → was.
questions.learning_tip: 'A great deal of applause' = one singular amount of applause. Past event → THERE WAS a great deal of applause.

questions.stem: The lead role in the school musical ________ to the student with the strongest voice and best stage presence.
questions.trap_type: The role was given (passive). Past passive = was given.
questions.learning_tip: The lead role was the receiver of the action. Past passive = WAS GIVEN. Passive = was/were + past participle.

questions.stem: The mentor told the aspiring writer ________ every rejection as a lesson rather than a failure.
questions.trap_type: Reported speech: told + object + to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told the writer TO + base verb': told the writer TO TREAT every rejection as a lesson.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Frequency adverbs)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Great talent (1)________ requires great effort — the two go together without exception.' Signal: without exception, 100% of the time = ALWAYS. The sentence states a universal truth.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'usually' (not 100%) instead of 'always' (100%). The sentence says 'without exception' = ALWAYS.
questions.learning_tip: ALWAYS = 100% of the time, without exception. Great talent ALWAYS requires effort = there are no exceptions to this rule.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The greatest performers (2)________ stop learning, no matter how successful they become.' Signal: 0% of the time, complete negation = NEVER. 'No matter how successful' = they continue learning at all times.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'rarely' (almost never, not absolute zero) instead of 'never' (0% = absolute). 'No matter how successful' = the negation is absolute.
questions.learning_tip: NEVER = 0% of the time, absolutely not. The greatest performers NEVER stop learning = it never happens, regardless of success.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'A young person who discovers a talent early (3)________ has an advantage over those who start later.' Signal: most of the time, but not always = USUALLY. An early start is generally (not always) an advantage.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'always' (100%) which is too absolute. USUALLY = most of the time, not invariably.
questions.learning_tip: USUALLY = most of the time. An early start USUALLY gives an advantage = this is generally true, though not without exception.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Young artists (4)________ feel nervous before performing in public, even after months of practice.' Signal: more often than not, frequently but not always = OFTEN. Feeling nervous is a frequent but not universal experience.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'always' (too absolute) or 'sometimes' (less frequent). OFTEN = frequently, more often than not.
questions.learning_tip: OFTEN = frequently, more often than not. Young artists OFTEN feel nervous = it happens frequently, not just occasionally.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Despite weeks of preparation, a performer (5)________ forgets a line or misses a note on stage.' Signal: happens on some occasions but not regularly = SOMETIMES. Forgetting a line is occasional, not frequent.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'often' (more frequent) or 'rarely' (less frequent). SOMETIMES = on some occasions, neither frequent nor rare.
questions.learning_tip: SOMETIMES = on some occasions, not regularly. A performer SOMETIMES forgets a line = it happens now and then, not all the time.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Competitions (6)________ have a panel of three or five judges who score each participant.' Signal: the standard or typical arrangement = NORMALLY. Three or five judges is the standard setup.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'usually' (already used in blank 3) or 'always'. NORMALLY = in the typical or standard case.
questions.learning_tip: NORMALLY = in the typical or standard situation. Competitions NORMALLY have a panel of judges = this is the standard arrangement.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(7)________, a truly exceptional performer emerges who changes the art form entirely.' Signal: rarely, only on special occasions = OCCASIONALLY. A performer who 'changes the art form entirely' = extremely rare event.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'sometimes' (more frequent) or 'rarely'. OCCASIONALLY = infrequently, on special rare occasions.
questions.learning_tip: OCCASIONALLY = from time to time, infrequently. OCCASIONALLY a performer emerges who changes art entirely = this is a rare event that happens sometimes across generations.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'True mastery is (8)________ achieved without years of daily practice and dedication.' Signal: almost never, but not absolute zero = RARELY. True mastery without years of practice is possible in theory but almost never happens.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'never' (absolute) or 'sometimes'. RARELY = almost never, but leaving a theoretical possibility open.
questions.learning_tip: RARELY = almost never, only in exceptional cases. True mastery is RARELY achieved without years of practice = it almost never happens.

C.passage: Great talent (1)________ requires great effort — the two go together without exception. The greatest performers (2)________ stop learning, no matter how successful they become. A young person who discovers a talent early (3)________ has an advantage over those who start later. Young artists (4)________ feel nervous before performing in public, even after months of careful practice. Despite weeks of preparation, a performer (5)________ forgets a line or misses a note on stage — and that is perfectly normal. Competitions (6)________ have a panel of three or five judges who score each participant on different areas. (7)________, a truly exceptional performer emerges who changes the art form entirely and inspires a whole generation. True mastery is (8)________ achieved without years of daily practice and deep dedication.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Every student has (1)________ — the ability to grow, improve and achieve great things if given the right opportunity and support. What separates those who succeed from those who do not is often not raw talent alone, but (2)________ — the willingness to practise, to fail and to try again every single day. A good (3)________ can make a huge difference in a young person's journey. This is someone who has experience and wisdom, and who guides a student not just in skill but in character. Many schools now provide opportunities for students to (4)________ their talents through performances, science fairs and art exhibitions. Having a clear (5)________ also helps — knowing what you want to achieve gives your effort direction and purpose.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'ability to grow, improve and achieve great things' = undeveloped ability waiting to be realised = potential.
questions.learning_tip: POTENTIAL = the ability to develop, grow or succeed in the future. Every student has POTENTIAL = the capacity for growth and achievement.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'willingness to practise, to fail and to try again every single day' = sustained commitment = dedication.
questions.learning_tip: DEDICATION = strong commitment to a goal, shown through consistent effort over time. DEDICATION is practising daily even when it is hard.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'someone who has experience and wisdom, and guides a student' = a more experienced guide = mentor.
questions.learning_tip: A MENTOR = an experienced and trusted person who guides and advises someone less experienced. A good MENTOR supports your growth in skill and character.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'through performances, science fairs and art exhibitions' = to display or present talents publicly = showcase.
questions.learning_tip: SHOWCASE = display or present talents, products or ideas to an audience. Schools SHOWCASE student talents through performances and exhibitions.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'knowing what you want to achieve gives your effort direction and purpose' = a strong desire to achieve something = ambition.
questions.learning_tip: AMBITION = a strong desire to achieve something great. Having AMBITION means knowing what you want and working towards it with purpose.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Adverb required after action verb (performed)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'confident' (adjective) after the action verb 'performed'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (performed), use an ADVERB: performed CONFIDENTLY. 'Confident' is an adjective — it describes nouns, not actions.

questions.error_type: Plural — consonant + y → drop y, add -ies (story → stories)
questions.trap_type: Students add -s to 'story', producing 'storys'. When a word ends in consonant + y, change y to i and add -es.
questions.learning_tip: 'Story' ends in consonant + y → change y to i and add -es: story → STORIES. Same rule: city → cities, discovery → discoveries.

questions.error_type: Spelling — -ing rule: silent -e dropped, consonant NOT doubled for 'write'
questions.trap_type: Students double the 't' in 'writing', writing 'writting'. 'Write' ends in vowel-consonant-e: drop the e and add -ing. Do NOT double t.
questions.learning_tip: 'Write' ends in vowel-consonant-e (-i-t-e): drop the -e and add -ing → WRITING. The t is NOT doubled because the vowel before it (i) is long, not short.

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the judges)
questions.trap_type: 'The judges' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: 'The judges' = plural → WERE impressed. WAS is only for singular subjects.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (performers', not performers's)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'performers's' adding an extra 's' after the apostrophe.
questions.learning_tip: Plural possessive for nouns ending in -s: add only an apostrophe: the PERFORMERS' costumes = the costumes of all the performers. Never 'performers's'.

E.passage: At last Friday's school concert, the young dancers performed confident (1) despite rehearsing for only two weeks. The audience was moved by their talent show, which included original storys (2) told through movement. One student spent three months writting (3) the narration that was read aloud during the dance. The judges was (4) so impressed that they awarded the class a special merit prize. After the show, the performers's (5) families gathered backstage to congratulate them with flowers and cheers.

questions.sentence_a: You believe in your talent and keep working hard.
questions.sentence_b: You will achieve your ambitions one day.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'If'.
questions.model_answer: If you believe in your talent and keep working hard, you will achieve your ambitions one day.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'If you will believe in your talent, you will achieve your ambitions' — adding 'will' in the 'if' clause.
questions.learning_tip: Conditional: IF + simple present, simple future. If you BELIEVE and KEEP working, you WILL ACHIEVE. Never 'will' in the 'if' clause.

questions.sentence_a: The young chef created a dish.
questions.sentence_b: The dish impressed every judge on the panel.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using the relative pronoun 'that'.
questions.model_answer: The young chef created a dish that impressed every judge on the panel.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'The young chef created a dish that it impressed every judge' — adding 'it' after 'that'.
questions.learning_tip: Use 'that' to add information about a THING. The young chef created a dish THAT impressed every judge. Never add 'it' after 'that'.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Twelve-year-old Clara studied the cello for three years. She was good — her teacher said so — but she could never quite believe it. Every time she made a mistake in class, she felt certain everyone was judging her.

The school's annual music recital was in three weeks. This year, Clara was asked to perform a solo. She had never performed alone in front of an audience before.

For the next three weeks, she practised every evening after dinner. She played the piece hundreds of times. She made mistakes, corrected them, and made them again. Slowly, the piece became part of her.

On the night of the recital, Clara sat in the wings backstage, listening to the other performers. Her hands were cold. When her name was called, she walked to the centre of the stage.

She closed her eyes, placed her bow on the strings and played the opening note. It was long and clear. Everything else — the audience, the lights, the cold hands — seemed to fall away.

When the last note ended, there was a pause. Then the hall filled with applause.

Afterwards, her teacher came backstage. 'You played every note,' she said. 'But what I heard tonight was more than the notes.'

mcq_questions.stem: What happened IMMEDIATELY AFTER Clara walked to the centre of the stage?

options.2: Her teacher came backstage to speak with her.
options.3: She closed her eyes and placed her bow on the strings.
options.4: She sat in the wings listening to the other performers.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking the applause happened next. But the applause came AFTER she played. IMMEDIATELY after she walked on stage = she closed her eyes and began.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: 'She CLOSED HER EYES, placed her BOW ON THE STRINGS and played.' This happened immediately after she walked to centre stage.

mcq_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Clara's teacher believed she was a good student? Give a reason from the passage.
mcq_questions.model_answer: True. The passage says 'She was good — her TEACHER SAID SO.' This shows the teacher believed Clara was skilled. Clara herself was the one who doubted it.
mcq_questions.trap_type: Students say 'False, Clara was not confident' — confusing Clara's self-doubt with the teacher's view. The teacher's view is clear: 'her teacher said so.'
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: 'She was good — HER TEACHER SAID SO.' The TEACHER believed she was good. It is TRUE. Clara was the one who did not believe it — not the teacher.

mcq_questions.stem: When Clara's teacher said 'what I heard tonight was more than the notes', what did she most likely mean?

options.1: Clara had added extra notes that were not in the score.
options.2: The performance was technically perfect in every way.
options.3: Clara's playing went beyond correct notes and showed genuine feeling, courage and meaning.
options.4: The teacher was not impressed and was trying to say something politely.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 2 thinking it was about technical perfection. But 'more than the notes' means something BEYOND technique.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: 'More than the notes' = beyond technical correctness. Clara's performance showed FEELING, COURAGE and MEANING — the difference between playing notes and making music.

open_ended_questions.stem: For how long had Clara been learning the cello before the recital?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Clara studied the cello for three years.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'a long time' which is too vague.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: 'Clara had been learning the cello for THREE YEARS.' Give the exact duration stated in the passage.

open_ended_questions.stem: What was the CAUSE of Clara's nervousness before the recital? What EFFECT did playing the opening note have on her?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: CAUSE: Clara had never performed alone in front of an audience before, and she always worried that people were judging her when she made mistakes. EFFECT: When she played the opening note — long and clear — everything else seemed to fall away, meaning her nervousness disappeared and she became fully focused on the music.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe only one element without the other.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: CAUSE: she NEVER PERFORMED ALONE before + feared being judged. EFFECT: the opening note made everything FELL AWAY = her fear disappeared once she started playing.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did Clara prepare for the recital over the three weeks before it?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: She practised every evening after dinner and played the piece hundreds of times, correcting her mistakes each time.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'she practised a lot' without giving the specific details of her preparation.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: 'She practised EVERY EVENING after dinner. She played the piece HUNDREDS OF TIMES.' Give both specific details.

open_ended_questions.stem: Find ONE phrase in paragraph 5 that shows Clara was fully absorbed in her music during the performance.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: 'Everything else — the audience, the lights, the cold hands — seemed to fall away.'
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students quote 'she closed her eyes' which is preparation, not full absorption during performance.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: 'everything else — the audience, the lights, the cold hands — seemed to FALL AWAY.' This phrase means she was so absorbed in the music that nothing else existed for her.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on her actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Clara with evidence from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Clara is a diligent and resilient person. Firstly, her diligence is shown by how she prepared for the recital — she practised every evening after dinner for three weeks and played the piece hundreds of times, correcting mistakes along the way. This sustained, dedicated effort shows she was willing to work hard to be ready. Secondly, her resilience is shown on the night itself — despite cold hands and deep nervousness, she walked onto the stage, closed her eyes and played, pushing through her fear rather than giving up.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say she is 'talented and shy' without naming precise character traits or giving specific evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Name precise TRAITS then give EVIDENCE: (1) DILIGENT — practised EVERY EVENING for three weeks, HUNDREDS OF TIMES; (2) RESILIENT — walked on stage despite cold hands and nervousness, pushed through fear.

questions.stem: The bus ________ at the stop just as the students arrived, so they did not have to wait.
questions.trap_type: 'Departed' means left; 'appeared' is too vague; 'flew' is for aeroplanes. 'Pulled up' = arrived and stopped at a kerb.
questions.learning_tip: PULLED UP = arrived and came to a stop at a kerb or bus stop. The bus PULLED UP just in time for the students to board.

questions.stem: Passengers are reminded to ________ their EZ-Link cards before leaving the station to avoid an incomplete journey.
questions.trap_type: 'Tap in' is for entering; 'tap out' is for exiting — students may confuse the two phrasal verbs.
questions.learning_tip: TAP OUT = press your transit card on the reader when exiting a bus or MRT station. Always TAP OUT to end your journey correctly.

questions.stem: The train was so ________ during peak hour that passengers could barely move inside the carriage.
questions.trap_type: 'Empty', 'deserted' and 'spacious' all describe the opposite of a crowded train. PACKED = completely full of people.
questions.learning_tip: PACKED = completely full, leaving little or no space. During peak hour, MRT trains are PACKED with commuters going to work or school.

questions.stem: The elderly man looked ________ as he studied the bus route map, unsure which service to take.
questions.trap_type: 'Confident' and 'relaxed' suggest ease; 'amused' = entertained. Only 'baffled' = completely confused and unable to work something out.
questions.learning_tip: BAFFLED = completely confused and unable to understand something. The man was BAFFLED by the bus map = he could not figure it out.

questions.stem: The announcement asked all passengers to ________ to the rear of the train to allow others to board.
questions.trap_type: 'Race' implies running; 'squeeze' = push through; 'retreat' = go back in a military sense. 'Move down' = shift towards the back of a vehicle.
questions.learning_tip: MOVE DOWN = shift towards the back or far end of a vehicle to create space near the entrance. Train announcements often say 'please MOVE DOWN the carriage'.

questions.stem: Every weekday, the MRT station near our school ________ very crowded between seven and nine in the morning.
questions.trap_type: 'Every weekday' = regular habit = simple present. 'The MRT station' is singular → verb needs -s.
questions.learning_tip: 'Every weekday' = regular habit = simple present. The MRT station (singular) → BECOMES crowded during peak hours.

questions.stem: The bus ________ before we reached the stop, and we had to wait for the next one.
questions.trap_type: 'Before we reached the stop' = completed past event. 'Leave' is regular: leave → left (irregular). Students write 'leaved'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Leave' is irregular: leave → LEFT. The bus LEFT before we arrived = it departed in the past.

questions.stem: The MRT ride during rush hour is ________ crowded than the same ride at midday.
questions.trap_type: Comparing two things (rush hour vs midday) = comparative = more crowded. 'Most' is superlative (for three or more).
questions.learning_tip: COMPARATIVE (-er / more + adj) for comparing TWO things. Rush hour is MORE CROWDED than midday. Use 'more' before longer adjectives.

questions.stem: Bus 65 is ________ reliable bus on this route — it almost never arrives late.
questions.trap_type: Superlative needed (best among all buses on the route). 'The most' + adjective = superlative form for longer adjectives.
questions.learning_tip: SUPERLATIVE (the most + adj / the -est) for comparing THREE or more things. Bus 65 is THE MOST RELIABLE bus = best of all the buses on the route.

questions.stem: There was ________ space left on the train, so many passengers had to wait for the next service.
questions.trap_type: 'Space' is uncountable → use 'little' or 'much'. 'Few' and 'a few' are for countable nouns.
questions.learning_tip: LITTLE = not much (uncountable). 'Space' is uncountable → there was LITTLE space left. FEW / A FEW are only for countable nouns.

questions.stem: The ride on the new Circle Line is just ________ smooth ________ the ride on the North-South Line.
questions.trap_type: Two things being equal → 'as … as' = equal comparison. 'More … than' or 'less … than' show a difference; 'the most' is superlative.
questions.learning_tip: AS … AS = equal comparison. The ride is just AS SMOOTH AS the other line = the smoothness is the same on both.

questions.stem: The new bus interchange ________ by the transport authority last year to improve connectivity.
questions.trap_type: The interchange was built by the authority (passive). Past passive = was built.
questions.learning_tip: The interchange was the receiver of the action. Past passive = WAS BUILT. Passive = was/were + past participle.

questions.stem: The transport officer told commuters ________ their bags on the priority seats.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told commuters NOT TO + base verb': told commuters NOT TO LEAVE their bags on priority seats.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Prepositions of direction and movement)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We stepped (1)________ the train carriage just before the doors closed.' Signal: entering an enclosed space (the carriage) = INTO. INTO = movement entering a space.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' (location) instead of 'into' (movement entering). INTO shows movement entering an enclosed space.
questions.learning_tip: INTO = moving and entering an enclosed space. We stepped INTO the carriage = we moved inside it. 'Into' shows entry movement.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Father walked (2)________ the ticket machine to top up his card.' Signal: moving in the direction of something = TOWARDS. TOWARDS = moving in the direction of a destination.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'to' (arrival at destination) instead of 'towards' (movement in the direction of). TOWARDS = moving in the direction of but not necessarily arriving.
questions.learning_tip: TOWARDS = moving in the direction of something. Father walked TOWARDS the ticket machine = he moved in its direction.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The train passed (3)________ a long underground tunnel before emerging at the next station.' Signal: entering one end and exiting the other end of an enclosed passage = THROUGH. THROUGH = complete passage inside something.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'across' (open surface) instead of 'through' (enclosed passage). THROUGH = passing inside an enclosed space from one end to the other.
questions.learning_tip: THROUGH = passing inside something from one end to the other. The train passed THROUGH the tunnel = entered one end and came out the other.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The bus drove (4)________ the bridge and into the city centre.' Signal: travelling from one side of an open surface to the other = ACROSS. ACROSS = crossing an open surface (bridge, road, field) from side to side.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'through' (enclosed passage) instead of 'across' (open surface). ACROSS = movement over an open surface.
questions.learning_tip: ACROSS = moving from one side of an open surface to the other. The bus drove ACROSS the bridge = from one side to the other side.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We drove (5)________ the old market and I pointed it out to my grandfather.' Signal: moved alongside and beyond without stopping = PAST. PAST = moving alongside and beyond something without stopping.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'by' (similar meaning but not in the box). PAST = moved alongside and beyond something.
questions.learning_tip: PAST = moved alongside and beyond something without stopping. We drove PAST the old market = we went by it without stopping.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The bus travelled (6)________ Orchard Road, stopping at each bay to pick up passengers.' Signal: following the length or direction of a route/road = ALONG. ALONG = following the length or direction of something extended.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'on' (surface) instead of 'along' (following the direction of a route). ALONG = following the direction and length of a road or path.
questions.learning_tip: ALONG = following the direction and length of a road, path or river. The bus travelled ALONG Orchard Road = it followed the road from one end towards the other.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The MRT track is built (7)________ the expressway at that stretch, so the train runs above the road.' Signal: above and spanning something = OVER. OVER = above and spanning something (not just higher, but crossing over it).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'above' (higher position, static) instead of 'over' (spanning, crossing above). OVER = built spanning above something.
questions.learning_tip: OVER = spanning or built above something. The track is built OVER the expressway = it crosses above it. ABOVE = simply at a higher level.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The feeder bus loops (8)________ the entire estate before returning to the interchange.' Signal: moving in a circular path encircling an area = AROUND. AROUND = moving in a circle or loop encircling something.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'along' (linear direction) instead of 'around' (circular/looping path). AROUND = moving in a loop or circle.
questions.learning_tip: AROUND = moving in a loop or circle encircling something. The bus loops AROUND the estate = it circles the whole area before coming back.

C.passage: Last Saturday, our family took the MRT for the first time in months. We stepped (1)________ the train carriage just before the doors closed with a soft chime. Father walked (2)________ the ticket machine at the platform to top up his EZ-Link card. The train passed (3)________ a long underground tunnel before emerging at the next brightly lit station. Then we took a bus that drove (4)________ the bridge and into the city centre. We drove (5)________ the old market where my grandfather used to sell vegetables when he was young. The bus travelled (6)________ Orchard Road, stopping at each bay to pick up passengers. At one stretch, the MRT track is built (7)________ the expressway, so you can look down at the cars below. Finally, the feeder bus loops (8)________ the entire estate before returning us to the interchange near our block.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Singapore has one of the most efficient public transport systems in the world. Every day, millions of people (1)________ to school and work by bus and MRT, making it easy to get around the island without a car. At busy (2)________ stations like Jurong East and Dhoby Ghaut, passengers can transfer between different train lines without leaving the building. The (3)________ for a journey depends on the distance travelled, and passengers tap their cards at the start and end of each trip so the correct amount is deducted. Public transport also helps reduce road (4)________, because fewer cars are needed when good bus and train services are available. Singapore's buses and trains are known for being (5)________ — they rarely arrive late, and passengers can plan their journeys around the published timetables.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'to school and work by bus and MRT every day' = travel regularly between home and work/school = commute.
questions.learning_tip: COMMUTE = travel regularly between home and work or school, usually by public transport. Millions of people COMMUTE by MRT every day.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'passengers can transfer between different train lines without leaving the building' = a transfer hub = interchange.
questions.learning_tip: An INTERCHANGE = a station where passengers can transfer between different bus or train lines. Jurong East is a major MRT INTERCHANGE.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'depends on the distance travelled' and 'correct amount is deducted' = the price paid for a journey = fare.
questions.learning_tip: A FARE = the price paid for a journey on public transport. The MRT FARE depends on how far you travel.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'fewer cars are needed' and 'reduce road ___' = traffic blocking the roads = congestion.
questions.learning_tip: CONGESTION = excessive traffic or overcrowding on roads. Good public transport reduces road CONGESTION by keeping cars off the streets.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'rarely arrive late' and 'plan journeys around published timetables' = arriving on time = punctual.
questions.learning_tip: PUNCTUAL = arriving or happening at the scheduled time. Singapore's buses and trains are PUNCTUAL = they arrive on time reliably.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — their (possessive) vs there (place/existence)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'their' (belonging to them) when the sentence needs 'there' (at that place). These homophones sound the same but have different meanings.
questions.learning_tip: THEIR = belonging to them (possessive). THERE = at that place or 'there is/are'. 'We waited THERE for twenty minutes' = at that place. Not 'their'.

questions.error_type: Adverb required after action verb (walked)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'quick' (adjective) after the action verb 'walked'. A verb needs an adverb to describe how.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (walked), use an ADVERB: walked QUICKLY. 'Quick' is an adjective — it describes nouns, not actions.

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the seats)
questions.trap_type: 'The seats' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: 'The seats' = plural → WERE all taken by the time we boarded. WAS is only for singular subjects.

questions.error_type: Comparative form — more + adjective (not add -er to 'crowded')
questions.trap_type: Students write 'crowder' adding -er to 'crowded'. Two-syllable+ adjectives use 'more', not -er.
questions.learning_tip: CROWDED is a long adjective (2+ syllables): use MORE CROWDED, not 'crowdeder' or 'more crowder'. Long adjectives always use MORE for comparative.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (passengers', not passengers's)
questions.trap_type: Students add 's after the apostrophe for a plural noun ending in -s. Just add the apostrophe alone.
questions.learning_tip: Plural possessive for nouns ending in -s: just add an apostrophe after the -s: PASSENGERS' bags = the bags belonging to all the passengers.

E.passage: Last Monday, our class went on a learning journey by MRT. We met at the platform and waited their (1) for five minutes until the train arrived. Our teacher walked quick (2) to the front of the queue and reminded us to tap our cards. When we boarded, we realised that the seats was (3) all taken, so we held the handrails instead. The afternoon train was more crowder (4) than the morning train because many students were heading home at the same time. At the end of the trip, the teacher collected all the passengers's (5) MRT cards and kept them safely in her bag.

questions.sentence_a: You tap your card when boarding the bus.
questions.sentence_b: You tap it again when you exit.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'As well as'.
questions.model_answer: As well as tapping your card when boarding the bus, you tap it again when you exit.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'As well as you tap your card when boarding' — forgetting to change the verb to the -ing form after 'as well as'.
questions.learning_tip: AS WELL AS + verb-ing: AS WELL AS TAPPING your card when boarding, you tap it again when you exit. After 'as well as', always use verb-ing.

questions.sentence_a: You do not tap out properly.
questions.sentence_b: You will be charged the maximum fare.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'Unless'.
questions.model_answer: Unless you tap out properly, you will be charged the maximum fare.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'Unless you will tap out properly' — adding 'will' in the 'unless' clause, which is incorrect (same rule as 'if' conditionals).
questions.learning_tip: UNLESS = if not. UNLESS you tap out properly, you WILL be charged the maximum fare. Never use 'will' in the 'unless' clause — same rule as 'if'.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
It was eleven minutes past ten when eleven-year-old Sam looked up at the departure board and felt his stomach drop. The last train to Boon Lay departed three minutes ago. He was stranded at City Hall station with an empty EZ-Link card and his phone showing four percent battery.

Sam pressed himself against the wall near the exit, trying to think. He stayed too long at his cousin's birthday party and ignored the two messages his mother sent reminding him to leave early.

A station officer in a green vest noticed him and walked over. 'Are you alright, young man?' she asked.

Sam explained his situation. The officer's name tag read 'Chloe'. She did not scold him. Instead, she led him to the station control room and helped him call his mother using the station's phone.

His mother arrived forty minutes later. She was not angry — she looked more worried than upset. 'Next time, you read my messages,' she said quietly.

On the drive home, Sam stared out of the window. He thought about how a single choice — staying just a little longer — had led to this entire situation. He resolved never to miss the last train again.

mcq_questions.stem: Why was Sam unable to take the last train home?

options.1: His EZ-Link card had no money.
options.2: The train broke down at the station.
options.3: He stayed too long at the party and missed the last train.
options.4: His mother told him to wait at the station.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 — his card was empty, but that is not why he missed the train. He missed it because he stayed too late.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'He had stayed TOO LONG at his cousin's birthday party.' That is why he missed the train. The empty card is a separate problem.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 1 has the same meaning as 'stuck with no way to leave'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick 'departed' which means left. 'Stranded' = unable to leave and having no way to get help.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: STRANDED = stuck in a place with no means of leaving. Sam was STRANDED at the station = he could not leave and had no way to get home.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 4, what does 'she' refer to in 'she led him to the station control room'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking his mother had arrived. But his mother arrived forty minutes later — in paragraph 4 'she' is still Officer Chloe.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: the officer 'whose name tag read Chloe' = she is the subject of 'she led him'. Sam's mother arrived much later in paragraph 5.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 5, is it True or False that Sam's mother was angry when she arrived? Give a reason from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says she 'was not angry — she looked MORE WORRIED THAN UPSET.' Her main feeling was worry, not anger.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, she was angry because she scolded him.' She said one quiet sentence but was described as worried, not angry.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: 'She was NOT ANGRY — she looked more WORRIED than upset.' This directly states she was not angry. The answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What TWO problems did Sam face when he realised he had missed the last train?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) His EZ-Link card was empty, so he could not pay for another journey. (ii) His phone battery was at four percent, so he could barely call for help.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students name only one problem. The passage mentions two distinct problems simultaneously.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: (1) 'EMPTY EZ-LINK card' = no money for transport; (2) 'phone showing FOUR PERCENT battery' = almost no way to call for help. Two separate problems.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did Officer Chloe help Sam? Give TWO things she did.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) She noticed Sam and approached him to ask if he was alright. (ii) She led him to the station control room and helped him call his mother using the station's phone.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say only 'she helped him call his mother' without describing the first action of approaching and asking if he was okay.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraphs 3–4: (1) she NOTICED him and asked if he was alright; (2) she led him to the CONTROL ROOM and helped him CALL HIS MOTHER. Two distinct actions.

open_ended_questions.stem: In paragraph 2, Sam 'ignored the two messages his mother sent.' What does this tell us about why he was in this situation?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: It tells us that Sam was warned in time but chose not to act on the warnings. His situation was caused by his own decision to ignore his mother's reminders, not by an unexpected event.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'his mother did not help him' — she did, by sending reminders. He chose to IGNORE them.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: Sam IGNORED the two messages. This shows the situation was his own responsibility — he was warned but did not act on it.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his actions in the passage, describe TWO character traits of Sam with evidence from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Sam is a reflective but irresponsible person. Firstly, his irresponsibility is shown at the start — he ignored his mother's two warning messages and stayed at the party too long, directly causing the entire problem. Secondly, his ability to reflect is shown at the end: on the drive home, he thought carefully about how 'a single choice' had led to his situation, and he resolved never to miss the last train again — showing he genuinely learned from the experience.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say he is 'careless and sorry' without naming precise character traits or providing specific evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Name precise TRAITS then give EVIDENCE: (1) IRRESPONSIBLE — IGNORED two warning messages; (2) REFLECTIVE — on the drive home, thought about his SINGLE CHOICE and resolved to change.

questions.stem: The dentist used a small mirror to ________ the back of Maya's mouth for any signs of decay.
questions.trap_type: 'Cover' and 'block' obstruct; 'ignore' means pay no attention. Only 'examine' = look at carefully and thoroughly.
questions.learning_tip: EXAMINE = look at something carefully to check its condition. The dentist EXAMINES your mouth to look for cavities and other problems.

questions.stem: After the filling, the dentist told Maya not to eat anything ________ for at least an hour.
questions.trap_type: 'Sweet' is about flavour not texture; 'solid' and 'soft' relate to hardness. After a filling, 'chewy' = sticky foods that pull at fillings are the concern.
questions.learning_tip: CHEWY = requiring a lot of chewing, often sticky. After a dental filling, avoid CHEWY foods like gum or toffee that might pull the filling out.

questions.stem: The dentist ________ a small amount of anaesthetic gel on Maya's gum so she would not feel the injection.
questions.trap_type: 'Poured' implies liquid in a container; 'spread' is general; 'swallowed' is wrong. 'Applied' = put on a surface carefully in the correct medical context.
questions.learning_tip: APPLIED = put a substance carefully onto a surface. The dentist APPLIED anaesthetic gel to the gum = placed it precisely where needed.

questions.stem: The waiting room was quiet except for the ________ sound of the drill coming from behind the closed door.
questions.trap_type: 'Thunderous' = extremely loud; 'melodious' = musical and pleasant; 'inaudible' = cannot be heard at all. Behind a closed door, the drill would sound 'muffled'.
questions.learning_tip: MUFFLED = quieter or less clear than normal, as if heard through a barrier. The drill behind the closed door was MUFFLED = heard but not loudly.

questions.stem: The dentist advised regular ________ visits to catch problems before they become serious.
questions.trap_type: 'Urgent' = emergency; 'decorative' and 'reluctant' are unrelated to dental care. 'Preventive' = done to prevent problems before they occur.
questions.learning_tip: PREVENTIVE = done to prevent problems from happening. PREVENTIVE dental visits = regular check-ups to catch issues early, before they become serious.

questions.stem: Every six months, our family ________ to the dental clinic for a routine check-up.
questions.trap_type: 'Every six months' = regular habit = simple present. 'Our family' as a group = plural → go.
questions.learning_tip: 'Every six months' = regular habit = simple present. 'Our family' treated as a group → GO to the clinic.

questions.stem: The dentist ________ three teeth before she realised one of them could be saved.
questions.trap_type: Completed past action. 'Examine' is regular: examine → examined.
questions.learning_tip: 'Before she realised' = completed past action. 'Examine' is regular: examine → EXAMINED.

questions.stem: Going to the dentist now is ________ than waiting until the toothache gets worse.
questions.trap_type: Comparing two options (going now vs waiting) = comparative. 'Wiser' is the correct comparative of 'wise' (-er for one-syllable adjectives).
questions.learning_tip: COMPARATIVE: one-syllable adjectives add -er. 'Wise' → WISER. Going now is WISER than waiting = of the two options, going now is the better choice.

questions.stem: Of all the children in the family, Kai has ________ teeth because he flosses every night.
questions.trap_type: Superlative needed (comparing among all children in the family). 'The cleanest' = superlative of 'clean'.
questions.learning_tip: SUPERLATIVE: comparing among three or more. 'Clean' → THE CLEANEST. Of all the children, Kai has THE CLEANEST teeth.

questions.stem: There was ________ bleeding after the extraction, so the dentist placed a cotton roll over the wound.
questions.trap_type: 'Bleeding' is uncountable → use 'a little' or 'much'. 'A few', 'many', 'several' are for countable nouns.
questions.learning_tip: A LITTLE = a small amount (uncountable). 'Bleeding' is uncountable → there was A LITTLE bleeding. 'A few' and 'several' are only for countable nouns.

questions.stem: The treatment here is not ________ expensive ________ at the specialist clinic downtown.
questions.trap_type: Equal comparison: 'not as expensive as' = the two prices are being compared for equality/inequality.
questions.learning_tip: AS … AS for equal comparisons. 'Not AS expensive AS' = the prices are not equal — this clinic is cheaper. The structure 'not as X as' shows one is less.

questions.stem: The broken tooth ________ repaired by the dentist during a thirty-minute appointment.
questions.trap_type: The tooth was the receiver of the action. Past passive = was repaired.
questions.learning_tip: The tooth was the receiver of the action. Past passive = WAS REPAIRED. Passive = was/were + past participle.

questions.stem: The dentist told the patient ________ sugary drinks for the rest of the day after the filling.
questions.trap_type: Reported speech: told + object + to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told the patient TO + base verb': told the patient TO AVOID sugary drinks after the filling.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Basic conjunctions)

questions.context_check: Passage: '(1)________ Liam was nervous about his dentist appointment, he walked in calmly.' Signal: contrast — nervous inside but calm outside = ALTHOUGH. ALTHOUGH = despite the fact that.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'because' (reason) instead of 'although' (contrast). ALTHOUGH shows a contrast between internal feeling and outward behaviour.
questions.learning_tip: ALTHOUGH = despite the fact that. ALTHOUGH he was nervous, he walked in calmly = these two facts contrast with each other.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'He breathed slowly (2)________ the dentist leaned the chair back.' Signal: at the moment/time that = WHEN. WHEN connects an ongoing action to the moment it happened.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'while' (two ongoing simultaneous actions) instead of 'when' (a point in time). 'The dentist leaned back' = a point in time, not an ongoing action.
questions.learning_tip: WHEN = at the moment that something happened. He breathed slowly WHEN the dentist leaned the chair back = at that specific moment.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Liam counted ceiling tiles (3)________ the dentist worked on his tooth.' Signal: two actions happening simultaneously (counting tiles + dentist working) = WHILE. WHILE = at the same time as.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'when' (single point in time) instead of 'while' (two ongoing simultaneous actions). Both actions were ongoing at the same time.
questions.learning_tip: WHILE = two ongoing actions happening at the same time. He counted tiles WHILE the dentist worked = both actions were happening simultaneously.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'He could not feel any pain (4)________ the anaesthetic had numbed the area.' Signal: the reason he felt no pain = BECAUSE. BECAUSE introduces the reason.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'since' (already planned for blank 5) or 'as'. BECAUSE is the most direct causal conjunction here.
questions.learning_tip: BECAUSE = the reason. He felt no pain BECAUSE the anaesthetic had numbed the area = the anaesthetic is the reason for no pain.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(5)________ the dentist knew Liam very well after five years of visits, she knew exactly how nervous he got.' Signal: a reason that is ongoing/long-established = SINCE. SINCE = given that (as a causal conjunction showing background reason).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'because' (already used in blank 4). SINCE = given that / because of an ongoing background fact.
questions.learning_tip: SINCE = given that, because of an ongoing background situation. SINCE she had been his dentist for five years, she understood him well.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'She told him to raise his hand (6)________ he felt any discomfort during the procedure.' Signal: conditional — the hand-raising depends on whether he feels discomfort = IF. IF = conditional trigger.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'when' (time) instead of 'if' (conditional). He may or may not feel discomfort — it is a condition, not a certain time.
questions.learning_tip: IF = a conditional. Raise your hand IF you feel discomfort = the action depends on whether the condition occurs. WHEN would suggest it definitely will happen.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The dentist said the decay would spread (7)________ the filling was done that day.' Signal: the decay will spread IF the filling is NOT done = UNLESS. UNLESS = if not / except if.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'if' instead of 'unless'. UNLESS = if not. 'Unless the filling was done' = 'if the filling was NOT done'.
questions.learning_tip: UNLESS = if not / except if. The decay would spread UNLESS the filling was done = it would spread IF the filling was NOT done.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(8)________ Liam left the clinic, he felt a wave of relief wash over him.' Signal: at the same time as / in the moment that he was leaving = AS. AS = at the same time as, used for gradual or simultaneous actions.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'when' (sudden point in time) or 'while'. AS = gradual or flowing simultaneous movement — natural for 'as he left'.
questions.learning_tip: AS = at the same time as, often for gradual actions. AS he left the clinic, he felt relief = the feeling came at the same time as he was walking out.

C.passage: (1)________ Liam was nervous about his dentist appointment, he walked in calmly and sat down in the waiting room. He breathed slowly (2)________ the dentist leaned the chair back and adjusted the overhead light. Liam counted ceiling tiles (3)________ the dentist worked carefully on his tooth. He could not feel any pain (4)________ the anaesthetic had numbed the area around his gum. (5)________ the dentist knew Liam very well after five years of visits, she knew exactly how nervous he got and always spoke to him in a calm, steady voice. She told him to raise his hand (6)________ he felt any discomfort during the procedure. The dentist said the decay would spread further (7)________ the filling was done that day, so Liam was glad he had not cancelled his appointment. (8)________ Liam left the clinic, he felt a wave of relief wash over him — and reached for his phone to tell his mother all was well.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Our dentist taught us a lot about keeping our teeth healthy during our last visit. She explained that (1)________ is a hard outer layer that protects the tooth from damage — and that eating too much sugar slowly wears it away. When bacteria combine with food particles, they form a sticky coating called (2)________ on the surface of the teeth. If not cleaned away regularly, this leads to tooth decay and a (3)________, which is a small hole that develops in the tooth. To prevent this, we should brush twice a day and (4)________ between our teeth every night to remove food particles that the toothbrush cannot reach. Before doing a filling, dentists inject medicine to (5)________ the area so the patient does not feel any pain during the procedure.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'hard outer layer that protects the tooth' = enamel.
questions.learning_tip: ENAMEL = the hard outer layer of a tooth that protects it from decay. Sugar slowly wears away ENAMEL.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'sticky coating formed by bacteria and food particles on teeth' = plaque.
questions.learning_tip: PLAQUE = a sticky film of bacteria that forms on teeth. If not removed by brushing, PLAQUE causes tooth decay.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'a small hole that develops in the tooth' = cavity.
questions.learning_tip: A CAVITY = a small hole in a tooth caused by tooth decay. Dentists fill a CAVITY to prevent it from getting larger.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'between our teeth every night to remove food particles the toothbrush cannot reach' = floss.
questions.learning_tip: FLOSS = use dental floss (a thin thread) to clean between teeth. You should FLOSS every day to remove plaque between teeth.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'inject medicine so the patient does not feel any pain' = make the area unable to feel = numb.
questions.learning_tip: NUMB = without feeling, unable to sense pain. Dentists inject anaesthetic to NUMB the area before doing a filling.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — its (possessive) vs it's (it is)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'its' (possessive pronoun) when the sentence needs 'it's' = it is. These look almost identical but have different meanings.
questions.learning_tip: ITS = belonging to it (possessive). IT'S = it is (contraction). 'IT'S important to brush your teeth' = 'It is important'. Use IT'S when you can replace it with 'it is'.

questions.error_type: Adverb required after action verb (brushed)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'gentle' (adjective) after the action verb 'brushed'. A verb needs an adverb to describe how.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (brushed), use an ADVERB: brushed GENTLY. 'Gentle' is an adjective — it describes nouns, not actions.

questions.error_type: Irregular plural — tooth → teeth
questions.trap_type: Students add -s to 'tooth', producing 'tooths'. 'Tooth' has a completely irregular plural form.
questions.learning_tip: 'Tooth' has an irregular plural: tooth → TEETH. Never write 'tooths'. Other irregular plurals: foot → feet, goose → geese.

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the children)
questions.trap_type: 'The children' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: 'The children' = plural → WERE given stickers at the end of their check-up. WAS is only for singular subjects.

questions.error_type: Comparative form — more + adjective for two-syllable+ words (not -er)
questions.trap_type: Students add -er to 'painful', producing 'painfuller'. Two-syllable+ adjectives use 'more', never -er.
questions.learning_tip: PAINFUL is a long adjective (2+ syllables): use MORE PAINFUL, not 'painfuller'. Long adjectives always use MORE for the comparative form.

E.passage: Our dentist always reminds us that its (1) important to brush our teeth before bed. At our last appointment, the hygienist showed us how to hold the toothbrush and brushed gentle (2) on the gum line to prevent damage. She also pointed out that two of our tooths (3) had early signs of plaque build-up. The children was (4) very cooperative during their check-up and followed every instruction carefully. The dentist mentioned that a toothache left untreated will become painfuller (5) over time, so early visits are always the wisest choice.

questions.sentence_a: She brushes her teeth every morning.
questions.sentence_b: She has never had a cavity.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'Since'.
questions.model_answer: Since she brushes her teeth every morning, she has never had a cavity.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'She brushes her teeth every morning since she has never had a cavity' — reversing the cause and result.
questions.learning_tip: SINCE = because of an ongoing or established fact. SINCE she brushes every morning, she has never had a cavity. The reason comes after 'since'.

questions.sentence_a: You floss every day.
questions.sentence_b: Your teeth will not be as healthy as they could be.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'Unless'.
questions.model_answer: Unless you floss every day, your teeth will not be as healthy as they could be.
questions.trap_type: Students add 'will' in the 'unless' clause: 'Unless you will floss every day' — incorrect.
questions.learning_tip: UNLESS + simple present, simple future. UNLESS you FLOSS every day, your teeth WILL NOT BE as healthy. Never 'will' after 'unless'.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Nine-year-old Priya had not been to the dentist in two years. Every time her mother suggested a visit, Priya found a reason to postpone it — a school project, a family outing, a stomach ache that appeared just in time.

But one Tuesday morning, Priya woke up with a sharp pain in her lower left molar. It throbbed steadily, like a tiny hammer tapping from the inside. She tried to ignore it, but by lunchtime, she could not chew her food properly.

Her mother made an appointment for that same afternoon. The clinic was small and brightly lit. Dr Nair, a tall woman with a gentle voice, welcomed Priya without any fuss. She examined the tooth quickly and explained that there was a cavity that needed to be filled.

'Will it hurt?' Priya asked.

'There will be a small pinch,' said Dr Nair. 'After that, you will feel nothing.'

She was right. The injection stung for two seconds. Then the whole left side of Priya's mouth felt like a thick cushion. The filling itself took twelve minutes.

Walking out, Priya felt something she had not expected: relief. Not just because it was over, but because it was so much smaller than the fear she carried for two years.

'You should have come sooner,' her mother said.

Priya nodded. She already knew.

mcq_questions.stem: Why had Priya not visited the dentist for two years?

options.1: Her mother forgot to make appointments.
options.2: There was no dentist near their home.
options.3: She always found excuses to avoid going.
options.4: She had no problems with her teeth.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 4 thinking she had no reason to go. But paragraph 1 says she found reasons to POSTPONE — implying she was avoiding it.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: 'Every time her mother suggested a visit, Priya FOUND A REASON TO POSTPONE IT.' She was making excuses to avoid going.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'pulsed with a steady pain'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick 'sharp' (the type of pain, not the rhythm) or 'tapping' (a simile, not the main word). 'Throbbed' = pulsed with a steady rhythm of pain.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: THROBBED = pulsed with a steady, rhythmic pain. 'It THROBBED steadily, like a tiny hammer tapping from the inside.' THROBBED = pulsed with steady pain.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 6, what does 'it' refer to in 'because it was so much smaller than the fear she carried for two years'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 2 thinking 'it' refers to the injection. But 'it' refers to the whole experience — the procedure — which was smaller than the FEAR she imagined.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: In context, 'IT had been so much smaller than the fear' = the entire dental PROCEDURE was far less frightening than the fear she built up over two years.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 5, is it True or False that the injection was completely painless? Give a reason from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says 'The injection STUNG FOR TWO SECONDS.' It was not completely painless — it hurt briefly, but only for a short moment.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, Dr Nair said it would not hurt.' Dr Nair said 'you will feel nothing' AFTER the pinch — she acknowledged there would be a pinch.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: 'The injection STUNG FOR TWO SECONDS.' It was not completely painless — there was a brief sting. The answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: How long did the filling procedure take?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: The filling took twelve minutes.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'a short time' which is too vague.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: 'The filling itself took TWELVE MINUTES.' Give the exact duration stated in the passage.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did Priya feel when she walked out of the clinic, and why was the feeling unexpected?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: She felt relief. It was unexpected because she had dreaded the visit for two years — but the procedure was so much easier and smaller than the fear she built up in her mind.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'she was happy' without explaining why the feeling was unexpected.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 6: She felt RELIEF — unexpected because the procedure was 'SMALLER THAN THE FEAR she had carried for two years.' The reality was much less frightening than the imagined fear.

open_ended_questions.stem: How do we know that Dr Nair was a kind and reassuring dentist? Give ONE piece of evidence from paragraph 3.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Dr Nair 'welcomed Priya without any fuss' and had a 'gentle voice', showing she was calm and reassuring rather than intimidating.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'she was kind' without quoting specific evidence from the passage.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: she 'welcomed Priya WITHOUT ANY FUSS' and had a 'GENTLE VOICE.' Both phrases show she was calm and reassuring — not intimidating or clinical.

open_ended_questions.stem: What is the most important lesson of this passage? Support your answer with TWO pieces of evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: The most important lesson is that fear of something is often worse than the thing itself — and that avoiding a problem only allows it to grow. Firstly, Priya avoided the dentist for two years and built up a large imagined fear, but the actual procedure took only twelve minutes and was far less painful than expected. Secondly, her delay caused the cavity to develop to the point where a filling was needed — had she gone earlier, the problem might have been caught sooner and treated more easily.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'we should brush our teeth' — too general. The lesson must be connected to specific events in the passage.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: LESSON: fear is often worse than reality; delaying makes problems worse. EVIDENCE: (1) the procedure was only TWELVE MINUTES — far smaller than two years of FEAR; (2) AVOIDING the dentist caused the cavity to worsen.

questions.stem: Grandma ________ her old photo albums to show her grandchildren what life was like when she was young.
questions.trap_type: 'Destroyed', 'hid' and 'discarded' all suggest the albums were not valued. Only 'treasured' = kept and valued something dearly.
questions.learning_tip: TREASURED = kept and valued something very dearly. Grandma TREASURED her photo albums = she valued them and kept them carefully.

questions.stem: Grandfather's stories of life in the kampung ________ the children, who had never seen a village like that.
questions.trap_type: 'Bored', 'frightened' and 'angered' are all negative reactions. Kampung stories that captivate children = fascinated.
questions.learning_tip: FASCINATED = held someone's complete interest and attention. Grandfather's stories FASCINATED the children = they were completely captivated.

questions.stem: My grandmother moves slowly and with great care, but her mind remains ________ and alert.
questions.trap_type: 'Dim', 'confused' and 'slow' all suggest mental weakness. 'Sharp' = mentally quick and clear even in old age.
questions.learning_tip: SHARP = mentally quick, alert and clear. Even in old age, Grandma's mind was SHARP = she was quick-thinking and mentally alert.

questions.stem: Grandfather spent hours ________ old furniture in the garage, sanding it down and painting it a new colour.
questions.trap_type: 'Destroying' and 'ignoring' are negative; 'selling' means giving away for money. 'Restoring' = repairing and returning to original condition.
questions.learning_tip: RESTORING = repairing and returning something old to its original good condition. Grandfather RESTORED old furniture = fixed and repainted it.

questions.stem: The afternoon visits to my grandparents were the most ________ part of my childhood — I remember every detail.
questions.trap_type: 'Forgettable', 'ordinary' and 'unpleasant' suggest unimportance or negativity. 'Cherished' = held dear in memory with great affection.
questions.learning_tip: CHERISHED = loved and kept in memory with deep affection. Those visits were CHERISHED memories = the most loved and treasured parts of childhood.

questions.stem: Every Sunday, my grandmother ________ a pot of chicken rice for the whole family.
questions.trap_type: 'Every Sunday' = regular habit = simple present. 'My grandmother' is singular → verb needs -s.
questions.learning_tip: 'Every Sunday' = regular habit = simple present. My grandmother (singular) → COOKS a pot of chicken rice.

questions.stem: Grandfather ________ us a long story about his school days whenever we visited him at his flat.
questions.trap_type: 'Whenever we visited' = past habit. 'Tell' is regular: tell → told (irregular). Students write 'telled'.
questions.learning_tip: 'Tell' is irregular: tell → TOLD. 'Whenever we visited' = past recurring action → TOLD us stories.

questions.stem: My grandfather is the ________ storyteller in our family — nobody can hold our attention the way he does.
questions.trap_type: Superlative needed (best among all family members). 'Good' → irregular superlative = 'the best'. 'Most good' is wrong.
questions.learning_tip: SUPERLATIVE of 'good' = THE BEST (irregular). He is THE BEST storyteller in the family = better than anyone else. Never 'the most good'.

questions.stem: Grandma's chicken rice is ________ tastier ________ any version I have tried at a restaurant.
questions.trap_type: 'Far ... than' = 'far' is an intensifier used with comparative. 'Far tastier than' = much tastier than. Students may choose 'more ... than' but 'tastier' is already in comparative form.
questions.learning_tip: FAR + comparative + THAN = intensified comparison. 'Far TASTIER THAN' = much tastier than. 'Far' intensifies the comparative. Do not add 'more' before an adjective already in -er form.

questions.stem: There is ________ advice I have received in life that was wiser than what my grandfather has given me.
questions.trap_type: 'Advice' is uncountable → use 'little' or 'much'. 'Few', 'a few', 'many' are for countable nouns.
questions.learning_tip: LITTLE = not much (uncountable). 'Advice' is uncountable → there is LITTLE advice wiser than what Grandfather gives. FEW is only for countable nouns.

questions.stem: Grandmother's handmade kueh is just ________ delicious ________ the kueh sold at Bengawan Solo.
questions.trap_type: Equal comparison: 'just as delicious as' = the two are equally good.
questions.learning_tip: AS … AS = equal comparison. Grandmother's kueh is just AS DELICIOUS AS the shop-bought kueh = their quality is equal.

questions.stem: The old rocking chair in the corner ________ by my grandfather himself when he was a young carpenter.
questions.trap_type: The chair was the receiver of the action. Past passive = was built.
questions.learning_tip: The rocking chair was the receiver of the action. Past passive = WAS BUILT. Passive = was/were + past participle.

questions.stem: Grandmother told the children ________ her silver bracelet without asking her first.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: 'Told the children NOT TO + base verb': told the children NOT TO TOUCH her silver bracelet without asking.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Personal pronouns — subject, object and possessive)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'My grandmother is eighty years old, but (1)________ still wakes up at five every morning.' Signal: blank = SUBJECT of 'wakes up'. My grandmother = female singular = SHE.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'her' (object form) instead of 'she' (subject). SHE is the subject pronoun for a female.
questions.learning_tip: SHE = subject pronoun for a female. My grandmother STILL WAKES UP — the subject is SHE. 'Her wakes up' is wrong.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'I visit (2)________ every Saturday morning without fail.' Signal: blank = OBJECT of 'visit'. Refers to grandmother (female) = HER (object pronoun).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'she' (subject) instead of 'her' (object after a verb).
questions.learning_tip: After the verb 'visit', use the OBJECT pronoun: visit HER. 'Visit she' is wrong.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Mother sometimes calls (3)________ to help carry the grocery bags.' Signal: blank = OBJECT of 'calls'. Refers to grandfather = male = HIM (third person singular male object pronoun).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'he' (subject form) instead of 'him' (object form after the verb 'calls').
questions.learning_tip: After the verb 'calls', use the OBJECT pronoun: calls HIM to help. 'Calls he' is wrong. HIM is the object pronoun for a male.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Grandfather is eighty-four and (4)________ still tends the small garden behind the flat every day.' Signal: blank = SUBJECT of 'tends'. Grandfather = male singular = HE.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'his' (possessive) instead of 'he' (subject pronoun). HE is the subject of 'tends'.
questions.learning_tip: HE = subject pronoun for a male. Grandfather STILL TENDS the garden — the subject is HE. 'His tends the garden' is wrong.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(5)________ hands are rough from years of work, but they are always warm when he holds mine.' Signal: blank = BEFORE noun 'hands' = possessive adjective. Grandfather = male = HIS hands.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'he' (subject pronoun) instead of 'his' (possessive adjective before a noun).
questions.learning_tip: Before 'hands' (a noun), use a POSSESSIVE ADJECTIVE: HIS hands. 'He hands' is wrong.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Together, (6)________ have taught me more about life than any book could.' Signal: blank = SUBJECT of 'have taught'. Refers to both grandparents (plural) = THEY.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'them' (object form) instead of 'they' (subject form).
questions.learning_tip: Both grandparents = plural = THEY have taught me. THEY is the subject pronoun for a group. 'Them have taught' is wrong.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(7)________ stories about growing up during a harder time in Singapore always leave me thinking.' Signal: blank = BEFORE noun 'stories' = possessive adjective. Both grandparents = THEIR stories.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'they' (subject) or 'them' (object) instead of 'their' (possessive adjective before 'stories').
questions.learning_tip: Before 'stories' (a noun), use a POSSESSIVE ADJECTIVE: THEIR stories. 'They stories' and 'them stories' are both wrong.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'I hope I can spend as much time with (8)________ as possible before they grow too old to remember.' Signal: blank = OBJECT of 'spend time with'. Refers to grandparents (plural) = THEM (object pronoun).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'they' (subject form) instead of 'them' (object form after a preposition).
questions.learning_tip: After the preposition 'with', use the OBJECT pronoun: spend time with THEM. 'With they' is wrong.

C.passage: My grandmother is eighty years old, but (1)________ still wakes up at five every morning to prepare breakfast. I visit (2)________ every Saturday morning without fail. Mother sometimes calls (3)________ to help carry the grocery bags. Grandfather is eighty-four and (4)________ still tends the small garden behind the flat every day. (5)________ hands are rough from years of work, but they are always warm when he holds mine. Together, (6)________ have taught me more about life than any book could ever do. (7)________ stories about growing up during a harder time in Singapore always leave me thinking for days. I hope I can spend as much time with (8)________ as possible before they grow too old to remember the stories they have shared with me.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Spending time with grandparents is one of the most valuable things a child can do.
