options.4: The number of neighbours on the floor

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'enough' refers to space in the flat. But Mdm Aisha was welcoming Mr Tan to join the meal — 'enough' = food and hospitality.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: Mdm Aisha said 'Come in — there is MORE THAN ENOUGH' while waving him forward to the FOOD and gathering. 'Enough' = plenty of food and welcome for one more guest.

mcq_questions.stem: Mr Tan said 'I did not expect to feel so at home.' What does this tell us about his experience?

options.1: He expected the food to remind him of his own home.
options.2: The visit surprised him — he felt more welcome and comfortable than he had imagined.
options.3: He was unhappy because the flat looked different from his own.
options.4: He visited Mdm Aisha's home many times before.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'at home' = comfortable with familiar food. But 'feel at home' = feel welcome and relaxed; he felt MORE welcome than he expected.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: 'Feel AT HOME' = feel relaxed, welcome and comfortable. Mr Tan had hesitated to enter, but ended up FEELING AT HOME = far more comfortable and happy than he expected.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Mdm Aisha only invited her Muslim neighbours to her open house? Give a reason from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says she opened her door to 'EVERYONE on the floor — regardless of race or religion', showing she welcomed all neighbours, not just Muslim ones.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, it is a Hari Raya celebration so only Muslims were invited.' The passage explicitly says 'regardless of race or religion'.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: 'EVERYONE on the floor — REGARDLESS OF RACE OR RELIGION.' This means she welcomes all people. The answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: Why did Mr Tan hesitate at the entrance?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: He moved in only three weeks before and felt unsure about intruding on what he thought was a private family occasion.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he was shy' — too vague. The passage gives the specific reason: he was new and worried about intruding.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: he moved in only THREE WEEKS before and felt unsure about 'intruding on a FAMILY OCCASION'. He was new and thought the gathering was private.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did Mdm Aisha and Rina make Mr Tan feel welcome? Give TWO specific details from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) Mdm Aisha waved him forward warmly and said 'There is more than enough', showing she was glad he came. (ii) Rina handed him a plate and explained what each dish was, helping him feel comfortable with the unfamiliar food.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'they were kind' without specific details.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraphs 3–4: (1) Mdm Aisha WAVED HIM FORWARD and said 'Come in'; (2) RINA handed him a plate and showed him what each dish was. Two specific welcoming actions.

open_ended_questions.stem: What does Mdm Aisha's final line — 'That is what an open house is for' — tell us about her purpose in hosting?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Her purpose was not just to celebrate her own festival, but to create a space where neighbours of different backgrounds could come together, feel welcome and form connections.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'she likes cooking for people' — misses the deeper purpose of community-building.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: 'THAT IS WHAT AN OPEN HOUSE IS FOR' = the purpose is to make people feel at home across differences. Her open house is about COMMUNITY and CONNECTION, not just food.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on her actions in the passage, describe TWO character traits of Mdm Aisha with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) GENEROUS: she has hosted everyone on her floor for over twenty years and always says 'there is more than enough', showing she gives without limit. (ii) INCLUSIVE: she welcomes neighbours regardless of race or religion, making her open house a true celebration of community.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say she is 'kind and friendly' without naming precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: GENEROUS = 'more than enough', 20 years of hosting. INCLUSIVE = 'regardless of race or religion'. Name the trait + give the evidence from the passage.

questions.stem: The waves at Siloso Beach were as ________ as a gentle song, rocking the swimmers back and forth.
questions.trap_type: 'Rough' and 'angry' suggest violent waves; 'loud' is about sound. SOOTHING = gentle and calming, like a song.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The waves were AS SOOTHING AS a gentle song = the simile compares the waves to music. SOOTHING = calming and peaceful.

questions.stem: The family decided to ________ the cable car and take it across to Sentosa Island.
questions.trap_type: 'Avoid' = stay away; 'build' = construct; 'describe' = explain. BOARD = get onto a vehicle or mode of transport.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: BOARD = get onto a vehicle (bus, train, cable car, plane). You BOARD the cable car = you get on. 'Board' is used for almost any vehicle you step into!

questions.stem: The theme park ride was so ________ that the children screamed with delight from start to finish.
questions.trap_type: 'Boring', 'slow' and 'ordinary' all describe dull experiences. THRILLING = causing great excitement and a rush of energy.
questions.learning_tip: THRILLING = causing great excitement and a rush of energy. A THRILLING ride = one that makes your heart beat fast with excitement.

questions.stem: The children built an ________ sandcastle with towers, a moat and a drawbridge out of sticks.
questions.trap_type: 'Ugly' and 'ordinary' are negative or plain; 'invisible' cannot be seen. ELABORATE = very detailed, complex and carefully planned.
questions.learning_tip: ELABORATE = very detailed and carefully constructed with many parts. An ELABORATE sandcastle has towers, a moat and a drawbridge — not just a mound of sand.

questions.stem: After a long day in the sun, the cool sea water felt ________ and washed away all the tiredness.
questions.trap_type: 'Cold' is a fact about temperature, not a feeling of benefit. 'Muddy' and 'dangerous' are negative. REFRESHING = making you feel energised and better after being tired.
questions.learning_tip: REFRESHING = making you feel better, cooler and more energised. A REFRESHING swim after a hot day = the swim washes away tiredness and makes you feel alive again.

questions.stem: Nobody in our group ________ the map properly, so we ended up walking in the wrong direction.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'reads' thinking 'Nobody' = singular → present tense, but the context is past ('ended up walking'). Past simple = read (past of read).
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY = Singular! But here the sentence is PAST → 'Nobody READ the map' = past simple. Nobody + past verb (no -s needed in past). 'Nobody reads' would be present.

questions.stem: Our class has ________ Sentosa three times this year as part of our outdoor education programme.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. 'Visit' is regular: visit → visited.
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Our class HAS VISITED Sentosa three times = these visits happened at some point this year. VISIT → VISITED (regular).

questions.stem: Sentosa is ________ visited tourist attraction in Singapore, welcoming millions of people each year.
questions.trap_type: Superlative needed — comparing Sentosa to all other attractions. THE MOST + multi-syllable adjective.
questions.learning_tip: THE MOST + long adj = superlative! Sentosa is THE MOST VISITED = more visited than any other attraction. Use THE MOST for long adjectives.

questions.stem: The children ________ sand sculptures when a sudden wave rushed up the beach and swept one away.
questions.trap_type: 'A wave rushed up' = sudden interrupting event. The children were already building = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The wave RUSHED UP = sudden past event. Children were already in the middle of building = WERE BUILDING. Past continuous = was/were + verb-ing.

questions.stem: There were ________ visitors at the beach than we expected — it was surprisingly peaceful.
questions.trap_type: 'Visitors' is countable → use FEWER. 'Less' is for uncountable nouns.
questions.learning_tip: FEWER + countable noun. Visitors = countable → FEWER visitors. LESS is for uncountable nouns like 'crowd' or 'noise'. Rule: FEWER for things you can COUNT.

questions.stem: You have been to Sentosa before, ________ you?
questions.trap_type: Positive present perfect ('have been') → negative question tag = haven't you.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present perfect → negative tag. 'You HAVE BEEN to Sentosa, HAVEN'T you?' Positive → negative tag. HAS/HAVE → HASN'T/HAVEN'T.

questions.stem: The new waterpark at Sentosa ________ by a team of international designers to attract families from all over Asia.
questions.trap_type: The waterpark was the receiver of the action. Past passive = was designed.
questions.learning_tip: WAS/WERE + past participle = passive! The waterpark WAS DESIGNED by designers = the designers did the action; the waterpark received it.

questions.stem: The lifeguard told swimmers ________ beyond the yellow buoys for safety.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: TOLD someone NOT TO + base verb. The lifeguard told swimmers NOT TO GO beyond the buoys. Formula: told + person + not to + verb.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Relative pronouns — note: 'who' and 'which' each used twice)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The lifeguard (1)________ rescued the boy was praised by everyone on the beach.' Signal: blank = relative pronoun replacing a PERSON (the lifeguard) as subject = WHO. WHO = replaces a person in a relative clause.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'which' (for things) instead of 'who' (for people). The lifeguard = a person → WHO.
questions.learning_tip: WHO = relative pronoun for PEOPLE. The lifeguard WHO rescued the boy = 'who' replaces 'the lifeguard' in the second clause. WHO is always for people.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The cable car, (2)________ runs between Mount Faber and Sentosa, offers a stunning view of the sea.' Signal: blank = relative pronoun replacing a THING (the cable car) = WHICH. WHICH = replaces a thing in a non-restrictive clause.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'who' (for people) instead of 'which' (for things). The cable car = a thing → WHICH.
questions.learning_tip: WHICH = relative pronoun for THINGS. The cable car, WHICH runs between Mount Faber and Sentosa = 'which' replaces 'the cable car'. WHICH is always for things.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The sandcastle (3)________ we built took over an hour to complete.' Signal: blank = relative pronoun in a restrictive clause defining which sandcastle = THAT. THAT = used in restrictive (defining) clauses for both people and things.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'which' (non-restrictive) instead of 'that' (restrictive/defining). The clause 'that we built' defines WHICH sandcastle, not just adds information.
questions.learning_tip: THAT = used in restrictive clauses that DEFINE which one. The sandcastle THAT we built = this tells us WHICH sandcastle (the one we built, not another). THAT = defining clause.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Palawan Beach is the place (4)________ my family always sets up our picnic.' Signal: blank = relative pronoun replacing a PLACE (Palawan Beach) = WHERE. WHERE = replaces a place in a relative clause.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'which' (thing, needs a preposition: 'at which') or 'that'. WHERE = the correct relative adverb for places.
questions.learning_tip: WHERE = relative pronoun for PLACES. Palawan Beach is the place WHERE my family picnics = 'where' replaces 'at that place'. WHERE is always for locations.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'I remember the summer (5)________ we first visited Sentosa as a family.' Signal: blank = relative pronoun replacing a TIME (the summer) = WHEN. WHEN = replaces a time expression in a relative clause.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'that' or 'which' instead of 'when'. WHEN = the correct relative adverb for times.
questions.learning_tip: WHEN = relative pronoun for TIMES. The summer WHEN we first visited = 'when' replaces 'at that time'. WHEN is always for time expressions.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The family (6)________ children built the biggest sandcastle won a small prize from the beach attendant.' Signal: blank = possessive relative pronoun linking 'family' to 'children' = WHOSE. WHOSE = possessive relative pronoun ('the family's children').
questions.trap_type: Students write 'who' (subject) or 'which' (thing) instead of 'whose' (possessive). WHOSE = belonging to the family.
questions.learning_tip: WHOSE = possessive relative pronoun. The family WHOSE children built the sandcastle = the family's children. WHOSE = 'belonging to whom'. Replace 'the family's' → 'whose'.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Anyone (7)________ wants to rent a kayak must register at the activity counter first.' Signal: blank = relative pronoun replacing a PERSON (anyone who) = WHO. 'Anyone who' = the person who.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'that' (also acceptable for people in informal English, but WHO is preferred for formal/exam contexts).
questions.learning_tip: WHO = preferred relative pronoun for PEOPLE in formal writing. Anyone WHO wants to rent a kayak = 'who' refers back to 'anyone' (a person). In exams, use WHO for people.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We took the monorail, (8)________ connects the different parts of Sentosa, to get back to the beach.' Signal: blank = relative pronoun adding extra information about a THING (the monorail) = WHICH. Non-restrictive clause (extra info, set off by commas).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'that' instead of 'which'. Non-restrictive clauses (extra info between commas) use WHICH, not THAT.
questions.learning_tip: WHICH = used in non-restrictive clauses (extra information between commas). We took the monorail, WHICH connects different parts of Sentosa. Commas + extra info = WHICH, not THAT.

C.passage: The lifeguard (1)________ rescued the boy was praised by everyone on the beach that afternoon. The cable car, (2)________ runs between Mount Faber and Sentosa, offers a stunning view of the sea below. The sandcastle (3)________ we built together took over an hour to complete. Palawan Beach is the place (4)________ my family always sets up our picnic mat. I still remember the summer (5)________ we first visited Sentosa as a family and saw the fireworks over the sea. The family (6)________ children built the biggest sandcastle won a small prize from the friendly beach attendant. Anyone (7)________ wants to rent a kayak must register at the activity counter first. We took the monorail, (8)________ connects the different parts of Sentosa, to get back to the main beach area.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Sentosa is a popular island (1)________ off Singapore's southern coast. Visitors can travel by road, by monorail, or by (2)________ car — a gondola suspended on wires high above the sea. From above, the island looks like a (3)________ green carpet with white beaches on every side. Its theme parks, hotels and beaches make it the most popular (4)________ for families. Its (5)________ white sand beaches and the sound of the sea make it hard to believe the city is just minutes away.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'island... connected to mainland... with beaches and theme parks' = a holiday/leisure destination = resort.
questions.learning_tip: A RESORT = a place that is popular for holidays, leisure and recreation. Sentosa is an island RESORT = a leisure destination with beaches and attractions.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'a gondola suspended on wires that carries passengers high above the sea' = cable car.
questions.learning_tip: A CABLE car = a gondola or cabin that hangs from a thick wire (cable) and travels between two points high above the ground.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'stretched out below, with white beaches on every side' + comparing to a carpet = bright, shining = gleaming.
questions.learning_tip: GLEAMING = shining brightly with reflected light. The island looks like a GLEAMING green carpet = it shines brightly in the sunlight.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'most popular ___ for families looking for fun' = a place or thing that draws visitors = attraction.
questions.learning_tip: An ATTRACTION = a place or feature that draws visitors. Theme parks and beaches are ATTRACTIONS that make Sentosa a popular destination.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'white sand beaches' that stretch widely = covering a large area in an irregular way = sprawling.
questions.learning_tip: SPRAWLING = spreading over a large area in an irregular or extended way. SPRAWLING white sand beaches = beaches that stretch widely along the shoreline.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the beaches)
questions.trap_type: 'The beaches' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! The beaches WERE clean and beautiful. WAS is only for ONE thing (singular). BEACHES = more than one → WERE.

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — its (possessive) vs it's (it is)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'its' (possessive) when the sentence needs 'it's' = it is.
questions.learning_tip: IT'S = it is (contraction). ITS = belonging to it. 'ITS great to be at the beach' → can you replace with 'it is'? YES → use IT'S. Remember: IT'S = IT IS.

questions.error_type: Spelling — ie/ei confusion (receive: after C, use EI)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'recieve' putting I before E after C. After the letter C, use EI, not IE.
questions.learning_tip: Rule: I before E, EXCEPT after C! reCEIve = after C → use EI ✅. 'Recieve' puts I before E after C = WRONG. Trick: 'C rules after reCEIve' — C always comes before EI.

questions.error_type: Adverb required after action verb (moved)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'quick' (adjective) after the action verb 'moved'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (moved), use an ADVERB: moved QUICKLY. Rule: verb + adverb (-ly). 'Quick' describes nouns. 'Quickly' describes actions.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — irregular plural possessive (children's, not childrens')
questions.trap_type: Students write 'childrens'' treating 'children' as a regular plural. 'Children' is already an irregular plural — add 's to form the possessive.
questions.learning_tip: 'Children' is ALREADY plural (irregular). Possessive = CHILDREN'S (add 's). NOT 'childrens'' — that adds an extra wrong -s. Irregular plural → add 's: children's bags.

E.passage: Last Saturday, our family spent the day at Sentosa. The beaches was (1) clean and the water was warm and clear. My sister said its (2) the best place for a family day out in Singapore. At the activity booth, we signed up to recieve (3) free kayaking lessons at three o'clock. The instructor moved quick (4) through the water to demonstrate the correct paddling technique. At the end of the day, the childrens' (5) sand sculptures were photographed by other visitors who walked past.

questions.sentence_a: The cable car broke down halfway.
questions.sentence_b: We would have been stranded above the sea.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'Unless'.
questions.model_answer: Unless the cable car breaks down halfway, we will not be stranded above the sea.
questions.trap_type: Students misuse the conditional structure. UNLESS = if not → rephrase in present conditional.
questions.learning_tip: UNLESS = if not. 'Unless the cable car BREAKS DOWN' (simple present in the unless clause) = if it does NOT break down. UNLESS + simple present, simple future.

questions.sentence_a: The sandcastle stood three feet tall.
questions.sentence_b: The sandcastle took two hours to build.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using the relative pronoun 'which'.
questions.model_answer: The sandcastle, which took two hours to build, stood three feet tall.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'The sandcastle which it took two hours to build stood three feet tall' — adding 'it' after 'which'.
questions.learning_tip: WHICH = relative pronoun for things. The sandcastle, WHICH took two hours to build, stood three feet tall. Commas + WHICH = extra info. Never add 'it' after 'which'.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
It was the last Saturday of the June holidays. The Sentosa Beach Festival had organised a sandcastle competition, and eight-year-old Kai planned his design for two weeks.

His plan was ambitious — a four-towered castle with a moat, a drawbridge made of driftwood and tiny flags made from paper clips and scraps of cloth. He had even drawn a blueprint on a piece of paper, which he kept folded in his pocket.

When the starting whistle blew, Kai's older sister Priya dug the foundations while Kai shaped the towers. They worked without stopping for an hour and a half.

With fifteen minutes left, disaster struck. A large wave slid up the beach and collapsed one entire wall of the castle.

Kai stared at the damage. Then, without a word, he began rebuilding.

They did not win first prize. A twelve-year-old boy named Sam built a replica of the Merlion that was judged the most creative entry. But Kai's castle won the special prize for Most Improved — because the judges watched him rebuild the fallen wall without complaint.

As the sky turned orange over the cable car station, Kai's father took a photograph of the battered castle standing proud in the late light. It was lopsided, shorter than planned and missing one tower entirely. But in the photograph, it looked exactly right.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'a detailed plan or drawing of a structure'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Design' is a general word; 'pocket' and 'paper' are objects. BLUEPRINT = a detailed technical drawing or plan.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: BLUEPRINT = a detailed technical drawing or plan of something to be built. Kai's BLUEPRINT was his detailed drawing of the castle layout.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 2, what does 'which' refer to in 'which he kept folded in his pocket'?

options.3: The blueprint Kai drew on paper

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'which' = the design (general). But 'which' refers specifically to the BLUEPRINT — the thing he drew on a piece of paper.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'He had drawn a BLUEPRINT on a piece of paper, WHICH he kept folded in his pocket.' WHICH = the blueprint (the piece of paper with the drawing).

mcq_questions.stem: Why did Kai win the 'Most Improved' prize rather than first prize?

options.1: The judges felt sorry for him because a wave destroyed his castle.
options.2: His castle was the most creative entry in the competition.
options.3: The judges saw him rebuild the collapsed wall calmly and without complaining, showing resilience.
options.4: He used the best materials of all the competitors.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking it was a sympathy prize. But the passage says the judges WATCHED him rebuild WITHOUT COMPLAINT — they were rewarding his resilience.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Last paragraph: the judges WATCHED him REBUILD the fallen wall WITHOUT COMPLAINT. The prize was for his RESILIENCE and positive attitude, not for the castle's design.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 4, is it True or False that the wave destroyed Kai's entire sandcastle? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The wave 'collapsed ONE ENTIRE WALL of the castle' — not the whole castle. The rest of the structure was still standing.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, the wave destroyed everything.' The passage says only ONE WALL collapsed.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'A large wave collapsed ONE ENTIRE WALL.' Only one wall fell — the rest was still standing. The answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: Who won first prize, and what did that person build?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: A twelve-year-old boy named Sam won first prize. He built a replica of the Merlion, which was judged the most creative entry.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'Kai won first prize' — he won the special prize, not first prize.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Last paragraph: 'a twelve-year-old boy named SAM built a replica of the MERLION that was judged the most creative entry.' Sam won first prize, not Kai.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did Kai's plan show he had prepared carefully? Give TWO details from paragraph 2.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) His plan included specific features: four towers, a moat, a driftwood drawbridge and tiny flags from paper clips and cloth. (ii) He had even drawn a blueprint — a detailed plan — which he kept in his pocket during the competition.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he planned for two weeks' — that is in paragraph 1, not paragraph 2.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: (1) he designed FOUR TOWERS, a moat, a driftwood drawbridge and paper-clip flags; (2) he drew a BLUEPRINT on paper and kept it in his pocket. Both show careful preparation.

open_ended_questions.stem: Find ONE phrase from paragraph 5 that shows how Kai responded when disaster struck.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: 'Without a word, he began rebuilding.'
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students quote 'He stared at the damage' — that shows his initial reaction, not his response.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: 'WITHOUT A WORD, he began REBUILDING.' This phrase shows he did not panic, complain or give up — he simply started again in silence.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his actions in the passage, describe TWO character traits of Kai with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) DETERMINED: he planned his castle for two weeks, drew a blueprint and worked for 90 minutes without stopping — showing he committed fully to his goal. (ii) RESILIENT: when the wave destroyed a wall, he stared at the damage then began rebuilding without a word — not giving up despite the setback.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he is creative and smart' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: DETERMINED = planned for two weeks, drew a blueprint, worked 90 minutes non-stop. RESILIENT = rebuilt the collapsed wall WITHOUT A WORD, no complaint.

questions.stem: True friendship is as ________ as gold — it is rare and worth protecting.
questions.trap_type: 'Heavy' describes weight; 'common' means ordinary; 'dull' = boring. PRECIOUS = extremely valuable and rare, like gold.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! True friendship is AS PRECIOUS AS gold = comparing friendship to gold to show its value. PRECIOUS = very valuable and rare.

questions.stem: When Lena forgot her lunch, her best friend immediately ________ half of her sandwich.
questions.trap_type: 'Gave up' = stopped trying; 'broke off' = snapped; 'threw away' = discarded. HANDED OVER = gave to someone else.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: HAND OVER = give something to someone else. She HANDED OVER half her sandwich = passed it to Lena. HAND + OVER work together as one phrase.

questions.stem: A true friend will ________ you even when others walk away.
questions.trap_type: 'Ignore', 'criticise' and 'avoid' are all negative responses. STAND BY = remain loyal and supportive.
questions.learning_tip: STAND BY = remain loyal and supportive to someone, especially when times are hard. A true friend STANDS BY you = stays with you no matter what.

questions.stem: After their argument, the two friends ________ their differences and agreed to move on.
questions.trap_type: 'Remembered' = recalled; 'deepened' = made worse; 'ignored' = did not address. RESOLVED = found a solution to a problem or conflict.
questions.learning_tip: RESOLVED = successfully dealt with a problem or disagreement. The friends RESOLVED their differences = they worked through the issue and came to an agreement.

questions.stem: Sharing your last biscuit with a hungry classmate is a small but ________ act of kindness.
questions.trap_type: 'Harmful' and 'meaningless' are negative. 'Ordinary' means unremarkable. SELFLESS = putting others' needs before your own without expecting a reward.
questions.learning_tip: SELFLESS = caring more about others than yourself. A SELFLESS act = doing something for someone else without expecting anything back. Opposite: selfish.

questions.stem: Someone ________ left a birthday card on Maya's desk before she arrived at school.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'have' thinking 'someone' = many people. SOMEONE = singular → HAS (present perfect auxiliary).
questions.learning_tip: SOMEONE = Singular! Use HAS, not HAVE. Someone HAS left a card = singular subject + present perfect. EVERYONE / SOMEONE / NOBODY = always singular.

questions.stem: Maya and Riya have ________ friends since they were in Primary One.
questions.trap_type: HAVE + past participle = present perfect. 'Be' is irregular: be → been.
questions.learning_tip: HAVE + past participle = present perfect. Maya and Riya HAVE BEEN friends since Primary One = they became friends then and still are. BE → BEEN (irregular).

questions.stem: Riya is a ________ more generous friend than anyone else I know.
questions.trap_type: FAR + comparative = intensified comparison. 'Very' and 'lot' are not used before comparatives. FAR MORE generous = much more generous.
questions.learning_tip: FAR + comparative = much more. Riya is FAR MORE GENEROUS = much more generous than others. Use FAR to make a comparative stronger. 'Very more' is WRONG.

questions.stem: The two girls ________ their secret hideout in the library when a teacher suddenly walked in.
questions.trap_type: 'A teacher suddenly walked in' = sudden interrupting event. The girls were already planning = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The teacher WALKED IN = sudden past event. The girls were already in the middle of planning = WERE PLANNING (past continuous).

questions.stem: There was ________ kindness in her simple act of sharing her umbrella in the rain.
questions.trap_type: 'Kindness' is uncountable → MUCH. 'A few', 'many', 'several' are for countable nouns.
questions.learning_tip: MUCH + uncountable noun. Kindness = uncountable → MUCH kindness. You cannot say 'many kindnesses' or 'a few kindness'. Use MUCH for feelings and abstract nouns.

questions.stem: You and Maya have been best friends for years, ________ you?
questions.trap_type: Positive present perfect → negative question tag. 'Have been' → haven't you.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present perfect → negative tag. 'You HAVE BEEN best friends, HAVEN'T you?' Positive → negative tag. HAVE → HAVEN'T.

questions.stem: The friendship award at the school assembly ________ by a student who had helped a classmate every day for a term.
questions.trap_type: The award was the receiver of the action. Past passive = was given.
questions.learning_tip: WAS/WERE + past participle = passive! The award WAS GIVEN by the school = the award received the action. Passive voice: receiver + WAS/WERE + past participle.

questions.stem: The teacher told the students ________ their snacks with classmates who had forgotten theirs.
questions.trap_type: Reported speech: told + object + to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: TOLD someone TO + base verb. The teacher told students TO SHARE their snacks. Formula: told + person + to + verb (infinitive).

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Pronouns — subject, object, possessive, reflexive)

questions.context_check: Passage: '(1)________ have been best friends with Siti since we were in kindergarten.' Signal: blank = SUBJECT of 'have been'. First person singular subject = I.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'Me' (object form). I is the SUBJECT pronoun. 'Me have been' is wrong.
questions.learning_tip: I = subject pronoun (does the action). I HAVE BEEN friends with Siti. 'Me' is the object — use ME after verbs: 'she helped ME'. Subject = I; Object = ME.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Siti always remembers (2)________ birthday without being reminded.' Signal: blank = POSSESSIVE ADJECTIVE before noun 'birthday'. First person = MY birthday.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'me' (object) or 'I' (subject) instead of 'my' (possessive adjective before a noun).
questions.learning_tip: MY = possessive adjective before a noun. MY birthday = the birthday belonging to me. 'Me birthday' is wrong — use MY before nouns.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'I made the birthday card (3)________ instead of buying one from the shop.' Signal: blank = reflexive pronoun, same subject as 'I'. I made it BY MYSELF = I alone, with no help = MYSELF.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'me' (object) instead of 'myself' (reflexive). 'I made it by me' is wrong.
questions.learning_tip: MYSELF = reflexive pronoun for I. I made it BY MYSELF = I alone, without help. Use MYSELF when the subject (I) and object refer to the same person.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Siti smiled when (4)________ saw the card — her eyes lit up with joy.' Signal: blank = SUBJECT of 'saw'. Siti = female singular subject = SHE.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'her' (object form) instead of 'she' (subject). 'Her saw the card' is wrong.
questions.learning_tip: SHE = subject pronoun for a female. SHE saw the card. 'Her' is the object: 'I gave it to HER'. Subject = SHE; Object = HER.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'I helped (5)________ carry her things home after she twisted her ankle on the way.' Signal: blank = OBJECT of 'helped'. Refers to Siti (female) as object = HER.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'she' (subject) instead of 'her' (object after the verb 'helped').
questions.learning_tip: After a verb (helped), use the OBJECT pronoun. I helped HER = HER is the object. 'I helped she' is WRONG. After verbs: use ME, HER, HIM, THEM (not I, she, he, they).

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Good friends like Siti and me — (6)________ are the ones you can call at any time of night.' Signal: blank = SUBJECT of 'are'. Siti and me = a group of people = THEY (third person plural subject).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'them' (object) or 'their' (possessive) instead of 'they' (subject).
questions.learning_tip: THEY = subject pronoun for a group. Good friends like Siti and me — THEY are the ones you can call. 'Them are the ones' is WRONG. Subject = THEY.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'I sat beside (7)________ on the bus every day for three years.' Signal: blank = OBJECT after preposition 'beside'. Refers to Siti (female) as object = HER.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'she' (subject) instead of 'her' (object after preposition). After prepositions, always use object pronouns.
questions.learning_tip: After a PREPOSITION (beside, with, for, to), use OBJECT pronoun. I sat beside HER. 'Beside she' is WRONG. Preposition + object pronoun: beside ME, with HER, for THEM.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Real friends never need to pretend — they can just be (8)________ around each other.' Signal: blank = reflexive pronoun for 'they' (plural third person). They can be THEMSELVES = their true selves. THEMSELVES = reflexive for they/them.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'them' (object) instead of 'themselves' (reflexive). 'Be them' is wrong.
questions.learning_tip: THEMSELVES = reflexive pronoun for they/them. They can be THEMSELVES = be their true selves, without pretending. Use THEMSELVES when the subject (they) and object are the same people.

C.passage: (1)________ have been best friends with Siti since we were in kindergarten. Siti always remembers (2)________ birthday without being reminded. I made the birthday card (3)________ instead of buying one from the shop, because I wanted it to feel more personal. Siti smiled when (4)________ saw the card — her eyes lit up with joy. When Siti twisted her ankle on the way home, I helped (5)________ carry her things. Good friends like Siti and me — (6)________ are the ones you can call at any time of night. I sat beside (7)________ on the bus every day for three years, and we never ran out of things to talk about. Real friends never need to pretend — they can just be (8)________ around each other.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: True friendship is built on more than spending time together. It requires (1)________ — genuine care for another person's feelings. A good friend is also (2)________ — they stay by your side even when things are hard. A friend who is (3)________ tells you the truth kindly. When arguments happen, the ability to (4)________ each other keeps the friendship alive. Over time, a strong (5)________ of trust grows between two people, making friendship one of the most valuable things in life.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'genuine care and understanding for another person's feelings and difficulties' = compassion.
questions.learning_tip: COMPASSION = a deep feeling of care and concern for someone who is suffering. A friend with COMPASSION understands how you feel and wants to help.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'stays by your side even when things are hard and does not abandon you' = loyal.
questions.learning_tip: LOYAL = remaining faithful and supportive to someone, especially in difficult times. A LOYAL friend does not leave when things get hard.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'tells you the truth kindly, rather than just saying what you want to hear' = sincere.
questions.learning_tip: SINCERE = genuine and honest, saying what you truly mean. A SINCERE friend tells you the truth even when it is uncomfortable to hear.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'move forward, keeps the friendship alive' after arguments = forgive.
questions.learning_tip: FORGIVE = stop feeling angry with someone for something they did wrong. The ability to FORGIVE each other is what keeps friendships strong after arguments.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'strong ___ of trust and shared experiences' = bond.
questions.learning_tip: A BOND = a strong connection or link between people. A BOND of trust = a deep connection built over time through shared experiences and mutual care.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — to (preposition) vs too (also/excessively)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'to' when the meaning is 'also'. TOO = also OR excessively.
questions.learning_tip: TOO = also or excessively. 'She wanted to join TOO' = also. 'TO' = direction or infinitive. Test: can you replace with 'also'? YES → use TOO. 'She wanted to join to' is WRONG.

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the friends)
questions.trap_type: 'The friends' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! The friends WERE very upset after the argument. WAS is only for singular subjects. FRIENDS = more than one → WERE.

questions.error_type: Spelling — ie/ei confusion (friend: I before E)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'freind' putting E before I. 'Friend' follows the I-before-E rule: frIEnd.
questions.learning_tip: Rule: I before E, except after C! frIEnd = I before E ✅. Remember: 'A frIEnd is nice till the END' — I before E, always in 'friend'.

questions.error_type: Adverb required after action verb (shared)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'happy' (adjective) after the action verb 'shared'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (shared), use an ADVERB: shared HAPPILY. Rule: verb + adverb (-ly). 'Happy' describes nouns. 'Happily' describes actions (how something was done).

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (friends', not friends's)
questions.trap_type: Students add 's after the apostrophe for a plural noun ending in -s.
questions.learning_tip: Plural possessive: just add apostrophe after -s! The FRIENDS' lunchboxes = the lunchboxes belonging to all the friends. Never 'friends's' — that is double-s and wrong.

E.passage: Last Thursday, our class celebrated Friendship Day. Mei wanted to join the group activity to (1). The friends was (2) nervous at first about sharing their drawings with the whole class. One student gave her freind (3) the last piece of cake without hesitation. Afterwards, they shared their snacks happy (4) and everyone felt closer by the end of the day. The teacher pinned all the friends's (5) drawings on the board to show what each person valued most in a friendship.

questions.sentence_a: You are honest with your friends.
questions.sentence_b: The friendship will grow stronger over time.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'As long as'.
questions.model_answer: As long as you are honest with your friends, the friendship will grow stronger over time.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'As long as you will be honest' — adding 'will' in the 'as long as' clause.
questions.learning_tip: AS LONG AS + simple present, simple future. AS LONG AS you ARE honest, the friendship WILL GROW. No 'will' after 'as long as'.

questions.sentence_a: The girl noticed her friend was upset.
questions.sentence_b: The girl sat with her friend without saying a word.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'Although'.
questions.model_answer: Although the girl noticed her friend was upset, she sat with her without saying a word.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'The girl noticed her friend was upset although she sat with her' — less powerful. ALTHOUGH at the start shows the contrast more clearly.
questions.learning_tip: ALTHOUGH + [first fact], [contrasting fact]. ALTHOUGH she noticed her friend was upset, she SAT WITH HER without speaking — a contrast between noticing and choosing silence.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
On the first day of school after the June holidays, twelve-year-old Anya sat down and noticed that the seat next to her was empty. Her best friend Jess moved to Australia.

The teacher introduced a new student. Her name was Clara, and she stood at the front with her eyes fixed on her shoes. Anya remembered her own first day at this school — how long the classroom had seemed, and how nobody had spoken to her for the entire morning.

She moved her bag off the chair beside her.

'You can sit here,' she said.

Clara looked up. She hesitated, then walked over and sat down.

They did not speak much for the first week. But Anya made sure to save the seat every day. On Friday, Clara brought two rice crispy treats wrapped in foil. She placed one quietly on Anya's desk.

Anya looked at the treat, then at Clara.

'Thank you,' she said.

Clara smiled — the first real smile Anya saw from her all week. 'Thank you for the seat,' Clara said.

By the end of the second week, they had discovered they both liked the same author. Anya lent Clara three books in a single afternoon. Clara returned them all the following Monday with tiny sticky notes inside marking her favourite lines. Neither of them mentioned the empty seat or the rice crispy treat again. They did not need to.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 1 has the same meaning as 'went to live in a different place'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Noticed' = observed; 'empty' = nothing in it; 'best' = finest. MOVED = went to live in a new place.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: MOVED = went to live in a different place. Jess MOVED to Australia = she went to live there permanently. 'Move' (to a new home or country) = relocate.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 2, what does 'her own first day' refer to?

options.1: Clara's first day at any school
options.2: Anya's first day at this particular school, when nobody spoke to her
options.3: The teacher's first day at the school
options.4: Jess's first day before she left for Australia

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 or 4 confusing whose first day is being described. 'HER OWN first day' = Anya's, and 'this school' = the current school.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'Anya remembered HER OWN first day at THIS SCHOOL — how long the classroom had seemed.' HER OWN = Anya's first day at the same school Clara just joined.

mcq_questions.stem: Clara said 'Thank you for the seat.' What does this tell us about what the seat meant to her?

options.1: She was grateful for a comfortable place to sit.
options.2: She was thanking Anya for the physical chair.
options.3: She understood that saving the seat every day was Anya's way of welcoming and including her.
options.4: She preferred to sit at the front of the class.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 2 thinking she was literally thanking Anya for the chair. But 'the seat' = Anya's daily act of inclusion and friendship, not just the furniture.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: 'Thank you for THE SEAT' = Clara understood that saving the seat EVERY DAY was Anya's way of saying 'you belong here.' The seat = an act of FRIENDSHIP and INCLUSION.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 2, is it True or False that Anya found her own first day at school easy? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says the classroom 'had seemed very long' and 'nobody had spoken to her for the entire morning' — showing she found her first day lonely and difficult.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, Anya was confident on her first day.' The passage says the opposite.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'NOBODY HAD SPOKEN to her for the ENTIRE MORNING' on her own first day. This shows it was lonely and difficult, not easy. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did Clara bring on Friday, and what did she do with it?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Clara brought two rice crispy treats wrapped in foil. She placed one quietly on Anya's desk.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'she brought food' without the specific detail.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 6: 'Clara brought two RICE CRISPY TREATS wrapped in foil. She placed one quietly on ANYA'S DESK.' Give both the item and the specific action.

open_ended_questions.stem: Why did Anya decide to offer her seat to Clara? Give TWO reasons from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) She remembered what it felt like to be new — her own first day had seemed very long and nobody had spoken to her. (ii) She saw Clara standing at the front with her eyes on her shoes, which showed she was shy and nervous.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'Anya was kind' without connecting to the specific evidence from the passage.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraphs 2–4: (1) Anya REMEMBERED her own lonely first day; (2) Clara stood with EYES ON HER SHOES = shy and nervous. Both details explain Anya's decision.

open_ended_questions.stem: Find ONE phrase from the passage that shows Anya's friendship was not through words but through action.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: 'Anya made sure to save the seat every day.'
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students quote 'You can sit here' — that IS a word-based action. The question asks for action WITHOUT words.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 6: 'Anya made sure to SAVE THE SEAT EVERY DAY' — she showed friendship through a consistent daily action, not through words or conversation.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on her actions in the passage, describe TWO character traits of Anya with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) EMPATHETIC: she remembered her own lonely first day and used that experience to understand how Clara felt — that memory drove her to offer the seat. (ii) CONSISTENT: she did not just offer the seat once; she saved it EVERY DAY for a week, showing her friendship was reliable, not just a single gesture.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'kind and caring' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: EMPATHETIC = used her own first-day experience to understand Clara's feelings. CONSISTENT = saved the seat EVERY DAY, not just once. Both are shown through specific actions.

questions.stem: The thunderclap was as ________ as a hundred drums beating at once, shaking the windows of every flat.
questions.trap_type: 'Quiet', 'soft' and 'gentle' describe the opposite of a loud thunderclap. DEAFENING = so loud it hurts your ears.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The thunderclap was AS DEAFENING AS a hundred drums. DEAFENING = so loud it feels like it blocks out all other sound.

questions.stem: The forecast warned of heavy rain, so Mother told us to ________ extra umbrellas before leaving home.
questions.trap_type: 'Lose', 'break' and 'hide' are negative actions. BRING ALONG = take something with you when you leave.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: BRING ALONG = take something with you. Mother told us to BRING ALONG extra umbrellas = take them with us when we left. BRING + ALONG = carry with you.

questions.stem: The rain fell in heavy ________, soaking everything within seconds.
questions.trap_type: 'Breezes' = wind; 'droplets' = tiny individual drops; 'wisps' = thin strands. SHEETS (of rain) = rain falling in dense walls.
questions.learning_tip: SHEETS of rain = rain falling in dense, flat walls of water. Heavy tropical rain falls in SHEETS — solid curtains of water that soak you instantly.

questions.stem: After the storm, the streets were ________ with fallen leaves, broken branches and puddles.
questions.trap_type: 'Decorated' sounds positive. 'Cleaned' and 'painted' make no sense after a storm. LITTERED = covered messily with objects that should not be there.
questions.learning_tip: LITTERED = covered untidily with scattered objects. After the storm, streets were LITTERED with leaves and branches = messy things were scattered all over. LITTER = rubbish/mess.

questions.stem: The sudden storm ________ the outdoor event, forcing everyone to take shelter inside the community hall.
questions.trap_type: 'Enhanced' and 'improved' mean made better. 'Continued' = kept going. DISRUPTED = interrupted and prevented something from continuing normally.
questions.learning_tip: DISRUPTED = interrupted and prevented something from continuing as planned. The storm DISRUPTED the event = it broke up the event and forced everyone indoors.

questions.stem: Nobody in the playground ________ the storm was coming until the first bolt of lightning lit up the sky.
questions.trap_type: Context is past ('lit up the sky'). NOBODY = singular. Past tense + nobody = knew (past of know).
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY = Singular! Past context → NOBODY KNEW = past simple, singular. 'Nobody know' (no -s in past) or 'nobody knew' (correct past). Singular + past → knew.

questions.stem: Singapore has ________ some of the most intense thunderstorms in South-East Asia in recent years.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. 'Experience' is regular: experience → experienced.
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Singapore HAS EXPERIENCED intense storms = it has had them recently, and the experience is relevant now. EXPERIENCE → EXPERIENCED (regular).

questions.stem: Yesterday's storm was the ________ one this year, cutting off power to three districts.
questions.trap_type: Superlative needed (comparing this storm to all storms this year). 'Severe' is multi-syllable → THE MOST SEVERE. 'Severest' is acceptable but less standard.
questions.learning_tip: THE MOST + long adj = superlative! THE MOST SEVERE storm = the most extreme one compared to all others. Use THE MOST for multi-syllable adjectives.

questions.stem: The children ________ in the puddles when their mother called them inside.
questions.trap_type: 'Their mother called them inside' = sudden interrupting event. The children were already splashing = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: Their mother CALLED THEM = sudden past event. Children were already splashing in puddles = WERE SPLASHING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing.

questions.stem: There was ________ lightning in the sky that the whole room lit up like daylight.
questions.trap_type: 'Lightning' is uncountable → SO MUCH. 'Many', 'a few', 'several' are for countable nouns.
questions.learning_tip: SO MUCH + uncountable noun. Lightning = uncountable → SO MUCH lightning. 'Many lightnings' or 'several lightning' are WRONG. Use MUCH/SO MUCH for uncountable things.

questions.stem: The roof of the old shelter didn't hold up very well, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Main clause is NEGATIVE past ('didn't hold up') → POSITIVE question tag. 'Didn't' → positive tag = did it.
questions.learning_tip: Negative statement → positive tag. 'The roof DIDN'T hold up well, DID it?' NEGATIVE → POSITIVE tag. Past 'didn't' → tag uses 'did'.

questions.stem: The flood warning notice ________ on all public screens across the island within minutes of the storm beginning.
questions.trap_type: The notice was the receiver of the action. Past passive = was displayed.
questions.learning_tip: WAS/WERE + past participle = passive! The notice WAS DISPLAYED = someone displayed it; the notice received the action. Passive: receiver + WAS/WERE + past participle.

questions.stem: The weather forecaster told residents ________ in low-lying areas during the heavy rain.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: TOLD someone NOT TO + base verb. The forecaster told residents NOT TO STAY in low-lying areas. Formula: told + person + not to + verb.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Basic conjunctions, expanded)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Thunder rumbled (1)________ lightning lit up the whole sky.' Signal: two simultaneous events joined together = AND. AND = addition of two equally happening things.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'but' (contrast) instead of 'and' (addition). Both events happened together, not in contrast.
questions.learning_tip: AND = joins two things happening together. Thunder rumbled AND lightning lit up the sky = both things happened at the same time. AND = addition.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We brought umbrellas (2)________ the wind turned them inside out immediately.' Signal: contrast — we prepared, but it did not help = BUT. BUT = unexpected contrast.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'and' (addition) instead of 'but' (unexpected contrast). The wind turning umbrellas inside out is the unexpected opposite result.
questions.learning_tip: BUT = contrast or unexpected result. We brought umbrellas BUT the wind turned them inside out = the unexpected opposite happened. BUT = surprise contrast.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The drain overflowed, (3)________ the road became flooded within minutes.' Signal: result/consequence = SO. The flooding is the RESULT of the drain overflowing.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'and' (addition) instead of 'so' (result). SO shows a cause → result relationship.
questions.learning_tip: SO = result or consequence. The drain overflowed, SO the road flooded = the flooding was the RESULT of the drain. SO = and as a result of that.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The children rushed inside (4)________ they were afraid of the lightning.' Signal: the REASON they rushed inside = BECAUSE. BECAUSE introduces a reason.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'so' (result) instead of 'because' (reason). BECAUSE = the reason for the action.
questions.learning_tip: BECAUSE = the reason. Children rushed inside BECAUSE they were afraid = BECAUSE tells us WHY they rushed in. BECAUSE = gives the reason.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(5)________ the rain was heavy, Father insisted on going to buy dinner for the family.' Signal: contrast — heavy rain + Father went out anyway = ALTHOUGH. ALTHOUGH = despite the fact that.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'because' (reason) instead of 'although' (contrast). ALTHOUGH = despite the difficult condition.
questions.learning_tip: ALTHOUGH = despite the fact that. ALTHOUGH the rain was heavy, Father went out = these two facts contrast. ALTHOUGH = even though something is difficult, the other thing still happened.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'You can wait for the rain to stop (6)________ take a taxi home instead.' Signal: a choice between two options = OR. OR = one option or the other.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'and' (both options) instead of 'or' (one of the two). These are alternative choices, not things to do together.
questions.learning_tip: OR = a choice between two options. Wait for the rain OR take a taxi = choose one. AND would mean doing both. OR = alternative choice.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(7)________ the storm began at noon, the sky has not brightened at all.' Signal: from a past point up to now = SINCE (background reason or time marker). SINCE = from a point in the past up to now.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'although' or 'because' instead of 'since' (causal/temporal: from that point until now).
questions.learning_tip: SINCE = from a past moment up to now, OR because of an ongoing background reason. SINCE the storm began = from the moment the storm started until now, the sky has stayed dark.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The match will be cancelled (8)________ the rain stops within the next thirty minutes.' Signal: the cancellation will happen IF the rain does NOT stop = UNLESS. UNLESS = if not.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'if' instead of 'unless'. IF the rain stops = the match continues. UNLESS the rain stops = the match is cancelled (if it does NOT stop).
questions.learning_tip: UNLESS = if not. The match will be cancelled UNLESS the rain stops = it will be cancelled IF the rain does NOT stop. UNLESS = negative condition.

C.passage: Thunder rumbled (1)________ lightning lit up the whole sky in a single bright flash. We brought umbrellas (2)________ the strong wind turned them inside out immediately. The drain overflowed, (3)________ the road became flooded within just a few minutes. The children rushed inside (4)________ they were afraid of the lightning flashing across the dark sky. (5)________ the rain was heavy, Father still insisted on going out to buy dinner for the whole family. You can wait for the rain to stop (6)________ take a taxi home instead — the choice is yours. (7)________ the storm began at noon, the sky has not brightened at all. The match will be cancelled (8)________ the rain stops within the next thirty minutes.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Singapore experiences thunderstorms frequently, especially in the afternoons. Before a major storm, the weather (1)________ often warns of strong winds and heavy rain. A sudden (2)________ of wind can bend small trees and rattle windows. Heavy rain can (3)________ anyone caught outside within seconds. During a storm, it is important to find (4)________ — a covered area away from trees. Heavy rain also reduces (5)________, making it difficult for drivers to see clearly ahead.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'warns of strong winds and heavy rain before a storm' = a weather prediction = forecast.
questions.learning_tip: A FORECAST = a prediction of what the weather will be. The weather FORECAST warns us of coming storms so we can prepare.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'sudden ___ of wind can bend trees' = a sudden strong burst of wind = gust.
questions.learning_tip: A GUST (of wind) = a sudden, strong burst of wind. A GUST can bend small trees and knock over lightweight objects.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'caught outside within seconds... even under an umbrella' = soaked completely = drench.
questions.learning_tip: DRENCH = soak something or someone completely with water. Heavy tropical rain can DRENCH you in seconds even if you have an umbrella.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'find ___ — a covered area away from trees and open fields' = a place of protection = shelter.
questions.learning_tip: SHELTER = a covered place that provides protection from the rain, wind or sun. During a storm, find SHELTER in a covered area away from trees.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'reduces ___, making it difficult for drivers to see clearly' = the ability to see = visibility.
questions.learning_tip: VISIBILITY = how far or clearly you can see. Heavy rain reduces VISIBILITY = you cannot see very far ahead. Low VISIBILITY makes driving dangerous.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the puddles)
questions.trap_type: 'The puddles' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! The puddles WERE everywhere after the rain. WAS is only for singular. PUDDLES = more than one → WERE.

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — they're (they are) vs their (possessive)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'they're' (they are) when the sentence needs 'their' (belonging to them).
questions.learning_tip: THEIR = belonging to them. THEY'RE = they are. 'They grabbed THEIR umbrellas' = umbrellas belonging to them. Test: 'They grabbed they are umbrellas' = WRONG. Use THEIR.

questions.error_type: Spelling — ie/ei confusion (weird: ei, exception to I-before-E rule)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'wierd' putting I before E. 'Weird' is an exception — it uses EI even though there is no C before it.
questions.learning_tip: WEIRD is an exception! I before E, except after C — but 'weird' breaks the rule. Remember: 'WEIRD is WEIRd' = spell it with EI. Just memorise this one: w-e-i-r-d.

questions.error_type: Adverb required after action verb (rained)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'heavy' (adjective) after the action verb 'rained'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (rained), use an ADVERB: rained HEAVILY. Rule: verb + adverb (-ly). 'Heavy' describes nouns (heavy rain). 'Heavily' describes the action (rained heavily).

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — singular possessive (teacher's, not teachers's)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'teachers's' adding an extra 's'. For a singular noun, add 's: teacher → teacher's.
questions.learning_tip: Singular possessive: noun + 's! The TEACHER'S umbrella = the umbrella belonging to one teacher. 'Teachers's' is wrong — 'teachers' is already plural. ONE teacher → teacher's.

E.passage: Yesterday afternoon, a thunderstorm hit our estate without warning. The puddles was (1) everywhere and the drains overflowed into the corridor. The children quickly grabbed they're (2) raincoats and boots before rushing outside to splash in the puddles. The sky had turned a wierd (3) yellow-green colour before the rain began. By four o'clock, it rained so heavy (4) that the bus was delayed by forty minutes. The teachers's (5) umbrella turned inside out as soon as she stepped out of the school building.

questions.sentence_a: You hear thunder.
questions.sentence_b: You should go indoors immediately.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'As soon as'.
questions.model_answer: As soon as you hear thunder, you should go indoors immediately.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'As soon as you will hear thunder' — adding 'will' in the 'as soon as' clause.
questions.learning_tip: AS SOON AS + simple present, imperative or simple future. AS SOON AS you HEAR thunder, you SHOULD go indoors. No 'will' after 'as soon as'.

questions.sentence_a: The storm knocked down an old tree.
questions.sentence_b: The old tree had stood at the corner of the road for fifty years.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using the relative pronoun 'which'.
questions.model_answer: The storm knocked down an old tree, which had stood at the corner of the road for fifty years.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'an old tree which it had stood' — adding 'it' after 'which'. Also, 'had stood' is acceptable here as it is in a relative clause describing a prior state.
questions.learning_tip: WHICH = relative pronoun for things. The storm knocked down a tree, WHICH had stood for fifty years. Non-restrictive clause (extra info, commas) → use WHICH. Never add 'it' after 'which'.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage_title: How to Stay Safe During a Thunderstorm
G.passage:
Singapore experiences thunderstorms more than 170 days a year, making it one of the world's most storm-prone countries. Understanding what happens during a thunderstorm and how to stay safe can make a real difference.

A thunderstorm forms when warm, moist air rises rapidly and meets cooler air high in the atmosphere. This creates large storm clouds that produce lightning and thunder. Lightning is a powerful electrical discharge, and the thunder we hear is the sound it makes as it heats the air around it. Because light travels faster than sound, we always see lightning before we hear thunder. Counting the seconds between the flash and the bang tells you how far away the storm is — roughly one kilometre for every three seconds.

During a thunderstorm, there are several safety rules to follow. You should stay indoors and away from windows. Avoid using electrical appliances and unplug devices where possible. If you are outdoors, do not shelter under a tree, as trees attract lightning. Move to a low-lying area instead and crouch down with your feet together and your hands over your ears.

Thunderstorms in Singapore usually pass within thirty to sixty minutes. After the rain stops, it is important to check for flooded paths and fallen branches before going outside.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'a release of electrical energy'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Atmosphere' is the sky; 'rapid' = fast; 'moist' = damp. DISCHARGE = a sudden release of electrical energy.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: DISCHARGE = a sudden release of energy, especially electrical energy. Lightning is an electrical DISCHARGE = a burst of electricity between clouds and the ground.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 2, what does 'it' refer to in 'the thunder we hear is the sound it makes'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'it' refers to the storm cloud. But 'it' refers to LIGHTNING, which heats the air and causes the sound of thunder.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'Lightning is a powerful electrical discharge, and the thunder we hear is the sound IT makes as it heats the air.' IT = LIGHTNING.

mcq_questions.stem: Why should you NOT shelter under a tree during a thunderstorm?

options.1: Trees are too wet to stand under.
options.2: You might be seen by lightning.
options.3: Trees attract lightning and could put you in danger.
options.4: Trees block the view of the storm.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking it is about getting wet. The passage specifically says trees 'attract lightning'.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: 'do not shelter under a tree, as TREES ATTRACT LIGHTNING.' If lightning hits the tree, you could be harmed. Move to a low-lying open area instead.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Singapore has thunderstorms on fewer than 100 days a year? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says Singapore experiences thunderstorms MORE THAN 170 DAYS A YEAR — far more than 100 days.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students may say 'True' guessing a lower number. The passage states '170 days a year' explicitly.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: Singapore has thunderstorms MORE THAN 170 DAYS A YEAR. 170 > 100, so the statement is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: How can you estimate how far away a thunderstorm is?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: You count the seconds between the lightning flash and the thunder, then divide by three. Each three seconds is roughly one kilometre.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'count the seconds' without explaining the calculation.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'roughly ONE KILOMETRE for every THREE SECONDS.' Count the seconds → divide by three → distance in kilometres.

open_ended_questions.stem: Give TWO things you should do if you are caught OUTDOORS during a thunderstorm.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) Do not shelter under a tree — move away from it. (ii) Move to a low-lying area and crouch down with feet together and hands over ears.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students give indoor safety tips. The question specifies OUTDOORS.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3 (OUTDOORS): (1) NOT UNDER A TREE (trees attract lightning); (2) CROUCH DOWN in a low-lying area, feet together, hands over ears. These are the two outdoor rules.

open_ended_questions.stem: Why do we see lightning before we hear thunder?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Because light travels faster than sound. We see the lightning flash first, then hear the thunder after.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'lightning comes before thunder' without explaining why.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'Because LIGHT TRAVELS FASTER THAN SOUND, we always see lightning before we hear thunder.' This is the scientific reason for the sequence.

open_ended_questions.stem: This passage is an informational text. Describe TWO features the writer uses to make it useful to readers.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) PRACTICAL SAFETY RULES: the writer gives specific things to do and not do (e.g., avoid trees, crouch down), making the information actionable. (ii) SCIENTIFIC EXPLANATION: the writer explains WHY lightning and thunder happen, helping readers understand and remember the advice.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students summarise the content rather than analysing the features of the text.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: FEATURES of an informational text: (1) practical SAFETY RULES that readers can follow; (2) SCIENTIFIC EXPLANATION of why things happen. Analyse HOW it is written, not WHAT it says.

questions.stem: The firefighter was as ________ as a lion when he ran into the burning building to save the child.
questions.trap_type: 'Timid' and 'fearful' = afraid; 'slow' = not fast. BRAVE = showing courage in the face of danger.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The firefighter was AS BRAVE AS a lion = comparing his courage to a lion's. 'As brave as a lion' is a common simile for great courage.

questions.stem: When the alarm went off, the firefighters ________ their gear and reached the fire truck in under a minute.
questions.trap_type: 'Threw away' and 'took off' mean removing; 'ignored' = paid no attention. PUT ON = dressed themselves in something.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: PUT ON = wear or dress in something. The firefighters PUT ON their gear = they dressed themselves in their protective suits and helmets quickly.

questions.stem: The fire engine ________ through the streets with its siren wailing loudly.
questions.trap_type: 'Crept' and 'tiptoed' suggest slow, quiet movement; 'floated' is for water or air. SPED = moved very fast.
questions.learning_tip: SPED = moved very quickly (past tense of 'speed'). The fire engine SPED through the streets = moved at high speed to reach the fire as fast as possible.

questions.stem: The firefighter worked quickly and carefully to ________ the people trapped inside the damaged building.
questions.trap_type: 'Forget', 'ignore' and 'delay' all mean not helping. RESCUE = save someone from danger.
questions.learning_tip: RESCUE = save someone from danger or a difficult situation. Firefighters RESCUE people trapped in fires or accidents — they bring them to safety.

questions.stem: The fire safety officer emphasised that prevention is always more ________ than responding to a fire after it starts.
questions.trap_type: 'Exciting' and 'dangerous' are irrelevant comparisons. 'Tiring' is negative. EFFECTIVE = producing the desired result successfully.
questions.learning_tip: EFFECTIVE = producing the best results. Prevention is MORE EFFECTIVE than responding after a fire starts = stopping a fire before it happens works better than fighting it after.

questions.stem: Everyone in the group ________ amazed when they saw how quickly the firefighters could suit up.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'were' thinking 'everyone in the group' = many people. EVERYONE = singular → WAS. Past context = WAS.
questions.learning_tip: EVERYONE = Singular! Past context → EVERYONE WAS amazed. 'Everyone were' is WRONG. EVERYONE / NOBODY / SOMEONE = always singular → IS / WAS / HAS.

questions.stem: Our class has ________ to the fire station twice before, but this year's visit was the most memorable.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. 'Go' is irregular: go → gone.
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Our class HAS GONE to the fire station twice = both visits happened before now. GO → GONE (irregular). Never 'has went'.

questions.stem: The fire station's ladder truck is the ________ vehicle in the whole fleet, able to extend to thirty metres.
questions.trap_type: Superlative needed (comparing to all vehicles in the fleet). 'Tall' → THE TALLEST (short adjective, add -est).
questions.learning_tip: THE + adjective + -EST = superlative for short adjectives! The TALLEST vehicle = taller than all others. TALL → TALLEST. Use -EST for one-syllable adjectives.

questions.stem: The firefighters ________ the hose when the fire captain gave the order to stand down.
questions.trap_type: 'The captain gave the order' = sudden past event. Firefighters were already rolling the hose = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The captain GAVE THE ORDER = sudden past event. Firefighters were already rolling the hose = WERE ROLLING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing.

questions.stem: There was ________ smoke coming from the roof when the crew arrived — they had caught it early.
questions.trap_type: 'Smoke' is uncountable → use 'little' or 'much'. 'A few', 'many', 'several' are for countable nouns.
questions.learning_tip: LITTLE + uncountable noun. Smoke = uncountable → LITTLE smoke. 'A few smoke' is WRONG. LITTLE = not much of something uncountable. They were lucky — only LITTLE smoke.

questions.stem: The fire safety equipment hasn't been checked this month, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Main clause is NEGATIVE present perfect ('hasn't been checked') → POSITIVE question tag. 'Hasn't' → positive tag = has it.
questions.learning_tip: Negative present perfect → positive tag. 'The equipment HASN'T been checked, HAS it?' NEGATIVE → POSITIVE tag. HAS → HASN'T; HASN'T → HAS.

questions.stem: The new fire safety leaflet ________ to every household in the estate last month.
questions.trap_type: The leaflet was the receiver of the action. Past passive = was delivered.
questions.learning_tip: WAS/WERE + past participle = passive! The leaflet WAS DELIVERED to households = the SCDF delivered it; the leaflet received the action.

questions.stem: The fire safety officer told residents ________ candles unattended near curtains or paper.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: TOLD someone NOT TO + base verb. The officer told residents NOT TO LEAVE candles unattended. Formula: told + person + not to + base verb.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Passive voice — 8 forms)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Every fire engine (1)________ thoroughly after each call-out.' Signal: present simple passive — regular/routine action = IS + past participle. Subject 'every fire engine' = singular.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'is cleaning' (active) instead of 'is cleaned' (passive). The engine does not clean itself — people clean it.
questions.learning_tip: IS + past participle = present simple passive. The engine IS CLEANED = someone cleans it. Passive: IS/ARE + past participle. Rule: receiver + IS/ARE + pp.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'All firefighters (2)________ for at least two years before they are allowed to attend a real fire.' Signal: present simple passive — plural subject 'all firefighters' = ARE + past participle.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'is trained' (singular) instead of 'are trained' (plural). 'All firefighters' = plural → ARE.
questions.learning_tip: ARE + past participle = present simple passive for PLURAL. All firefighters ARE TRAINED = they receive training (plural subject). ARE for plural; IS for singular. Rule: plural + ARE + pp.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'This fire station (3)________ in 1987 and has served the community ever since.' Signal: past simple passive — one completed past action = WAS + past participle. Subject 'this fire station' = singular.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'were built' (plural past) instead of 'was built' (singular past).
questions.learning_tip: WAS + past participle = past simple passive for SINGULAR. This station WAS BUILT in 1987 = someone built it then. Singular + WAS + pp. Rule: singular + WAS; plural + WERE.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Three people (4)________ from the burning flat by the crew last Tuesday.' Signal: past simple passive — plural subject ('three people') + completed past action = WERE + past participle.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'was rescued' (singular past) instead of 'were rescued' (plural past).
questions.learning_tip: WERE + past participle = past simple passive for PLURAL. Three people WERE RESCUED = the crew rescued them. Plural + WERE + pp. Rule: plural past passive = WERE + pp.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The fire safety manual (5)________ three times since it was first published.' Signal: present perfect passive — singular subject 'the manual' + action from past to now = HAS BEEN + past participle.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'have been updated' (plural) instead of 'has been updated' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: HAS BEEN + past participle = present perfect passive for SINGULAR. The manual HAS BEEN UPDATED = it was updated at some point(s) and is relevant now. Singular = HAS BEEN.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'New smoke detectors (6)________ in every flat in the estate since last year.' Signal: present perfect passive — plural subject 'new smoke detectors' = HAVE BEEN + past participle.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'has been installed' (singular) instead of 'have been installed' (plural).
questions.learning_tip: HAVE BEEN + past participle = present perfect passive for PLURAL. New detectors HAVE BEEN INSTALLED = they were installed (from past to now). Plural = HAVE BEEN.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'One of the hoses (7)________ right now after it was damaged during last week's call-out.' Signal: present continuous passive — singular subject 'one of the hoses' + happening right now = IS BEING + past participle.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'is repaired' (simple present passive) instead of 'is being repaired' (continuous passive, right now).
questions.learning_tip: IS BEING + past participle = present continuous passive. The hose IS BEING REPAIRED = it is being repaired right now. Rule: IS/ARE + BEING + pp = happening now (passive).
