questions.context_check: Passage: 'The new ladder truck (8)________ when the alarm suddenly sounded for a real fire.' Signal: past continuous passive — singular subject + ongoing past action interrupted = WAS BEING + past participle.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'was tested' (simple past passive, completed) instead of 'was being tested' (past continuous passive, ongoing when interrupted).
questions.learning_tip: WAS BEING + past participle = past continuous passive. The truck WAS BEING TESTED (ongoing) when the alarm sounded (interruption). Rule: WAS/WERE + BEING + pp = ongoing past passive.

C.passage: Every fire engine (1)________ thoroughly after each call-out to ensure it is always ready for the next emergency. All firefighters (2)________ for at least two years before they are allowed to attend a real fire. This fire station (3)________ in 1987 and has served the community ever since. Three people (4)________ from the burning flat by the crew last Tuesday evening. The fire safety manual (5)________ three times since it was first published, to include new guidelines for high-rise buildings. New smoke detectors (6)________ in every flat in the estate since last year as part of a government safety programme. One of the hoses (7)________ right now after it was damaged during last week's call-out. The new ladder truck (8)________ when the alarm sounded for a real fire.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Singapore Civil Defence Force firefighters are among the most highly trained (1)________ in the world. During school visits, they use a training room to (2)________ a fire emergency safely. Students learn to identify a fire (3)________ — anything that could start or spread a fire. They are also taught how to (4)________ a building quickly using stairways instead of lifts. Firefighters use specialist (5)________ such as breathing equipment and hydraulic cutting tools to carry out rescues.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'most highly trained ___ in the world' = the people who work there = personnel.
questions.learning_tip: PERSONNEL = the people who work in an organisation. SCDF PERSONNEL = the firefighters and staff who work for SCDF.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'to ___ a fire emergency... without any real danger' = create a realistic copy of = simulate.
questions.learning_tip: SIMULATE = create a realistic copy or model of a situation for training purposes. Firefighters SIMULATE emergencies to train safely.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'anything that could start or spread a fire' = a source of danger = hazard.
questions.learning_tip: A HAZARD = a source of potential danger. An overloaded electrical socket is a fire HAZARD = it could cause a fire.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'leave a building quickly and safely using stairways' = evacuate.
questions.learning_tip: EVACUATE = leave a building or area quickly because of danger. During a fire, you must EVACUATE = exit the building immediately using the staircase.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'specialist ___ such as breathing equipment, hydraulic cutting tools and hoses' = specialised equipment = apparatus.
questions.learning_tip: APPARATUS = specialised equipment or tools for a particular purpose. Firefighters use specialist APPARATUS including breathing gear and hydraulic tools.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the firefighters)
questions.trap_type: 'The firefighters' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! The firefighters WERE already dressed when the alarm rang. WAS is only for singular. FIREFIGHTERS = more than one → WERE.

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — its (possessive) vs it's (it is)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'its' (possessive) when the sentence needs 'it's' = it is.
questions.learning_tip: IT'S = it is. ITS = belonging to it. 'ITS important to test your smoke alarm' → can you replace with 'it is'? YES → use IT'S. Remember: IT'S = IT IS.

questions.error_type: Spelling — ie/ei confusion (piece: I before E)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'peice' putting E before I. 'Piece' follows the I-before-E rule: pIEce.
questions.learning_tip: Rule: I before E, except after C! pIEce = I before E ✅. Remember: 'A pIEce of PIE' — the word PIE is hidden inside PIECE, with I before E.

questions.error_type: Adverb required after action verb (spread)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'rapid' (adjective) after the action verb 'spread'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (spread), use an ADVERB: spread RAPIDLY. Rule: verb + adverb (-ly). 'Rapid' describes nouns (a rapid spread). 'Rapidly' describes actions (spread rapidly).

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — singular possessive (firefighter's = one firefighter)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'firefighters'' (plural possessive) when the sentence refers to one firefighter. ONE firefighter → firefighter's.
questions.learning_tip: Singular possessive: ONE firefighter → FIREFIGHTER'S helmet. FIREFIGHTERS' helmet (plural) would mean one helmet belonging to many firefighters. Check: is it ONE or MANY? ONE → 's.

E.passage: Last Friday, our class visited Bukit Timah Fire Station for a learning journey. The firefighters was (1) already dressed in their full gear when we arrived, ready to demonstrate a mock rescue. The officer in charge said its (2) essential to check your smoke alarm every month. He showed us a peice (3) of melted plastic — the result of leaving a phone charger plugged in overnight. A small electrical fire can spread rapid (4) throughout a room in just two minutes if nothing is done. We also tried on the firefighters' (5) heavy breathing mask, which weighed almost five kilograms.

questions.sentence_a: You test your smoke alarm regularly.
questions.sentence_b: You may not know it has stopped working.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'Unless'.
questions.model_answer: Unless you test your smoke alarm regularly, you may not know it has stopped working.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'Unless you will test' — adding 'will' in the 'unless' clause.
questions.learning_tip: UNLESS + simple present, simple future/modal. UNLESS you TEST your smoke alarm regularly, you MAY NOT KNOW it has stopped. No 'will' after 'unless'.

questions.sentence_a: The firefighter entered the burning building.
questions.sentence_b: She rescued two children from the third floor.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'After'.
questions.model_answer: After entering the burning building, the firefighter rescued two children from the third floor.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'After the firefighter entered the burning building, she rescued two children' — acceptable, but the model answer uses the -ing reduction.
questions.learning_tip: AFTER + verb-ing (same subject): AFTER ENTERING the building, the firefighter rescued two children. When the subject is the same for both actions, 'after + -ing' is elegant and concise.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
The alarm sounded at 2.47 in the afternoon. By 2.48, Senior Station Inspector Ravi had already led his team out of the station.

The call was for a kitchen fire in a third-floor flat on Clementi Avenue. When the engine arrived, smoke was pouring from an open window. Ravi's team pulled on their breathing masks and went in.

The fire was small — a forgotten pan on the stove. They put it out in under two minutes. But in the corridor outside, they found an elderly man who could not walk. He was trying to reach the staircase when the smoke overcame him.

Ravi lifted the man onto his back and carried him down three flights of stairs without stopping.

The paramedics were waiting outside. The man, who was seventy-eight years old, was taken to hospital and later confirmed to be in stable condition.

At the debrief that evening, Ravi reminded his team: 'The fire was the easy part. It is always the person who needs the most time.'

Ravi did not speak on the way back to the station. At the debrief, he set his helmet on the table and looked at his team. Each of them knew what the other was thinking: the man in the corridor could have been anyone's grandfather. That thought did not make the work harder. It made it more important.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'flowing out in large amounts'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Arrived' = reached a place; 'pulled' = drew; 'open' = not closed. POURING = flowing out continuously and in large amounts.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: POURING = flowing out steadily and in large amounts. Smoke was POURING from the window = coming out in a continuous stream. 'Pour' = flow freely and in volume.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'them' refer to in 'They put it out in under two minutes'?

options.1: The smoke and flames from the fire

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 2 thinking 'it' = the pan. But 'put it out' = extinguished the FIRE. 'It' = the fire.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: 'The fire was small... They PUT IT OUT in under two minutes.' IT = the FIRE. 'Put out' = extinguish. They extinguished the fire in under two minutes.

mcq_questions.stem: Ravi said 'The fire was the easy part. It is always the person who needs the most time.' What did he mean?

options.1: Fires are usually small and easy to put out.
options.2: Rescuing people requires more care, effort and time than extinguishing the fire itself.
options.3: The team should have arrived faster.
options.4: Elderly people should not live in high-rise flats.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking he was dismissing the fire. His message is about what is truly difficult — the human rescue.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Ravi means: putting out the fire is technically straightforward, but RESCUING a PERSON — carrying them safely to safety — requires more time, care and effort. People are the priority.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that the team took more than two minutes to leave the station after the alarm? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The alarm sounded at 2.47 and 'BY 2.48, Senior Station Inspector Ravi had already LED HIS TEAM OUT of the station' — showing they left within one minute.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, it takes time to prepare.' The passage gives exact times — they left within one minute.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: alarm at 2.47, team out by 2.48 = ONE MINUTE. 'By 2.48, Ravi had ALREADY led his team out.' They left in under one minute. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What caused the fire, and where was it?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: The fire was caused by a forgotten pan left on the stove. It was in the kitchen of a third-floor flat on Clementi Avenue.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'a kitchen fire' without identifying the specific cause.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: 'a FORGOTTEN PAN on the stove' was the cause. Location: kitchen of a THIRD-FLOOR flat on Clementi Avenue. Give both the cause and the location.

open_ended_questions.stem: What TWO challenges did Ravi's team face that were more difficult than putting out the fire?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) They found an elderly man who could not walk and was overcome by smoke while trying to reach the staircase. (ii) Ravi had to carry the man on his back down three flights of stairs without stopping — a physically demanding and time-consuming rescue.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe the fire as a challenge. The question asks what was MORE DIFFICULT than the fire.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraphs 3–4: (1) finding a man who COULD NOT WALK and was overcome by smoke; (2) Ravi carrying him down THREE FLIGHTS of stairs on his back. The HUMAN rescue was the real challenge.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did the firefighters know where to go when they arrived at the flat?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: They could see smoke pouring from an open window, which showed them where the fire was.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'they got a call' — the call told them the address, but the visual clue (smoke from window) directed them to the exact location.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'SMOKE was POURING from an OPEN WINDOW.' This visual clue told them exactly where the fire was in the building. They could see it from outside.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his actions and words in the passage, describe TWO character traits of Ravi with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) DECISIVE: Ravi had his team out of the station within one minute of the alarm — no hesitation, immediate action. (ii) COMPASSIONATE: when he found the elderly man who could not walk, he lifted him onto his back and carried him down three flights of stairs without stopping, putting the man's safety entirely first.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'brave and fast' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: DECISIVE = team out within ONE MINUTE, no hesitation. COMPASSIONATE = carried the elderly man on his BACK down THREE FLIGHTS without stopping — putting the person first.

questions.stem: The chapteh champion was as ________ as a cat, catching the feathered shuttlecock before it touched the ground.
questions.trap_type: 'Slow', 'clumsy' and 'heavy' all suggest the opposite of fast, skilled movement. QUICK = moving fast and reacting immediately.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The champion was AS QUICK AS a cat = the simile compares his speed to a cat's. QUICK = fast and light in movement.

questions.stem: Despite losing five rounds in a row, the young player refused to ________ and kept trying until the very end.
questions.trap_type: 'Continue', 'practise' and 'improve' all mean the opposite of stopping. GIVE UP = stop trying because something is too difficult.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: GIVE UP = stop trying because something feels too hard. The player refused to GIVE UP = he kept going despite losing. GIVE + UP work together — never split them!

questions.stem: The kite flew higher and higher until it was barely ________, just a tiny speck against the blue sky.
questions.trap_type: 'Colourful' describes colour, not whether it can be seen from far away. 'Heavy' and 'broken' make no sense. VISIBLE = able to be seen.
questions.learning_tip: VISIBLE = able to be seen. The kite was barely VISIBLE = it was so far away it could hardly be seen. Opposite: invisible.

questions.stem: The old man showed the children how to ________ the gasing top so that it spun perfectly on the ground.
questions.trap_type: 'Break' = damage; 'ignore' = pay no attention; 'sell' = give for money. LAUNCH = send something into motion with force.
questions.learning_tip: LAUNCH = send something into motion with a controlled release of force. To LAUNCH a gasing top = to throw and release it so it spins perfectly.

questions.stem: The five stones game requires great ________ — both hands and eyes must work together at exactly the right moment.
questions.trap_type: 'Strength' = physical power; 'speed' = fast movement; 'silence' = no noise. COORDINATION = the ability to use hands and eyes together smoothly and accurately.
questions.learning_tip: COORDINATION = the ability to control different parts of your body together smoothly. Five stones needs great COORDINATION = your hands and eyes must work together at exactly the right time.

questions.stem: Everyone in the playground ________ a different traditional game during recess.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'play' thinking 'everyone in the playground' = many people. EVERYONE = singular → verb must have -S in present tense.
questions.learning_tip: EVERYONE / NOBODY / SOMEONE = Singular! ALWAYS use verb+S. Everyone PLAYS = add -S. 'Everyone play' or 'Everyone are playing' are WRONG.

questions.stem: Our school has ________ a traditional games festival every year since it was founded.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. 'Hold' is irregular: hold → held.
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Our school HAS HELD a festival every year = from the past until now. HOLD → HELD (irregular).

questions.stem: The gasing top spun ________ longer than the chapteh shuttlecock stayed in the air.
questions.trap_type: FAR + comparative = intensified comparison. 'Very' is not used with comparatives. FAR LONGER = much longer.
questions.learning_tip: FAR + comparative = much more. The gasing spun FAR LONGER THAN the chapteh stayed in the air. FAR makes the comparison stronger. 'Very longer' is WRONG.

questions.stem: The children ________ their kites on the open field when a strong gust of wind suddenly snapped the string.
questions.trap_type: 'A gust snapped the string' = sudden interrupting event. The children were already flying kites = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: A gust SNAPPED the string = sudden past event. Children were already in the middle of flying kites = WERE FLYING (past continuous). Past continuous = was/were + verb-ing.

questions.stem: There was ________ space left on the mat for the five stones players to sit comfortably.
questions.trap_type: 'Space' is uncountable → use LITTLE. 'Few', 'many' and 'a few' are for countable nouns.
questions.learning_tip: LITTLE + uncountable noun. Space = uncountable → LITTLE space. 'Few space' or 'a few space' are WRONG. LITTLE = not much (uncountable).

questions.stem: Traditional games are more educational than most people think, ________ they?
questions.trap_type: Positive statement ('are more educational') → negative question tag. 'Are' → aren't they.
questions.learning_tip: Positive statement → negative tag. Traditional games ARE more educational, AREN'T they? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE tag. ARE → AREN'T.

questions.stem: The zero-point rubber band rope ________ by the students before each game to make sure it was the right length.
questions.trap_type: The rope was the receiver of the action. Past passive: was/were + past participle.
questions.learning_tip: WAS/WERE + past participle = passive! The rope WAS MEASURED = someone measured it. The rope received the action. NEVER: 'was being measured' (P5 level).

questions.stem: The games teacher told the students ________ their tops on the tiled corridor in case the surface was too slippery.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: TOLD someone NOT TO + base verb. The teacher told students NOT TO SPIN their tops on the tiles. Formula: told + person + not to + verb.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Prepositions of place and direction)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We played five stones (1)________ the void deck of our block after school.' Signal: enclosed space (void deck) = IN. IN = inside an enclosed or defined space.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'at' (general location) instead of 'in' (inside an enclosed space).
questions.learning_tip: IN = inside an enclosed space. We played IN the void deck = inside that covered area. IN is for spaces you can be inside of.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Kai placed the gasing top (2)________ the smooth concrete surface and gave it a strong spin.' Signal: surface contact = ON. ON = touching the top of a surface.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' (enclosed space) instead of 'on' (surface contact).
questions.learning_tip: ON = on top of / touching a surface. The top is placed ON the concrete surface = it sits on top of it. ON is for surfaces.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The children met (3)________ the corner of the field every Saturday morning to play chapteh.' Signal: a specific point or meeting place = AT. AT = at a specific point or location.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' (enclosed) instead of 'at' (specific point). AT is used for specific points, not enclosed spaces.
questions.learning_tip: AT = a specific point or location. We met AT the corner of the field = at that exact spot. AT is for specific places or points.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The kite flew (4)________ the tallest tree in the park before the wind changed direction.' Signal: movement above and across = OVER. OVER = above something, crossing from one side to the other.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'above' (not in word box) or 'through'. OVER = passing above and across.
questions.learning_tip: OVER = above something, moving from one side to the other. The kite flew OVER the tree = it passed above the tree. OVER shows crossing movement above.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Priya hid the five stones bag (5)________ the bench so that nobody would take it during the break.' Signal: below and covered by = UNDER. UNDER = below and covered by something.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'behind' (at the back) instead of 'under' (below). The bag is below the bench, not at the back of it.
questions.learning_tip: UNDER = below something that is above you. The bag is UNDER the bench = below the seat of the bench. UNDER means something is directly above you.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The rubber band rope stretched (6)________ the narrow gap between the two pillars.' Signal: from one side to the other, passing inside = THROUGH. THROUGH = entering one side and exiting the other.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'over' (above) instead of 'through' (passing inside). The rope passes inside the gap, not over it.
questions.learning_tip: THROUGH = entering at one side and coming out the other. The rope stretched THROUGH the gap = it passed inside and came out the other side.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'He ran (7)________ the courtyard and grabbed the chapteh before it landed.' Signal: movement from outside to inside (entering) = INTO. INTO = movement entering an enclosed space.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' (static location) instead of 'into' (movement entering). INTO shows the direction of movement, not a static position.
questions.learning_tip: INTO = movement from outside to inside. He ran INTO the courtyard = he was outside, then moved inside. IN = where you are; INTO = the direction you move.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The slowest player had to stand (8)________ the line and wait for the next round.' Signal: at the back of something = BEHIND. BEHIND = at the back of or further back than.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'under' (below) instead of 'behind' (at the back). The player is at the back of the line, not below it.
questions.learning_tip: BEHIND = at the back of something. Stand BEHIND the line = stand at the back, further away. BEHIND is about being at the rear or back of something.

C.passage: We played five stones (1)________ the void deck of our block after school every day. Kai placed the gasing top (2)________ the smooth concrete surface and gave it a strong spin. The children met (3)________ the corner of the field every Saturday morning to play chapteh. The kite flew (4)________ the tallest tree in the park before the wind changed direction. Priya hid the five stones bag (5)________ the bench so nobody would take it during the break. The rubber band rope stretched (6)________ the narrow gap between the two pillars perfectly. He ran (7)________ the courtyard and grabbed the chapteh before it landed. The slowest player had to stand (8)________ the line and wait for the next round.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Games like chapteh, gasing and five stones are part of Singapore's cultural (1)________ — people played them for generations and they connect us to our roots. These (2)________ games do not need expensive equipment or a large space, which makes them easy for anyone to enjoy. In a game of zero-point, a player must jump over a rope held by the (3)________ without touching it. Chapteh tests a player's (4)________ — the ability to move quickly and change direction without losing balance. After a round of five stones, players (5)________ the small cloth bags and prepare for the next throw.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'played for generations and connect us to our roots' = cultural legacy = heritage.
questions.learning_tip: HERITAGE = traditions and practices passed down through generations. These games are part of Singapore's cultural HERITAGE = they belong to our shared history.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'have been played for generations' = old and long-established = traditional.
questions.learning_tip: TRADITIONAL = following practices that have been done for a long time. TRADITIONAL games are ones passed down from older generations.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'jump over a rope held by the ___' = the other player in the game = opponent.
questions.learning_tip: An OPPONENT = the other player or team you are playing against. In zero-point, the OPPONENT holds the rope for you to jump over.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'move quickly and change direction without losing balance' = agility.
questions.learning_tip: AGILITY = the ability to move quickly and change direction smoothly. Chapteh tests your AGILITY — you must react fast and shift your body with control.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'pick up the cloth bags to prepare for the next throw' = retrieve.
questions.learning_tip: RETRIEVE = go and get something after it has been used or lost. Players RETRIEVE the five stones bags = they pick them up to use again.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the players)
questions.trap_type: 'The players' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! The players WERE excited to compete. WAS is only for ONE thing. 'The players' = more than one → WERE.

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — there (place) vs their (possessive)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'there' (at that place) when the sentence needs 'their' (belonging to them).
questions.learning_tip: THEIR = belonging to them. The players held THEIR tops ready. THERE = at that place. Test: replace with 'belonging to them'. If YES → use THEIR.

questions.error_type: Spelling — ie/ei confusion (achieve: I before E)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'acheive' putting E before I. The correct spelling is achIEve — I before E.
questions.learning_tip: Rule: I before E, except after C! achIEve = I before E ✅. Remember: 'achIEve' has IE in the middle — like 'PIE' — I before E always in this word!

questions.error_type: Adverb required after action verb (wrapped)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'careful' (adjective) after the action verb 'wrapped'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (wrapped), use an ADVERB: wrapped CAREFULLY. Rule: verb + adverb (-ly). 'Careful' describes nouns; 'carefully' describes actions.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (players', not players's)
questions.trap_type: Students add 's after the apostrophe for a plural noun ending in -s.
questions.learning_tip: Plural possessive: just add apostrophe! The PLAYERS' tops = the tops belonging to all the players. NEVER 'players's' — the -s after the apostrophe is wrong for plural nouns.

E.passage: Last Saturday, our class took part in the Traditional Games Carnival. The players was (1) lined up at the starting zone, each holding a top or a shuttlecock. They gripped there (2) tops tightly, waiting for the signal to begin. Every child wanted to acheive (3) the highest score and win the golden trophy. The teacher wrapped the gasing rope careful (4) around each top before handing it to the players. At the end of the day, the judges announced the players's (5) final scores and everyone cheered.

questions.sentence_a: You practise chapteh every day.
questions.sentence_b: You will improve your coordination and balance.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'If'.
questions.model_answer: If you practise chapteh every day, you will improve your coordination and balance.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'If you will practise' — adding 'will' in the 'if' clause.
questions.learning_tip: IF + simple present, simple future. IF you PRACTISE every day, you WILL IMPROVE. NEVER use 'will' after 'if' in the condition clause.

questions.sentence_a: The gasing competition was held at the community centre.
questions.sentence_b: The gasing competition attracted players from five different schools.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using the relative pronoun 'which'.
questions.model_answer: The gasing competition, which attracted players from five different schools, was held at the community centre.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'The gasing competition which it attracted' — adding 'it' after 'which'.
questions.learning_tip: WHICH = relative pronoun for things. The competition, WHICH attracted players from five schools, was held at the centre. NEVER add 'it' after 'which'.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
It was the final round of the gasing competition, and nine-year-old Arif had one chance left.

All morning, he watched the older boys launch their tops with a single, practiced flick of the wrist. Their tops spun for minutes at a time, gliding slowly across the smooth concrete pad. Arif's best spin so far had lasted forty-three seconds.

His grandfather, who had taught him everything he knew about gasing, sat in the third row of the plastic chairs. He did not wave or call out. He simply watched.

Arif stepped to the line. He wound the rope around the top slowly, the way his grandfather had shown him — tight, even, patient.

He threw.

The top landed perfectly and spun without wobbling. Arif did not watch it. He watched his grandfather's face instead.

At sixty seconds, the crowd began to count. At seventy, some stood up. At eighty-three seconds, the judge raised the green flag.

Arif looked at his grandfather. The old man pressed his lips together and nodded once — the same nod he gave when something was done correctly.

That was enough.

Outside, the other competitors had already left. Arif stayed a little longer, watching the empty concrete pad where the tops had spun. He wanted to remember exactly how the rope felt in his hands.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'moving smoothly without effort'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Spun' = rotated; 'practiced' = well-rehearsed; 'launched' = sent into motion. GLIDING = moving smoothly and effortlessly.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: GLIDING = moving smoothly, without effort or sound. The tops were GLIDING across the concrete = moving in a slow, effortless way.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'He' refer to in 'He simply watched'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 2 thinking 'He' = Arif. But the paragraph is describing Arif's grandfather — 'He' = the grandfather.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: 'His GRANDFATHER... sat in the third row. HE did not wave or call out. HE simply watched.' HE = the grandfather, not Arif.

mcq_questions.stem: Why did Arif watch his grandfather's face instead of his spinning top?

options.1: He was nervous and could not look at the top.
options.2: He could not see the top from where he was standing.
options.3: His grandfather's reaction meant more to him than the result on the judge's card.
options.4: He wanted to make sure his grandfather was safe.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking he was simply too nervous. But the whole passage builds to this moment — Arif cares deeply about his grandfather's approval.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Arif did not check the judge — he watched his GRANDFATHER'S FACE. This shows that his grandfather's reaction (approval, pride) meant MORE to him than the official result.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 2, is it True or False that Arif's best spin before the final lasted more than one minute? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says 'Arif's best spin so far had lasted FORTY-THREE SECONDS' — which is less than one minute (sixty seconds).
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, the older boys' tops spun for minutes.' That is the older boys, not Arif.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'Arif's best spin had lasted FORTY-THREE SECONDS.' 43 seconds < 60 seconds (one minute). The answer is FALSE. Read carefully — the older boys spun longer, not Arif.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did Arif prepare the gasing top before throwing it?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: He wound the rope around the top slowly, tightly and evenly — exactly the way his grandfather had taught him.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he got ready' — too vague. The passage gives specific details about how he wound the rope.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'He WOUND THE ROPE around the top SLOWLY — tight, even, patient.' Give these specific details, not a general answer.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did the crowd's reaction change as Arif's top kept spinning? Give TWO details from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) At sixty seconds, the crowd began to count — showing they were engaged and tracking the time. (ii) At seventy seconds, some stood up — showing their excitement was growing.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe only one stage of the reaction.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 7: At SIXTY seconds = crowd BEGAN TO COUNT. At SEVENTY seconds = some STOOD UP. These are two distinct reactions that show growing excitement.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did Arif's grandfather's nod mean to Arif?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: It meant that Arif did something correctly — it was his grandfather's sign of quiet approval and pride.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'the grandfather was happy' — too vague. The nod has a specific meaning explained in the passage.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Last paragraph: 'the same nod he gave when something was done CORRECTLY.' The nod = quiet signal of approval. That was enough for Arif.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his actions in the passage, describe TWO character traits of Arif with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) PATIENT: he wound the rope slowly and carefully — 'tight, even, patient' — not rushing despite the pressure of the final round. (ii) RESPECTFUL: instead of celebrating or checking the judge, he watched his grandfather's face — showing his grandfather's approval mattered most to him.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'brave and good at gasing' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE formula: TRAIT = evidence from text. PATIENT = wound rope 'SLOWLY, TIGHT, EVEN' despite final-round pressure. RESPECTFUL = watched GRANDFATHER'S FACE (not the judge). For G8, always name the TRAIT first, then give EVIDENCE from the passage.

questions.stem: The dragonfly hovered above the pond, its wings as ________ as paper, so delicate that sunlight shone right through them.
questions.trap_type: 'Heavy' and 'thick' are the opposite of delicate. 'Dark' doesn't fit because sunlight shines through them. THIN = having very little thickness, delicate and fine.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The wings were AS THIN AS paper = comparing their delicate thinness to paper. THIN = very little thickness. A dragonfly's wings are among the thinnest structures in nature.

questions.stem: The scientist decided to ________ the rare beetle specimen carefully so it would not be damaged.
questions.trap_type: 'Destroy', 'ignore' and 'hide' are all harmful or unhelpful actions. LOOK AFTER = take care of something to keep it safe.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: LOOK AFTER = take care of something or someone. She decided to LOOK AFTER the beetle = keep it safe and in good condition. LOOK + AFTER work together — never split!

questions.stem: The butterfly ________ from a dull brown caterpillar into a creature with dazzling orange and black wings.
questions.trap_type: 'Disappeared' = vanished; 'shrank' = became smaller; 'escaped' = got away. TRANSFORMED = changed completely in form or appearance.
questions.learning_tip: TRANSFORMED = changed completely into something very different. The caterpillar TRANSFORMED into a butterfly = it became something entirely new and beautiful.

questions.stem: The firefly's gentle light ________ in the darkness of the garden like a tiny dancing star.
questions.trap_type: 'Faded', 'disappeared' and 'shrank' all mean the light was going away or getting smaller. FLICKERED = shone with a rapidly changing, unsteady light.
questions.learning_tip: FLICKERED = shone with a rapidly changing, unsteady light. The firefly's light FLICKERED = it blinked on and off quickly, like a tiny flame.

questions.stem: Ants are ________ insects — a single colony can contain millions of individuals all working together.
questions.trap_type: 'Solitary' = living alone; 'fragile' = easily broken; 'silent' = making no sound. SOCIAL insects live and work in large organised groups.
questions.learning_tip: SOCIAL insects = insects that live and work together in large organised groups. Ants are SOCIAL insects — they communicate, cooperate and build together as a community.

questions.stem: Nobody in the science class ________ that the stick insect on the leaf is actually a living creature.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'notice' thinking 'nobody in the science class' = many people. NOBODY = singular → verb must have -S in present tense.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY = Singular! ALWAYS use verb+S in present tense. Nobody NOTICES = add -S. 'Nobody notice' or 'Nobody are noticing' are WRONG.

questions.stem: Our school has ________ an insect garden in the science corner since last year.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. 'Create' is regular: create → created.
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Our school HAS CREATED an insect garden = it was created at some point and is still there now. CREATE → CREATED (regular).

questions.stem: The grasshopper can jump ________ than fifty times its own body length in a single leap.
questions.trap_type: Comparative needed (comparing to a standard distance). 'Far' → comparative = FARTHER (or further). 'Very' cannot be used with comparatives.
questions.learning_tip: FARTHER = comparative of 'far'. The grasshopper jumps FARTHER THAN fifty times its length = it goes more distance than that. FARTHER = more distance. 'Very farther' is WRONG.

questions.stem: The students ________ the monarch butterfly when it suddenly flew out of the net.
questions.trap_type: 'It suddenly flew out of the net' = sudden interrupting event. Students were already observing = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The butterfly FLEW OUT = sudden past event. Students were already observing = WERE OBSERVING (past continuous). Past continuous = was/were + verb-ing.

questions.stem: There is ________ information about beetles in this book — it covers almost every species in South-East Asia.
questions.trap_type: 'Information' is uncountable → use 'a lot of' or 'much'. 'A few', 'many' and 'several' are for countable nouns.
questions.learning_tip: A LOT OF = large amount for BOTH countable and uncountable nouns. 'Information' is uncountable → A LOT OF information. 'Many information' or 'a few information' are WRONG.

questions.stem: The firefly display in the mangrove forest was the most beautiful thing you have ever seen, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Main clause uses 'you have ever seen' = present perfect positive → negative question tag = haven't you.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present perfect → negative tag. 'The most beautiful thing you HAVE ever seen, HAVEN'T you?' HAVE → HAVEN'T. Positive → negative tag.

questions.stem: The rare Atlas moth specimen ________ to the national museum after it was discovered in the jungle last week.
questions.trap_type: The moth specimen was the receiver of the action. Past passive = was donated.
questions.learning_tip: WAS/WERE + past participle = passive! The specimen WAS DONATED = someone donated it; the specimen received the action. NEVER use 'was being donated' (P5 level).

questions.stem: The nature guide told the children ________ the praying mantis or it might strike at their fingers.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: TOLD someone NOT TO + base verb. The guide told children NOT TO TOUCH the mantis. Formula: told + person + not to + verb.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Personal pronouns — subject and object)

questions.context_check: Passage: '(1)________ spotted a bright green praying mantis on the wall of the science room.' Signal: blank = SUBJECT of 'spotted'. First person singular subject = I.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'Me' (object form). I is the SUBJECT pronoun — it does the action.
questions.learning_tip: I = subject pronoun — it DOES the action. I spotted the mantis. ME = object — it receives the action ('The mantis surprised ME'). SUBJECT = I; OBJECT = ME.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'My teacher asked (2)________ to draw the mantis in my science journal.' Signal: blank = OBJECT of 'asked'. The teacher asked → me (first person singular object). 'My teacher asked me' = ME is the receiver of asking.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'I' (subject) instead of 'me' (object after a verb).
questions.learning_tip: After a verb (asked), use OBJECT pronoun. My teacher asked ME = ME is what the verb 'asked' points to. 'My teacher asked I' is WRONG. After verbs: use ME, HIM, HER, THEM.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'My classmate Dion is the insect expert in our class — (3)________ knows the name of almost every bug.' Signal: blank = SUBJECT of 'knows'. Dion = male singular subject = HE.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'him' (object form) instead of 'he' (subject).
questions.learning_tip: HE = subject pronoun for a male. HE knows the names = HE does the action. 'Him knows' is WRONG. HE = subject; HIM = object (e.g., 'I told HIM').

questions.context_check: Passage: 'I always ask (4)________ for help when I cannot identify an insect.' Signal: blank = OBJECT of 'ask'. I ask → him (male singular object after a verb).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'he' (subject) instead of 'him' (object after a verb).
questions.learning_tip: After a verb (ask), use OBJECT pronoun. I always ask HIM for help = HIM is the receiver of asking. 'I ask he' is WRONG. After verbs: HIM, not HE.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Our science teacher loves insects — (5)________ once kept a pet stick insect for a whole year.' Signal: blank = SUBJECT of 'kept'. Science teacher = female singular subject = SHE.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'her' (object form) instead of 'she' (subject).
questions.learning_tip: SHE = subject pronoun for a female. SHE kept a pet stick insect = SHE does the action. 'Her kept' is WRONG. SHE = subject; HER = object (e.g., 'I saw HER').

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The stick insect surprised (6)________ by shedding its skin overnight without any warning.' Signal: blank = OBJECT of 'surprised'. The insect surprised → her (female singular object after a verb).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'she' (subject) instead of 'her' (object after a verb).
questions.learning_tip: After a verb (surprised), use OBJECT pronoun. The insect surprised HER = HER is the receiver of 'surprised'. 'Surprised she' is WRONG. After verbs: HER, not SHE.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Ants are fascinating creatures — (7)________ can carry fifty times their own body weight.' Signal: blank = SUBJECT of 'can carry'. Ants = plural subject = THEY.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'them' (object form) instead of 'they' (subject).
questions.learning_tip: THEY = subject pronoun for a group. THEY can carry fifty times their weight = THEY do the action. 'Them can carry' is WRONG. THEY = subject; THEM = object.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Scientists have studied (8)________ for thousands of years and still have new discoveries to make.' Signal: blank = OBJECT of 'studied'. Scientists studied → them (ants, plural object after a verb).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'they' (subject) instead of 'them' (object after a verb).
questions.learning_tip: After a verb (studied), use OBJECT pronoun. Scientists studied THEM = THEM is the receiver of 'studied'. 'Studied they' is WRONG. After verbs: THEM, not THEY.

C.passage: (1)________ spotted a bright green praying mantis on the wall. My teacher asked (2)________ to draw it. My classmate Dion is the insect expert — (3)________ knows the name of every bug. I always ask (4)________ for help when I cannot identify an insect. Our science teacher loves insects — (5)________ once kept a pet stick insect on her desk. The stick insect surprised (6)________ by shedding its skin overnight. Ants are fascinating creatures — (7)________ can carry fifty times their weight. Scientists have studied (8)________ for thousands of years.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Insects have developed amazing ways to survive. Many use (1)________ to blend in with surroundings and hide from enemies. The stick insect looks exactly like a twig. A (2)________ is an animal that hunts and eats other animals. Insects use their (3)________ — the long feelers on their heads — to sense vibrations and communicate. Some insects begin life as (4)________, worm-like young that hatch from eggs. A healthy garden provides the ideal (5)________ for many insect species.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'blending in with surroundings to hide' = camouflage.
questions.learning_tip: CAMOUFLAGE = the ability to blend in with surroundings so as not to be seen. The stick insect uses CAMOUFLAGE = it looks like a twig so predators cannot spot it.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'an animal that hunts and eats other animals' = predator.
questions.learning_tip: A PREDATOR = an animal that hunts and eats other animals. Birds and lizards are PREDATORS of insects = they catch and eat them.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'long feelers on their heads — to sense vibrations, smell food and communicate' = antennae.
questions.learning_tip: ANTENNAE = the long, thin feelers on an insect's head used to sense the world. Insects use their ANTENNAE to detect smells, sounds and vibrations.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'worm-like young that hatch from eggs before growing into their adult form' = larvae.
questions.learning_tip: LARVAE = the worm-like young of insects that hatch from eggs. Caterpillars are the LARVAE of butterflies. LARVA (singular) → LARVAE (plural).

questions.trap_type: The clue 'ideal ___ for many insect species to feed, breed and shelter' = natural home = habitat.
questions.learning_tip: A HABITAT = the natural environment where a living thing normally lives. A healthy garden is the ideal HABITAT for insects to feed, breed and shelter.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the butterflies)
questions.trap_type: 'The butterflies' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! The butterflies WERE resting on the flower. WAS is only for ONE thing (singular). BUTTERFLIES = more than one → WERE.

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — its (possessive) vs it's (it is)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'its' (possessive) when the meaning is 'it is'.
questions.learning_tip: IT'S = it is (contraction). ITS = belonging to it. 'ITS amazing how far ants can carry things' → can you say 'it is amazing'? YES → use IT'S. IT'S = IT IS.

questions.error_type: Spelling — ie/ei confusion (chief: I before E)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'cheif' putting E before I. 'Chief' follows I-before-E: chIEf.
questions.learning_tip: Rule: I before E, except after C! chIEf = I before E ✅. Remember: the 'chIEf' has a PIE hidden inside him — chIEf. I before E!

questions.error_type: Adverb required after action verb (moved)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'slow' (adjective) after the action verb 'moved'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (moved), use an ADVERB: moved SLOWLY. Rule: verb + adverb (-ly). 'Slow' describes nouns; 'slowly' describes HOW something moves.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (scientists', not scientist's)
questions.trap_type: Students use singular possessive (scientist's) when the sentence refers to many scientists.
questions.learning_tip: SCIENTISTS' = belonging to many scientists (plural). 'The SCIENTISTS' findings' = what many scientists found. SCIENTIST'S = only ONE scientist. Check: ONE or MANY?

E.passage: Our class went on a nature walk to study insects in the school garden. The butterflies was (1) resting on the flowers when we arrived, their wings open in the warm sunlight. its (2) hard to believe that such delicate creatures can migrate across entire continents. The teacher pointed to a trail of ants and told us that the cheif (3) worker always leads the group back to the nest. The green caterpillar moved slow (4) along the branch, searching for fresh leaves to eat. At the end of the walk, the scientist's (5) notes and photographs were collected and used to create a class insect guide.

questions.sentence_a: You remove fallen leaves and dead branches from your garden.
questions.sentence_b: You reduce the number of hiding places for harmful insects.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'As long as'.
questions.model_answer: As long as you remove fallen leaves and dead branches from your garden, you reduce the number of hiding places for harmful insects.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'As long as you will remove' — adding 'will' in the 'as long as' clause.
questions.learning_tip: AS LONG AS + simple present, simple present/future. AS LONG AS you REMOVE fallen leaves, you REDUCE hiding places. No 'will' after 'as long as'.

questions.sentence_a: The firefly produces light using a chemical reaction in its body.
questions.sentence_b: The firefly uses light to attract a mate.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'Since'.
questions.model_answer: Since the firefly produces light using a chemical reaction in its body, it uses this light to attract a mate.
questions.trap_type: Students reverse the logic: 'The firefly uses light to attract a mate since it produces light using a chemical reaction' — acceptable but less natural as a causal structure.
questions.learning_tip: SINCE = because of a background reason. SINCE the firefly PRODUCES light using chemistry, IT USES this light to attract a mate. The background cause comes after 'since'.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Most people know that bees make honey. But the engineering inside a beehive is just as remarkable as the honey itself.

Bees build their hives from wax, which they produce inside their own bodies. A single worker bee produces only about one gram of wax in its entire lifetime. Yet a large hive may contain over one hundred thousand individual wax cells, all built to exactly the same six-sided shape.

The six-sided shape, called a hexagon, is not chosen by accident. It is the most efficient shape that exists: it uses the least amount of wax to create the most amount of storage space. Engineers and architects have studied the hexagon for centuries because of this property.

Inside each cell, bees store honey, pollen or eggs. The temperature inside the hive is kept at exactly thirty-five degrees Celsius at all times — warm enough for eggs to develop, cool enough to preserve the honey.

When a hive becomes too crowded, the queen bee leaves with half the colony to build a new home. The remaining bees raise a new queen. In this way, the colony survives and grows, generation after generation.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 3 has the same meaning as 'using the smallest amount of resources to get the best result'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Hexagon' is a shape; 'property' = a characteristic; 'chosen' = selected. EFFICIENT = using the least resources to produce the best result.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: EFFICIENT = using the least amount of resources to produce the best result. The hexagon is the most EFFICIENT shape = it uses the least wax but stores the most.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 4, what does 'this' refer to in 'The temperature inside the hive is kept at exactly thirty-five degrees Celsius at all times'?

options.3: A specific constant temperature maintained inside the hive
options.4: The number of bees in the colony

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 2 thinking 'this' refers to the cells. But the paragraph shifts to temperature — 'this' = the specific temperature of 35°C.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'The temperature inside the hive is kept at exactly THIRTY-FIVE DEGREES CELSIUS at all times.' THIS = this specific maintained temperature.

mcq_questions.stem: Why does the writer mention that 'engineers and architects have studied the hexagon for centuries'?

options.1: To show that humans are smarter than bees.
options.2: To suggest that bees learned to build from human engineers.
options.3: To show that bees discovered a mathematically perfect shape long before humans studied it.
options.4: To explain why beehives are always round.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking it is about human superiority. The writer's purpose is the opposite — to show that bees naturally discovered what humans took centuries to study.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: engineers studied the hexagon BECAUSE of its efficiency — the bees were already using it. This shows bees discovered a perfect shape BEFORE humans understood it scientifically.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 2, is it True or False that a single bee produces enough wax to build a complete hive on its own? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says a single worker bee produces only about ONE GRAM OF WAX in its entire lifetime — far too little to build a whole hive.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, bees make their own wax.' They do make their own wax, but each bee only makes one gram — far too little to build an entire hive alone.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'a single worker bee produces only about ONE GRAM of wax in its ENTIRE LIFETIME.' One gram is a tiny amount — one bee alone could never build a hive. FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: Name THREE things that bees store inside the cells of the hive.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Bees store honey, pollen and eggs inside the cells of the hive.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students name only one or two items.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'Inside each cell, bees store HONEY, POLLEN or EGGS.' All three are listed clearly in the passage. Name all three for full marks.

open_ended_questions.stem: Why is the hexagon shape so useful for building a beehive? Give TWO reasons from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) It uses the least amount of wax — meaning bees do not waste resources. (ii) It creates the most amount of storage space — so the bees can store the maximum amount of honey, pollen and eggs.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'it is strong and neat' — these may be true but are not stated in the passage.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: (1) uses the LEAST AMOUNT OF WAX; (2) creates the MOST AMOUNT OF STORAGE SPACE. Both are stated directly. Use the passage's own words.

open_ended_questions.stem: What happens when a beehive becomes too crowded?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: The queen bee leaves with half the colony to build a new home, while the remaining bees raise a new queen.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'the bees move away' — too vague. The passage gives specific details about what happens.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: 'The QUEEN BEE leaves with HALF the colony to build a new home. The remaining bees RAISE A NEW QUEEN.' Both actions are part of the answer.

open_ended_questions.stem: This passage is an informational text. Describe TWO techniques the writer uses to make the information interesting and clear.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) SURPRISING FACTS: the writer begins with what people already know ('bees make honey'), then immediately reveals something unexpected — that the engineering of the hive is equally remarkable. (ii) SPECIFIC NUMBERS: the writer uses exact figures (one gram of wax, one hundred thousand cells, thirty-five degrees) to make the facts feel real and precise.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students summarise the content instead of analysing the writer's techniques.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TECHNIQUES of an informational text: (1) SURPRISING CONTRAST = writer says 'you know bees make honey — but the ENGINEERING is just as remarkable' = hooks the reader with an unexpected comparison. (2) SPECIFIC NUMBERS = 'one gram of wax', '100,000 cells', '35 degrees' = exact figures make information feel credible and precise. Analyse HOW the text is written, not WHAT it says.

questions.stem: Early in the morning, the farm was as ________ as a library — not a single animal had woken up yet.
questions.trap_type: 'Loud', 'busy' and 'dark' all suggest activity or noise. QUIET = making no or very little sound.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The farm was AS QUIET AS a library = comparing the farm's silence to a library's. QUIET = making no sound. Similes always use 'as ... as'.

questions.stem: Before the storm arrived, the farmer told his children to ________ for the market immediately.
questions.trap_type: 'Return' = come back; 'wait' = stay; 'sleep' = rest. SET OFF = begin a journey.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: SET OFF = start a journey or begin moving toward a destination. The farmer told them to SET OFF immediately = to start going right away. SET + OFF work together.

questions.stem: The farmer ________ the soil carefully before planting the seeds to make sure it was loose and rich.
questions.trap_type: 'Watered' = poured water; 'ignored' = paid no attention; 'painted' = applied colour. TILLED = turned over and prepared the soil for planting.
questions.learning_tip: TILLED = turned over and prepared the soil for planting. Farmers TILL the soil = they loosen it and enrich it before seeds are planted.

questions.stem: The goats were ________ in the meadow, eating grass and wandering wherever they pleased.
questions.trap_type: 'Sleeping' = resting; 'hiding' = concealing themselves; 'racing' = running fast competitively. GRAZING = eating grass or plants slowly while moving around.
questions.learning_tip: GRAZING = eating grass slowly while moving around a field. Goats and cows GRAZE in meadows = they wander and eat the grass as they go.

questions.stem: The old farmer's vegetable garden was ________ — every patch of soil was used to grow something useful.
questions.trap_type: 'Empty' = nothing there; 'damp' = slightly wet; 'ordinary' = unremarkable. PRODUCTIVE = producing a large amount of useful output.
questions.learning_tip: PRODUCTIVE = producing a large useful output. A PRODUCTIVE garden = one where every patch grows food. Farmers want their land to be PRODUCTIVE = to yield as much as possible.

questions.stem: Everyone on the farm ________ a different job to do before the sun rises each morning.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'have' thinking 'everyone on the farm' = many people. EVERYONE = singular → verb must be HAS in present tense.
questions.learning_tip: EVERYONE = Singular! Use HAS, not HAVE. Everyone HAS a job = singular. 'Everyone have a job' is WRONG. EVERYONE / NOBODY / SOMEONE = always singular → IS / HAS / verb+S.

questions.stem: The farmer has ________ vegetables at the weekend market for over thirty years.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. 'Sell' is irregular: sell → sold.
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. The farmer HAS SOLD vegetables for thirty years = started then, still selling now. SELL → SOLD (irregular).

questions.stem: The harvest this year is much ________ than last year because of the long dry spell.
questions.trap_type: Comparing two harvests (this year vs last year) = comparative. 'Small' → SMALLER (short adjective adds -er).
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective + -ER = comparative. Small → SMALLER. The harvest is SMALLER THAN last year = comparing two harvests. 'Smallish' is informal and not standard.

questions.stem: The children ________ the pigs when their father called them in for breakfast.
questions.trap_type: 'Their father called them in' = sudden interrupting event. The children were already feeding the pigs = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: Their father CALLED THEM = sudden past event. Children were already feeding the pigs = WERE FEEDING (past continuous). Past continuous = was/were + verb-ing.

questions.stem: There were ________ eggs in the basket — not enough to sell at the market.
questions.trap_type: 'Eggs' is countable → use FEW or A FEW. 'Little' and 'much' are for uncountable nouns. FEW = not many (negative implication).
questions.learning_tip: FEW = not many (countable noun, negative implication). EGGS = countable → FEW eggs. LITTLE is for uncountable nouns like 'milk'. FEW = not enough of something countable.

questions.stem: The cockerel crows every morning without fail, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive simple present ('crows') → negative question tag. 'Crows' (singular present) → doesn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive simple present (third person singular) → negative tag. The cockerel CROWS every morning, DOESN'T it? DOES → DOESN'T. Positive → negative tag.

questions.stem: The freshly picked vegetables ________ to the market in a covered truck every Saturday at dawn.
questions.trap_type: The vegetables were the receivers of the action. Past passive: was/were + past participle.
questions.learning_tip: WAS/WERE + past participle = passive! The vegetables WERE DELIVERED = someone delivered them; vegetables received the action. WERE for plural subject.

questions.stem: The farmer told his children ________ the greenhouse door open or the seedlings would dry out.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: TOLD someone NOT TO + base verb. The farmer told his children NOT TO LEAVE the door open. Formula: told + person + not to + verb.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Time and condition conjunctions)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The rooster crows (1)________ the sun begins to rise over the mountains.' Signal: at the same time as / at the moment that = WHEN. WHEN = at the moment something happens.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'while' (ongoing duration) instead of 'when' (at a specific moment).
questions.learning_tip: WHEN = at the moment something happens (a point in time). The rooster crows WHEN the sun rises = at that specific moment. WHEN = one event triggers another.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Father mends the fence (2)________ Mother tends to the vegetable patch nearby.' Signal: two actions happening at the same time, both ongoing = WHILE. WHILE = during the same period as.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'when' (moment trigger) instead of 'while' (same ongoing period).
questions.learning_tip: WHILE = during the same period as another ongoing action. Father mends WHILE Mother tends = both doing their tasks at the same time. WHILE = two ongoing actions together.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(3)________ the weather stays dry this week, we will harvest the sweet potatoes on Friday.' Signal: conditional — the harvest depends on dry weather = IF. IF = standard conditional.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'when' (certain event) instead of 'if' (uncertain conditional). The weather staying dry is uncertain.
questions.learning_tip: IF = uncertain condition. IF the weather stays dry = it might stay dry or it might not. WHEN = certain event. IF + simple present, simple future.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(4)________ the milk is ready, Grandma pours it into glass bottles for the morning delivery.' Signal: immediately when something happens = AS SOON AS. AS SOON AS = immediately when.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'when' (at the moment) instead of 'as soon as' (immediately, with emphasis on speed).
questions.learning_tip: AS SOON AS = immediately when something happens (emphasis on speed). AS SOON AS the milk is ready, she pours it = the moment it is ready, she acts immediately.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The crops must be watered daily (5)________ the rainy season begins.' Signal: continuing up to a point = UNTIL. UNTIL = continuing up to that moment in time.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'before' (earlier than) instead of 'until' (continuously up to that point). The watering continues all the way to the rainy season.
questions.learning_tip: UNTIL = continue doing something all the way up to a point. Water the crops UNTIL the rainy season = keep watering right up to that point. UNTIL = ongoing action up to a limit.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The children feed the chickens (6)________ they leave for school each morning.' Signal: the feeding happens earlier in time than leaving for school = BEFORE.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'after' (later than) instead of 'before' (earlier than). The feeding comes first, then school.
questions.learning_tip: BEFORE = earlier in time. The children feed the chickens BEFORE they leave for school = the feeding happens first, then they go to school. BEFORE = the first action.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(7)________ the harvest is complete, the whole family gathers to share a meal together.' Signal: following the completion of the harvest = AFTER. AFTER = later in time, following an event.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'before' (earlier than) instead of 'after' (following). The meal comes after the harvest is done.
questions.learning_tip: AFTER = later in time, following another event. AFTER the harvest is complete, they gather = the meal comes after the harvest finishes. AFTER = the second action.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(8)________ the sun sets over the farm, the animals find their way back to the shelter on their own.' Signal: happening at the same time as / at the same rate as = AS. AS = happening simultaneously, or in proportion.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'when' (point trigger) instead of 'as' (gradual simultaneous process). The sun setting is gradual, not a single point.
questions.learning_tip: AS = happening at the same time as a gradual process. AS the sun SETS = while it is setting (gradual). AS shows two gradual things happening together. Different from WHEN (a single moment).

C.passage: Life on a farm follows the rhythm of the sun. The rooster crows (1)________ the sun begins to rise over the mountains each morning. Father mends the broken fence (2)________ Mother tends to the vegetable patch nearby. (3)________ the weather stays dry this week, we will harvest the sweet potatoes on Friday afternoon. (4)________ the milk is ready, Grandma pours it carefully into glass bottles for the morning delivery. The crops must be watered daily (5)________ the rainy season begins next month. The children feed the chickens (6)________ they leave for school each morning, rain or shine. (7)________ the harvest is complete, the whole family gathers to share a meal together. (8)________ the sun sets over the farm, the animals find their way back to the shelter on their own.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: A successful farm depends on the natural (1)________ — knowing when to plant, water and gather crops. Farmers (2)________ their plants from tiny seedlings into healthy produce using the right soil and water. The soil must be (3)________ — rich in nutrients to support healthy root growth. Many farms also keep (4)________ such as chickens, cows and pigs for eggs, milk and meat. At the end of each growing cycle, the farmer gathers the (5)________ — all the ripe fruits and vegetables ready to sell.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'knowing when to plant, water and gather' = the natural cycle of time on a farm = season.
questions.learning_tip: A SEASON = a period of time in the natural yearly cycle with specific weather and conditions. Farmers follow the SEASON = they know which activities belong to which part of the year.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'from tiny seedlings into strong, healthy produce by giving them the right care' = nurture.
questions.learning_tip: NURTURE = help something grow by giving it care, attention and the right conditions. Farmers NURTURE their plants = tend to them carefully from seedling to harvest.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'rich in nutrients and able to support healthy root growth' = fertile.
questions.learning_tip: FERTILE = (of soil) rich in nutrients and able to support healthy plant growth. FERTILE soil = the best kind for farming — plants grow well and produce a lot.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'chickens, cows and pigs — provide eggs, milk and meat' = livestock.
questions.learning_tip: LIVESTOCK = farm animals kept for their products or for food. Chickens, cows and pigs are all examples of LIVESTOCK kept on a working farm.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'fruits, vegetables and grains that are ready to be sold or stored' after the growing cycle = harvest.
questions.learning_tip: A HARVEST = the gathering of crops at the end of the growing season. The farmer gathers the HARVEST = all the crops that are ripe and ready.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the goats)
questions.trap_type: 'The goats' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! The goats WERE grazing in the meadow. WAS is only for ONE thing. GOATS = more than one → WERE.

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — too (also/excessively) vs to (preposition/infinitive)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'too' (also/excessively) when the sentence needs 'to' (infinitive marker).
questions.learning_tip: TO = infinitive marker before a verb (to water) or direction preposition. TOO = also or excessively. 'Forgot too water' is WRONG — 'to water' = the infinitive. Use TO before verbs.

questions.error_type: Spelling — ie/ei confusion (field: I before E)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'feild' putting E before I. 'Field' follows I-before-E: fIEld.
questions.learning_tip: Rule: I before E, except after C! fIEld = I before E ✅. Remember: 'the fIEld has a PIE in the middle' — fIEld. I before E always!

questions.error_type: Adverb required after action verb (crowed)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'loud' (adjective) after the action verb 'crowed'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (crowed), use an ADVERB: crowed LOUDLY. Rule: verb + adverb (-ly). 'Loud' describes nouns; 'loudly' describes HOW the rooster crowed.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — singular possessive (farmer's, not farmers's)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'farmers's' adding an extra 's'. For one farmer: farmer → farmer's.
questions.learning_tip: Singular possessive: noun + 's! ONE FARMER'S market stall = the stall belonging to one farmer. 'Farmers's' is wrong — 'farmers' is already plural. ONE farmer → farmer's.

E.passage: Last weekend, our class visited a working farm in Lim Chu Kang. The goats was (1) grazing peacefully in the meadow when we arrived, barely looking up from the grass. Our guide told us that one student forgot too (2) water the seedlings the previous week and several of them dried out. We walked across the large feild (3) behind the main barn, passing rows of cabbages and sweet potatoes stretching all the way to the trees. At five o'clock in the morning, the old rooster crowed so loud (4) that the farmer woke up without needing an alarm clock. At the end of our visit, we saw the farmers's (5) freshly harvested vegetables packed neatly into crates for delivery.

questions.sentence_a: The soil is rich and well-watered.
questions.sentence_b: The crops will grow quickly and produce a large harvest.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'If'.
questions.model_answer: If the soil is rich and well-watered, the crops will grow quickly and produce a large harvest.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'If the soil will be rich' — adding 'will' in the 'if' clause.
questions.learning_tip: IF + simple present, simple future. IF the soil IS rich, the crops WILL GROW quickly. NEVER use 'will' after 'if' in the condition clause.

questions.sentence_a: The old barn stood at the edge of the paddy field.
questions.sentence_b: The old barn was built by the farmer's grandfather fifty years ago.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using the relative pronoun 'which'.
questions.model_answer: The old barn, which was built by the farmer's grandfather fifty years ago, stood at the edge of the paddy field.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'The old barn which it was built by' — adding 'it' after 'which'.
questions.learning_tip: WHICH = relative pronoun for things. The old barn, WHICH was built by the farmer's grandfather, stood at the edge of the field. NEVER add 'it' after 'which'.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Eleven-year-old Priya grew up in a flat in Ang Mo Kio. She never visited a farm before.

On the first morning, she woke at five to help her aunt milk the cows. It was still dark. Everything smelled of earth and animals. She held the bucket so tightly her knuckles went white.

Her aunt did not explain. She simply showed her — slow, even strokes, the same rhythm again and again. Priya tried. The cow shifted, and she spilled half the bucket.

'Again,' said her aunt. There was no irritation in her voice. Just the word.

On the second morning, Priya woke at four-thirty — half an hour early. She was already in the barn when her aunt arrived.

'You came back,' said her aunt.

'I spilled,' said Priya.

Her aunt handed her the bucket. 'That is why you came back.'

By seven o'clock, the milk was done and the cows were calm. Priya's arms ached, but she did not mention it.

On the bus home, Priya sat without speaking. Her arms still ached. She looked at her hands and thought about the rhythm her aunt had shown her — slow, even, patient. She realised she could still feel the motion, like a small muscle memory she had not owned before that morning.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 4 has the same meaning as 'annoyance or frustration'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Rhythm' = pattern; 'shifted' = moved; 'simply' = in a plain way. IRRITATION = a feeling of mild anger or annoyance.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: IRRITATION = mild annoyance or frustration. 'There was no IRRITATION in her voice' = she was not annoyed at all, even though Priya spilled the milk.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 7, what does 'That' refer to in 'That is why you came back'?

options.3: The fact that Priya had spilled the milk and wanted to correct it

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'That' refers only to the spilled milk. But the aunt means the desire to come back and correct the mistake — the spilling and its consequence.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 7: Priya said 'I SPILLED.' Her aunt replied 'THAT is why you came back.' THAT = the fact that she spilled = the mistake that motivated her to return early to correct it.

mcq_questions.stem: Why does the writer end with 'Priya's arms ached, but she did not mention it'?

options.1: To show that Priya was too shy to talk to her aunt.
options.2: To show that Priya grew — she chose to complete the work quietly without complaining.
options.3: To show that the work was too hard for an eleven-year-old.
options.4: To show that her aunt would not have listened anyway.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 3 thinking the work was simply too hard. But the writer's point is about Priya's growth — she did not complain despite the pain.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: The ending shows Priya's growth: her arms ACHED (real physical pain), but she did not MENTION it = she chose to endure silently, without needing praise or comfort. This shows maturity.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Priya visited a farm many times before this visit? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says Priya 'had never been on a farm before' — this was her first time on a farm.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, she visited her aunt's farm' — the visit being described is her first time.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: 'She HAD NEVER BEEN ON A FARM BEFORE.' This clearly states it was her first experience on a farm. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What time did Priya arrive at the barn on the second morning?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: She arrived before four-thirty — she was already in the barn when her aunt arrived at four-thirty.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'five o'clock' (the first morning's time) instead of the second morning's time.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: 'On the second morning, Priya woke at FOUR-THIRTY — half an hour early. She was ALREADY IN THE BARN when her aunt arrived.' Second morning = four-thirty.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did Priya's aunt teach her? Give TWO specific details from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) She did not explain with words — she simply showed Priya by demonstrating the correct technique: 'slow, even strokes, the same rhythm again and again.' (ii) When Priya spilled, her aunt said only one word — 'Again' — without irritation, giving Priya the space to try again without embarrassment.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'she taught her patiently' without giving specific details from the text.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraphs 3–4: (1) Aunt SHOWED HER (demonstrated), not explained; (2) said only 'AGAIN' with NO IRRITATION — silent, patient encouragement. Two specific details.

open_ended_questions.stem: What reason does Priya's aunt give for why Priya came back early on the second morning?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Her aunt says Priya came back because she had spilled — the mistake itself was what motivated her to return and try again.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'she wanted to learn more' — too vague. The aunt's specific point is that SPILLING itself = the reason.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 8: 'That is why you CAME BACK' — the aunt means: SPILLING = the reason for returning. Making a mistake and caring about it enough to return is the point.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on her actions across BOTH mornings, describe TWO character traits of Priya with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) DETERMINED: on the second morning, she woke half an hour earlier than required and was already in the barn before her aunt arrived — she returned to face the same task that had defeated her. (ii) RESILIENT: despite her arms aching by seven o'clock, she did not mention it — she finished the work without complaining.
