open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'hard-working and kind' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE formula: TRAIT = evidence from text. DETERMINED = woke at FOUR-THIRTY, ALREADY IN THE BARN before her aunt arrived. RESILIENT = arms ACHED but she DID NOT MENTION IT — endured without complaint. For G8, always: (i) Trait name: evidence. (ii) Trait name: evidence.

questions.stem: The librarian's memory was as ________ as a blade — she could recall the exact shelf location of any book within seconds.
questions.trap_type: 'Heavy', 'dull' and 'cold' do not describe a keen, precise memory. SHARP = quick and accurate in thinking and memory.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! Her memory was AS SHARP AS a blade = comparing her precise memory to the sharpness of a blade. SHARP = quick, accurate and precise.

questions.stem: The children quickly ________ of stickers for decorating their reading journals and had to ask for more.
questions.trap_type: 'Gave up' = stopped trying; 'found out' = discovered; 'looked after' = cared for. RAN OUT OF = used up the entire supply of something.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: RUN OUT OF = use up the entire supply of something. They RAN OUT OF stickers = they used every single one and had none left. RUN + OUT + OF work together.

questions.stem: The library's reading room was completely ________ — not one person was talking above a whisper.
questions.trap_type: 'Crowded' = many people; 'colourful' = many colours; 'broken' = not working. SILENT = making no sound at all.
questions.learning_tip: SILENT = making no sound at all. The room was completely SILENT = nobody was talking, every sound was absent. Even a whisper would have been too loud.

questions.stem: The librarian gently ________ the damaged page with clear tape so the book could still be used.
questions.trap_type: 'Tore' = damaged further; 'removed' = took away; 'replaced' = put something new. REPAIRED = fixed something that was damaged.
questions.learning_tip: REPAIRED = fixed something that was broken or damaged. The librarian REPAIRED the page = she mended it so the book could be used again.

questions.stem: The library's archive held rare ________ — old handwritten letters and maps that could not be found anywhere else.
questions.trap_type: 'Paintings', 'medals' and 'photographs' are specific formats. DOCUMENTS = written or printed records, especially rare or official ones.
questions.learning_tip: DOCUMENTS = written or printed records, especially formal or important ones. Rare DOCUMENTS = old handwritten letters or maps with historical value.

questions.stem: Somebody in the reading room ________ their mobile phone on silent, and it keeps vibrating loudly on the table.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'forget' thinking 'somebody in the reading room' = plural. SOMEBODY = singular → present tense → FORGETS.
questions.learning_tip: SOMEBODY / SOMEONE / EVERYBODY / NOBODY = Singular! ALWAYS use verb+S. Somebody FORGETS = add -S. 'Somebody forget' is WRONG.

questions.stem: Our school has ________ a reading corner in the library with bean bags and floor cushions.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. SET UP is a phrasal verb; past participle = 'set up' (no change in past participle form).
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Our school HAS SET UP a reading corner = it was created at some point and is still there. SET UP (phrasal verb) → SET UP (past participle).

questions.stem: The new library building is far ________ than the old one, with three floors and a rooftop garden.
questions.trap_type: Comparative needed (comparing new vs old building). 'Large' → LARGER (short adjective adds -er). 'More larger' is wrong (double comparative).
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective + -ER = comparative. Large → LARGER. The new library is LARGER THAN the old one. NEVER 'more larger' — that is a double comparative error.

questions.stem: The students ________ their book reports when the librarian announced the start of story time.
questions.trap_type: 'The librarian announced story time' = sudden interrupting event. Students were already writing = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The librarian ANNOUNCED story time = sudden past event. Students were already writing = WERE WRITING (past continuous). Past continuous = was/were + verb-ing.

questions.stem: There are ________ picture books in the children's section than in any other part of the library.
questions.trap_type: Comparing quantities of books = comparative 'more'. 'Much' and 'a little' are for uncountable; 'a few' is a small number, not comparative.
questions.learning_tip: MORE + countable plural noun = comparative quantity. There are MORE picture books = a larger number compared to other sections. 'Much books' is WRONG — MUCH is for uncountable.

questions.stem: You haven't returned last week's library book yet, ________ you?
questions.trap_type: Negative present perfect ('haven't returned') → positive question tag = have you.
questions.learning_tip: Negative present perfect → positive tag. 'You HAVEN'T returned the book, HAVE you?' NEGATIVE → POSITIVE tag. HAVEN'T → HAVE.

questions.stem: The most popular book in the library ________ thirty times in a single month.
questions.trap_type: The book was the receiver of the action. Past passive = was borrowed.
questions.learning_tip: WAS/WERE + past participle = passive! The book WAS BORROWED thirty times = people borrowed it; the book received the action. Singular → WAS.

questions.stem: The librarian asked the children ________ their voices down while others were reading.
questions.trap_type: Requested action reported speech: asked + object + to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: ASKED someone TO + base verb. The librarian asked children TO KEEP their voices down. Formula: asked + person + to + verb (positive reported speech).

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Verb 'read' — 8 forms; note: 'read' appears twice: present/base AND past tense, same spelling, different pronunciation)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Aisha (1)________ at least two books every week.' Signal: 'every week' = regular habit = simple present. Subject 'Aisha' = singular → reads.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'read' (base or past) instead of 'reads' (third person singular present).
questions.learning_tip: Regular habit = simple present. Aisha (singular) → READS every week. Add -S for he/she/it in simple present. 'Aisha read every week' is WRONG — that is ambiguous past/present.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'She enjoys (2)________ adventure stories more than any other genre.' Signal: 'enjoys + ___' = gerund (verb-ing). Pattern: enjoy + verb-ing → reading.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'to read' (infinitive) instead of the gerund after 'enjoys'.
questions.learning_tip: ENJOY + verb-ing (gerund). She enjoys READING = the -ing form. NEVER 'enjoys to read' — after ENJOY, always use -ing. LIKE/LOVE/ENJOY + verb-ing.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Last Saturday, she (3)________ a whole novel in a single afternoon.' Signal: 'Last Saturday' = past. 'Read' is irregular: read (present) → read (past) — same spelling, different pronunciation (present: /riːd/, past: /rɛd/).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'readed' not knowing 'read' is irregular with identical past and present spellings.
questions.learning_tip: READ is an irregular verb: read (present, /riːd/) → READ (past, /rɛd/). Same spelling — different pronunciation! 'Last Saturday' = past → use READ (pronounced 'red'). NEVER 'readed'.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'While she (4)________ the final chapter, the library lights flickered twice.' Signal: 'while she ___' = ongoing background past action. Subject 'she' = singular → was reading. Interrupted by 'lights flickered'.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'read' (simple past) missing the 'while' ongoing signal.
questions.learning_tip: 'While she ___' = ongoing past background action = past continuous. She WAS READING the final chapter when the lights flickered = she was in the middle of it.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Her two younger brothers (5)________ picture books nearby at the same time.' Signal: same past time frame, plural subject 'her two brothers' + ongoing parallel action → were reading.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'was reading' (singular) instead of 'were reading' (plural).
questions.learning_tip: Her brothers = plural (more than one). Past continuous plural → WERE READING (not 'was reading'). WERE for plural; WAS for singular. They were doing it at the same past moment.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'After the lights came back on, she continued (6)________ without missing a single word.' Signal: 'continued + ___' = can take to-infinitive or -ing. Here we use 'continued to read' = infinitive. Pattern: continue + to + base verb.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'reading' (also valid for 'continue', but 'to read' is in the word_box). Only 'to read' is available in the word_box.
questions.learning_tip: CONTINUE + to + base verb = one option. She continued TO READ without missing a word. 'Continue' can be followed by BOTH 'to read' OR 'reading' — here we use 'to read' from the word box.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Her library target is to (7)________ fifty books before the end of Primary Three.' Signal: 'to + ___' = infinitive = base verb. 'To' is already there → only base form follows.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'reads' (third person present, adds -s) after 'to', forgetting that after 'to' the base form is always used.
questions.learning_tip: After 'TO', ALWAYS use the BASE form (no -s, no -ing, no -ed). To READ fifty books — never 'to reads' or 'to reading'. This is the infinitive = to + base verb.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Right now, Aisha (8)________ a book about ancient Egyptian civilisations.' Signal: 'Right now' = present continuous. Subject 'Aisha' = singular → is reading.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'reads' (simple present habit) missing the 'right now' signal for present continuous.
questions.learning_tip: 'Right now' = present continuous. Aisha (singular) → IS READING a book right now. 'Reads' would mean she reads regularly as a habit. 'IS READING' = doing it at this moment.

C.passage: Aisha (1)________ at least two books every week without fail. She enjoys (2)________ adventure stories more than any other genre in the library. Last Saturday, she (3)________ a whole novel in a single afternoon without stopping for lunch. While she (4)________ the final chapter, the library lights flickered twice and then came back on. Her two younger brothers (5)________ picture books nearby at the same time, keeping themselves quietly entertained. After the lights came back on, she continued (6)________ without missing a single word of the story. Her library target is to (7)________ fifty books before the end of Primary Three this year. Right now, Aisha (8)________ a book about ancient Egyptian civilisations that she found on the top shelf.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: A public library contains many types of books. Readers often (1)________ the shelves freely, picking up books that catch their eye. Many libraries have an online (2)________ — a searchable list of every book available. Books in the (3)________ section, such as encyclopaedias, cannot be borrowed and must be used inside. Readers borrow (4)________ — made-up stories — for pleasure. If a book is not returned by the due date, it becomes (5)________ and a small fine may be charged.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'picking up books that catch their eye before deciding what to borrow' = browse.
questions.learning_tip: BROWSE = look casually at items without a specific goal. You BROWSE the shelves = you look along them, picking up books that interest you without a fixed plan.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'a searchable list of every book and resource available' = catalogue.
questions.learning_tip: A CATALOGUE = a complete searchable list of all available items. A library CATALOGUE = the system that lists every book and tells you where to find it.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'encyclopaedias and atlases... cannot be borrowed... used inside the library' = reference section.
questions.learning_tip: A REFERENCE section = the part of a library containing books like encyclopaedias that cannot be borrowed and must be used inside. You go there to look up specific information.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'stories that are made up and not based on real events' = fiction.
questions.learning_tip: FICTION = stories that are made up and imaginary (not real). Novels, fairy tales and adventure stories are FICTION. Opposite: non-fiction = true or factual.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'not returned by the due date... a small fine may be charged' = overdue.
questions.learning_tip: OVERDUE = not returned or completed by the required date. A library book is OVERDUE = it should have been returned but has not been yet. A fine is charged as a reminder.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the books)
questions.trap_type: 'The books' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! The books WERE arranged neatly on the shelf. WAS is only for ONE thing (singular). BOOKS = more than one → WERE.

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — they're (they are) vs their (possessive)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'they're' (they are) when the sentence needs 'their' (belonging to them).
questions.learning_tip: THEIR = belonging to them. Students must return THEIR books on time. THEY'RE = they are. Test: can you replace with 'they are'? 'they are books' — NO. Use THEIR.

questions.error_type: Spelling — ie/ei confusion (grief: I before E)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'greif' putting E before I. 'Grief' follows I-before-E: grIEf.
questions.learning_tip: Rule: I before E, except after C! grIEf = I before E ✅. The story was full of grIEf — remember: grief has an IE inside, like beLIEve and frIEnd.

questions.error_type: Adverb required after action verb (spoke)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'soft' (adjective) after the action verb 'spoke'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (spoke), use an ADVERB: spoke SOFTLY. Rule: verb + adverb (-ly). 'Soft' describes nouns; 'softly' describes HOW someone speaks.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — singular possessive (librarian's = one librarian)
questions.trap_type: Students use plural possessive (librarians') when only one librarian is meant.
questions.learning_tip: ONE LIBRARIAN'S desk = the desk belonging to one librarian. LIBRARIANS' desk = belonging to many librarians. Check: is it ONE or MANY? ONE → librarian's.

E.passage: Every Tuesday afternoon, our class visits the school library for reading time. The books was (1) arranged neatly on the shelves, sorted by subject and author. Students must remember to return they're (2) borrowed books by Friday or they will receive an overdue notice. In one of the storybooks, the main character experienced great greif (3) when her favourite library was closed down to make way for a new road. The librarian spoke soft (4) to each student, helping them find a book that matched their interests. After the session, we tidied the librarians' (5) desk and placed all the returned books in the sorting trolley.

questions.sentence_a: You read at least thirty minutes a day.
questions.sentence_b: Your vocabulary and comprehension will improve significantly.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'As long as'.
questions.model_answer: As long as you read at least thirty minutes a day, your vocabulary and comprehension will improve significantly.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'As long as you will read' — adding 'will' in the 'as long as' clause.
questions.learning_tip: AS LONG AS + simple present, simple future. AS LONG AS you READ thirty minutes a day, your vocabulary WILL IMPROVE. NEVER 'will' after 'as long as'.

questions.sentence_a: The library holds a rare collection of old maps.
questions.sentence_b: The rare collection is not available to borrow.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using the relative pronoun 'which'.
questions.model_answer: The library holds a rare collection of old maps, which is not available to borrow.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'a rare collection which it is not available' — adding 'it' after 'which'.
questions.learning_tip: WHICH = relative pronoun for things. A rare collection of old maps, WHICH is not available to borrow. NEVER add 'it' after 'which'. The collection is the antecedent.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
The book was always in the same corner. Every Saturday, nine-year-old Jonas walked past the other shelves — the adventure books, the science books, the graphic novels — and went straight to that corner.

The book was too difficult for him. He knew that. The words were long and the sentences ran over two lines. But he liked the cover: a boy standing at the edge of a cliff, looking out at a sea of clouds.

He never borrowed it. He just sat down and tried to read it. Sometimes he got through one page. Once, on a day when the library was particularly quiet, he got through three.

One Saturday, the corner was empty. The book was gone.

Jonas stood and stared at the gap in the shelf for a long time. Then he went to the librarian.

'Someone borrowed the book in the corner,' he said. 'The one with the boy on the cliff.'

The librarian checked the screen. 'It will be back in three weeks,' she said.

Jonas nodded. 'I'll be here,' he said.

He sat down in the corner with a different book. But he did not read it. He thought about the boy on the cliff and the sea of clouds below.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 3 has the same meaning as 'especially or noticeably'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Difficult' = hard; 'borrowed' = taken from the library; 'sometimes' = occasionally. PARTICULARLY = especially or to a notable degree.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: PARTICULARLY = especially or to a notable degree. 'The library was PARTICULARLY quiet' = noticeably quieter than usual, more so than normally.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 6, what does 'It' refer to in 'It will be back in three weeks'?

options.3: The book with the boy on the cliff

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 2 thinking 'it' refers to the empty shelf. But Jonas asked about the book — the librarian's 'it' = the book.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 6: Jonas told the librarian about THE BOOK in the corner. The librarian replied 'IT will be back in three weeks.' IT = the book Jonas asked about.

mcq_questions.stem: Jonas sat with a different book but 'did not read it'. What does this tell us about his feelings?

options.1: He was too tired to read anything.
options.2: He could only think about the book on the cliff — he was so attached to it that no other book could hold his attention.
options.3: He had already read every other book in the library.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking he was tired. But the passage ends with him thinking about the boy and the cliff — showing deep attachment to that specific book.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Last paragraph: Jonas sat with another book but THOUGHT ABOUT THE BOY ON THE CLIFF. He could not read anything else because his mind was fully on that one book — deep attachment.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 2, is it True or False that Jonas found the book easy to read? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says 'The book was too difficult for him' — the words were long and the sentences ran over two lines.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, he read it every week.' He tried to read it every week — but the passage says it was too difficult for him.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'The book was TOO DIFFICULT for him. The WORDS WERE LONG and the sentences RAN OVER TWO LINES.' He tried but it was hard. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: Why did Jonas like the book even though it was too hard for him?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: He liked the cover — a boy standing at the edge of a cliff, looking out at a sea of clouds.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he liked the story' — the passage says he liked the COVER, not the story content.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'he liked the COVER: a boy standing at the EDGE OF A CLIFF, looking out at a SEA OF CLOUDS.' It was the cover image that drew him to the book.

open_ended_questions.stem: How does the passage show that Jonas visited the library regularly and with a clear purpose? Give TWO details.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) He visited 'every Saturday' — showing a consistent, weekly pattern. (ii) He walked past the adventure books, science books and graphic novels and went 'straight to that corner' — showing he had a specific destination in mind.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he liked reading' — too vague.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: (1) 'EVERY SATURDAY' = consistent weekly visits; (2) he walked 'straight to THAT CORNER' = he had a clear, specific purpose every time he came.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did Jonas say when the librarian told him the book would be back in three weeks?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: He said 'I'll be here' — meaning he would come back to the library in three weeks to get the book.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students paraphrase without quoting — 'he said he would come back.' The question expects the exact words.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 7: 'I'LL BE HERE.' Jonas said this = he committed to returning in three weeks when the book comes back. Quote the exact words from the passage.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Jonas with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) PERSISTENT: Jonas tried to read the same difficult book every Saturday for many weeks, getting through only one or three pages at a time — he did not give up despite the difficulty. (ii) DEVOTED: when the book was gone, he told the librarian exactly what it was and declared 'I'll be here' in three weeks — showing how attached he was to it.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'patient and curious' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE formula: TRAIT = evidence. PERSISTENT = went EVERY SATURDAY, got through '1 or 3 pages at a time' despite difficulty. DEVOTED = found it gone, told the librarian, said 'I'LL BE HERE' in 3 weeks. Always: trait name + exact words or action from text.

questions.stem: The rubbish collector's bag was as ________ as a boulder by the time he reached the end of the street.
questions.trap_type: 'Light', 'colourful' and 'soft' do not describe a full, loaded bag. HEAVY = having great weight.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The bag was AS HEAVY AS a boulder = comparing its weight to a large rock. AS + adj + AS = simile comparing two things.

questions.stem: The detective needed to ________ who took the missing package from the letterbox.
questions.trap_type: 'Forget', 'ignore' and 'create' are all the wrong actions for a detective. FIND OUT = discover information through investigation.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: FIND OUT = discover a piece of information through effort or investigation. The detective needed to FIND OUT who took the package = discover the answer. FIND + OUT work together.

questions.stem: The paramedic worked quickly and ________, knowing that every second counted in an emergency.
questions.trap_type: 'Slowly' and 'carelessly' are dangerous in an emergency; 'quietly' is irrelevant. EFFICIENTLY = doing the task quickly and without wasting any time or effort.
questions.learning_tip: EFFICIENTLY = doing something well and without wasting time or effort. In an emergency, a paramedic must work EFFICIENTLY = fast, accurate and without any wasted movement.

questions.stem: The postman ________ every letter and parcel into the correct pigeonhole before starting his delivery round.
questions.trap_type: 'Lost', 'ignored' and 'opened' all describe the wrong treatment of mail. SORTED = organised into the correct groups or places.
questions.learning_tip: SORTED = organised into groups or put into the correct places. The postman SORTED the letters = placed each one in the correct pigeonhole for the right address.

questions.stem: The police officer's role in the community is not just to enforce rules but also to build ________ with the people she serves.
questions.trap_type: 'Walls', 'fences' and 'distance' all suggest separation. TRUST = confident belief in the reliability and honesty of another person.
questions.learning_tip: TRUST = confident belief in someone's honesty and reliability. Building TRUST = creating a positive relationship where people feel safe and respected.

questions.stem: Each community helper ________ an important role in keeping our neighbourhood safe and clean.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'play' thinking 'each community helper' = many people. EACH = singular → verb must have -S in present tense.
questions.learning_tip: EACH = Singular! ALWAYS use verb+S in present tense. Each helper PLAYS a role = add -S. 'Each helpers play' is WRONG. EACH / EVERY / SOMEONE = singular verb.

questions.stem: Our town council has ________ a new community garden near the bus interchange.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. 'Build' is irregular: build → built.
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. The council HAS BUILT a garden = it was built at some point and is there now. BUILD → BUILT (irregular).

questions.stem: The new clinic is much ________ to the housing estate than the old one, making it easier for residents to visit.
questions.trap_type: Comparative needed (comparing old and new clinic locations). 'Close' → CLOSER (short adjective adds -er). 'Closely' is an adverb, not an adjective.
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective + -ER = comparative. Close → CLOSER. The new clinic is CLOSER TO the estate = comparing two distances. 'Very close' would be ok too, but 'closer' is comparative.

questions.stem: The cleaner ________ the glass doors of the community centre when the first visitors began to arrive.
questions.trap_type: 'The first visitors began to arrive' = sudden interrupting event. The cleaner was already wiping the doors = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The visitors BEGAN TO ARRIVE = sudden past event. The cleaner was already in the middle of wiping = WAS WIPING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing.

questions.stem: There is ________ litter in this park today — the volunteer cleaners did a wonderful job this morning.
questions.trap_type: 'Litter' is uncountable → use LITTLE. 'Few', 'a few' and 'many' are for countable nouns.
questions.learning_tip: LITTLE + uncountable noun. Litter = uncountable → LITTLE litter. 'Few litter' is WRONG — you cannot count individual pieces of litter. LITTLE = not much (uncountable).

questions.stem: The ambulance arrived within four minutes of the emergency call, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive simple past ('arrived') → negative question tag. 'Arrived' (past simple) → didn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive simple past → negative tag. The ambulance ARRIVED within four minutes, DIDN'T it? Positive → negative tag. Past 'arrived' → tag uses 'did/didn't'.

questions.stem: The road in front of the school ________ after the heavy rain damaged the surface last month.
questions.trap_type: The road was the receiver of the action. Past passive = was repaired.
questions.learning_tip: WAS/WERE + past participle = passive! The road WAS REPAIRED = workers repaired it; the road received the action. WAS for singular subject.

questions.stem: The police officer told residents ________ valuables in their cars overnight.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: TOLD someone NOT TO + base verb. The officer told residents NOT TO LEAVE valuables in cars. Formula: told + person + not to + verb.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Result, completion and sequence adverbs)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'When the emergency call came in, the paramedic team responded (1)________ without any delay.' Signal: 'without any delay' = at once, with no pause = IMMEDIATELY.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'soon' (in a short while) instead of 'immediately' (at once, with no delay at all).
questions.learning_tip: IMMEDIATELY = at once, with no delay whatsoever. The team responded IMMEDIATELY = the instant they got the call, they moved. SOON = in a short while; IMMEDIATELY = right now.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'By the time the doctor arrived, the nurses had (2)________ prepared the patient for treatment.' Signal: done sooner than expected = ALREADY. ALREADY = completed before a reference point.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'yet' (expected but not done) instead of 'already' (done before expected).
questions.learning_tip: ALREADY = done sooner than expected. By the time the doctor arrived, nurses had ALREADY prepared the patient = done before the doctor even got there. ALREADY = sooner than expected.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The rubbish truck has not collected the bins on our street (3)________.' Signal: expected but has not happened up to now = YET (used in negatives and questions). YET = expected but not done.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'still' (ongoing state) instead of 'yet' (expected but not completed). YET is used in negatives.
questions.learning_tip: YET = expected to happen but has not happened so far (used in negatives/questions). 'Has not collected YET' = we expect it to come but it has not come. YET is used with negatives.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The postman is (4)________ making his rounds in our estate even though it is almost noon.' Signal: ongoing state that has continued without stopping = STILL. STILL = continuing into the present moment.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'yet' (expected but not done, used in negatives) instead of 'still' (ongoing positive state).
questions.learning_tip: STILL = continuing without stopping into the present moment. The postman is STILL making rounds = he started and he is continuing now. STILL = an ongoing action.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'A new community centre was (5)________ opened in our neighbourhood, just two weeks ago.' Signal: in the near past, not long ago = RECENTLY. RECENTLY = a short time ago.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'soon' (in the future) instead of 'recently' (in the near past). 'Two weeks ago' = past, close to now.
questions.learning_tip: RECENTLY = a short time ago, in the near past. A centre was RECENTLY opened = it opened just two weeks ago = not long ago. SOON = in the near future; RECENTLY = in the near past.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The repair team said the broken streetlight would be fixed (6)________ — within the next two days.' Signal: in the near future, a short time from now = SOON. SOON = in a short while.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'recently' (near past) instead of 'soon' (near future). 'Within the next two days' = future.
questions.learning_tip: SOON = in a short while, in the near future. The streetlight will be fixed SOON = it will happen within two days. RECENTLY = near past; SOON = near future.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'After three weeks of searching, the team (7)________ found the source of the water leak.' Signal: after a long process or difficulty, the result is achieved = FINALLY. FINALLY = at last, after a long time.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'eventually' (also correct but less emphatic for a defined search period) instead of 'finally' (emphasises the end of a specific process).
questions.learning_tip: FINALLY = at last, after a long time or process. After THREE WEEKS of searching, they FINALLY found it = it happened after everything else, at the end of the process.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The new recycling bins were resisted by many residents at first, but they (8)________ accepted them as part of daily life.' Signal: after a long time and gradual change = EVENTUALLY. EVENTUALLY = after a long gradual process.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'finally' (end of a specific task) instead of 'eventually' (gradual acceptance over time). EVENTUALLY suggests a slow, natural change.
questions.learning_tip: EVENTUALLY = after a long time, through gradual change. Residents EVENTUALLY accepted the bins = slowly, over time, they came to accept them. FINALLY = end of a specific task; EVENTUALLY = slow natural change.

C.passage: When the emergency call came in, the paramedic team responded (1)________ without delay. By the time the doctor arrived, the nurses had (2)________ prepared the patient. The rubbish truck has not collected the bins on our street (3)________. The postman is (4)________ making his rounds in our estate. A new community centre was (5)________ opened just two weeks ago. The repair team said the broken streetlight would be fixed (6)________. After three weeks, the team (7)________ found the source of the water leak. The new recycling bins were resisted at first, but residents (8)________ accepted them as part of daily life.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Singapore is served by many dedicated community helpers. A trained (1)________ gives immediate first aid at emergencies before a doctor arrives. Community police officers (2)________ the neighbourhood at regular hours to prevent crime and keep residents safe. Many Singaporeans also (3)________ their free time to helping others without pay, visiting nursing homes or tutoring students. These helpers (4)________ themselves fully to improving the community. All community helpers — from doctors and teachers to cleaners and postmen — are (5)________ to a well-functioning society.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'trained medical worker who responds to emergencies before a doctor arrives, giving first aid' = paramedic.
questions.learning_tip: A PARAMEDIC = a trained medical worker who gives emergency treatment before or instead of a doctor. PARAMEDICS arrive first at emergencies and stabilise patients.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'walk around the neighbourhood at regular hours to prevent crime' = patrol.
questions.learning_tip: PATROL = walk regularly around an area to watch for problems and keep people safe. Police officers PATROL the neighbourhood = they move through it regularly to prevent crime.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'help others without pay' = volunteer.
questions.learning_tip: To VOLUNTEER = offer your time and energy to help others without being paid. People who VOLUNTEER at nursing homes or clean parks choose to do it freely.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'making the community a better place — giving their efforts fully to a goal' = dedicate.
questions.learning_tip: DEDICATE = commit yourself fully to a cause or person. They DEDICATE themselves to the community = they give their time and energy wholeheartedly to help others.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'necessary to a well-functioning society' = essential.
questions.learning_tip: ESSENTIAL = absolutely necessary, cannot be done without. Community helpers are ESSENTIAL to society = society would not function properly without them.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the nurses)
questions.trap_type: 'The nurses' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! The nurses WERE on duty throughout the night. WAS is only for ONE (singular). NURSES = more than one → WERE.

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — their (possessive) vs there (place/existence)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'their' (belonging to them) when the sentence needs 'there' (at that place).
questions.learning_tip: THERE = at that place. The doctor stood THERE by the door. THEIR = belonging to them. Test: can you replace with 'at that place'? YES → use THERE.

questions.error_type: Spelling — ie/ei confusion (niece: I before E)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'neice' putting E before I. 'Niece' follows I-before-E: nIEce.
questions.learning_tip: Rule: I before E, except after C! nIEce = I before E ✅. Remember: your nIEce has a PIE — nIEce. I comes before E always in this word!

questions.error_type: Adverb required after action verb (worked)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'brave' (adjective) after the action verb 'worked'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (worked), use an ADVERB: worked BRAVELY. Rule: verb + adverb (-ly). 'Brave' describes nouns; 'bravely' describes HOW someone works.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (nurses', not nurses's)
questions.trap_type: Students add 's after the apostrophe for a plural noun ending in -s.
questions.learning_tip: Plural possessive: just add apostrophe after -s! The NURSES' station = the station belonging to all the nurses. NEVER 'nurses's' — the extra -s after apostrophe is wrong for plural nouns.

E.passage: Last month, our class visited a community polyclinic for a learning journey. The nurses was (1) busy attending to patients when we arrived, moving quickly and quietly between the rooms. The doctor stood their (2) at the entrance and welcomed us warmly. She told us that her own neice (3) had inspired her to become a doctor after recovering from a serious illness as a child. Throughout the visit, the medical staff worked brave (4) and calmly, even when several patients arrived at the same time. At the end of the visit, we signed our names in the nurses's (5) appreciation book and thanked the whole team for their time.

questions.sentence_a: You do not report a broken streetlight to the town council.
questions.sentence_b: It may stay unrepaired for weeks.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'Unless'.
questions.model_answer: Unless you report a broken streetlight to the town council, it may stay unrepaired for weeks.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'Unless you will report' — adding 'will' in the 'unless' clause.
questions.learning_tip: UNLESS + simple present, simple future/modal. UNLESS you REPORT the broken streetlight, it MAY STAY unrepaired. Never 'will' after 'unless'.

questions.sentence_a: The paramedic rushed to the scene.
questions.sentence_b: The paramedic treated three patients in under ten minutes.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'After'.
questions.model_answer: After rushing to the scene, the paramedic treated three patients in under ten minutes.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'After the paramedic rushed to the scene, she treated' — acceptable, but model answer uses -ing reduction elegantly.
questions.learning_tip: AFTER + verb-ing (same subject): AFTER RUSHING to the scene, the paramedic treated three patients. Same subject → 'after + -ing' is concise and elegant.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Marcus worked as a cleaner at Changi Airport for eleven years. He worked the night shift — from ten at night until six in the morning — when the terminals were quieter and the floors could be cleaned properly.

Most passengers did not notice him. They were tired, or rushing, or looking at their phones. A woman once walked straight through his wet-mopped section without pausing, leaving footprints across the section he had just finished.

Marcus did not say anything. He mopped it again.

There was a boy, perhaps nine or ten, who watched him one night from a seat near Gate C12. The boy's family was waiting for a late flight. He watched Marcus work for almost twenty minutes.

Then the boy walked over.

'Why do you clean at night?' he asked.

Marcus stopped and thought about it. 'Because when the sun comes up,' he said, 'I want everything to be ready.'

The boy looked around at the gleaming floor. 'I never thought about who cleans,' he said.

Marcus smiled. 'Not many people do,' he said. 'But someone has to.'

Marcus picked up his mop and cart and moved on to Gate C13. There were still four more sections to finish before six.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 1 has the same meaning as 'areas inside an airport where passengers wait'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Shift' = a period of work; 'properly' = correctly; 'quieter' = less noisy. TERMINALS = the large buildings at an airport where passengers wait and board.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: TERMINALS = the large airport buildings where passengers check in, wait and board. Changi Airport has multiple TERMINALS — large waiting and departure areas.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 2, what does 'his' refer to in 'the section he had just finished'?

options.1: The boy watching from the seat

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 3 thinking 'his' refers to the passenger. But the whole paragraph is about Marcus — 'his' = Marcus's section.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'A woman walked through HIS WET-MOPPED SECTION... the section HE had just finished.' HIS and HE = MARCUS, the cleaner being described throughout.

mcq_questions.stem: Why does the writer include the detail about the woman who walked through the wet floor?

options.1: To show that the woman was rude.
options.2: To show that Marcus's work was difficult and easily undone, but he redid it without complaint.
options.3: To prove that the airport floor was always wet.
options.4: To show that passengers should not use their phones.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking the writer's purpose is to criticise the woman. The writer's purpose is to show Marcus's quiet professionalism — he simply re-did the work.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2–3: the woman ruined his work; Marcus DID NOT SAY ANYTHING and MOPPED IT AGAIN. The writer includes this to show his professionalism — he redid it without complaint.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Marcus works during the daytime? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says he works 'from ten at night until six in the morning' — this is the night shift, not the daytime.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, he works at the airport.' He works at the airport, but on the night shift, not during the day.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: 'He worked the NIGHT SHIFT — from TEN AT NIGHT until SIX IN THE MORNING.' This is nighttime work. The answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did the boy notice about the airport floor when he looked around?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: The boy noticed that the floor was gleaming — it was shining cleanly, the result of Marcus's work.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'the floor was clean' — the passage uses the specific word 'gleaming' which should be quoted or explained.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 8: 'The boy looked around at the GLEAMING FLOOR.' GLEAMING = shining brightly and cleanly. This was the result of Marcus's work through the night.

open_ended_questions.stem: How does the passage show that most passengers do not appreciate Marcus's work? Give TWO details.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) The passage says most passengers 'did not notice him' — they were too tired, rushing or on their phones to see him. (ii) A woman 'walked straight through his wet-mopped section without pausing' — undoing his work without even looking up.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'people were rude' without quoting specific details.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: (1) most passengers 'DID NOT NOTICE HIM' = they were too busy; (2) a woman 'WALKED STRAIGHT THROUGH his wet-mopped section WITHOUT PAUSING' = she didn't even see the wet floor.

open_ended_questions.stem: What reason did Marcus give for cleaning at night?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: He said that when the sun comes up, he wants everything to be ready — he cleans at night so the airport is perfect by the time passengers arrive in the morning.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'because it is quieter' — that is mentioned in paragraph 1, but Marcus's OWN reason is about wanting things to be ready.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 7: 'Because when the SUN COMES UP, I want everything to be READY.' Marcus cleans at night so the airport is perfect for the morning. This is his own stated reason.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his words and actions, describe TWO character traits of Marcus with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) PROFESSIONAL: when the woman walked through his clean floor, he said nothing and simply mopped it again — he did his job without complaint or distraction. (ii) PURPOSEFUL: he explained that he cleans at night so 'everything is ready' when the sun comes up — showing he takes real pride in his work and cares about the result.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'hardworking and kind' without precise traits or evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE formula: TRAIT = evidence. PROFESSIONAL = said NOTHING when woman ruined his work, MOPPED IT AGAIN without complaint. PURPOSEFUL = 'when the SUN COMES UP, I want EVERYTHING TO BE READY' = clear motivation and pride. Always quote or paraphrase the evidence.

questions.stem: The injured kitten was as ________ as a feather when the volunteer picked it up — it did not struggle at all.
questions.trap_type: 'Heavy' and 'rough' are the opposite of delicate. 'Loud' describes sound, not touch. GENTLE = soft and careful in movement or touch.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The kitten was AS GENTLE AS a feather = comparing its soft stillness to a feather. GENTLE = calm, soft and careful. Similes always use 'as ... as'.

questions.stem: For an experienced rescue diver, recovering a trapped dolphin was ________ — she completed the mission in under twenty minutes.
questions.trap_type: 'Impossible' and 'a big challenge' mean it was difficult. 'Very tiring' describes effort. A PIECE OF CAKE = something very easy to do.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: A PIECE OF CAKE = something very easy. 'The rescue was a piece of cake for her' = she found it very easy. Idioms cannot be understood word by word — 'a piece of cake' is NOT about food!

questions.stem: The wildlife officer decided to ________ the injured eagle until its wing healed completely.
questions.trap_type: 'Release' = set free (the opposite of what is needed while injured); 'ignore' = pay no attention; 'photograph' = take a picture. CARE FOR = look after and tend to something.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: CARE FOR = look after someone or something that needs help. The officer decided to CARE FOR the eagle = tend to it, feed it and help it recover. CARE + FOR work together.

questions.stem: The rescue team moved with great ________, avoiding any sudden movements that might scare the trapped animal.
questions.trap_type: 'Speed', 'noise' and 'strength' would all alarm an injured animal. CAUTION = great care to avoid danger or harm.
questions.learning_tip: CAUTION = careful attention to avoid risk. The team moved with CAUTION = slowly and carefully so as not to frighten the animal. 'With caution' is a set phrase meaning very carefully.

questions.stem: The community centre set up a temporary ________ for animals affected by the flash flood, providing food and shelter.
questions.trap_type: 'Market', 'school' and 'clinic' are all real places but not places set up for flood-affected animals. SHELTER = a place providing temporary protection and care.
questions.learning_tip: A SHELTER = a place of temporary protection. An animal SHELTER = a place where rescued or homeless animals are cared for until they find a permanent home.

questions.stem: Anyone who witnesses an injured animal on the road ________ the ACRES hotline immediately.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'call' thinking 'anyone who witnesses' = many people. ANYONE = singular → verb+S in present tense.
questions.learning_tip: ANYONE / EVERYONE / NOBODY / SOMEONE = Singular! Always use verb+S. Anyone CALLS = add -S. 'Anyone call' is WRONG. Singular indefinite pronouns take singular verbs.

questions.stem: Our school has ________ over five hundred dollars for the wildlife rescue centre this year.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. 'Raise' is regular: raise → raised.
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Our school HAS RAISED five hundred dollars = started raising this year and the result is here now. RAISE → RAISED (regular verb).

questions.stem: The rescued sea turtle is far ________ than it was when it first arrived at the rescue centre three weeks ago.
questions.trap_type: Comparing two conditions (now vs three weeks ago) = comparative. 'Healthy' → HEALTHIER (short adjective: add -ier replacing -y).
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective ending in -Y → change Y to I, add -ER. Healthy → HEALTHIER. The turtle is HEALTHIER THAN before = comparing two points in time. 'Most healthy' is superlative (for three or more).

questions.stem: The volunteers ________ the injured otter back to the river when the rescue coordinator called them back.
questions.trap_type: 'The coordinator called them back' = sudden interrupting event. Volunteers were already in the middle of carrying = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The coordinator CALLED THEM BACK = sudden past event. Volunteers were already carrying the otter = WERE CARRYING (past continuous). Past continuous = was/were + verb-ing.

questions.stem: There was ________ information about the animal's injuries in the rescue report — the vet could not tell what had happened.
questions.trap_type: 'Information' is uncountable → use LITTLE. 'Few', 'a few' and 'many' are for countable nouns.
questions.learning_tip: LITTLE + uncountable noun. Information = uncountable → LITTLE information. 'Few information' is WRONG — you cannot count individual pieces of information. LITTLE = not much.

questions.stem: The wild boar rescue operation was the most dangerous mission the team had ever attempted, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive past simple ('was the most dangerous') → negative question tag. 'Was' → wasn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive past 'to be' → negative tag. The operation WAS the most dangerous, WASN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE tag. WAS → WASN'T.

questions.stem: The injured pangolin ________ to the wildlife recovery centre by a team of trained volunteers last Friday.
questions.trap_type: The pangolin received the action. Past passive: was/were + past participle.
questions.learning_tip: WAS/WERE + past participle = passive! The pangolin WAS TRANSPORTED = volunteers transported it; the pangolin received the action. NEVER 'was being transported' (P5 level).

questions.stem: The rescue centre manager told the new volunteers ________ the animals without proper gloves or protective gear.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: TOLD someone NOT TO + base verb. The manager told volunteers NOT TO HANDLE the animals. Formula: told + person + not to + verb (base form).

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Comparative and superlative structures)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'A healthy adult otter can swim (1)________ a champion swimmer.' Signal: comparing two things of equal speed = AS + adj + AS. AS FAST AS = equal comparison.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'faster than' (unequal comparison) instead of 'as fast as' (equal).
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = equal comparison. The otter swims AS FAST AS a champion swimmer = the same speed. 'Faster than' = one is faster; 'as fast as' = both are the same speed.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Of all the animals at the rescue centre, the pygmy slow loris is (2)________, fitting in the palm of one hand.' Signal: comparing more than two items = superlative THE + adj + -EST.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'the smaller' (comparative, for two items) instead of 'the smallest' (superlative, for three or more).
questions.learning_tip: THE + adj + -EST = superlative (comparing THREE or more). Of all the animals, this one IS THE SMALLEST = the most small of all. THE SMALLEST = the one that beats all the rest.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The adult monitor lizard that arrived Monday is clearly (3)________ the young one we rescued last month.' Signal: comparing two lizards, unequal size = comparative adjective + THAN.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'the biggest' (superlative) instead of 'bigger than' (comparative between two).
questions.learning_tip: adj + -ER + THAN = comparative (comparing two things). The adult is BIGGER THAN the young one = comparing just these two. BIGGER THAN = unequal comparison between two.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'After a week without food, the rescued eagle was (4)________ a healthy wild eagle of the same species.' Signal: unequal comparison, the eagle is weaker = NOT AS + adj + AS.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'weaker than' (acceptable but NOT in word_box) instead of 'not as strong as' (negative equal form).
questions.learning_tip: NOT AS + adj + AS = negative comparison. NOT AS STRONG AS = less strong than. 'He is not as strong as his brother' = his brother is stronger. NOT AS = one falls short of the other.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The male sea turtle we found is (5)________ the female, weighing almost twice as much.' Signal: large difference in comparison = FAR + comparative. FAR HEAVIER THAN = much heavier.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'heavier than' (correct but lacks intensifier) instead of 'far heavier than' (intensified comparison in word_box).
questions.learning_tip: FAR + comparative = much more than. FAR HEAVIER THAN = a great deal heavier. FAR makes the comparison stronger. 'Very heavier' is WRONG — use FAR with comparatives.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'We received two injured civets — (6)________ needed surgery while the smaller one only needed rest.' Signal: choosing between exactly two items = THE + comparative + OF THE TWO.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'the biggest' (superlative, for three+) instead of 'the bigger of the two' (comparative for exactly two).
questions.learning_tip: THE + comparative + OF THE TWO = when choosing between exactly two. THE BIGGER OF THE TWO = the larger one when there are only two options. Never use superlative for just two things.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Without treatment, the animal grew (7)________ until the vet finally arrived to help.' Signal: gradual progressive change = comparative + AND + comparative.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'weaker' (single comparative) instead of the progressive form 'weaker and weaker'.
questions.learning_tip: comparative + AND + comparative = progressive change over time. WEAKER AND WEAKER = getting weaker little by little. More and more, faster and faster — this pattern shows gradual change.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Rescuing a wild crocodile is (8)________ animal mission our team has ever faced.' Signal: comparing all missions (more than two) to find the one that tops all others = THE MOST + long adj.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'most dangerous' (missing 'the') instead of 'the most dangerous' (superlative with THE).
questions.learning_tip: THE MOST + long adjective = superlative. THE MOST DANGEROUS = nothing is more dangerous than this. ALWAYS use THE before 'most + adjective'. 'Most dangerous' without THE is WRONG.

C.passage: A healthy adult otter can swim (1)________ a champion swimmer. Of all the animals at our centre, the pygmy slow loris is (2)________, fitting in the palm of one hand. The adult monitor lizard that arrived Monday is (3)________ the young one we rescued last month. After a week without food, the rescued eagle was (4)________ a healthy wild eagle. The male sea turtle we found is (5)________, weighing almost twice as much. We received two injured civets — (6)________ needed surgery while the smaller one only needed rest. Without treatment, the animal grew (7)________ until the vet arrived. Rescuing a wild crocodile is (8)________ animal mission our team has ever faced.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Animal rescue work needs both skill and compassion. When an injured creature arrives, it first receives (1)________ care — trained doctors examine its wounds and begin treatment. Many rescued animals are (2)________ — easily hurt by sudden movements — so handlers must stay calm. Some animals are found (3)________ by their owners, left alone without food or shelter. Once fully recovered, the team will (4)________ the animal back into its natural habitat. For animals that cannot survive alone, the centre serves as a permanent (5)________ — a safe haven for life.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'trained animal doctors' = veterinary (relating to animal medicine).
questions.learning_tip: VETERINARY = relating to the medical care of animals. A VETERINARY clinic = an animal hospital. A VET (short for veterinarian) = an animal doctor.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'easily hurt by sudden movements or loud noises' = fragile.
questions.learning_tip: FRAGILE = easily damaged or broken. Injured animals are FRAGILE = they can be hurt by rough handling. Handle with care — fragile things break easily.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'left alone without food or shelter by owners who can no longer care for them' = abandoned.
questions.learning_tip: ABANDONED = left alone and without care, especially by an owner. An ABANDONED animal = one that was left behind with no one to look after it.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'return it back into its natural habitat after recovery' = release.
questions.learning_tip: RELEASE = set free. To RELEASE an animal back into the wild = to let it go so it can live freely in its natural environment.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'a safe haven where they can live out their lives in peace' = sanctuary.
questions.learning_tip: A SANCTUARY = a safe place of refuge and protection. An animal SANCTUARY = a protected space where animals live safely, free from harm.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the rescuers)
questions.trap_type: 'The rescuers' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! The rescuers WERE careful around the frightened animal. WAS is only for ONE thing (singular). RESCUERS = more than one → WERE.

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — your (possessive) vs you're (you are)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'your' (belonging to you) when the meaning is 'you are'.
questions.learning_tip: YOU'RE = you are (contraction). YOUR = belonging to you. Test: 'your ready to help' → can you say 'you are ready to help'? YES → use YOU'RE. YOU'RE = YOU ARE.

questions.error_type: Spelling — ie/ei confusion (thief: I before E)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'theif' putting E before I. 'Thief' follows I-before-E: thIEf.
questions.learning_tip: Rule: I before E, except after C! thIEf = I before E ✅. Remember: 'the thIEf stole a PIE' — thIEf has IE inside, just like PIE. I before E always in this word!

questions.error_type: Adverb required after action verb (appeared)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'sudden' (adjective) after the action verb 'appeared'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (appeared), use an ADVERB: appeared SUDDENLY. Rule: verb + adverb (-ly). 'Sudden' describes nouns; 'suddenly' describes HOW something appears.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (rescuers', not rescuers's)
questions.trap_type: Students add 's after the apostrophe for a plural noun ending in -s.
questions.learning_tip: Plural possessive: just add apostrophe after -s! The RESCUERS' equipment = the equipment belonging to all the rescuers. NEVER 'rescuers's' — extra -s after apostrophe is wrong for plurals ending in -s.

E.passage: Last Tuesday, a group of students helped to rescue a family of otters near the canal. The rescuers was (1) trained to approach wild animals slowly and without making noise. One student called out to her friend, 'Your (2) going to need to stay very still or the mother otter will panic!' A young theif (3) bird swooped past, startling the team just as they were about to secure the net. The mother otter appeared sudden (4) from behind the reeds, dragging one of her pups by the scruff of the neck. After the rescue was complete, the rescuers's (5) report was sent to ACRES for the centre's records.

questions.sentence_a: You spot an injured animal near your home.
questions.sentence_b: You should call the wildlife rescue hotline right away.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'Since'.
questions.model_answer: Since you spot an injured animal near your home, you should call the wildlife rescue hotline right away.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'Since you will spot' — adding 'will' in the 'since' clause.
questions.learning_tip: SINCE = because of a known or given fact. SINCE you spot an injured animal, you SHOULD CALL the hotline. 'Since' introduces the reason; the result clause follows.

questions.sentence_a: The vet asked a question.
questions.sentence_b: Is the fox badly injured?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The vet asked...'
questions.model_answer: The vet asked if the fox was badly injured.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'The vet asked if the fox is badly injured' (no tense shift) or 'The vet asked if was the fox badly injured' (wrong word order).
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: asked + IF/WHETHER + subject + verb. 'Is the fox...?' → asked IF THE FOX WAS... Normal word order (no inversion). Tense shifts: is → was.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Ten-year-old Mei had never seen a pangolin before. She was cycling home from school when she spotted the creature by the drain — curled into a ball, completely still.

She knew enough not to touch it. Instead, she took a photograph with her mother's phone and called the wildlife rescue number on a poster at the library.

The officer who answered was calm and asked her clear questions: Where exactly was she? Was the animal breathing? Was there any blood? Mei answered each one carefully, keeping her eyes on the pangolin.

Thirty minutes later, a rescue van arrived. The officer — a tall woman named Dr Farah — crouched down beside the pangolin. 'It's dehydrated and frightened,' she said, 'but it will be fine.'

She lifted the pangolin gently into a ventilated box lined with dry leaves, then turned to Mei.

'You did exactly the right thing,' she said. 'Most people either run away or try to pick it up. You stayed calm and called for help.'

Mei watched the van drive away. She thought about the pangolin — one of the world's most trafficked animals — and decided, right there on the pavement, that she wanted to work with animals one day.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 4 has the same meaning as 'lacking enough water in the body'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Frightened' = scared; 'ventilated' = allowing air to flow; 'crouched' = bent down low. DEHYDRATED = not having enough water in the body.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: DEHYDRATED = lacking enough water in the body. 'DE-' means removal. The pangolin was DEHYDRATED = it lost too much water and was not getting enough to drink.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'one' refer to in 'The officer who answered was calm and asked her clear questions'?

options.3: The rescue officer who answered the phone

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'one' refers to the number. But 'The officer who answered' = one (person) who picked up the call.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: 'The officer who answered WAS CALM and asked clear questions.' The 'officer' = the person who picked up the wildlife rescue call. Context: she called the number → an officer answered.

mcq_questions.stem: Why does Dr Farah say 'You did exactly the right thing'?

options.1: Because Mei was the first person ever to call the wildlife hotline.
options.2: Because Mei stayed calm, did not touch the animal and called for expert help instead.
options.3: Because Mei is planning to be a wildlife officer.
options.4: Because Mei found a very rare species of animal.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 4 thinking the praise was about finding the pangolin. Dr Farah's praise is specifically about Mei's behaviour: staying calm and calling for help.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 6: 'Most people either RUN AWAY or TRY TO PICK IT UP. You STAYED CALM and CALLED FOR HELP.' These three actions (not touching, staying calm, calling) are exactly why Dr Farah praised her.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 2, is it True or False that Mei picked up the pangolin to look at it more closely? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says 'She knew enough not to touch it' — she took a photograph and called for help instead of picking it up.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, she got closer to help it.' She stayed near but knew not to touch it.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'She knew enough NOT TO TOUCH IT.' She took a PHOTOGRAPH and CALLED the rescue number. She did NOT pick it up. The answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What three questions did the rescue officer ask Mei on the phone?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: The officer asked: (1) Where exactly was she? (2) Was the animal breathing? (3) Was there any blood?
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students give only one or two questions.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: Three clear questions — (1) WHERE was she? (2) Was the animal BREATHING? (3) Was there any BLOOD? All three are listed directly in the passage.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did Mei feel when she first spotted the pangolin? Give TWO pieces of evidence from the passage.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) She felt curious and concerned — she took a photograph and stayed near the pangolin instead of walking away, showing she cared about what happened to it. (ii) She felt calm and focused — she answered each of the officer's questions carefully while keeping her eyes on the pangolin throughout.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'she felt happy' without evidence. The passage shows CURIOSITY (she stayed and photographed) and CALMNESS (answered questions while watching).
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: For EMOTION questions: name the feeling + give evidence from the passage. 'She felt CURIOUS = she took a photo and stayed near it.' FEELING + EVIDENCE = full marks.

open_ended_questions.stem: What decision did Mei make at the end of the passage, and what made her make it?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Mei decided she wanted to work with animals one day. She was moved by the pangolin rescue and by learning that pangolins are among the world's most trafficked animals.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'she decided to call the hotline again' — that already happened. The decision is about her future career.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Last paragraph: 'she decided she wanted to WORK WITH ANIMALS one day.' The reason: she thought about the pangolin — 'one of the world's MOST TRAFFICKED ANIMALS.' This fact moved her to make the decision.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on her actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Mei with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) RESPONSIBLE: Mei knew not to touch the pangolin and called the wildlife rescue number instead — she took the correct action even without being told what to do. (ii) OBSERVANT: she answered the officer's questions carefully while keeping her eyes on the pangolin — she stayed alert and noticed the details needed to help.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'kind and brave' without precise traits linked to textual evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: RESPONSIBLE = knew NOT TO TOUCH IT, CALLED the rescue number. OBSERVANT = answered questions CAREFULLY, kept her EYES ON the pangolin throughout. Name the trait, then give the evidence.

questions.stem: The view from the plane window was as ________ as an ocean — clouds stretched in every direction without end.
questions.trap_type: 'Small' and 'narrow' describe limited space. 'Dark' is about light. VAST = extremely large in area or extent.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The view was AS VAST AS an ocean = comparing the endless sky to an ocean's expanse. VAST = extremely large, stretching without limits.

questions.stem: The pilot announced that the turbulence stopped the plane from taking off on time, but the delay came ________ and surprised all the passengers.
questions.trap_type: 'Very slowly', 'little by little' and 'on purpose' do not capture sudden unexpectedness. OUT OF THE BLUE = completely unexpectedly, with no warning.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: OUT OF THE BLUE = happening completely unexpectedly, with no warning. The delay came OUT OF THE BLUE = nobody expected it at all. Blue sky has no warning signs — it appears from nowhere.

questions.stem: After the long queue at immigration, the family finally watched their plane ________ into the bright afternoon sky.
questions.trap_type: 'Land' = come down; 'sink' = go under; 'stop' = cease movement. TAKE OFF = leave the ground and begin flying.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: TAKE OFF = (of a plane) leave the ground and begin to fly. The plane TOOK OFF into the sky = it left the runway and flew upward. TAKE + OFF work together.

questions.stem: Passengers must show their ________ at the boarding gate before being allowed onto the plane.
questions.trap_type: 'Suitcase' = luggage; 'passport photo' = just a photo; 'travel guide' = a book. A BOARDING PASS = the ticket that allows a passenger to board the plane.
questions.learning_tip: A BOARDING PASS = the document or card that authorises a passenger to board a specific flight. Without a BOARDING PASS, you cannot get onto the plane.

questions.stem: The flight attendant was calm and ________ — she handled the nervous passenger with patience and professionalism.
questions.trap_type: 'Rude', 'clumsy' and 'distracted' all describe negative qualities. COMPOSED = calm and in control of one's feelings, especially in a difficult situation.
questions.learning_tip: COMPOSED = calm and in control even under pressure. The attendant was COMPOSED = she stayed cool and professional. COMPOSE yourself = make yourself calm.

questions.stem: Everyone on board ________ their seatbelt fastened during take-off and landing.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'keep' thinking 'everyone on board' = many people. EVERYONE = singular → verb+S in present tense.
questions.learning_tip: EVERYONE / NOBODY / SOMEONE = Singular! Always use verb+S. Everyone KEEPS their seatbelt fastened = add -S. 'Everyone keep' is WRONG. Singular indefinite → singular verb.

questions.stem: Changi Airport has ________ the world's best airport award for the eighth year running.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. 'Win' is irregular: win → won.
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Changi HAS WON the award for eight years = started winning in the past and keeps winning now. WIN → WON (irregular).

questions.stem: Terminal 3 is much ________ than Terminal 1, with three times as many shops and restaurants.
questions.trap_type: Comparing two terminals = comparative. 'Large' → LARGER (short adjective adds -er). 'More larger' is double comparative (WRONG).
questions.learning_tip: Short adjective + -ER = comparative. Large → LARGER. Terminal 3 is LARGER THAN Terminal 1. 'More larger' is WRONG — never add 'more' AND '-er'. Choose one.

questions.stem: The passengers ________ their bags through the X-ray machine when the security alarm went off.
questions.trap_type: 'The alarm went off' = sudden interrupting event. Passengers were already passing bags = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The alarm WENT OFF = sudden past event. Passengers were already in the middle of passing their bags = WERE PASSING (past continuous). Past continuous = was/were + verb-ing.

questions.stem: There are ________ seats available on this flight — the airline is fully booked for the holiday weekend.
questions.trap_type: 'Seats' is countable. 'Little' and 'a little' are for uncountable nouns; 'much' needs a negative. NO = zero (works for both countable and uncountable).
questions.learning_tip: NO = zero, none available. There are NO seats = not even one seat. NO works with both countable and uncountable nouns. 'Little seats' is WRONG — seats are countable.

questions.stem: The flight delay disappointed all the passengers on board, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive past simple ('disappointed') → negative question tag. 'Disappointed' → didn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive past simple → negative tag. The delay DISAPPOINTED everyone, DIDN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE tag. Past simple → did/didn't.

questions.stem: All carry-on luggage ________ before boarding to ensure it fits the airline's size requirements.
questions.trap_type: The luggage received the action. Past passive: was/were + past participle.
questions.learning_tip: WAS/WERE + past participle = passive! The luggage WAS MEASURED = staff measured it; the luggage received the action. WERE for plural subject.

questions.stem: The flight attendant asked the passengers ________ their tray tables and return their seats to the upright position.
questions.trap_type: Positive reported speech: asked + object + to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: ASKED someone TO + base verb. The attendant asked passengers TO FOLD their tray tables. Formula: asked + person + to + verb (positive reported speech).

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Quantity adjectives — advanced group)

questions.context_check: Passage: '(1)________ passenger must show their boarding pass at the gate before boarding.' Signal: each individual one in a group (emphasises ALL individuals) = EVERY. EVERY + singular noun.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'each' (also correct in some contexts) but EVERY emphasises the collective rule applying to ALL without exception.
questions.learning_tip: EVERY + singular noun = each one without exception (rule-like). EVERY passenger must show a pass = there are no exceptions. EVERY emphasises that the rule covers ALL.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(2)________ seat on the plane comes with a personal screen and a set of headphones.' Signal: referring to individual items one by one = EACH. EACH + singular noun (individual focus).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'every' (rule emphasis) instead of 'each' (individual focus). EACH is used when thinking about items one by one.
questions.learning_tip: EACH + singular noun = thinking about items one by one. EACH seat comes with a screen = focusing on individual seats. EACH = one by one; EVERY = the whole group without exception.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(3)________ passengers must fasten their seatbelts during turbulence, without exception.' Signal: the entire group together = ALL. ALL + plural noun.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'every' (singular noun required) instead of 'all' (plural noun).
questions.learning_tip: ALL + plural noun = the entire group together. ALL passengers = every single one of them as a group. ALL is followed by PLURAL; EVERY is followed by SINGULAR.

questions.context_check: Passage: '(4)________ travellers arrive at the airport at least two hours before their flight to avoid missing check-in.' Signal: the majority, but not all = MOST. MOST = the larger part of a group.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'all' (every single one) instead of 'most' (the majority). The passage implies some do not arrive two hours early.
questions.learning_tip: MOST = the majority (more than half, but not all). MOST travellers arrive early = most, but not every single one. MOST ≠ ALL. ALL = every one; MOST = the largest part.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Make sure you have (5)________ time to clear security before your flight departs.' Signal: a sufficient amount = ENOUGH. ENOUGH = as much as needed.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'plenty of' (more than enough) instead of 'enough' (just sufficient). The passage is about having the minimum required.
questions.learning_tip: ENOUGH = as much as is needed, not more. Make sure you have ENOUGH time = the right amount to clear security. ENOUGH = sufficient. PLENTY OF = more than enough (surplus).

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The departure lounge has (6)________ seating, so passengers can relax comfortably before boarding.' Signal: more than enough, an abundance = PLENTY OF. PLENTY OF = more than sufficient.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'enough' (just sufficient) instead of 'plenty of' (abundance). The lounge has MORE than enough seating.
questions.learning_tip: PLENTY OF = a large amount, more than enough. The lounge has PLENTY OF seating = many seats, more than needed. PLENTY OF = abundance. Works with both countable and uncountable nouns.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'There is (7)________ food allowed past the security checkpoint — all snacks must be consumed or discarded beforehand.' Signal: zero, nothing allowed = NO. NO = not any.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'none' (pronoun, stands alone) instead of 'no' (adjective before noun). 'No food' = NO + noun. 'None' cannot directly precede a noun.
questions.learning_tip: NO + noun = zero of that thing. There is NO food allowed = not any food at all. NONE = pronoun (stands alone): 'None is allowed.' NO = adjective before a noun: 'NO food'.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The airline checked the overhead compartments — (8)________ of the bags were oversized, so boarding was smooth.' Signal: not any of a previously mentioned group = NONE (pronoun referring back). NONE OF + noun phrase.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'no' (adjective) instead of 'none' (pronoun). 'None of the bags' = NONE OF (pronoun construction). 'No of the bags' is ungrammatical.
questions.learning_tip: NONE OF + noun phrase = not any of them. NONE of the bags were oversized = not a single one of them. NONE OF = pronoun construction. Compare: NO bags (adjective) vs NONE of the bags (pronoun).

C.passage: (1)________ passenger must show their boarding pass at the gate before boarding. (2)________ seat on the plane comes with a personal screen and headphones. (3)________ passengers must fasten their seatbelts during turbulence. (4)________ travellers arrive at the airport at least two hours before their flight to avoid missing check-in. Make sure you have (5)________ time to clear security before departure. The lounge has (6)________ seating, so passengers can relax before boarding. There is (7)________ food allowed past the security checkpoint — all snacks must be discarded. The airline checked the overhead compartments — (8)________ of the bags were oversized, so boarding was smooth.
