D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: A plane journey begins long before take-off. At the airport, travellers check in at the (1)________ hall and drop off their luggage. The plane then taxis along the (2)________, the long flat strip where aircraft take off and land. Pilots sit in the (3)________ at the front, surrounded by controls and screens. Once airborne, the plane climbs to a cruising (4)________ of about ten thousand metres above sea level. During the flight, passengers may feel bumps caused by (5)________ — sudden changes in air movement that rock the aircraft.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'check in and drop off luggage before heading to the gate' = departure hall.
questions.learning_tip: DEPARTURE = the act of leaving. A DEPARTURE hall = the area in an airport where passengers check in and start their journey. DEPART = leave; DEPARTURE = the act of leaving.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'the long flat strip where aircraft take off and land' = runway.
questions.learning_tip: A RUNWAY = the long paved strip at an airport where planes take off and land. RUNWAY = the road for planes.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'at the front of the aircraft, surrounded by hundreds of controls and screens' where pilots sit = cockpit.
questions.learning_tip: The COCKPIT = the front section of a plane where the pilot and co-pilot sit and control the aircraft. Only the flight crew can enter the COCKPIT.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'about ten thousand metres above sea level' = altitude (height above the ground).
questions.learning_tip: ALTITUDE = height above sea level, especially of an aircraft. The plane flies at a cruising ALTITUDE of 10,000 metres = that height above the earth.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'bumps and shaking caused by sudden changes in air movement that rock the aircraft' = turbulence.
questions.learning_tip: TURBULENCE = sudden, irregular air movements that cause a plane to shake and bump. TURBULENCE is normal but can be alarming for nervous flyers.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the passengers)
questions.trap_type: 'The passengers' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! The passengers WERE excited to board. WAS is only for ONE (singular). PASSENGERS = more than one → WERE.

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — whose (possessive) vs who's (who is/has)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'whose' (possessive pronoun) when the meaning is 'who is'.
questions.learning_tip: WHO'S = who is OR who has (contraction). WHOSE = belonging to whom. 'Whose flying the plane today?' → can you say 'Who is flying the plane'? YES → use WHO'S. WHO'S = WHO IS.

questions.error_type: Spelling — ie/ei confusion (relief: I before E)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'releif' putting E before I. 'Relief' follows I-before-E: relIEf.
questions.learning_tip: Rule: I before E, except after C! relIEf = I before E ✅. Remember: 'What a relIEf — the PIE is safe!' — relIEf has IE just like PIE. I before E!

questions.error_type: Adverb required after action verb (landed)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'safe' (adjective) after the action verb 'landed'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (landed), use an ADVERB: landed SAFELY. Rule: verb + adverb (-ly). 'Safe' describes nouns (a safe landing); 'safely' describes HOW something lands.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (pilots', not pilots's)
questions.trap_type: Students add 's after the apostrophe for a plural noun ending in -s.
questions.learning_tip: Plural possessive: just add apostrophe after -s! The PILOTS' cabin = the cabin belonging to all the pilots. NEVER 'pilots's' — the extra -s after the apostrophe is wrong for plural nouns ending in -s.

E.passage: Last school holiday, my family flew to Tokyo for a week. The passengers was (1) buzzing with excitement as we queued at the gate to board our flight. A young boy standing ahead of us asked his father, 'Whose (2) flying the plane today?' Everyone smiled at his question. After a smooth take-off, the pilot announced we were flying at thirty-five thousand feet and expressed his releif (3) that the weather ahead was clear and calm. Our plane landed safe (4) at Narita Airport just after dinner time, and we were glad to stretch our legs after the long flight. As we left the aircraft, we could hear the pilots's (5) voices thanking the ground crew through the intercom.

questions.sentence_a: You do not check in online before arriving at the airport.
questions.sentence_b: You may have to wait in a long queue at the counter.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'Unless'.
questions.model_answer: Unless you check in online before arriving at the airport, you may have to wait in a long queue at the counter.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'Unless you will check in' — adding 'will' in the 'unless' clause.
questions.learning_tip: UNLESS + simple present, modal verb. UNLESS you CHECK IN online, you MAY HAVE TO wait. Never use 'will' after 'unless'. UNLESS = if not.

questions.sentence_a: The passenger asked a question.
questions.sentence_b: What is the departure time for flight SQ317?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The passenger asked...'
questions.model_answer: The passenger asked what the departure time for flight SQ317 was.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'The passenger asked what was the departure time' — wrong word order (question inversion kept). In reported speech, use normal word order.
questions.learning_tip: WH-question → reported speech: ASKED + WH-word + subject + verb (normal order). 'What IS the time?' → asked WHAT the time WAS. NEVER 'asked what WAS the time'. Word order flips to normal in reported speech.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Eight-year-old Zara never flew on a plane before this trip. She expected it to be loud, and it was. But it was also — unexpectedly — beautiful.

From her window seat, she watched the ground disappear. Singapore shrank below her: highways became threads, buildings became squares, and the sea turned into a flat silver mirror. Then the clouds rose up around the plane, and she could no longer see the ground at all.

She pressed her nose against the cold glass and stared.

Her father, who was sitting in the middle seat reading a magazine, glanced up. 'You all right?'

'Dad,' said Zara quietly, 'is this what the world looks like from up here all the time?'

Her father smiled. 'Every time,' he said.

Zara turned back to the window. Below her, the clouds formed a white landscape. Hills of cloud. Plains of cloud. A whole other world above the one she knew from the ground.

She did not touch her in-flight meal. She did not use the entertainment screen. She sat with her face turned to the window for the entire four-hour flight, watching the light change across the clouds as the sun moved slowly west.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'became smaller in the distance'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Disappeared' = vanished completely; 'turned' = changed direction or form; 'formed' = took shape. SHRANK = became smaller.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: SHRANK = past tense of 'shrink' = became smaller. Singapore SHRANK below her = it looked smaller and smaller as the plane climbed. SHRINK → SHRANK (irregular past).

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 7, what does 'one' refer to in 'A whole other world above the one she had always known'?

options.2: The world she knew on the ground — the everyday world below the clouds

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'the one' = the clouds. But 'the one she had always known' = the world she knew before — the ground-level world.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 7: 'A whole other world ABOVE the one she had ALWAYS KNOWN.' The one she always knew = the world on the GROUND. The new world = the cloud landscape above. ONE = the ground-level world.

mcq_questions.stem: Why does the writer say Zara 'did not touch her in-flight meal' and 'did not use the entertainment screen'?

options.1: To show that Zara was feeling unwell during the flight.
options.2: To show that the food and screen were not working properly.
options.3: To show that watching the clouds was far more absorbing to Zara than anything else on the flight.
options.4: To show that Zara was afraid to move from her seat.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking she was sick. But the passage shows she was captivated by the clouds — not unwell.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Last paragraph: she 'did NOT TOUCH the meal' and 'did NOT USE the screen' — she sat watching the clouds for the ENTIRE FOUR HOURS. The writer shows the view was so absorbing it replaced everything else.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Zara had flown on a plane before? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says Zara 'had never been on a plane before' — this was her first flight.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True' because she knows it is loud. She was told it would be loud — but she had never flown herself.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: 'Zara HAD NEVER BEEN ON A PLANE BEFORE.' She was told about the noise, but this was her FIRST FLIGHT. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did Singapore look from the plane window after take-off? Give TWO details.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Highways looked like thin threads, and buildings looked like small squares. The sea became a flat silver mirror.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'it looked small' — too vague. The passage gives three specific visual details.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: highways became THREADS, buildings became SQUARES, the sea turned into a FLAT SILVER MIRROR. These are specific visual images — give at least two of them.

open_ended_questions.stem: How does the writer show that Zara was completely absorbed by the view? Give TWO details from the final paragraph.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) She did not touch her in-flight meal — she was too focused on the clouds to eat. (ii) She sat watching the clouds for the entire four-hour flight without using the entertainment screen.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'she looked out the window' — too vague. The specific details are about what she chose not to do.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Final paragraph: (1) DID NOT TOUCH the in-flight meal; (2) sat watching for the ENTIRE FOUR-HOUR flight without the entertainment screen. These show complete absorption in the view.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did Zara see when she looked out of the window after the clouds rose up around the plane?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: She saw a white landscape of clouds — hills of cloud and plains of cloud — like a whole other world above the one she knew.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'she saw clouds' — too vague. The passage describes the cloud landscape in specific terms.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 7: 'HILLS OF CLOUD. PLAINS OF CLOUD. A WHOLE OTHER WORLD above the one she had always known.' These specific images make the answer complete.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on her behaviour throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Zara with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) CURIOUS: she pressed her nose against the glass, stared at the view and asked her father if the world always looked like this — showing genuine wonder and a hunger to understand. (ii) FOCUSED: she ignored her meal and entertainment screen for the entire four-hour flight, keeping her face at the window — showing deep, unwavering concentration.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'excited and quiet' without precise traits linked to evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: CURIOUS = pressed nose against glass, asked 'Is this what the world looks like?'. FOCUSED = did NOT touch meal, did NOT use screen, watched for ENTIRE FOUR HOURS. Name trait → give evidence.

questions.stem: The explanation in the science textbook was as ________ as a glass of water — easy to understand and perfectly transparent.
questions.trap_type: 'Heavy', 'cold' and 'slow' do not describe clarity of explanation. CLEAR = easy to understand, transparent and straightforward.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The explanation was AS CLEAR AS a glass of water = comparing its clarity to pure, transparent water. CLEAR = easy to understand, with nothing hidden or confusing.

questions.stem: Even though she felt ________ that morning, the young scientist dragged herself to the lab because the experiment could not wait.
questions.trap_type: 'Excited', 'on top of the world' and 'over the moon' all describe feeling good. UNDER THE WEATHER = feeling unwell or slightly ill.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: UNDER THE WEATHER = feeling unwell or slightly ill. She felt UNDER THE WEATHER = she was not feeling well that morning. When you are sick, you feel like bad weather is hanging over you!

questions.stem: The science club decided to ________ a new experiment to test whether plants grow faster with or without music.
questions.trap_type: 'Stop' and 'give up' mean not doing it; 'look after' = care for. CARRY OUT = perform or conduct (a task or experiment).
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: CARRY OUT = perform or complete a task or experiment. The club decided to CARRY OUT the experiment = conduct it from start to finish. CARRY + OUT work together.

questions.stem: The scientist recorded every detail of the experiment in a ________, noting the time, temperature and results for each trial.
questions.trap_type: 'Storybook' and 'novel' are fiction; 'poster' is a display. A LOGBOOK = an official record where observations, data and notes are written down in order.
questions.learning_tip: A LOGBOOK = a detailed record of events, observations and data. Scientists keep a LOGBOOK so they can review and share their findings. LOG = record; LOGBOOK = the book of records.

questions.stem: During the experiment, the students noticed a significant ________ in the colour of the liquid after adding the acid.
questions.trap_type: 'Smell', 'weight' and 'change' are all possible but 'change in colour' specifically refers to a chemical reaction. REACTION = a process in which substances interact to produce new substances or changes.
questions.learning_tip: A REACTION = a chemical or physical process triggered by combining substances. When acid is added to the liquid, a REACTION occurs = the chemicals interact and the colour changes.

questions.stem: Nobody in the science class ________ how to explain the results of the experiment without looking at the data.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'know' thinking 'nobody in the science class' = many people. NOBODY = singular → verb+S in present tense.
questions.learning_tip: NOBODY / EVERYONE / ANYONE = Singular! ALWAYS use verb+S. Nobody KNOWS = add -S. 'Nobody know' is WRONG. Singular indefinite → singular verb in present tense.

questions.stem: Our science team has ________ the winning prize at the National Science Fair two years in a row.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. 'Win' is irregular: win → won.
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Our team HAS WON the prize two years in a row = started winning before and just did it again. WIN → WON (irregular past participle).

questions.stem: The results from Group A were far ________ than those from Group B, because Group A followed the method more carefully.
questions.trap_type: Comparing two groups = comparative. 'Accurate' (3+ syllables) → MORE + adj. 'Most accurate' is superlative; 'accurately' is an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: Long adjective (3+ syllables) → MORE + adjective = comparative. Group A's results were MORE ACCURATE THAN Group B's. NEVER 'accurater' — use MORE for long adjectives.

questions.stem: The students ________ the final measurements when the fire alarm interrupted the lesson.
questions.trap_type: 'The fire alarm interrupted' = sudden event. Students were already in the middle of recording = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The alarm INTERRUPTED = sudden past event. Students were already recording = WERE RECORDING (past continuous). Was/were + verb-ing = action in progress when interrupted.

questions.stem: There was ________ equipment left in the science room — the other classes used it all during the morning session.
questions.trap_type: 'Equipment' is uncountable → use LITTLE. 'Few', 'a few' and 'many' are for countable nouns.
questions.learning_tip: LITTLE + uncountable noun. Equipment = uncountable → LITTLE equipment. You cannot say 'a few equipment' or 'few equipment'. LITTLE = not much (for uncountable things).

questions.stem: The science fair was the most exciting event of the school year, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive past 'to be' ('was') → negative question tag. 'Was' → wasn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive past 'to be' → negative tag. The fair WAS the most exciting, WASN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE tag. WAS → WASN'T.

questions.stem: The results of the experiment ________ by the teacher before they were shared with the other classes.
questions.trap_type: The results received the action. Past passive: was/were + past participle. Plural subject (results) → were.
questions.learning_tip: WAS/WERE + past participle = passive! The results WERE CHECKED = the teacher checked them; results received the action. WERE for plural subject.

questions.stem: The teacher asked the students ________ their experiment data in the shared folder before the end of the period.
questions.trap_type: Positive reported speech: asked + object + to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: ASKED someone TO + base verb. The teacher asked students TO SAVE their data. Formula: asked + person + to + verb. 'Asked to saving' or 'asked save' are WRONG.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Modal and obligation verbs — advanced)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'All students (1)________ wear safety goggles before starting any experiment.' Signal: strong obligation/rule, no choice = MUST. MUST = strong necessity.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'should' (not in word_box) instead of 'must' (strong rule obligation).
questions.learning_tip: MUST = strong obligation (rule or necessity). Students MUST wear goggles = it is a non-negotiable rule. MUST is stronger than 'should'. Breaking this rule is not acceptable.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'You (2)________ record your observations at every stage, not just at the end.' Signal: practical necessity for a specific task = NEED TO. NEED TO = it is necessary.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'must' (stronger obligation) instead of 'need to' (practical necessity). NEED TO is softer — it focuses on what is required to get a good result.
questions.learning_tip: NEED TO = it is necessary to do this (practical requirement). You NEED TO record observations at every stage = you must do this to get complete data. NEED TO focuses on what is required.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Scientists (3)________ check their equipment before starting to make sure nothing is broken or missing.' Signal: moral or good practice recommendation = OUGHT TO. OUGHT TO = should (moral advisability).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'must' (strict rule) instead of 'ought to' (recommendation/good practice).
questions.learning_tip: OUGHT TO = should, it is morally right or good practice to do this. Scientists OUGHT TO check their equipment = it is the right thing to do. OUGHT TO is like SHOULD but slightly more formal.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'If the experiment takes more than one hour, students (4)________ get permission from the teacher to stay after class.' Signal: external rule/obligation imposed by others = HAVE TO. HAVE TO = external requirement.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'must' (personal obligation) instead of 'have to' (rule imposed by others — the teacher's rule).
questions.learning_tip: HAVE TO = external obligation, a rule or requirement set by others. Students HAVE TO get permission = the school rule requires it. MUST = personal sense of obligation; HAVE TO = rule from outside.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'With enough practice, a Primary Three student (5)________ set up a simple circuit independently.' Signal: capability/ability = IS ABLE TO. IS ABLE TO = can (emphasising capability).
questions.trap_type: Students write 'can' (not in word_box) instead of 'is able to' (same meaning, formal ability).
questions.learning_tip: IS ABLE TO = has the skill/capability to do something. A student IS ABLE TO set up a circuit = she has the skill and knowledge to do it. IS ABLE TO = 'can' (more formal, emphasises achievement of ability).

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Our science lab (6)________ have only one microscope, but now we have eight for the whole class to share.' Signal: past habit or past state that is no longer true = USED TO.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'would' (repeated past action) instead of 'used to' (past state that no longer exists). 'Used to have' = a state in the past, now changed.
questions.learning_tip: USED TO = a past habit or state that is no longer true now. The lab USED TO have only one microscope = in the past it had one, but now it has eight. USED TO describes past situations that have changed.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'You (7)________ write down your hypothesis before starting, or the teacher will not accept your report.' Signal: strong warning/advice with consequence = HAD BETTER. HAD BETTER = strong advice with implied warning.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'should' (not in word_box) instead of 'had better' (stronger, implied warning/consequence).
questions.learning_tip: HAD BETTER = strong advice with an implied warning. You HAD BETTER write down your hypothesis = if you don't, something bad will happen (the teacher won't accept the report). HAD BETTER is stronger than 'should'.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'When given a choice, most students (8)________ do a hands-on experiment than copy notes from the board.' Signal: preference between two options = WOULD RATHER. WOULD RATHER + base verb.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'prefer' (not in word_box) instead of 'would rather' (same meaning, modal preference).
questions.learning_tip: WOULD RATHER + base verb = preference. Students WOULD RATHER do an experiment THAN copy notes = they prefer the experiment. WOULD RATHER ... THAN ... = choosing between two options.

C.passage: The science laboratory has rules that every student (1)________ follow without exception. Before starting, you (2)________ record observations at every stage — not just at the end. Scientists (3)________ check their equipment before starting to make sure nothing is broken. If an experiment takes more than one hour, students (4)________ get permission from the teacher to continue. With enough practice, a Primary Three student (5)________ set up a simple circuit independently. Our science lab (6)________ have only one microscope, but now we have eight for the whole class. You (7)________ write down your hypothesis before starting, or the teacher will not accept your report. When given a choice, most students (8)________ do a hands-on experiment than copy notes.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Every good science investigation follows a clear process. First, a scientist forms a (1)________ — a prediction about what will happen. Then, they design and conduct an (2)________ to test this prediction. During the test, they carefully (3)________ what is happening and note every detail. A scientist must change only one (4)________ at a time — for example, only the temperature — while keeping everything else the same. At the end, the scientist draws a (5)________, explaining what the results show and whether the original prediction was correct.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'a prediction about what will happen based on what they already know' = hypothesis.
questions.learning_tip: A HYPOTHESIS = a scientific prediction made before an experiment. You think: 'I BELIEVE that...' — that is your HYPOTHESIS. It may be right or wrong; the experiment tests it.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'design and conduct an ___ to test this prediction' = experiment.
questions.learning_tip: An EXPERIMENT = a scientific test carried out to discover or prove something. Scientists design EXPERIMENTS to test whether their hypothesis is correct.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'carefully ___ what is happening and write down every detail' = observe.
questions.learning_tip: OBSERVE = watch carefully and notice what is happening. Scientists OBSERVE during an experiment = they look, listen and notice every detail.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'change only one ___ at a time — for example, only the amount of water' = variable.
questions.learning_tip: A VARIABLE = a factor that can change in an experiment. To make an experiment fair, you only change ONE VARIABLE at a time while keeping everything else the same.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'drawn at the end, explaining what the results show' = conclusion.
questions.learning_tip: A CONCLUSION = the final statement that explains what the experiment showed. The CONCLUSION answers: Was the hypothesis correct? What did we learn from the results?

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the results)
questions.trap_type: 'The results' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! The results WERE surprising. WAS is only for ONE (singular). RESULTS = more than one thing → WERE.

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — wear (to put on clothing) vs where (a place)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'wear' (put on clothing) when the sentence needs 'where' (at which place).
questions.learning_tip: WHERE = at which place (location). WEAR = to put on clothing. 'The lab wear we store the equipment' → should 'where' be here? YES — it is a place. WHERE = location; WEAR = clothing.

questions.error_type: Spelling — ie/ei confusion (yield: I before E)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'yeild' putting E before I. 'Yield' follows I-before-E: yIEld.
questions.learning_tip: Rule: I before E, except after C! yIEld = I before E ✅. Remember: 'the fIEld will yIEld a PIE' — yIEld and fIEld both have IE. I before E!

questions.error_type: Adverb required after action verb (measured)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'careful' (adjective) after the action verb 'measured'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (measured), use an ADVERB: measured CAREFULLY. Rule: verb + adverb (-ly). 'Careful' describes nouns; 'carefully' describes HOW the measuring was done.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (groups', not groups's)
questions.trap_type: Students add 's after the apostrophe for a plural noun ending in -s.
questions.learning_tip: Plural possessive: just add apostrophe after -s! The GROUPS' findings = the findings belonging to all the groups. NEVER 'groups's' — extra -s after apostrophe is WRONG for plural nouns ending in -s.

E.passage: Last Friday, our class did a science experiment about the effect of sunlight on plant growth. The results was (1) recorded in a table and checked against our original predictions. We moved our equipment to the room wear (2) the large windows let in the most sunlight. Our teacher told us that the experiment might yeild (3) surprising findings if we used different types of soil. Each student measured the height of their plant careful (4) using a ruler and noted the measurement in their logbook. At the end of the session, the groups's (5) observations were compared and the class agreed on a shared conclusion.

questions.sentence_a: The experiment produced unexpected results.
questions.sentence_b: The students were still able to write a clear conclusion.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'Although'.
questions.model_answer: Although the experiment produced unexpected results, the students were still able to write a clear conclusion.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'Although the experiment produced unexpected results but...' — adding 'but' redundantly after 'although'.
questions.learning_tip: ALTHOUGH introduces a contrast clause. ALTHOUGH the results were unexpected, the students STILL wrote a clear conclusion. NEVER use 'but' after 'although' — 'although' already shows the contrast.

questions.sentence_a: The teacher asked a question.
questions.sentence_b: What does the experiment show?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The teacher asked...'
questions.model_answer: The teacher asked what the experiment showed.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'The teacher asked what does the experiment show' — keeping question word order. In reported speech, use normal word order.
questions.learning_tip: WH-question → reported speech: ASKED + WH-word + subject + verb (normal order). 'What DOES the experiment SHOW?' → asked WHAT the experiment SHOWED. No inversion. Present → past (shows → showed).

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage_title: Why Do Ice Cubes Melt Faster in Salt Water?
G.passage:
Have you ever noticed that roads are sprinkled with salt during winter in cold countries? The reason is connected to a simple scientific principle: salt lowers the freezing point of water.

Pure water freezes at zero degrees Celsius. When salt is added to water, the water molecules become harder to freeze, so the freezing point drops below zero. This means that a saltwater solution stays liquid at temperatures where pure water would already be solid ice.

This same principle explains why ice cubes melt faster in salt water than in plain water. When you drop an ice cube into a glass of salt water, the salt water immediately begins pulling heat from the ice. The more salt there is in the water, the lower the freezing point drops, and the faster the ice melts.

You can test this yourself. Fill two identical glasses — one with plain water and one with salt water — and add a same-sized ice cube to each. Observe what happens over five minutes and record the results.

This kind of experiment is called a controlled experiment. You change only one variable — the salt — and keep everything else the same: the amount of water, the size of the ice cube, the room temperature. This way, you can be sure that any difference in the results is caused by the salt alone.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'a mixture of a substance dissolved in liquid'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Molecule' = a tiny unit of matter; 'principle' = a basic rule; 'temperature' = degree of heat. SOLUTION = a mixture where a substance is dissolved in a liquid.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: A SOLUTION = a liquid mixture in which a substance (like salt) is completely dissolved. A SALTWATER SOLUTION = salt dissolved in water. In science, solution ≠ answer — it means a dissolved mixture.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'This same principle' refer to?

options.1: The method of sprinkling salt on roads
options.2: The fact that salt lowers the freezing point of water
options.3: The speed at which ice cubes melt

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'this principle' = road salt. The principle is the scientific fact — that salt lowers the freezing point.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2 ends: 'salt lowers the FREEZING POINT OF WATER.' Paragraph 3 begins: 'THIS SAME PRINCIPLE explains why ice melts faster in salt water.' THIS SAME PRINCIPLE = the freezing point principle from paragraph 2.

mcq_questions.stem: Why is it important to keep the size of the ice cube and the room temperature the same in the experiment described in paragraph 5?

options.1: To make the experiment look neat and organised.
options.2: To make sure only the salt can explain any difference in the results.
options.3: To save time when recording the observations.
options.4: Because bigger ice cubes would not fit in the glasses.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking it is about presentation. The scientific reason is about controlling variables.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: 'You change only ONE VARIABLE — the salt — and keep everything else the SAME... so you can be sure the difference is caused by the SALT ALONE.' Keeping other things the same = controls variables so only salt can explain differences.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 2, is it True or False that pure water and salt water have the same freezing point? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says pure water freezes at ZERO degrees Celsius, but salt lowers the freezing point BELOW ZERO — so salt water has a lower freezing point than pure water.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, both are water.' Salt changes the freezing point — so they are different.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: pure water freezes at ZERO DEGREES. Salt water's freezing point drops BELOW ZERO. The two are NOT the same. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: According to paragraph 3, what happens when you drop an ice cube into a glass of salt water?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: The salt water immediately begins pulling heat from the ice, causing it to melt faster.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'the ice melts' — correct but not specific enough. The passage explains why.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: 'the salt water IMMEDIATELY begins PULLING HEAT from the ice.' This heat transfer causes the ice to MELT FASTER. Give the mechanism, not just the result.

open_ended_questions.stem: Describe the experiment suggested in paragraph 4. What do you need and what do you do?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) You need two identical glasses — one with plain water and one with salt water — and two same-sized ice cubes. (ii) You add one ice cube to each glass, then observe and record what happens over five minutes.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students describe only one glass or forget the timing.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: (1) TWO IDENTICAL GLASSES = one plain water, one salt water; same-sized ice cubes. (2) Observe for FIVE MINUTES and record results. Both steps needed for full marks.

open_ended_questions.stem: What is a 'controlled experiment', according to the passage?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: A controlled experiment is one where you change only one variable and keep everything else the same, so you can be sure what caused the difference in results.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'a careful experiment' — too vague.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: 'you change only ONE VARIABLE... and keep EVERYTHING ELSE THE SAME.' This is the definition of a CONTROLLED EXPERIMENT — isolating the single cause.

open_ended_questions.stem: This passage is an informational text. Describe TWO techniques the writer uses to help readers understand the scientific information.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) QUESTION HOOK: the passage begins with a question ('Have you ever noticed...?') to connect the reader's everyday experience to the science. (ii) HANDS-ON EXAMPLE: the writer suggests a simple home experiment in paragraph 4, turning abstract science into something the reader can do and see for themselves.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students summarise the science rather than analysing the writing techniques.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TECHNIQUES: (1) QUESTION HOOK = 'Have you ever noticed...?' = makes the reader think about real life before the science; (2) HANDS-ON EXAMPLE in paragraph 4 = reader can try it themselves, making the concept concrete and memorable.

questions.stem: The vegetables at the wet market were as ________ as a morning breeze — still cool and dewy from the early delivery.
questions.trap_type: 'Expensive', 'loud' and 'heavy' do not describe how a vegetable feels or smells. FRESH = recently harvested, not stale or wilted.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The vegetables were AS FRESH AS a morning breeze = comparing their freshness to cool morning air. FRESH = recently harvested and still in perfect condition.

questions.stem: After the food blogger visited, the auntie's noodle stall at the wet market became ________ — people queued for over an hour to try her laksa.
questions.trap_type: 'A piece of cake' = something easy; 'out of the blue' = unexpectedly; 'under the weather' = feeling unwell. THE TALK OF THE TOWN = the most popular topic that everyone is discussing.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: THE TALK OF THE TOWN = something or someone that everyone is talking about and interested in. The stall became THE TALK OF THE TOWN = everyone was talking about it and going there.

questions.stem: The fishmonger was generous and decided to ________ a few extra prawns with every purchase over ten dollars.
questions.trap_type: 'Keep' = hold on to; 'hide' = conceal; 'sell' = exchange for money. GIVE AWAY = give something for free without charge.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: GIVE AWAY = give something to people for free. The fishmonger GAVE AWAY extra prawns = he added them at no extra cost. GIVE + AWAY work together.

questions.stem: The ________ at the wet market was lively and colourful — stalls stretched from one end of the hall to the other.
questions.trap_type: 'Library', 'clinic' and 'playground' are different places. A BAZAAR = a marketplace or market, especially a busy, colourful one.
questions.learning_tip: A BAZAAR = a busy marketplace or market hall where different goods are sold. Wet markets can also be called BAZAARS — lively places with many stalls selling food, spices and goods.

questions.stem: The elderly vendor ________ her regulars with a warm smile and remembered each person's usual order without being told.
questions.trap_type: 'Ignored', 'avoided' and 'confused' describe negative or unhelpful behaviour. GREETED = welcomed someone with a friendly word or gesture.
questions.learning_tip: GREETED = welcomed someone in a friendly way when they arrive. The vendor GREETED her regulars = she warmly welcomed the customers she recognised.

questions.stem: Somebody at the vegetable stall ________ the price tag every morning to match the day's supply and demand.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'update' thinking 'somebody at the stall' = many people. SOMEBODY = singular → verb+S in present tense.
questions.learning_tip: SOMEBODY / NOBODY / EVERYONE = Singular! Always use verb+S. Somebody UPDATES the price tag = add -S. 'Somebody update' is WRONG. Singular indefinite → singular present verb.

questions.stem: The wet market vendor has ________ fresh fish to this neighbourhood for over twenty years.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. 'Sell' is irregular: sell → sold.
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. The vendor HAS SOLD fish for over twenty years = started selling long ago and is still selling today. SELL → SOLD (irregular).

questions.stem: The fish stall on the left is much ________ than the one at the entrance — the owner has more variety and keeps things cleaner.
questions.trap_type: Comparing two stalls = comparative. 'Popular' (3+ syllables) → MORE + adj. 'Most popular' = superlative; 'very popular' is not comparative.
questions.learning_tip: Long adjective (3+ syllables) → MORE + adjective = comparative. MORE POPULAR THAN = comparing two stalls. 'Popularer' is WRONG — always use MORE for long adjectives.

questions.stem: The vendor ________ a customer's order when another regular arrived and asked for the last piece of pork belly.
questions.trap_type: 'Another regular arrived' = sudden interrupting event. The vendor was already wrapping = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The regular ARRIVED = sudden past event. The vendor was already in the middle of wrapping = WAS WRAPPING (past continuous). Past continuous = was/were + verb-ing.

questions.stem: There were ________ mangoes left at the fruit stall by noon — the morning crowd had bought them all within an hour.
questions.trap_type: 'Mangoes' is countable → use FEW (not little/much). FEW = not many (countable, negative implication).
questions.learning_tip: FEW = not many (countable noun). MANGOES = countable → FEW mangoes. LITTLE is for uncountable nouns (water, sugar). FEW mangoes = not enough mangoes left.

questions.stem: The wet market has been part of this community for over forty years, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive present perfect ('has been') → negative question tag. 'Has' → hasn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present perfect → negative tag. The market HAS been part of the community, HASN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE tag. HAS → HASN'T.

questions.stem: The pork ribs ________ in a special marinade for three hours before being sent to the restaurant next door.
questions.trap_type: The ribs received the action. Past passive: was/were + past participle. Plural subject (ribs) → were.
questions.learning_tip: WAS/WERE + past participle = passive! The ribs WERE SOAKED = someone soaked them; the ribs received the action. WERE for plural subject.

questions.stem: The fishmonger asked the customer ________ back the next morning if she wanted the freshest prawns.
questions.trap_type: Positive reported speech: asked + object + to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: ASKED someone TO + base verb. The fishmonger asked the customer TO COME back the next morning. Formula: asked + person + to + verb. 'Asked coming' or 'asked come' are WRONG.

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Time prepositions — specific time and duration)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The wet market opens (1)________ five o'clock in the morning, when the first delivery trucks arrive.' Signal: specific clock time = AT. AT + specific time of day.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' (used for morning/afternoon, not clock time) instead of 'at' (specific clock time).
questions.learning_tip: AT + specific clock time. The market opens AT five o'clock = at that exact time. AT = precise point in time (AT 5am, AT noon, AT midnight). IN the morning = general time of day.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The busiest day at the wet market is (2)________ Sunday, when whole families come to do their weekly shopping.' Signal: day of the week = ON. ON + day of the week.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' or 'at' instead of 'on'. ON is always used with days of the week.
questions.learning_tip: ON + day of the week. The market is busiest ON SUNDAY = on that specific day. ON Monday, ON Tuesday, ON weekends = always use ON for days.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The durian season usually arrives (3)________ June, bringing larger crowds and stronger smells to every stall.' Signal: month of the year = IN. IN + month or year.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'on' (used for days) or 'at' (specific time) instead of 'in' (month/season).
questions.learning_tip: IN + month, year or season. Durian season is IN JUNE = in that month. IN June, IN 2024, IN summer = always use IN for months, years and seasons.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'This family has been buying vegetables from the same stall (4)________ thirty years.' Signal: a duration of time = FOR. FOR + length of time.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'since' (not in word_box) or 'during' instead of 'for' (duration).
questions.learning_tip: FOR + duration of time. The family has bought from the same stall FOR THIRTY YEARS = the duration is thirty years. FOR answers 'how long?' SINCE answers 'since when?'

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The original wet market building was built over fifty years (5)________, when this area was still a fishing village.' Signal: measured distance from now into the past = AGO. Number + time + AGO.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'before' (relative to another past event) instead of 'ago' (measured from the present moment).
questions.learning_tip: AGO = measured time before now. Fifty years AGO = fifty years before now (the present). 'Before' compares to another past event; 'ago' counts back from today.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Most of the fresh produce sold here is delivered (6)________ twelve hours of being harvested.' Signal: inside a time limit = WITHIN. WITHIN = before a time limit expires.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'in' (used for months/general time) instead of 'within' (inside a time limit).
questions.learning_tip: WITHIN + time period = before that time has ended. Delivered WITHIN twelve hours = before twelve hours pass. WITHIN = inside the limit. 'In twelve hours' = after twelve hours; 'within twelve hours' = before.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The smell of spices and fresh herbs fills every corner of the market (7)________ the day.' Signal: from start to end of a period, continuously = THROUGHOUT. THROUGHOUT = all the way through.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'during' (not in word_box) instead of 'throughout' (from start to end, continuously).
questions.learning_tip: THROUGHOUT = all the way through a period of time, from beginning to end. The smell fills the market THROUGHOUT the day = all day, from opening to closing, without stopping.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'The vendor promises that all orders placed before nine o'clock will be ready (8)________ noon.' Signal: no later than a time = BY. BY = at or before a deadline.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'at' (exact point) instead of 'by' (deadline — at or before that time).
questions.learning_tip: BY + time = at or before that time (a deadline). Ready BY noon = finished at noon or earlier. AT noon = at exactly noon. BY = deadline; AT = exact point.

C.passage: The wet market opens (1)________ five o'clock each morning when delivery trucks arrive. The busiest day is (2)________ Sunday, when families come for weekly shopping. Durian season arrives (3)________ June, bringing large crowds to every stall. This family bought vegetables from the same stall (4)________ thirty years. The original market building was built over fifty years (5)________, when this area was a fishing village. Most produce here is delivered (6)________ twelve hours of harvesting to stay fresh. The smell of spices fills every corner (7)________ the day. The vendor promises morning orders will be ready (8)________ noon.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: A visit to a wet market is a rich experience. Each (1)________ is run by a family who specialise in one type of food — fish, pork or vegetables. The (2)________ arranges produce in an attractive (3)________ so customers can see everything clearly before deciding what to buy. Experienced shoppers know how to (4)________ — they compare prices and ask for a discount when buying a lot. Some popular items are (5)________, meaning they are only available at certain times of the year.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'run by a single family specialised in one type of food' = stall.
questions.learning_tip: A STALL = a small shop or table in a market where goods are sold. A wet market has many individual STALLS, each selling something different.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'arranges the produce' and runs the stall = vendor (the seller).
questions.learning_tip: A VENDOR = a person who sells goods, especially at a market stall or street stall. The VENDOR at the wet market = the person running and selling from that stall.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'arranged on a table so customers can see everything clearly before buying' = display.
questions.learning_tip: A DISPLAY = an arrangement of goods set out for people to see. The vendor creates an attractive DISPLAY = lays everything out so customers can see it clearly.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'compare prices and politely ask for a better deal when buying in large quantities' = bargain.
questions.learning_tip: To BARGAIN = negotiate a price by asking for a discount or better deal. At wet markets, customers sometimes BARGAIN = politely ask for a lower price, especially when buying a lot.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'only available at certain times of the year, such as rambutans in summer' = seasonal.
questions.learning_tip: SEASONAL = only available at a particular time of year. SEASONAL fruits and vegetables = they grow and ripen during one specific season, not all year round.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the vegetables)
questions.trap_type: 'The vegetables' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! The vegetables WERE laid out neatly. WAS is only for ONE thing (singular). VEGETABLES = more than one → WERE.

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — hear (to listen) vs here (at this place)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'hear' (use ears to detect sound) when the sentence needs 'here' (at this place).
questions.learning_tip: HERE = at this place. HEAR = use your ears. 'Come hear!' → can you replace with 'at this place'? YES → use HERE. HERE contains the word 'here' in 'where' — both are about PLACE.

questions.error_type: Spelling — ie/ei confusion (pier: I before E)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'peir' putting E before I. 'Pier' follows I-before-E: pIEr.
questions.learning_tip: Rule: I before E, except after C! pIEr = I before E ✅. Remember: 'the pIEr serves PIE by the sea' — pIEr has IE inside. I before E!

questions.error_type: Adverb required after action verb (called)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'loud' (adjective) after the action verb 'called'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (called), use an ADVERB: called LOUDLY. Rule: verb + adverb (-ly). 'Loud' describes nouns; 'loudly' describes HOW someone calls out.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (vendors', not vendors's)
questions.trap_type: Students add 's after the apostrophe for a plural noun ending in -s.
questions.learning_tip: Plural possessive: just add apostrophe after -s! The VENDORS' stalls = the stalls belonging to all the vendors. NEVER 'vendors's' — extra -s after apostrophe is WRONG for plural nouns ending in -s.

E.passage: Last Saturday morning, my grandmother took me to the wet market near our flat for the first time. The vegetables was (1) laid out neatly on wide bamboo trays, and the fish glittered under the bright lights. 'The freshest prawns are sold hear, (2) not at the supermarket!' Grandma said, gesturing at the stall near the old peir (3) painting on the wall. One uncle called out loud (4) to passing customers, waving a bunch of fresh spinach and offering it at a special price. By the time we left, the vendors's (5) trays were nearly empty and the morning crowd was beginning to thin out.

questions.sentence_a: The vendor sees a customer approaching.
questions.sentence_b: She immediately begins to arrange the freshest produce at the front of the stall.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'As soon as'.
questions.model_answer: As soon as the vendor sees a customer approaching, she immediately begins to arrange the freshest produce at the front of the stall.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'As soon as the vendor will see' — adding 'will' in the 'as soon as' clause.
questions.learning_tip: AS SOON AS + simple present, simple present or future. AS SOON AS the vendor SEES a customer, she BEGINS to arrange. 'As soon as' = immediately when. Never 'will' after 'as soon as'.

questions.sentence_a: The customer asked the fishmonger a question.
questions.sentence_b: How much do the vegetables cost?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The customer asked...'
questions.model_answer: The customer asked how much the vegetables cost.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'The customer asked how much do the vegetables cost' — keeping question word order. In reported speech, normal word order is used.
questions.learning_tip: WH-question → reported speech: ASKED + WH-word + subject + verb (normal order). 'How much DO the vegetables COST?' → asked HOW MUCH the vegetables COST. No inversion. Tense stays the same in present tense reported speech.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
Every Saturday, nine-year-old Wei woke early and followed his grandfather to the wet market at Tekka. It was their ritual — just the two of them, before the rest of the family stirred.

His grandfather moved through the stalls like water, pausing here, nodding there, tasting a sliver of something before deciding. Wei knew enough to be patient. The market was not a place to rush.

At the fish stall, Uncle Raju always saved the best threadfin for their family. 'For you, Mr Lim — still swimming when it arrived this morning,' he would say, and grandfather would inspect it closely, turn it once, then nod.

Wei did not eat fish. But he liked the ceremony of it.

At the tofu stall, the auntie sliced quickly and silently — cubes of white, firm and soft, stacked in a green basin. She never needed to be told how much. She knew.

On the way home, grandfather carried the bags. Wei always asked to carry one, and grandfather always let him — the lightest one. Neither mentioned this.

At home, grandmother would begin to cook while grandfather washed the vegetables over the sink. Wei sat at the kitchen table, and the smell of garlic and old wood filled the flat.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'a very thin piece cut from something'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Ritual' = a regular custom; 'pausing' = stopping briefly; 'stirred' = woke up. SLIVER = a very thin, small slice or piece.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: A SLIVER = a very thin, small piece cut or broken off something. Grandfather tasted 'a SLIVER of something' = a tiny thin piece. SLIVER = a thin slice.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does 'it' refer to in 'grandfather would inspect it closely'?

options.3: The threadfin fish that Uncle Raju saved for them

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'it' = the stall. But the sentence is about what Uncle Raju saved — the threadfin fish.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: 'Uncle Raju always saved the best THREADFIN for their family.' Then 'grandfather would inspect IT closely.' IT = the threadfin fish — the specific fish being discussed.

mcq_questions.stem: Why does the writer say 'Neither mentioned this' in paragraph 6?

options.1: To show that neither Wei nor his grandfather could speak.
options.2: Because grandfather quietly let Wei carry a bag without drawing attention to the fact that he chose the lightest one for him.
options.3: To show that Wei was too tired to talk on the way home.
options.4: To show that the bags were too heavy for anyone to talk about.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 3 thinking they were tired. But the writer shows a quiet, unspoken understanding between grandfather and grandson.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 6: Wei asked to carry a bag; grandfather let him carry THE LIGHTEST ONE. NEITHER MENTIONED THIS = both understood without saying it. It was a quiet, kind gesture — grandfather protecting Wei's pride without drawing attention.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 1, is it True or False that Wei and his grandfather went to the wet market with the whole family? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says it was 'just the two of them, before the rest of the family stirred' — only Wei and his grandfather went.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, the whole family went to the market.' The passage says 'just the two of them' — the rest of the family was still asleep.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 1: 'JUST THE TWO OF THEM, before the rest of the FAMILY STIRRED.' STIRRED = woke up. The others were still asleep. Only Wei and grandfather went. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: What did Uncle Raju say to grandfather about the threadfin?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Uncle Raju said that the fish was still swimming when it arrived that morning — meaning it was very fresh.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he saved the best fish' — that is what he did, not what he said.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 3: Uncle Raju said: 'STILL SWIMMING WHEN IT ARRIVED THIS MORNING.' This is what he SAID — it is a quote from the passage showing how fresh the fish was.

open_ended_questions.stem: How does the writer show that grandfather was experienced at shopping at the wet market? Give TWO details.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) He moved through the stalls 'like water' — pausing, nodding and tasting before deciding — showing he knew exactly what he was looking for. (ii) He inspected the fish closely and turned it once before nodding — showing he could judge quality with skill.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'he went every week' — that is about Wei, not specifically grandfather's skill.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: Grandfather moved 'LIKE WATER' — pausing, nodding, tasting. Paragraph 3: he INSPECTED the fish CLOSELY, turned it ONCE, then nodded. Both show experienced, confident shopping skill.

open_ended_questions.stem: How did the tofu stall auntie show that she knew the family well?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: She sliced the tofu quickly and silently without being told how much — she already knew exactly how much their family wanted.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'she cut the tofu' — too vague. The point is she knew without being told.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 5: 'She NEVER NEEDED TO BE TOLD how much. SHE KNEW.' = the auntie knew the family's regular order by heart, without asking. This shows a long, familiar relationship.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on his actions throughout the passage, describe TWO character traits of Wei's grandfather with evidence.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: (i) DISCERNING: grandfather paused, tasted and inspected before deciding what to buy — he judged quality carefully and did not just take the first thing offered. (ii) GENTLE: on the way home, he quietly let Wei carry a bag — always the lightest one — without mentioning it, protecting Wei's feelings while keeping the ritual kind.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'experienced and kind' without precise traits or textual evidence.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: TRAIT INFERENCE: DISCERNING = paused, tasted, INSPECTED CLOSELY — careful judge of quality. GENTLE = let Wei carry THE LIGHTEST BAG, NEITHER MENTIONED THIS — quiet, unspoken kindness. Name trait → give evidence.

questions.stem: The warning light on the laptop was as ________ as a torch, flashing in the dark room and impossible to miss.
questions.trap_type: 'Quiet', 'small' and 'slow' do not describe the intensity of light. BRIGHT = giving out a strong, clear light.
questions.learning_tip: AS + adj + AS = Simile! The warning light was AS BRIGHT AS a torch = comparing its light intensity to a torch. BRIGHT = giving out strong, clear light that is hard to miss.

questions.stem: The new phone model was released last month but it ________ — it was priced at over two thousand dollars.

options.2: cost an arm and a leg

questions.trap_type: 'Was very popular' describes demand; 'was a piece of cake' = easy; 'came out of the blue' = unexpectedly. COST AN ARM AND A LEG = was extremely expensive.
questions.learning_tip: IDIOM: COST AN ARM AND A LEG = be extremely expensive. The phone COST AN ARM AND A LEG = it was priced so high it felt like giving up a body part to buy it! Idioms cannot be understood word by word.

questions.stem: Students must ________ to the school portal every morning to check their homework assignments.
questions.trap_type: 'Turn off' = switch off; 'give up' = stop trying; 'break down' = stop working. LOG ON = connect to a computer system using a username and password.
questions.learning_tip: PHRASAL VERB: LOG ON = connect and sign in to a computer system or website. Students LOG ON to the school portal = they enter their details and access the system. LOG + ON work together.

questions.stem: Being online for too long can affect your ________ — it is important to take regular breaks and rest your eyes.
questions.trap_type: 'Strength' = physical power; 'schedule' = timetable; 'homework' = school work. WELLBEING = the state of being comfortable, healthy and happy.
questions.learning_tip: WELLBEING = the state of being healthy, happy and comfortable. Spending too long online affects your WELLBEING = your physical and mental health. Taking breaks protects your WELLBEING.

questions.stem: The student kept her password ________ — she never wrote it down or shared it with anyone, not even her best friend.
questions.trap_type: 'Public', 'visible' and 'complicated' are all inappropriate for password security. CONFIDENTIAL = kept secret and not to be shared with others.
questions.learning_tip: CONFIDENTIAL = secret and not to be shared. She kept her password CONFIDENTIAL = she told nobody. Passwords must be CONFIDENTIAL to keep your accounts safe.

questions.stem: Each student in our school ________ a unique password to access the online learning platform.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'need' thinking 'each student' = many people. EACH = singular → verb+S in present tense.
questions.learning_tip: EACH / EVERY / EVERYONE / NOBODY = Singular! Always use verb+S. Each student NEEDS a password = add -S. 'Each student need' is WRONG. EACH is always singular.

questions.stem: Our school has ________ a new set of cyber wellness guidelines since the start of this year.
questions.trap_type: HAS + past participle = present perfect. 'Introduce' is regular: introduce → introduced.
questions.learning_tip: HAS + past participle = present perfect. Our school HAS INTRODUCED new guidelines = it was done this year and the guidelines are in effect now. INTRODUCE → INTRODUCED (regular).

questions.stem: The new cyber safety lesson is far ________ than last year's version — it covers more topics and uses real-life examples.
questions.trap_type: Comparing two versions (this year vs last year) = comparative. Long adjective → MORE + adj. 'Comprehensiver' is WRONG (never add -er to long adjectives).
questions.learning_tip: Long adjective (4+ syllables) → MORE + adjective = comparative. MORE COMPREHENSIVE THAN = comparing two versions. 'Comprehensiver' is WRONG. For long adjectives, always use MORE.

questions.stem: The student ________ her password when the school's online system sent her a security alert.
questions.trap_type: 'The system sent a security alert' = sudden event. The student was already in the middle of changing = past continuous.
questions.learning_tip: The system SENT an alert = sudden past event. The student was already changing her password = WAS CHANGING (past continuous). Past continuous = was/were + verb-ing.

questions.stem: There was ________ guidance about online safety in the school handbook — students had to search for information themselves.
questions.trap_type: 'Guidance' is uncountable → use LITTLE. 'Few', 'a few' and 'many' are for countable nouns.
questions.learning_tip: LITTLE + uncountable noun. Guidance = uncountable → LITTLE guidance. 'Few guidance' is WRONG — you cannot count pieces of guidance. LITTLE = not much (uncountable).

questions.stem: Protecting your personal information online is extremely important, ________ it?
questions.trap_type: Positive present simple ('is') → negative question tag. 'Is' → isn't it.
questions.learning_tip: Positive present 'to be' → negative tag. Protecting information IS important, ISN'T it? POSITIVE → NEGATIVE tag. IS → ISN'T.

questions.stem: The cyberbullying complaint ________ by the school counsellor before any action was taken.
questions.trap_type: The complaint received the action. Past passive: was/were + past participle.
questions.learning_tip: WAS/WERE + past participle = passive! The complaint WAS INVESTIGATED = the counsellor investigated it; complaint received the action. NEVER 'was being investigated' (P5 level).

questions.stem: The teacher asked students ________ their devices during the assembly.
questions.trap_type: Negative reported speech: told/asked + object + not to + base verb.
questions.learning_tip: ASKED someone NOT TO + base verb. The teacher asked students NOT TO USE their devices. Formula: asked + person + not to + verb (base form).

C.label: Section C – Grammar Cloze (Adverbs of manner)

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Read all messages (1)________ before clicking any link, especially from unknown senders.' Signal: doing something with care and attention = CAREFULLY.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'slowly' (not in word_box) instead of 'carefully' (with attention and caution).
questions.learning_tip: CAREFULLY = with great attention and caution. Read messages CAREFULLY = pay close attention before clicking anything. CAREFULLY describes HOW to read (verb + adverb).

questions.context_check: Passage: 'If you receive a suspicious message, (2)________ close the window and tell a trusted adult.' Signal: doing something immediately and without delay = QUICKLY.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'fast' (also means rapidly, but QUICKLY fits better for deliberate immediate action) instead of 'quickly'.
questions.learning_tip: QUICKLY = immediately and without delay. Close the window QUICKLY = do it right away, with no hesitation. QUICKLY describes an action done in a short time.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Cyberbullying can happen (3)________ — victims may suffer without anyone around them knowing.' Signal: without noise or visible action, undetected = SILENTLY.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'quietly' (not in word_box) instead of 'silently' (without any sound or visible sign).
questions.learning_tip: SILENTLY = without making any sound or sign. Cyberbullying happens SILENTLY = it occurs without anyone else seeing or hearing. SILENT = no sound; SILENTLY = in a silent way.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Students who understand online safety usually perform (4)________ when asked to identify suspicious websites.' Signal: in a good and skilled manner = WELL (adverb form of 'good').
questions.trap_type: Students write 'good' (adjective, WRONG after a verb) instead of 'well' (adverb).
questions.learning_tip: WELL = adverb form of 'good'. They perform WELL = they do it in a good, skilled way. NEVER 'perform good' — after a verb (perform), use the ADVERB: WELL, not GOOD.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Developers work (5)________ to create firewalls that block harmful content from reaching young users.' Signal: with great effort and energy = HARD (adverb). HARD ≠ HARDLY.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'hardly' (meaning almost not at all, OPPOSITE meaning) instead of 'hard' (with great effort).
questions.learning_tip: HARD (adverb) = with great effort. They work HARD = they put in a lot of effort. HARDLY = almost not at all (opposite meaning!). 'Work hardly' = they barely work. HARD ≠ HARDLY — very different!

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Online misinformation spreads (6)________ — a false story can reach millions of people within hours.' Signal: moving or happening with great speed = FAST.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'quickly' (already used in C2) instead of 'fast' (rapid speed/movement).
questions.learning_tip: FAST (adverb) = with great speed. Misinformation spreads FAST = it moves very quickly from person to person. FAST describes speed of movement or spreading.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'Children who learn safe online habits from an early age use the internet (7)________ and responsibly as they grow older.' Signal: in a content and positive way = HAPPILY.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'confidently' (not in word_box) instead of 'happily' (in a pleased and positive manner).
questions.learning_tip: HAPPILY = in a happy, content and positive manner. Use the internet HAPPILY = they enjoy it and feel good about it. HAPPILY describes how they use it — with pleasure and confidence.

questions.context_check: Passage: 'When correcting a friend who has shared false information online, do it (8)________ so they do not feel embarrassed.' Signal: with care not to cause pain or embarrassment = GENTLY.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'kindly' (not in word_box) instead of 'gently' (with soft, careful handling).
questions.learning_tip: GENTLY = in a soft, careful way that avoids causing pain or upset. Correct your friend GENTLY = in a way that is sensitive and does not humiliate them. GENTLY describes a considerate, careful manner.

C.passage: Using the internet safely requires good habits. Read all messages (1)________ before clicking any link, especially from unknown senders. If you receive a suspicious message, (2)________ close the window and tell a trusted adult. Cyberbullying can happen (3)________ — victims may suffer without anyone knowing. Students who understand online safety usually perform (4)________ when asked to identify suspicious websites. Developers work (5)________ to create firewalls that block harmful content. Online misinformation spreads (6)________ — a false story can reach millions within hours. Children who learn safe online habits use the internet (7)________ as they grow older. When correcting a friend who shared false information, do it (8)________ so they do not feel embarrassed.

D.label: Section D – Vocabulary Cloze
D.passage: Cyber wellness means using technology safely and responsibly. One of the first steps is to create a strong (1)________ for every online account — it should include letters, numbers and symbols. Managing (2)________ is equally important: too many hours on screens can affect your sleep and mood. Some people use the internet to harm others. A (3)________ is someone who hurts or threatens another person online, often hiding behind an (4)________ identity with no real name. Living well in the (5)________ age means knowing how to enjoy technology and when to put it down.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'for every online account, at least eight characters long, includes letters, numbers and symbols' = password.
questions.learning_tip: A PASSWORD = a secret combination of characters used to access an online account. A strong PASSWORD is long and hard for others to guess.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'hours looking at a phone or computer screen — affects sleep, eyesight and mood' = screen time.
questions.learning_tip: SCREEN TIME = the amount of time a person spends looking at a digital screen. Managing SCREEN TIME = controlling how long you use devices each day.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'uses online platforms to hurt, threaten or embarrass another person' = cyberbully.
questions.learning_tip: A CYBERBULLY = a person who uses the internet to hurt, threaten or embarrass someone else. CYBER = online; BULLY = someone who harms others deliberately.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'hiding behind an ___ identity — does not reveal their real name' = anonymous.
questions.learning_tip: ANONYMOUS = not revealing one's name or identity. Cyberbullies sometimes act behind an ANONYMOUS identity = no one knows who they really are.

questions.trap_type: The clue 'the ___ age — knowing how to enjoy technology' = digital age.
questions.learning_tip: DIGITAL = relating to computers and electronic technology. The DIGITAL age = the current period in history where computers and the internet are central to life.

E.label: Section E – Editing

questions.error_type: Subject-verb agreement — plural subject (the students)
questions.trap_type: 'The students' is plural. Students write 'was' (singular).
questions.learning_tip: Plural subject → plural verb! The students WERE reminded to protect their passwords. WAS is only for ONE (singular). STUDENTS = more than one → WERE.

questions.error_type: Homophone confusion — no (negative/zero) vs know (to have knowledge)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'no' (zero/negative) when the meaning is 'know' (to have knowledge of something).
questions.learning_tip: KNOW = to have knowledge or information. NO = not any / negative answer. 'You should no how to spot a fake website' → can you say 'to have knowledge how to'? YES → use KNOW. KNOW = knowledge.

questions.error_type: Spelling — ie/ei confusion (shield: I before E)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'sheild' putting E before I. 'Shield' follows I-before-E: shIEld.
questions.learning_tip: Rule: I before E, except after C! shIEld = I before E ✅. Remember: 'a shIEld in the fIEld' — shIEld and fIEld both have IE. I before E!

questions.error_type: Adverb required after action verb (report)
questions.trap_type: Students write 'immediate' (adjective) after the action verb 'report'. A verb needs an adverb.
questions.learning_tip: After an action verb (report), use an ADVERB: report IMMEDIATELY. Rule: verb + adverb (-ly). 'Immediate' describes nouns; 'immediately' describes HOW quickly to report something.

questions.error_type: Possessive apostrophe — plural possessive (students', not students's)
questions.trap_type: Students add 's after the apostrophe for a plural noun ending in -s.
questions.learning_tip: Plural possessive: just add apostrophe after -s! The STUDENTS' accounts = the accounts belonging to all the students. NEVER 'students's' — extra -s after apostrophe is WRONG for plural nouns ending in -s.

E.passage: Last week, our school held a Cyber Wellness Day for all primary students. The students was (1) taught how to recognise phishing emails — messages that try to trick you into giving away your personal details. 'You should no (2) the warning signs: strange email addresses, urgent language and requests for your password,' said the speaker. She also explained how a strong password acts like a sheild (3) that protects your accounts from hackers. Students were told to report any suspicious activity immediate (4) to their parents or teachers without waiting to see what happens next. At the end of the session, the students's (5) feedback forms were collected, and many said they felt more confident about staying safe online.

questions.sentence_a: You use a strong and unique password for each account.
questions.sentence_b: Your personal information will be much safer online.
questions.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using 'As long as'.
questions.model_answer: As long as you use a strong and unique password for each account, your personal information will be much safer online.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'As long as you will use' — adding 'will' in the 'as long as' clause.
questions.learning_tip: AS LONG AS + simple present, simple future. AS LONG AS you USE a strong password, your information WILL BE safer. NEVER 'will' after 'as long as'.

questions.sentence_a: The teacher asked a question.
questions.sentence_b: Do you share your password with anyone?
questions.instruction: Combine into one sentence using reported speech. Begin: 'The teacher asked...'
questions.model_answer: The teacher asked if we shared our passwords with anyone.
questions.trap_type: Students write 'The teacher asked if do we share our password' — keeping question word order. In reported speech, normal word order is used.
questions.learning_tip: YES/NO question → reported speech: ASKED + IF/WHETHER + subject + verb (normal order). 'Do YOU SHARE your password?' → asked IF WE SHARED our passwords. Word order flips to normal. 'Do' disappears.

G.label: Section G – Comprehension
G.passage:
It started with one message.

Nina received it on the class chat group on a Monday morning: a photo of her, taken at Sports Day, with a caption that made fun of the way she ran. She did not know who sent it — the account used a fake name she did not recognise.

By lunchtime, twelve people laughed at it.

Nina did not go to the canteen that day. She sat at her desk and stared at her pencil case.

Her form teacher, Mrs Tan, noticed. At the end of the day, she asked Nina to stay behind.

'I didn't want to make a fuss,' Nina said.

Mrs Tan sat down across from her. 'Making a fuss,' she said quietly, 'is exactly what we need to do when something like this happens. Not to punish. To fix.'

Nina showed her the screenshot. Mrs Tan took her time looking at it, then nodded.

'This is not a joke,' she said. 'It is not harmless. And it is not going to continue.'

By the next morning, the post was removed and the fake account was reported. Nina did not know what the school said to the students involved. But the laughing stopped.

mcq_questions.stem: Which word in paragraph 2 has the same meaning as 'a short description or title added to a photo'?
mcq_questions.trap_type: 'Account' = a user profile; 'message' = written communication; 'group' = a collection of people. CAPTION = a short description or title added to a photo or image.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: A CAPTION = a short text placed under or over a photo to describe or comment on it. The photo had a CAPTION that made fun of her = a mocking label was placed on the image.

mcq_questions.stem: In paragraph 5, what does 'it' refer to in 'Mrs Tan noticed'?

options.1: The message on the class chat
options.2: That Nina did not go to the canteen and sat alone

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking 'it' = the message. But Mrs Tan noticed Nina's behaviour — she was sitting alone at her desk.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 4: 'Nina did not go to the canteen. She sat at her desk and stared at her pencil case.' Paragraph 5: 'Mrs Tan NOTICED.' She noticed NINA'S BEHAVIOUR — sitting alone, not eating, looking distressed.

mcq_questions.stem: What does Mrs Tan mean when she says 'Not to punish. To fix'?

options.1: She wants to punish the students who laughed.
options.2: She does not believe any punishment is needed.
options.3: She wants to address the situation to stop the harm, not just to get someone in trouble.
options.4: She plans to fix Nina's phone settings.

mcq_questions.trap_type: Students pick option 1 thinking Mrs Tan wants revenge. Her statement clarifies that her goal is to stop the harm, not to punish.
mcq_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 7: 'NOT TO PUNISH. TO FIX.' Mrs Tan is saying: the reason to act is not revenge or punishment — it is to STOP the situation and make things right. She focuses on the OUTCOME, not retribution.

open_ended_questions.stem: Based on paragraph 2, is it True or False that Nina knew who sent the message? Give a reason.
open_ended_questions.model_answer: False. The passage says 'the account had a fake name she did not recognise' — so Nina could not identify who sent the message.
open_ended_questions.trap_type: Students say 'True, she saw the message.' She saw it, but she did not know who sent it.
open_ended_questions.learning_tip: Paragraph 2: 'The ACCOUNT HAD A FAKE NAME she DID NOT RECOGNISE.' Nina could not tell who sent it because the sender used a false identity. Answer is FALSE.

open_ended_questions.stem: Why did Nina not go to the canteen at lunchtime?
open_ended_questions.model_answer: Nina was upset about the photo and mocking caption on the class chat — twelve people laughed at it, and she did not want to face them in the canteen.
